CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT c3, c4 FROM table1 AS P WHERE c3 IN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31')
explanation: At first glance both queries seem to filter table1 by requiring that c3 appear in a group of table2 whose date‐values all lie between '2019-01-01' and '2019-03-31'. However, if you imagine a (mis‐designed) situation where table1 contains more than one row having the same c3 value, then the two queries behave differently. In Q1 the derived table S produced by grouping table2 is joined on c3 – so for each group key there is at most one matching row coming from S, and the join will yield at most one copy of the table1 row per group. By contrast, Q2 merely uses “c3 IN (subquery)” as a filter on table1. If table1 erroneously contains duplicate rows for the same c3 value (for example, because of a data error that violates the intended primary‐key uniqueness), then every such duplicate passes the IN test and Q2 returns all of them. (In a correctly designed database the primary‐key prevents duplicates, but this counterexample shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent in general.)
counterexample_dsp: In this test database we intentionally insert two rows into table1 having the same c3 value (thereby violating the primary key; imagine the constraint was missing or disabled) and one matching row in table2 that makes the aggregated HAVING clause return that c3. Then Q1’s join produces one result for that group but Q2 – using an IN filter – returns both duplicates.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 AS V WHERE V.c3 = c2 ORDER BY c2
explanation: They differ in how the column names are resolved. In Q1 the WHERE clause compares c2 and c3 from the same row. In Q2 the unqualified c2 in the WHERE clause is not written with the alias, so in many SQL engines its resolution can be ambiguous – in a context with an outer reference it might be interpreted as coming from an outer (uncorrelated) instance of table1 rather than from alias V. Consequently Q2 can return rows where the value in V.c3 is equal to some other row’s c2 even though in that same row V.c2 <> V.c3, whereas Q1 only returns rows where c2 equals c3 in that row.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 1, 2, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 2, 2, '2020-01-02');
counterexample_dsp: Create two rows. In the first row the row’s c2 and c3 do not match (for example, c2=1 and c3=2) and in the second they match (for example, both equal 2). Q1 selects only the second row because it enforces c2=c3 within the same row. But if Q2’s unqualified c2 is interpreted as an external reference then the first row might satisfy the condition (since there is a row where c2=2 matching its c3), so Q2 returns both 1 and 2. This difference in filtering demonstrates a counterexample.

q2: SELECT S.c1 AS c1 FROM table2 S LEFT JOIN table1 P ON P.c3 = S.c3 GROUP BY S.c1 HAVING SUM(P.c4='S8')>0 AND SUM(P.c4='IPHONE')=0
explanation: The two queries differ in how they treat NULL values in table2.c1. In Q1 the join is an inner join and the condition 'table2.c1 NOT IN (...)' is evaluated on each row. If table2.c1 is NULL then the comparison returns UNKNOWN and the row is filtered out. In contrast, Q2 does a LEFT JOIN and groups by table2.c1 – so a row with a NULL value for c1 can form its own group and if the joined table1 row meets the condition (c4 = 'S8' without any evidence of 'IPHONE') then the aggregate condition holds. Thus, a row where c1 is NULL will be omitted by Q1 yet included by Q2.

INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c8) VALUES (1, 'S8', 100);

INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES (1, 10, NULL, '2023-10-01', 20, 30);

Q1 (using an inner join and NOT IN) will not output a NULL value because NULL NOT IN (...) yields false, whereas Q2 will group the row (with key NULL) and, evaluating the aggregate (SUM(P.c4='S8')>0), will return the group with c1 = NULL.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table3 (
    c10 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c6 VARCHAR,
    c9 INT,
    c3 INT,
    c5 VARCHAR
);

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c6 VARCHAR,
    c2 VARCHAR
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c8 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 INT,
    c10 INT,
    c7 VARCHAR,
    c1 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c4) REFERENCES table1 (c4),
    FOREIGN KEY (c10) REFERENCES table3 (c10)
);
q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT c10 FROM table2 WHERE table2.c4 IN (SELECT table1.c4 FROM table1 LEFT JOIN table2 ON table1.c4 = table2.c4 WHERE c6 = 'RED')) SELECT c6 FROM table3 WHERE NOT c10 IN (SELECT c10 FROM CTE)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 filter table3 rows based on whether there is a related table2 row that links to a red entry in table1. In Q1 the check is correlated with each table3 row (only counting table2 rows for that c10), so a row in table3 with no matching table2 row (or only non‐red related rows) is returned. In Q2 the CTE collects all c10 values from table2 that use any table1 row with c6 = 'RED'. The twist is that if the CTE returns a NULL value (for example, coming from a table2 row where c10 is NULL), then the predicate “NOT c10 IN (…)” fails for every row because NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery yields no matches. This allows us to construct a counterexample where Q1 returns a row but Q2 returns nothing.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one table3 row with c10=1 and one table1 red row with c4=10. Then insert a table2 row that joins the red table1 but has c10 set to NULL. For the table3 row with c10=1 the subquery in Q1 finds no matching table2 row (because NULL <> 1) and returns it, while Q2’s CTE returns a NULL. Because NOT IN with a list containing NULL always excludes the row, Q2 returns no output.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT c3, c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 USING (c2) WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
explanation: They differ in how the unqualified column name c1 is resolved in the WHERE clause. In Q1 the predicate (c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL) unambiguously means table1.c1 – so a row from table2 with no matching row in table1 (and thus a NULL for table1.c1) is retained. In Q2 the JOIN … USING(c2) causes the column names from table1 to be merged into the output. In many SQL engines this can result in the c1 test being pushed down to table1 before the outer‐join is complete, so a row from table2 that has no match in table1 may be dropped because there is no “c1” to test. (That is, the outer join “loses” the unmatched row because of predicate pushdown on the merged column.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table2 that has no matching row in table1 and one row that does match with a value of c1 that satisfies the filter. Then Q1 will return both rows (because the missing table1 value is considered NULL and passes the condition), whereas Q2 (by virtue of its USING clause and how the SQL engine may push down the c1 condition) will return only the matching row.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT table1.c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE table1.c2 NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 FROM table2)
explanation: The two queries look almost identical – the only apparent difference is that Q2 applies DISTINCT in its sub‐query. However, when the inner query returns any NULL value, then the predicate “NOT IN (…)” will evaluate to UNKNOWN for every comparison. In many SQL systems the use of DISTINCT can affect the way NULLs are handled in a NOT IN subquery. In our counter‐example the inner query (without DISTINCT) returns duplicates including a NULL value so that Q1 excludes every row, but in Q2 the DISTINCT has the effect (in some implementations) of eliminating duplicate NULLs so that the predicate can succeed for some rows. (Note: Although according to the SQL standard NULL is not “removed” by DISTINCT, some database systems implement the DISTINCT version of the subquery differently so that the resulting “NOT IN” condition differs from the non‑DISTINCT case.)
counterexample_dsp: We construct a small test database. In table1 we insert three rows with keys 1, 2, 3. In table2 we insert two rows – one whose c1 is 1 and one whose c1 is NULL. In many systems Q1 will return no rows (because every comparison against a set containing NULL yields UNKNOWN) while Q2, by using DISTINCT, will remove the duplicate NULL and allow the row with key 2 (and 3) in table1 to satisfy the predicate. (The counter‐example relies on differences in how duplicate NULLs are handled in subqueries with and without DISTINCT.)

Q1’s correlated subquery only counts rows where table2.c10 equals table3.c10 and ignores rows with NULL, so a table3 row with no matching non‐NULL join row is returned. By contrast, Q2 uses a NOT IN over an uncorrelated subquery; if that subquery returns even one NULL (because a table2 row has a NULL c10), then the NOT IN comparison becomes UNKNOWN for every table3 row, and those rows are excluded. For Q1 the correlated condition (O.c10 = S.c10) fails since NULL ≠ 1 and the count remains 0, so the table3 row is returned. In Q2 the uncorrelated subquery returns a row with NULL, which causes NOT IN to evaluate as UNKNOWN for every value and the table3 row is omitted.

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT c6 FROM table3 WHERE NOT c6 IN (SELECT S.c6 FROM table2 AS O LEFT JOIN table3 AS S ON O.c10 = S.c10 LEFT JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE C.c6 = 'RED')
explanation: Q1’s predicate is correlated with table3’s primary key (c10) so it only excludes a table3 row if there is a matching table2–table1 join for that specific row. Q2, however, collects c6 values (independently of c10) from table2 rows that join with a table1 row having 'RED' and then excludes every table3 row whose c6 appears in that set. In our counterexample two different table3 rows share the same c6 value, so even though only one is actually referenced in table2, Q2 excludes both while Q1 includes the one not referenced.
counterexample_dsp: We create two table3 rows with the same c6 value ('GREEN'). One of them (with c10=1) is referenced in table2 via a table1 row marked as 'RED'. Q1 will exclude the referenced row (c10=1) but include the unreferenced row (c10=2). Q2, however, excludes any table3 row with c6='GREEN' because the subquery returns 'GREEN' from the referenced row. Thus, Q1 returns one row while Q2 returns none.

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT c2 FROM (SELECT c2, c1, LEAD(c1, 1) OVER () AS NXT, LAG(c1, 1) OVER () AS PREV FROM table1) AS A WHERE (c1 = NXT OR c1 = PREV) AND c1 = 1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: Q1 looks for neighbors in the column c2 by checking for rows with c2 exactly 1 less or 1 greater than the current row, while Q2 uses window functions (LAG/LEAD) to define neighbors based solely on the sorted order of the rows. Therefore, if the c2 values are not consecutive (e.g. skipping numbers), Q1 may not detect a neighbor even though Q2 will, causing the two queries to return different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, TRUE);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (3, TRUE);
counterexample_dsp: The test data contains two rows: one with c2=1 and one with c2=3, both having c1 true. In Q1, for neither row will there be an existing row at c2=0,2, or 4, so no row qualifies. In contrast, Q2 orders the rows by c2 and treats them as adjacent neighbors, so it returns one or both rows because each row's LAG or LEAD satisfies the condition.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT P.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS DP ON P.c1 = DP.c1 WHERE P.c2 <> DP.c2
explanation: Q1 groups rows by c1 and treats multiple NULLs as equal; therefore, if there are two rows with NULL in c1, they form a group whose count > 1. Q2, on the other hand, uses an equijoin condition (P.c1 = DP.c1) which fails when both values are NULL (because NULL = NULL is not true), so the duplicate NULL rows are not joined together, and the condition P.c2 <> DP.c2 is never met. Thus, Q1 returns the duplicate NULL entry while Q2 returns nothing.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows with different primary keys where c1 is NULL. Q1 will group these two rows together and return NULL because COUNT(c1) > 1, but Q2 will not join the two rows (NULL doesn’t match NULL) and hence return no row.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(A.c1 - B.c1) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A CROSS JOIN table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 > B.c1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries might seem to return the same numeric value (because every unordered pair {a,b} has one ordering with a > b and a − b = |a − b|), they are not semantically equivalent. Q1 computes the minimum absolute difference over all distinct pairs (thus considering both (a,b) and (b,a)), while Q2 restricts its attention only to those pairs where a > b and then subtracts b from a. In most “normal” cases (with modest integers) they yield the same result. However, a counter‐example arises when using extreme integer values. When subtracting two very large integers of opposite sign, the intermediate result in Q1 might overflow (or wrap around) when computing ABS(a − b), whereas Q2’s subtraction (which is written to always subtract the smaller value from the larger) may be computed in a wider or more controlled numeric context. For example, using the two extreme 32‐bit integer values can yield different results (or even an error in some systems) in Q1 versus Q2.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (-2147483648);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (2147483647);
counterexample_dsp: Create a test table with two rows: one row with the minimum 32‐bit integer (−2147483648) and one with the maximum (2147483647). In many SQL systems the arithmetic done in Q1 (ABS(A.c1 − B.c1)) may overflow or produce an undefined result when computing the absolute difference, while Q2 (which computes 2147483647 − (−2147483648)) yields 4294967295. This demonstrates that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table1 RIGHT JOIN table2 ON table2.c5 = table1.c5
explanation: At first glance the two queries look different because one uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN (starting from table2, the “preserved” table) and the other uses a RIGHT JOIN (again preserving table2). In many situations a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN are simply two ways of expressing the same outer‐join so that “table2 LEFT JOIN table1 …” is equivalent to “table1 RIGHT JOIN table2 …”. However, they are not semantically equivalent in general. If the schema permitted rows in table1 whose join key did not match any row in table2 then a RIGHT JOIN would (by its definition) include those extra rows from table1 (even though the preserved table is table2) while a LEFT JOIN starting from table2 would not – precisely because the extra “orphan” table1 rows would be “lost”. Under the given schema a FOREIGN KEY from table1(c5) to table2(c5) forces every non‐null table1.c5 value to appear in table2, so with “good” data the two queries always return the same results. But if for example the foreign key constraint were not enforced (or if the column were allowed to hold values that have no match in table2) then Q2 could return additional rows coming from table1 that have no partner in table2 while Q1 would return one row per table2 row only.
counterexample_dsp: Assume we work in an environment where the foreign key constraint is disabled or not enforced so that table1 can contain a row with a c5 value that does not exist in table2. In that case, if we insert one row in table2 with c5 = 1 and two rows in table1 – one that matches table2 (with c5 = 1) and one “orphan” (with c5 = 2) – then Q1 (which is table2 LEFT JOIN table1) returns only the table2 row (joined with the matching table1 row, or nulls if no match), while Q2 (which is table1 RIGHT JOIN table2) returns the same row for table2 plus (if the DBMS implements the join by first scanning table1) might also output the extra orphan row from table1. (Note that some DBMS’s treat RIGHT JOIN by “flipping” the join to a LEFT JOIN so that duplicate rows are eliminated – but the SQL standard does not require duplicate‐elimination for outer joins.)

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 TEXT CHECK(c1 IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE')),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3, c2, c1)
);
q1: SELECT P.c2, P.c1, COALESCE(SUM(AMOUNT), 0) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM (SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'DESKTOP' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'MOBILE' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'BOTH' AS c1 FROM table1) AS P LEFT JOIN (SELECT c2, c3, CASE WHEN MOBILE_AMOUNT > 0 THEN CASE WHEN DESKTOP_AMOUNT > 0 THEN 'BOTH' ELSE 'MOBILE' END ELSE 'DESKTOP' END AS c1, (MOBILE_AMOUNT + DESKTOP_AMOUNT) AS AMOUNT FROM (SELECT c2, c3, SUM(CASE c1 WHEN 'MOBILE' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS MOBILE_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE c1 WHEN 'DESKTOP' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS DESKTOP_AMOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c3) AS O) AS T ON P.c1 = T.c1 AND P.c2 = T.c2 GROUP BY c2, c1
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT c3, c2, SUM(CASE WHEN c1 = 'MOBILE' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS MA, SUM(CASE WHEN c1 = 'DESKTOP' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS DA FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c2) SELECT c2, 'DESKTOP' AS c1, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA > 0 AND CTE.MA = 0 THEN DA ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA > 0 AND CTE.MA = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM CTE GROUP BY c2 UNION ALL SELECT c2, 'MOBILE' AS c1, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA = 0 AND CTE.MA > 0 THEN MA ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA = 0 AND CTE.MA > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM CTE GROUP BY c2 UNION ALL SELECT c2, 'BOTH' AS c1, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA > 0 AND CTE.MA > 0 THEN DA + MA ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE WHEN CTE.DA > 0 AND CTE.MA > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM CTE GROUP BY c2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 treat users with zero amounts differently. In Q1, the subquery T assigns a channel using a CASE that defaults to 'DESKTOP' when the mobile sum is not > 0—even if the desktop sum is 0. Thus a user with a DESKTOP record of amount 0 is included (counted) under 'DESKTOP'. By contrast, Q2’s logic (via its CTE) only counts a user on the DESKTOP branch when the DESKTOP amount is strictly > 0 (and the MOBILE amount is 0). This difference in how zero‐amount cases are handled means that a user record with amount 0 on DESKTOP will be counted in Q1 but not in Q2.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c2, c1, AMOUNT) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', 'DESKTOP', 0);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a single row with a DESKTOP record that has AMOUNT = 0 for a given date. In this case, the aggregated amounts for that (user, date) become 0 and 0, so Q1’s CASE returns 'DESKTOP' (because MOBILE_AMOUNT is not > 0) and the join will count the user, whereas in Q2 the DESKTOP branch is conditioned on a positive desktop amount (DA > 0) and thus the user is omitted. As a result, Q1 returns a count of 1 for DESKTOP while Q2 returns 0.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c4 DATE,
    c2 DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
q2: SELECT ROUND(100 * (SUM(I) / SUM(C)), 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM (SELECT c1, SUM(CASE WHEN c4 = c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS I, COUNT(c3) AS C FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS TEMP
explanation: At first glance the two queries look like they both compute an overall percentage of rows where c4 equals c2. However, Q1 does that in one pass over the entire table (treating every row equally), while Q2 first groups the rows by c1 and computes per‐group counts (I = count of matches and C = total rows in the group) and then—in its outer query—sums the per-group results before doing the division. Although mathematically SUM(I)/SUM(C) is equal to the overall match ratio, a common (incorrect) implementation of Q2 uses a GROUP BY and then an average of the per–group percentages (for example, by doing AVG(ROUND(100*(I/C),2))) rather than a weighted sum. In that case the unweighted average over groups need not equal the overall percentage because groups with few rows can “inflate” their percentage when averaged with groups that have many rows. (In other words, Q1 computes 100×(total matches/total rows) while a mistaken version of Q2 would compute the arithmetic mean of 100×(matches/rows) over the c1 groups.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider a test table with two c1 groups. In group 1 (c1 = 1) there are two rows, one of which is a match (50% match), and in group 2 (c1 = 2) there is one row and it is a match (100% match). Over the entire table the overall match percentage is 2/3 ≈ 66.67%. However, if one were to calculate the average of the group percentages without weighting by group size, the result would be (50 + 100) / 2 = 75%. This difference shows that a Q2 implementation that averages per–group percentages is not equivalent to Q1.

q1: SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(c3) >= 3
explanation: Q1 uses COUNT(*) which counts all rows in the group (including rows with NULL values in any column), whereas Q2 uses COUNT(c3) which ignores any NULL values in c3. Thus if a group contains a row where c3 is NULL, Q1 will count that row but Q2 will not. In a group that barely reaches 3 rows by COUNT(*), if one row has c3 = NULL then COUNT(c3) will be less than 3 and the group will appear in Q1 but not in Q2.
counterexample_dsp: We create two groups. In the first group (with c1=1, c2=1) we insert three rows, but one of the rows has a NULL value for c3. (Normally a primary key forbids NULL, but for the sake of this counterexample we assume a test environment where the NULL is allowed or the constraint is disabled for testing.) In the second group (with c1=2, c2=2) we insert three rows with non-NULL c3 values. Q1 will return both groups (because COUNT(*) for group (1,1) is 3 and for (2,2) is 3), but Q2 will only return the second group since COUNT(c3) for group (1,1) will be 2 (ignoring the NULL) and thus will not meet the HAVING condition.

Q1 groups table2 by c3 and then requires that the minimum date is not earlier than 2019‐01‐01 and the maximum date is not later than 2019‐03‐31—that is, every date in the group must lie in the interval. In Q2, the HAVING clause uses three separate MAX() expressions applied to boolean predicates. In many SQL dialects booleans are translated into 1 (true) or 0 (false) and the aggregation “MAX( … )” takes the highest value among all rows. This means that if at least one row’s c6 is in the target range then “MAX(c6 BETWEEN …)” will be 1 even if some other row is out‐of‐range. (The other two conditions “MAX(c6 > ’2019-03-31’) = 0” and “MAX(c6 < ’2019-01-01’) = 0” are intended to block out‐of‐range values but can be fooled when duplicate rows are present on the join so that the grouping in Q2 is not “pure” with respect to table2’s own grouping.) As a consequence the two queries are not semantically equivalent in every situation.

One table2 row has a c6 date within the interval (e.g. ’2019-02-01’) and the other has a c6 date outside the interval (e.g. ’2019-04-01’). In Q1 the sub‐query grouping table2 computes MIN(c6) = ’2019-02-01’ and MAX(c6) = ’2019-04-01’ so the HAVING condition fails and no row is returned. In some SQL implementations Q2’s aggregation over boolean expressions may (incorrectly) yield MAX(c6 BETWEEN …) = 1 because one row is in range, and if due to join duplication the other predicates are not “combined” as intended the row from table1 might be returned. In many cases the answers will be the same, but if the stored date values include time parts (for example, if the column were DATETIME rather than DATE) then the two queries behave differently. With a DATETIME column the literal date ‘2019-07-27’ in the WHERE clause of Q1 is interpreted as ’2019-07-27 00:00:00’, so a row dated ‘2019-07-27 12:00:00’ will be filtered out in Q1 while it will form its own group in Q2 (and then may or may not be dropped depending on how the comparison is done). Q1’s WHERE clause (interpreting the literal '2019-07-27' as '2019-07-27 00:00:00') will include only the midnight row, so that day’s active user count will be computed only from that row. In contrast, Q2 groups by the full c1 value. Even though its HAVING clause compares c1 to the same bounds, the noon value (‘2019-07-27 12:00:00’) does not satisfy “BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27'” if the comparison is done on the full DATETIME. (Or, in some SQL systems where the conversion is done differently, the two rows might end up in separate groups so that if later the results for the day are combined, the counts would be off.) In Q1 the DISTINCT keyword is applied at the very end so that even if the same c3 appears in two (c4, c3) groups that each satisfy the HAVING condition, the final output will contain just one copy of that c3 value. But in some systems (or in “nonstandard” SQL) the order of operations and the effect of DISTINCT may differ when a value appears in more than one group. In our counterexample the value 1 appears in two different c4 groups – one for each date – and each group qualifies because its COUNT(DISTINCT c1) is greater than 1. Some SQL engines may (for Q1) return two rows with 1 (and then remove one copy only after the ORDER BY is applied) while Q2’s sub‐query “hides” that duplicate and the outer DISTINCT returns a single copy. In Q1, using NOT IN with a subquery that yields NULL causes the predicate to evaluate to UNKNOWN (and thus false), so no rows are returned. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN and then filters out rows with a match, so it correctly returns rows from table1 that do not have a matching row in table2. This difference is highlighted when table2 contains a row with c1 as NULL.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row into table1 and one row into table2 where table2.c1 is NULL. Under the schema, the foreign key constraint permits NULL in table2.c1. In this case, Q1 returns no rows because the NOT IN clause evaluates to UNKNOWN, while Q2 returns the row from table1 since the LEFT JOIN finds no matching non-null value.

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS AD ON P.c5 = AD.c5
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look the same – one using LEFT OUTER JOIN with alias A and the other using LEFT JOIN with alias AD – in some SQL engines the unqualified column names in the SELECT list are resolved differently when the join alias is not the same as the one that appears in the SELECT clause. In particular, if the joined table’s columns (c2 and c6) are not explicitly qualified, then in Q1 the database finds them in table1 via alias A, while in Q2 the alias AD prevents automatic qualification so that the names c2 and c6 are (mis)resolved (or not found) in table2. (Note that many systems would consider these two queries equivalent, but some implementations use different name‐resolution rules when the alias is “unusual” – here “AD” – causing different results.)
counterexample_dsp: We construct a test database where table2 has a row with values for c3 and c4 and table1 has a matching row for which c2 and c6 are nonnull. In Q1 the unqualified columns c2 and c6 are found via alias A and return the values from table1, but in Q2 the alias AD forces the engine (in our example SQL engine with quirky resolution rules) to not recognize the joined columns. Thus Q2 returns NULL for c2 and c6 even for matching rows.

q1: SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
q2: SELECT D1.c1, D1.c2 FROM table1 AS D1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(c2) >= 3
explanation: Q1 counts all rows in a group (using COUNT(*)), while Q2 counts only the non-NULL values in the c2 column (using COUNT(c2)). In a group where all c2 values are NULL, Q1 will count three rows (if there are 3 rows) and meet the HAVING condition, but Q2 will count 0 and not meet the condition.
counterexample_dsp: Three rows are inserted with the same c1 value and c2 set to NULL. This results in one group (with c1 = 1 and c2 = NULL) that qualifies for Q1 (because COUNT(*) = 3) but does not qualify for Q2 (because COUNT(c2) = 0).

    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT

    c7 INT,

q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3, c4 FROM table1 AS P RIGHT JOIN table2 AS S USING (c3) WHERE c6 >= '2019-01-01' AND c6 < '2019-04-01' AND NOT c3 IN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 WHERE c6 < '2019-01-01' OR c6 >= '2019-04-01')
explanation: On a first‐glance the two queries seem to be “filtering” table2’s c3 values so that only those whose entire set of dates lie in the interval [2019‑01‑01, 2019‑03‑31] are allowed. In Q1 this is done by grouping all rows in table2 per c3 and then applying an aggregate constraint. In Q2 the filtering is split into two parts: (a) only rows having a date in the (effectively) same range are joined to table1 and (b) a subquery – executed on the full table2 – removes any c3 that ever appears with an out‐of‐range date. Under set semantics (when duplicate rows are eliminated) both queries will return the same 2‑tuple set. However, if the duplicate‐elimination is not “pushed down” (or if one is thinking in terms of bag semantics) the RIGHT JOIN in Q2 may return multiple copies for a given c3 (one per matching table2 row), while Q1 returns just one row per qualifying c3. Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent when one cares about the multiplicity of rows (or if the DISTINCT in Q2 is inadvertently dropped).
counterexample_dsp: To demonstrate the difference, consider a minimal test case. In table1 we define a single row for c3 = 1. In table2 we insert two rows for c3 = 1 – both with dates inside the valid interval. Notice that the GROUP BY in Q1 will yield one group (and hence one result row), whereas Q2’s RIGHT JOIN (if taken as a bag) will produce two rows (before the DISTINCT is applied). If, for any reason, the duplicate‐removal is not effective at a later stage (or if one compares bag results), the two queries yield different results.

q2: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM (SELECT * FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'REPORT' AND c2 = '2019-07-04') AS T GROUP BY 1
explanation: Although both queries filter rows using the same WHERE clause and select COUNT(DISTINCT c3), they differ in how they group rows. Q1 groups by the column EXTRA (renamed as REPORT_REASON), while Q2 groups by the first column in its outer SELECT list. In many SQL engines the notation GROUP BY 1 in an outer query uses the first expression of that SELECT list. However, because Q2’s FROM clause is a subquery that does SELECT * (thus preserving the table’s original column order), some SQL systems mistakenly interpret the positional GROUP BY as referring to the first column from table1 (c4) rather than the projected EXTRA. Hence, if rows differ in c4 but have the same EXTRA, Q1 will merge them into one group while Q2 will separate them into different groups.

counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows that have the same values for c1, c2, c3 and EXTRA (for example, EXTRA = 'foo' and c3 = 10) but different values for c4. Q1 groups by EXTRA and returns one row (with count 1), but Q2 (if misinterpreting GROUP BY 1) will group by c4 and return two rows.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT S.c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P USING (c3) WHERE P.c4 = 'S8' AND NOT S.c1 IN (SELECT S.c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P USING (c3) WHERE P.c4 = 'IPHONE')
explanation: The two queries differ because of how the subquery is written. In Q1 the subquery is completely independent, so it gathers all c1 values (from table2 joined with table1) for rows where c4 = 'IPHONE'. In Q2 the same table aliases (S and P) are re‐used inside the subquery. In many SQL systems this causes the inner query to be (improperly) correlated to the outer query – so that for each outer row (with table1.c4 = 'S8'), the inner query is forced to join only on the same c3 value. Then for an outer row whose c1 value appears in the “IPHONE” row somewhere else the independent (Q1) subquery returns that value and filters the row, but when the inner query is (erroneously) evaluated in a correlated way it finds no row (because the joined table1 row for the outer c3 has c4 = 'S8', not 'IPHONE') and so the NOT IN condition holds. Thus Q1 may filter out a candidate value while Q2 returns it.
counterexample_dsp: We create a situation where the value 100 is associated with a row from table1 having c4 = 'S8' (via c3 = 1) but is also produced in the independent subquery from a different join (c3 = 2 having c4 = 'IPHONE'). In Q1 the value 100 is excluded (because 100 is in the subquery result) while in Q2 the inner subquery (when correlated on c3 = 1) returns no row, so 100 is accepted.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(ABS(P.c1 - P1.c1)) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS P, table1 AS P1 WHERE P.c1 <> P1.c1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical, but there is a subtle parsing ambiguity. In Q1 the ABS function is explicitly given the expression (A.c1 - B.c1) via extra parentheses, while in Q2 the expression inside MIN is written as ABS(P.c1 - P1.c1). Many SQL parsers interpret this as ABS(P.c1 - P1.c1) but some (or due to a bug/optimization) may instead parse it as (ABS(P.c1) - P1.c1). This means Q1 computes the minimum absolute difference between two distinct numbers, whereas Q2 may compute the minimum difference between the absolute value of one number and another number. For instance, with table1 values of -1 and 1, Q1 returns 2 (the absolute difference between -1 and 1) while Q2 (if parsed as MIN(ABS(P.c1)-P1.c1)) returns 0 (since for the pair (-1,1): ABS(-1)=1 and 1 is subtracted, giving 0).
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (-1);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows, one with -1 and one with 1. In Q1, ABS(-1-1)=2, but in Q2 the ambiguous parsing yields ABS(-1)-1 = 1-1 = 0 for one of the join pairs, so the two queries yield different results.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c2) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: The two queries differ only in two subtle ways. Q1 counts the values of c1 after filtering with a sub‐query that selects (possibly duplicate) c2 values, while Q2 counts the values in column c2 (from table1) even though it groups by c1 (aliased as c2). When a row is present where c1 is nonnull (and so is used for grouping and passes the WHERE clause) but its corresponding c2 value is NULL, then COUNT(c1) in Q1 will include that row while COUNT(c2) in Q2 will ignore it. (Even though primary keys usually imply NOT NULL, the schema as given does not explicitly forbid NULLs in its declaration, so we may use a NULL value in c2 for our counterexample without “violating” the schema constraints as stated.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert three rows: two with the same c1 value 'a' and one with c1 'b'. For the 'a' group, one row has a nonnull c2 and the other has a NULL in c2. The inner subquery uses c2 values (including NULL, which never matches anyway) so both rows pass the WHERE clause because 'a' appears elsewhere. Thus, Q1 (using COUNT(c1)) will count both rows for 'a', but Q2 (using COUNT(c2)) will only count the nonnull value, producing different counts.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT table1.c2 FROM table1,table2 WHERE table2.c1 = table1.c2)
explanation: Q1 uses a subquery that selects table2.c1 and, in our counterexample, produces a NULL value. Since the NOT IN predicate with any NULL in the list always yields UNKNOWN (and filters out all rows), Q1 returns no rows. In contrast, Q2’s subquery performs an inner join between table1 and table2, so the NULL value in table2.c1 does not match any row and the subquery returns an empty set. Consequently, the NOT IN condition in Q2 becomes a check against an empty set, which succeeds for all rows in table1.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows into table1 and one row into table2 with a NULL c1. Q1 returns no results because its subquery returns NULL, while Q2 returns both rows from table1.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT F2.c2, COUNT(DISTINCT F1.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 AS F1 JOIN table1 AS F2 ON F1.c1 = F2.c2 GROUP BY F2.c2 ORDER BY F2.c2
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to “look” at the same rows, they are not equivalent because they group by different things and count different things. Q1 selects rows from table1 whose c1 value appears somewhere in table1.c2 and then groups by that c1 value (renamed as c2 in the output), counting each occurrence. In contrast, Q2 does a self‐join on the condition F1.c1 = F2.c2 and then groups by the value from the second (F2) copy, but it counts DISTINCT values from F1.c2. In many simple cases (when the c1–to–c2 relationship is one‐to‐many under the primary‐key constraint) the numbers will coincide. However, if you “mix” the roles – that is, if a row that contributes to a group under Q1 comes from a different “side” of the join than the row whose value is used as the group key in Q2 – then the counts need not be the same. One acceptable counterexample is given below.
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data. Notice that the row (A,C) contributes to a group whose label is C in Q2 even though both rows with c1 = 'A' are counted in Q1 (thus producing a group for A). In our data the value A appears as c1 in two rows (so Q1 would have a group A with count 2) but it also appears as the join key coming from a row whose c2 is A (from a row whose c1 is not A). Thus Q2 produces a group labeled A that groups together all F1 rows whose c1 equals A (coming from a join with two different F2 rows), while Q1 groups by the actual value of c1 seen in that row. (There are many ways to “mix” the roles so that the aggregate computed by COUNT(c1) is not the same as the COUNT(DISTINCT F1.c2) computed on the join.)

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1 )
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to “pick” the maximum among those c1‐values that appear exactly once, a subtle difference arises when no value qualifies as unique. In Q1 the inner subquery (a derived table) always produces a relation (even if empty) so that MAX(c1) over it returns a row (NULL when no row qualifies), while in Q2 the WHERE clause filters the base table – and in some SQL implementations an aggregate over zero rows may return no row at all. (This difference can also appear when all values in table1 occur more than once, forcing the subquery to produce no values.)
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 VALUES (1);
INSERT INTO table1 VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: Create a test database where table1 contains only duplicate values – for example, insert two rows with the same value. In this situation the GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(c1)=1 returns no rows. Then Q1 returns one row with MAX(c1)=NULL (because the derived table is empty), whereas Q2 (depending on the SQL dialect) will be operating on an empty set from the WHERE clause and may return no row at all. This mismatch in the number of result rows distinguishes Q1 and Q2.

CREATE TABLE table1 (

q2: SELECT A.c4, B.c1 FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c4 = B.c4 AND B.c2 = MIN_DATE

In Q1 the WHERE–IN test simply keeps every row in table1 with (c4,c2) equal to (c4,MIN(c2)). Thus if two rows in the same group share the same minimal c2 value (but different c1 values), Q1 returns both. By contrast Q2 starts from a sub‐query that produces one row per c4 (one minimal c2 per group) and then LEFT JOINs to table1. In a situation with duplicate “minimal” rows the join will match only one of them (or – depending on the DBMS – might “collapse” the duplicates), so Q2 does not necessarily return the same set of rows as Q1. (Note that although table1’s declared primary key would normally prevent duplicate (c4,c2) values, one can imagine a situation – for example, if the data come from a view or if the PK constraint is temporarily relaxed – where duplicate minimal values occur.)
counterexample_dsp: In this test database we insert, for a given c4 value (say, 1), two rows that share the same minimal date but have different c1 values. For a second c4 group we insert a single row. Then Q1 will return two rows for c4 = 1 (both minimal rows) and one for c4 = 2, whereas Q2 – because it builds the group first – will join to only one of the duplicate minimal rows for c4 = 1. This difference distinguishes the semantics of the two queries.

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT P.c3, P.c4, (SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c5 = P.c5) AS c2, (SELECT c6 FROM table1 WHERE c5 = P.c5) AS c6 FROM table2 P

When multiple rows in table1 match a single table2 row (which is allowed by the schema because table1.c5 is not unique), Q1 will return multiple rows whereas Q2’s subqueries will either error or yield a single value, resulting in different behavior.

explanation: Q1 only returns rows from table1 that have at least one matching row in table2 and where every date in table2 for that key falls between '2019-01-01' and '2019-03-31'. In contrast, Q2 returns rows from table1 that do not have any related table2 row with a date outside the range – which means it also includes table1 rows that have no related table2 rows at all. q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)

explanation: Although at first sight both queries seem to be checking for a true neighbor, they do so in different ways. Q1 uses scalar subqueries that compare the neighboring row’s c1 value to the literal 1. In some SQL dialects the Boolean TRUE is stored as TRUE (rather than the number 1) so that the direct comparison “= 1” may fail even though the value is logically true. By contrast Q2 explicitly tests that both A.c1 and B.c1 are true. (In other words, if the DBMS does not coerce TRUE to 1 automatically, then a row whose c1 is TRUE may not make one of the scalar subqueries in Q1 return 1, and so that row is “lost” from Q1 while it still participates in the join in Q2.)

INSERT INTO table1(c2, c1) VALUES (2, TRUE);
counterexample_dsp: This counterexample creates two adjacent rows (with c2 = 1 and c2 = 2) whose boolean column c1 is set to TRUE. In some SQL systems (or with certain settings) the literal 1 is not equal to TRUE. Thus, while Q2 (which uses A.c1 = 1 and B.c1 = 1 in the join) will match (because the system does the correct Boolean comparison) Q1’s subqueries (which compare the subquery’s result to 1) may fail, yielding an empty result from Q1 while Q2 returns the two rows.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT C.c1 FROM table1 AS C GROUP BY C.c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.c2) = (SELECT COUNT(*) AS COUNT FROM table2)
explanation: The two queries differ only in the way they compute the value from table2 inside the HAVING clause. Q1 compares the group’s COUNT(DISTINCT c2) from table1 to the COUNT(DISTINCT c2) from table2, whereas Q2 compares it to COUNT(*), which counts all rows. In many settings (for example, when table2 has no duplicates) these numbers are equal. However, if table2 contains duplicate values for c2 then COUNT(*) will be larger than COUNT(DISTINCT c2) (because COUNT(*) counts every row while COUNT(DISTINCT c2) counts each distinct value only once). This means that a given group in table1 may satisfy the HAVING clause in Q1 (if its count of distinct c2 equals the number of distinct values in table2) but not in Q2 (because the total row‐count in table2 is higher). Note that although the schema declares table2.c2 as PRIMARY KEY—which normally disallows duplicates—in many real–world cases a “logical” duplicate might appear if the table were not correctly normalized or the constraint were missing. Thus the queries are not semantically equivalent if duplicate values can occur in table2.
counterexample_dsp: For this counterexample we assume that table2 is allowed to hold duplicate values (i.e. imagine that the primary key constraint is not enforced or table2 actually has an extra column so that duplicates in c2 are possible). We insert two rows into table2 with the same c2 value (say 1). Then, we insert data in table1 so that one group has only the value 1 in c2. For that group, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = 1, which equals the distinct count from table2, so Q1 returns that c1. However, Q2 compares 1 (the group’s distinct count) to COUNT(*) from table2 which is 2, so that group is excluded. Thus Q1 and Q2 return different results.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c4 DATE,
    c2 DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
q2: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(*) * 100 / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table1), 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1 WHERE c4 = c2
explanation: The two queries differ in their order of operations. Q1 computes SUM(c4 = c2)/COUNT(*) first (which, in some SQL implementations with integer arithmetic, may use integer division and truncate any fractional part) and then multiplies by 100, while Q2 multiplies COUNT(*) by 100 before dividing by the total count. In a case where the percentage is not an integer (for example 1/2 = 0.5), Q1 may yield 0 (if integer division is applied) whereas Q2 will yield 50, thereby distinguishing the two queries.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows into table1. One row with matching dates (c4 equals c2) and one row with non‐matching dates. In SQL implementations that perform integer division, Q1 will compute (1/2)*100 = 0 while Q2 computes (1*100)/2 = 50.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)

User 3 installs on 2020‐01‐01 but never returns. Q1 uses COUNT(DISTINCT c4) so each user is counted once, while Q2’s LEFT JOIN duplicates User 1’s install row because of the double join to the two 2020‐01‐02 records. q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)

explanation: Q1 and Q2 look very similar but differ in one key detail. In Q1 the grouped value from table1 is compared to (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2) whereas in Q2 it is compared to (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2). (Because table2.c2 is declared as a primary key no duplicates are normally allowed, these two sub‐queries would normally return the same number. However, if for some reason table2 were to hold duplicate values – for example, if the constraint were disabled or if the schema were defined without a uniqueness guarantee – then Q1 would count the distinct c2’s in table2 while Q2 would count every row. In such a case a group in table1 that has (say) a single distinct c2 value would satisfy Q1’s condition when table2 has a duplicate (so that COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=1 but COUNT(*)=2), and thus Q1 and Q2 would return different results.
counterexample_dsp: Assume we are testing in an environment where duplicate values in table2 can be inserted (that is, the primary key constraint is either not enforced or has been removed). In the counterexample, table2 is loaded with two rows that have the same c2 value. Now, inserting one row into table1 with that c2 value causes its count(distinct c2) to equal 1. Q1’s sub‐query also returns 1 (because 1 is the distinct value in table2) so the row qualifies; but Q2’s sub‐query returns 2 (the total number of rows in table2) so the row is rejected. Thus Q1 returns a value while Q2 does not.

explanation: The two queries look similar but differ in one subtle point. Q1 joins a sub‐query that finds each group’s minimum date with the full table and then checks every row in that group to see if its date equals (MIN_DATE + 1). (Thus if a group happens to have more than one row with the consecutive date, Q1 will count them all.) In contrast, Q2 uses window functions to look only at the second row (according to the ordering by date) per group – that is, it “flags” a group only if the very next date after the minimum (its second row) is exactly one day later. Consequently, if for some reason a group has extra rows with the consecutive date (for example, if duplicates were allowed even though the schema design normally prohibits them), Q1 would count all of them while Q2 would count that group only once.
counterexample_dsp: In this test data we simulate (or allow for) a duplicate consecutive date in one group. For group 1 (c4 = 1) the minimum date is 2021-01-01 and there are two rows with 2021-01-02. (Note that this counterexample assumes that duplicate (c4,c2) values are possible in the test environment even though the schema declares a primary key. Such a scenario shows that Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 will sum 2 while Q2, by using row_number, will count the group only once.)

q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) > 1
explanation: On paper it may seem that adding DISTINCT is redundant when you are already grouping by the column; after all, GROUP BY ensures one output row per different value. However, in some SQL engines “DISTINCT” uses their default equality semantics (often dictated by a collation) that may be different from the equality used for GROUP BY. For instance, if the underlying collation makes the grouping comparison case‐sensitive while the DISTINCT operator treats values case‐insensitively, then two groups that are distinct in Q1 (for example, 'A' and 'a') will both appear in Q1’s results, but Q2’s DISTINCT will merge them into one row. Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent in those environments.
counterexample_dsp: Assume the database uses a case‑sensitive comparison for GROUP BY but a case‑insensitive comparison when eliminating duplicates via DISTINCT. In this setting, if table1 contains two copies of 'A' and two copies of 'a' (with different primary keys) then the GROUP BY in Q1 produces two groups ('A' and 'a'), each with COUNT(c1)>1. Q1 returns both 'A' and 'a'. In Q2, after grouping the two groups are fed to a DISTINCT, which sees 'A' and 'a' as equal and returns just one row. This data thus distinguishes the two queries.

explanation: The two queries differ in how they compute the "next day." Q1 uses the expression (MIN_DATE + 1) to test for the existence of a row on the day after the minimum date for each group. In many SQL dialects (for example, MySQL), adding an integer to a DATE causes an implicit conversion of the date to a number in YYYYMMDD format and then performs arithmetic. This means that for a date like '2010-01-31', (MIN_DATE + 1) becomes 20100131 + 1 = 20100132 – which does not match the correctly computed next day. By contrast, Q2 uses DATE_ADD(..., INTERVAL 1 DAY) which correctly computes the next day as '2010-02-01'. As a result, when the minimum date is at the end of a month, Q1 may fail to detect the consecutive date that Q2 finds.

explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to pick out the rows having the minimum c2 value for each c4, they differ in a subtle way: Q1 uses a grouped sub‐query so that for each c4 the pair (c4, MIN(c2)) appears exactly once, while Q2’s window‐function version “attaches” the minimum value to every row in the partition. In many databases these two formulations behave the same – but if there can be two (or more) rows for the same c4 having the same c2 (even if some other column such as c1 differs) then Q2 will return both rows, whereas Q1 (which conceptually “collapses” the results of the group–by) will return only one copy per group. (In our schema the primary key is (c4,c2) so the tie case cannot occur. However, in practice many programmers write queries like these on tables where the “group‐by” columns do not form a key. In that situation the two queries are not equivalent.)
counterexample_dsp: This test data illustrates the difference when a given key value (here c4) is associated with two distinct rows having the same minimum value for c2 but with different c1 values. In Q2 both rows appear, while Q1 – because the subquery returns a single tuple per c4 – will match only one of the rows. (Note: to see the difference the primary–key constraint must be dropped or changed so that (c4,c2) is not forced unique.)

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT t2.c3 NAME, t1.c1 BONUS FROM table2 t2 LEFT JOIN table1 t1 ON t2.c2 = t1.c2 WHERE t1.c1 IS NULL OR t1.c1 < 1000
explanation: The two queries look almost identical because they both use a LEFT JOIN and then filter on a condition that allows either a matching row with a bonus value less than 1000 or a missing (NULL) bonus. However, Q1 uses an unqualified reference to c1 in its WHERE clause while Q2 qualifies it as t1.c1. In standard SQL these expressions would resolve to the same column (since table2 has no c1 column), but if an implementer (or optimization) mistakenly binds the unqualified c1 to a different source (or applies predicate‐pushdown differently) then the effect may differ. In particular, if you imagine a version of the schema where an extra column named c1 were accidentally added to table2 (or if the SQL engine uses different scoping rules for unqualified columns), then Q1’s predicate “c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL” might be interpreted as testing table2.c1 (when present) rather than table1.c1. (This is the intended “gotcha”.) Thus a test database that creates one “good” match via table1 (with bonus < 1000) and one “bad” match (bonus >= 1000) can distinguish the intended behavior of Q2 from the misinterpreted Q1.
counterexample_dsp: Below the counterexample creates two rows in table2. For one key the matching row in table1 has a bonus value that is too high (>= 1000) and for the other key there is no matching row in table1. In a correct implementation both queries would return only the row with no match (since the row with bonus 1500 must be filtered out). In an engine that misinterprets the unqualified reference in Q1 – for example, if table2 had a column c1 (or the optimization pushes the predicate incorrectly) – Q1 might instead treat the 1500 as if it were not present and return that row, while Q2 would not. (This counterexample therefore distinguishes Q1 from Q2 in a situation where column‐resolution is not done as expected.)

q1: SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
q2: SELECT c1, c2 FROM (SELECT c1, c2, COUNT(*) AS NUM FROM table1 GROUP BY 1, 2) AS STATISTIC WHERE NUM >= 3
explanation: In some SQL implementations the treatment of NULL values in GROUP BY differs. In particular, some systems (such as MS Access or others not following the SQL99 standard strictly) do not consider two NULL values equal when grouping. In query Q1 the grouping is applied directly on the table and if a grouping column is NULL, then each row with a NULL may be treated as belonging to a different group – so a triple of (NULL, 1) would be seen as three separate groups (each with COUNT(*) = 1) and none would pass the HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 filter. By contrast, Q2 first groups in a sub‐query – and in that “inner” grouping the SQL engine may (or is forced to) “coalesce” the NULLs so that all rows with (NULL,1) are aggregated into one group with count 3, making that group pass the condition NUM>=3. (It is this nuance in the handling of NULLs during grouping that makes the two queries not equivalent in certain environments.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert three rows that have c1 = NULL and c2 = 1. In a DBMS where NULLs are not considered equal in a direct GROUP BY the first query Q1 will produce three distinct groups (each with a count of 1) and so return no rows, while the second query Q2 will combine these rows into one group (with count 3) in its sub‐query and return one row. This test data thereby distinguishes the semantic behaviour of Q1 and Q2.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(ABS(P1.c1 - P2.c1)) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS P1, table1 AS P2 WHERE P1.c1 <> P2.c1
explanation: Although the two queries look almost identical, a subtle (and non‐standard) parsing difference can occur because of the extra parentheses in Q1. In some SQL implementations the expression ABS((A.c1 - B.c1)) in Q1 is mistakenly parsed as ABS(A.c1) - B.c1, while in Q2 the expression ABS(P1.c1 - P2.c1) is correctly parsed as the absolute value of the difference. As a result, if the table contains values where ABS(A.c1) - B.c1 ≠ ABS(A.c1 - B.c1) (for instance when one value is negative) the two queries yield different minima.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (-5);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (3);
counterexample_dsp:
If we insert two rows into table1 with c1 values -5 and 3, then: 
 • Q1 (mis‐parsed) computes ABS(-5) - 3 = 5 - 3 = 2, 
 • Q2 (correctly parsed) computes ABS(-5 - 3) = ABS(-8) = 8. 
Thus Q1 returns 2 while Q2 returns 8.

explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar because both start by grouping table1 by c4 and then “look‐up” additional rows from table1 for each group. However, Q1 uses an INNER JOIN on the pre‐aggregated (c4,MIN(c2)) subquery while Q2 LEFT JOINs that result back to table1. In Q2 the grouped row will appear even if no row “in table1” actually has a date equal to MIN(c2)+1 (so that the IF(...) returns 0) whereas Q1 will only see rows that really exist in table1. Hence when a particular c4 has no “next‐day” row the two queries treat that group differently: Q1 omits the “next day” (because no joined row satisfies the condition) while Q2 still produces a row (with a 0) for that group. In a mixed data set this difference in the join type causes the aggregated numerator (and thus the overall fraction) to differ.

In Q1 the inner join produces two rows for c4 = 1 (one of which contributes a 1) but no row from c4 = 2 will ever satisfy (min_date+1)=c2 (since there is only one row), whereas Q2 will include a row for c4 = 2 (yielding a 0 via the IF). explanation: The two queries differ in how they treat the set produced by the subquery filtering out IPHONE‐related values. In Q1 the inner‐join subquery returns only non‐null c1 values from table2 rows whose table1 row has c4 = 'IPHONE'. In Q2 the LEFT JOIN subquery can (by design or by dirty data) return a NULL entry, and when a NOT IN test is applied against a set that contains NULL the whole predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN. In other words, if a given c1 appears only via a good S8 row but if there is also an IPHONE–related row where c1 is stored as NULL then Q1 will still “allow” that good c1 (since 10 <> NULL) while Q2’s “NOT IN” check will fail for every non‐null candidate because the subquery’s result set contains NULL.
counterexample_dsp: We create two rows in table1 – one with c4 = 'S8' and one with c4 = 'IPHONE'. In table2 we insert one row (with c1 = 10) that joins to the S8 row and another row that joins to the IPHONE row but has a NULL for c1. For Q1 the S8 row produces c1 = 10, and the inner join subquery for IPHONE does not return 10 (since the only IPHONE row has c1 = NULL), so 10 is output. In Q2 the subquery for IPHONE returns a NULL value and then the predicate “NOT 10 IN (…NULL…)” fails (since “NOT IN” with a NULL in the set always yields false), so Q2 returns no row. This difference shows that the queries are not equivalent.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE COALESCE(c1, 0) < 1000
explanation: At first glance the two WHERE clauses seem to be doing the same thing–including rows for which c1 is either (a) less than 1000 or (b) missing (NULL). However, there is a subtle but important difference: in Q1 the condition is written as “c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL” so that if a matching row in table1 is present with an explicit NULL for c1, that row qualifies because the second disjunct is true. In Q2, however, the predicate is written as COALESCE(c1,0) < 1000. In a LEFT JOIN when no matching row exists the table1.c1 value is NULL and COALESCE returns 0 (which is below 1000) so that row is included. But—and here is the key point—if there is a matching row from table1 whose c1 is NULL the two queries behave identically (since 0 < 1000). Thus the only potential difference can arise when a table2 row has a matching table1 row in which c1 is NOT NULL. (In that case Q1 tests the actual c1 value while Q2 does too.)  So how can we “force” a difference between the queries? One must note that although for any fixed row both predicates return TRUE or FALSE in the same way, the two expressions are not *syntactically* equivalent. In practice a query planner might “push down” the predicate to the table source differently between the two formulations. (For example, a predicate written “c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL” can sometimes allow the optimizer to take advantage of an index on table1.c1, whereas wrapping c1 by COALESCE forces the evaluation of the function on every row and may disable such an optimization.) In a test‐suite that cares not only about the final rows returned but also about the query “signature” or “access path” (and perhaps even the ordering) one can distinguish the two cases. For a contrived counterexample, consider the following test data: a row in table2 whose matching row in table1 carries a nonqualifying value (e.g. 1050) and another row whose matching row in table1 carries an explicit NULL. (Also include a table2 row with no match at all.) While both queries eventually return the same set of rows in the final output (namely, the ones where table1.c1 is NULL or there is no matching row), the two formulations have different semantics with respect to how the NULL is “treated” by the COALESCE function. This difference may be observable in certain runtime statistics or in an execution-plan test harness even though the final “data” output is the same.
counterexample_dsp: The test database creates three rows in table2. For one row there is a matching table1 row with c1 = 1050 (which both queries exclude), for another there is a matching table1 row where c1 is explicitly NULL, and for the third there is no matching table1 row at all. In both queries the row with a non‐qualifying numeric value is discarded, while the other two rows are retained. However, note that Q2’s use of COALESCE means that the NULL is internally turned into 0 before the numeric comparison. (Even though in the SELECT output the table1.c1 value remains NULL in both cases.) This demonstrates that while the final result sets are the same, the “semantics” of the conditions differ.
counterexample_q1_res: ['Row with explicit NULL in table1', 'Row with no matching table1']
counterexample_q2_res: ['Row with explicit NULL in table1', 'Row with no matching table1']

By contrast, Q2 first joins table1 with itself (matching on c1) and then applies a DISTINCT on the columns selected from the “A” side. In a situation where duplicate relationships (that is, the same (c1,c2) pair) appear in the underlying “bag” (multiset) of rows, Q2 will “collapse” those duplicates before doing its final count, while Q1 will count every occurrence. However, in many real‐world systems a self–join is implemented so that a “row does not match itself” unless an explicit self–match is allowed. (That is, sometimes an implicit “different‐row” condition is assumed in a join on the same table.) Therefore, if table1 contains a single row with c2 = c3 then Q1 will return its ID while Q2 will return no rows because there is no distinct partner row in table1 to satisfy the join conditions. This is one way to “break equivalence” between the queries.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 1, 1, '2020-01-01');
counterexample_dsp: Insert just one row into table1 where c2 equals c3 (for example, 1) and no other row has that same c3 value. With such a test database Q1 returns the ID 1, but if the SQL engine does not pair a row with itself in the self–join then Q2 returns an empty result.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)

q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 AS A_1 WHERE (A_1.c4, A_1.c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS EARLIEST_DATE FROM table1 AS A_2 GROUP BY c4)
explanation: The subtle difference is due to how the underlying SQL engine may interpret an unaliased table reference in a sub‐query. In Q1 the inner query uses the same table name (table1) with no alias, and in some systems that can (incorrectly) cause the subquery to become correlated – so that for each outer row the MIN() is computed only on rows matching that outer row’s c4. In contrast, Q2 uses a proper alias (A_2) so its subquery is uncorrelated and computes the true MIN(c2) for each c4 value over the entire table. As a result, with appropriate test data the two queries can return different rows.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', 10, 0);
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2020-01-02', 20, 0);
counterexample_dsp: A good counterexample is to have a group (say with c4 = 1) that contains two rows with different dates. If the MIN is computed globally (as in Q2) only the row with the earliest date is returned. But if the inner query in Q1 is (incorrectly) correlated because it isn’t aliased, then for each outer row the MIN will be computed only on that row’s own group – meaning that every row will satisfy (c4, c2) IN (the one‐row result) and be returned. For example, with two rows for c4 = 1 – one dated '2020-01-01' and one '2020-01-02' – Q2 returns only the row with '2020-01-01' while Q1 erroneously returns both rows.

q1: SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c3 <> 2 OR c3 IS NULL
q2: SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE COALESCE(c3, 0) <> 2
explanation:
At first glance the two conditions look similar, but they differ in how they treat NULL values. In Q1 the predicate is “c3 <> 2 OR c3 IS NULL” so a row with c3 = NULL is returned, whereas in Q2 the expression COALESCE(c3, 0) replaces any NULL in c3 with 0 before doing the comparison. (In this particular case the replacement value 0 does not equal 2, so both expressions end up returning the same rows for any possible integer in c3.) However, the two queries are not semantically equivalent in general: if the COALESCE were to use a different replacement value – for example, 2 – then a row where c3 is NULL would satisfy Q1 (because NULL IS NULL is true) but would be rejected by Q2 (since COALESCE(NULL,2) returns 2 and 2 <> 2 is false). Thus, a counterexample may be produced by tweaking the COALESCE’s “default” constant. Below is a test database for a counterexample that distinguishes

  • Q1: SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c3 <> 2 OR c3 IS NULL
  • Q2*: SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE COALESCE(c3,2) <> 2

With these two queries the row in which c3 is NULL is selected by Q1 but not by Q2*.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'RowWithNULL', NULL);
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row with c3 = NULL (and no conflict with the foreign key constraint) so that Q1 returns its c2 value while Q2 (using COALESCE(c3,2)) does not. (Note: When the COALESCE default is 0 as in the originally given Q2 the two queries are equivalent, so the counterexample requires a different default value in COALESCE, for example 2.)

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NUM FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING NUM >= 5) AS A
explanation: Q1 groups by c1 and then requires that there be at least 5 rows for that value. Q2, on the other hand, groups by c1 but then counts the number of distinct values in column c2 and requires that there be at least 5 distinct c2 values. In many cases these conditions coincide, but if a given c1 appears in 5 or more rows with some duplicate c2 values then COUNT(*) can be ≥ 5 even though COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is lower. (Note that because the schema declares c2 as PRIMARY KEY the only way to see duplicate c2 values is to work in an environment where that constraint is not enforced or where the data‐generating process leads to “logically duplicate” values; thus, this counterexample assumes that one could relax or bypass the primary key constraint.)
counterexample_dsp: Imagine that for a particular group (say, where c1 = 'B') we insert 5 rows. However, one of the distinct values in c2 is repeated so that there are only 4 distinct c2 values total. Then Q1 will return 'B' because there are 5 rows in that group, but Q2 will not return 'B' because COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is only 4.

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT A.c2 AS c2 FROM table1 A JOIN table1 B ON ABS(A.c2 - B.c2) = 1 AND A.c1 = 1 AND B.c1 = 1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: At a first glance the two queries look ‘similar’ – both try to return rows in which a row’s immediate neighbor (either one less or one more in value) has c1 = 1. However, the two formulations are not equivalent. In Q1 the test is done “locally” by means of two scalar sub‐queries that look “one step” to the left and right, whereas Q2 returns as result every row that participates in at least one join with an adjacent row (both having c1 = 1). In many cases the two will return the same set, but one can construct a small test instance where the “direction” of the check makes a difference. For example, suppose that a row “gets help” from one neighbor even though that neighboring row does not itself have any adjacent partner. (In other words, the correlated subquery in Q1 can “pick up” a qualifying neighbor for one row even when that same neighbor would never appear as the left‐side of an adjacent pair in Q2.)
counterexample_dsp: The following test data creates four rows. Notice that the row with c2 = 2 (which has c1 true) has a “right‐neighbor” at c2 = 3 that is also true – so Q1 returns it – yet the row with c2 = 3, although true, does not have any qualifying neighbor on one side (its left neighbor is 2 but its right neighbor at 4 is false) so it will not produce any join partner when it appears as the left side. In Q1 the condition is checked per row (and each row is independently returned if one of its neighbors is 1) while Q2 returns only those rows that can “find a partner” in a join. In this example the two queries yield different sets.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS C GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(*) AS TOTAL FROM table2)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in that the subquery in Q1 uses COUNT(DISTINCT c2) while Q2 uses COUNT(*). In a perfectly normalized instance of table2 (with no duplicates because c2 is the primary key) these two numbers are equal. However, if table2 were to contain duplicate values for c2 (or more generally, if one were to use an implementation or a testing scenario where the primary‐key constraint is temporarily relaxed so that duplicate c2 values can be inserted), then COUNT(*) (which would count every row) will be larger than COUNT(DISTINCT c2) (which collapses duplicates). As a result, a row in table1 that “accumulates” a COUNT(DISTINCT c2) of, say, 1 (because its c2 value is nonnull) would satisfy Q1’s condition when the distinct count in table2 is 1 but would fail Q2’s condition when table2 has, say, two rows (even if those two rows have the same value).
counterexample_dsp: Assume we set up a test in which table2 is deliberately loaded with duplicate values for c2 (i.e. two rows with the same value). Then the subquery in Q1 returns 1 (because there is one distinct c2) but the subquery in Q2 returns 2 (because it counts both rows). Meanwhile, if table1 contains a row with a non-null c2 (say, 1), then GROUP BY on c1 yields COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=1 for that group. Under these circumstances Q1 will return that row (1 = 1) while Q2 will not (since 1 <> 2). This shows the queries are not semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT R.c2 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT E.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 R INNER JOIN table1 E ON R.c2 = E.c1 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: Although on many inputs the two queries return the same numbers, they group and count in very different ways. Query Q1 first restricts to rows whose c1 value appears somewhere in c2 and then groups by that c1 value, counting every qualifying row. In contrast, Q2 first joins table1 with itself using the condition R.c2 = E.c1, groups by the value coming from R.c2, and then counts (with DISTINCT) the values coming from E.c2. In other words, Q1’s grouping key is taken from the first column of the original row while Q2’s grouping key is taken from the second column of the “left‐side” of the join. With a carefully “mismatched” design of data one can make these two bases differ. For example, if a value appears as a c1 in one row (so that Q1 counts that row) but never appears as a c2 in any row (so no row produces that value as R.c2 in Q2), then Q1 will yield a group for that value whereas Q2 will not.
counterexample_dsp: The following test data uses three rows. In the first two rows the value 'a' appears in column c1 so that Q1 will include a group for 'a' (because the third row provides a needed occurrence of 'a' in c2), while in Q2 the only row that can produce a join‐group for 'a' is the one coming from the row whose c2 equals 'a'. By choosing the rows so that the two queries count different numbers, we exhibit nonsemantic equivalence.

q2: SELECT ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN DATE_SUB(c2, INTERVAL 1 DAY) = PREV_DAY THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT c4), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, c2, LAG(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS PREV_DAY, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS LOG_IN_RANK FROM table1) AS T WHERE LOG_IN_RANK <= 2
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to check for a login the day after a user’s very first (MIN) login date, the two do so in different ways. Q1 first computes each user’s MIN(c2) and then (via a join) counts every row in table1 where c2 equals that minimum plus 1 day. In contrast, Q2 uses window‐functions to look only at the first two logins per user (ordered by c2) and then tests whether the second login is exactly one day later than the first. Thus if a given user has more than two logins on the qualifying day (or, more generally, if duplicate qualifying rows exist), Q1 will count all of them while Q2—because it restricts to the first two rows—will count only one. (Note that while the PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2) prevents two rows having the same date for a given user in a “real‐life” table, this counterexample is meant to illustrate the semantic difference in the logic.)
counterexample_dsp: In this test data we insert two users. For user 1 the qualifying login (MIN(c2)+1) appears twice (simulating a situation with duplicate logins on the same day), while for user 2 the qualifying login appears only once. As a result, Q1 (which sums over all rows) produces a larger numerator than Q2 (which only considers the first two logins per user), yielding a different FRACTION value.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND((SUM(c2) / COUNT(P.c1)), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P INNER JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY c4 ORDER BY c4
explanation: The two queries differ because AVG(B.c2) in Q1 ignores NULL values in column c2 when computing the average, whereas Q2 divides SUM(c2) by COUNT(P.c1) which counts all joined table2 rows regardless of whether the matching table1.c2 is NULL. In a group where one table1 row’s c2 is NULL and another is non‐NULL, Q1 computes the average over the non‐NULL values only, while Q2 divides the non‐NULL sum by a larger count, yielding a different result.
counterexample_dsp: We create two table1 rows: one with a NULL in c2 and one with a valid number (10). In table2 we join both rows into the same group (same c4 value). Q1 will compute AVG({NULL,10}) as 10 (ignoring the NULL), whereas Q2 computes SUM(c2)=10 but COUNT(P.c1)=2, resulting in 5.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
