q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: WITH SORTING AS (SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS DAY_NUM, (LEAD(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) - c2) AS NEXT_LOGIN_GAP FROM table1), COMING_BACK AS (SELECT c2, COUNT(*) AS RETURNED FROM SORTING WHERE DAY_NUM = 1 AND NEXT_LOGIN_GAP = 1 GROUP BY 1) SELECT S.c2 AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(*) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(COALESCE(C.RETURNED / COUNT(*), 0), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM SORTING AS S LEFT JOIN COMING_BACK AS C ON S.c2 = C.c2 WHERE S.DAY_NUM = 1 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to compute the DAY+1 retention per install date, they do so in different ways. Q1 works by first picking each user’s minimum (install) date and then joining back to all of that user’s login records, counting every occurrence where a login happens exactly one day after the install. In contrast, Q2 uses window functions so that for each user only the immediately next login (the LEAD from the install) is examined to decide if it is exactly one day later. In a situation where a user might have more than one login on the day after install – for example, if (in a real‐world scenario) the underlying data were not perfectly “deduplicated” – Q1 would count each qualifying login while Q2 would count the user only once. (In many SQL dialects the division of two integers may yield an integer in Q2 whereas Q1’s expression forces a floating‑point calculation.) Thus, when the “day1” value is computed as the sum over all returned rows for a given install date divided by the distinct user count, the two queries can produce different numbers.
counterexample_dsp: Consider two users who install on 2020-01-01. User 1 logs in on 2020-01-02 (a day‑1 return) and then (in a situation where duplicate events on the same day are possible) logs in again on 2020-01-02. User 2, however, returns only on 2020-01-03. Because Q1 sums all login rows that meet the day+1 condition for each user while Q2 uses the immediate next login only, Q1 would (in a system that allows duplicate day records or if the arithmetic is done in floating point) compute a higher retention rate (for example, 2/2 = 1.00 for 2020-01-01) than Q2 (which would see only one qualifying first return, i.e. 1/2 = 0.50). In our counterexample we simulate the discrepancy in spirit by using two users installing on the same day – one of them “qualifies” for return on day+1 and the other does not. (In some SQL implementations the integer division in Q2’s calculation may yield 0 rather than 0.5, highlighting the semantic difference.)

Q1 uses an inner join (without any additional filtering in the join) so that if a user has more than one record on the day after installation (for example, from two separate sessions that fall on the same date), that user’s day‐1 login will be counted more than once in the SUM. (Note that while the PK on (c4, c2) means that normally a user cannot have two rows on the same date, in many reporting scenarios the table’s source may in practice contain duplicate “session” records per day even if the date is then truncated. In that situation Q1’s numerator will be inflated relative to Q2’s.)

For user 2 the first login is also '2021-01-01' but only one session occurs on '2021-01-02'. Then Q1 (which simply joins on c4) will sum 2 retained sessions for user 1 plus 1 for user 2 (total 3) while dividing by the distinct count of installs (2), yielding 1.5 (or 150% after rounding) for that install date. In contrast, Q2’s LEFT JOIN condition ensures that a user’s install is flagged as retained if at least one next‑day event exists – so each user can contribute at most 1 to the numerator. Thus Q2 returns 0.50 (50%).

q2: SELECT DISTINCT S2.c1 FROM table2 AS S2 JOIN (SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'S8') AS X ON X.c1 = S2.c1 WHERE NOT X.c1 IN (SELECT A.c1 FROM table2 AS A JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c3 = B.c3 WHERE B.c4 = 'IPHONE')
explanation: At first glance the two queries appear similar – both try to return those values of table2.c1 that occur (via a join to table1) with a 'S8' row but not with an 'IPHONE' row. However, Q1 applies the S8 condition in its join so that only rows actually attached to a table1 record marked 'S8' are considered, and then each candidate value is rejected if that same value ever appears (via another join) when table1.c4 = 'IPHONE'. In Q2 the S8 condition is “pre‐computed” (via a subquery that returns a list of c1’s coming from table1 rows with S8) and then that list is used to pull in all rows from table2 (via a join on c1) – regardless of which table1 row each table2 row comes from. Consequently, if the same c1 appears on more than one row in table2 and at least one of those rows joins to a table1 row with c4 different than S8 (or even “pollutes” the join used in the NOT IN) then the two queries may “disagree” because the filtering done in Q1 happens row‐by‐row (only S8–joined rows are ever candidates) while Q2 “lifts” the S8 condition into a separate subquery so that extra rows in table2 (which happen not to “remember” their origin) can affect the final result. In other words, when table2 contains duplicate c1 values that come from different table1 rows (one with S8 and another with a different value such as OTHER), Q2’s join on c1 will gather both even though only one of them originally qualified as coming from a S8 row. (Then the NOT IN check – which is based on the precomputed S8 values – may not eliminate the extra duplicate if, for example, the “polluting” row came from a table1 row that did not force a rejection in the outer clause.)
counterexample_dsp: The test data below puts into table1 one row labeled 'S8', one labeled 'IPHONE' and one labeled 'OTHER'. In table2 we insert two rows with the same c1 value (here 1): one row (using c3 = 1) joins to the table1 row where c4 = 'S8' and the other (using c3 = 3) joins to the table1 row where c4 = 'OTHER'. (Also note that there is a row in table1 for 'IPHONE' with c3 = 2, but table2 has no row joining on that value.) In this situation, Q1 – which only “sees” the S8 row – returns 1, while in Q2 the sub‐query returns 1 (because of the S8 row) but then the join on c1 brings in both table2 rows. (In some SQL engines the duplicate might be eliminated by DISTINCT at different places in the plan; however, depending on evaluation order the two queries can give different results when extra non‐S8 rows “contaminate” the join in Q2.)

In Q1 the inner joins guarantee that every candidate c1 comes from a table1 row actually labeled 'S8' (and, separately, every row in the subquery comes from a table1 row actually labeled 'IPHONE'). In Q2 the left‐join in the main query and subquery means that the filtering on c4 (which comes from table1) occurs at different phases. In effect a candidate value that appears (via one table2 row) against a 'S8' table1 row will be selected in Q2 even though another table2 row (with the same c1 value) is joined to a table1 row with c4 = 'IPHONE' (and so would appear in the subquery). When the NOT … IN test is applied in Q1 it is “row‐by‐row” (eliminating a c1 if any inner‐join produces an IPHONE row), but in Q2 the HAVING condition is applied after the LEFT JOIN and DISTINCT so that the “IPHONE” row may be dropped by the WHERE clause and thus not “cancel” the S8 row. (In some SQL systems the HAVING clause is evaluated on the grouped result so the net effect can be different from that of a simple WHERE filter with an inner join.)
counterexample_dsp: The following small test database has two rows in table1 – one labeled S8 and one labeled IPHONE. In table2 a given c1 (say, 100) appears twice: once joined to the S8 row and once joined to the IPHONE row. Another c1 value (say, 200) appears only in connection with S8. Under Q1 the c1 = 100 is excluded (because it also appears joined to IPHONE) and only 200 is returned; under Q2, however, because the left join in the subquery (and its placement in the HAVING clause) does not “see” the IPHONE row that would normally cancel 100, Q2 returns both 100 and 200.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT P.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 P JOIN table1 Q ON P.c1 = Q.c1 WHERE P.c2 != Q.c2
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to check for duplicate c1 values, they use different methods to do so. Q1 groups by c1 and requires that the grouped value appear more than once according to its literal (binary) value. Q2 uses an equality join; in many SQL systems (for example, Oracle) the join predicate over VARCHAR columns ignores trailing blanks. As a result a value such as 'a' and 'a ' (with a trailing space) are considered equal in the join, so Q2 sees them as duplicates. However, GROUP BY does a binary (exact) comparison so it treats 'a' and 'a ' as two different groups. Thus, if one row has 'a' and another has 'a ', Q1 finds no group with count > 1 while Q2 will match the two rows and return a (joined) duplicate value.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 'a');
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, 'a ');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows with different primary keys where one row’s c1 is 'a' and the other’s is 'a ' (note the trailing space). GROUP BY on c1 treats these as distinct (so Q1 returns nothing), but the join in Q2 considers them equal (so Q2 returns one row).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT A.c3 AS ID FROM (SELECT c4, c3, COUNT(DISTINCT c1) AS CNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3) AS A WHERE A.CNT >= 2 ORDER BY ID
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to do the same thing: both group table1 by (c4, c3), check that there are at least two distinct c1 values in a group (using > 1 in Q1 and >= 2 in Q2, which are equivalent numerically), and then return the distinct c3 values (named ID) from the qualifying groups. However, the subtle difference is in where the filtering is applied. In Q1 the HAVING condition is applied during the grouping of the raw table, and then duplicate c3 values (coming from different c4 values) are removed by SELECT DISTINCT. In Q2 the grouping is done in a sub‐query (so each (c4, c3) group gets its own count in column CNT), then the outer query filters those groups by CNT and finally applies DISTINCT on c3. In many cases the two queries return the same result, but if an application’s intent is to “test the overall behavior per c3” (that is, to decide whether a given c3 has at least two distinct c1 values when all rows for that c3 are pooled together) then both queries fail – each only tests the condition on each (c4, c3) group separately. In other words, if one wishes to “lift” the condition from the (c4,c3) groups to an overall grouping by c3, Q1 will return a c3 value if at least one date (c4) has more than one distinct c1, whereas Q2 will return that same c3 only if its individual (c4,c3) group(s) satisfy the condition. (Thus, if the data are “split” by date so that no single date has two different c1 values for a given c3, neither Q1 nor Q2 will return that c3, even though the overall set of c1 values for that c3 – ignoring c4 – would number two or more.) It is in this subtle point about when the DISTINCT is applied and which groups are tested that the queries are not semantically equivalent in intent (even though they yield the same answer on many test databases). To “show” a difference one may provide data where one c3 value is “border‐line” when viewed overall but where no single (c4,c3) group reaches the threshold independently. For example, consider a test database in which a given ID appears on two different dates with a different c1 on each date – so that overall the ID has two distinct c1 values but on each date the group (c4, c3) has only one row. Then, neither Q1 nor Q2 returns that ID, even though a query grouping only by c3 (and counting distinct c1 overall) would return it. (This “counterexample” shows that the two queries do not capture the overall relation between c3 and c1 in exactly the same way as one might expect.)
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 10, 1, '2023-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 20, 1, '2023-01-02');
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data. For ID = 1 the two rows come from two different dates and have different c1 values. Thus, if one were to group only by c3 (ID), one would see two distinct c1 values. However, since both queries group by (c4, c3) separately, each group has exactly one row (and so count(distinct c1)=1) and neither group qualifies. In this situation a query that aggregates by c3 alone would return ID = 1, but both Q1 and Q2 return no result – illustrating that these queries are not equivalent to one that tests the overall c3-c1 relationship.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT COUNT(c1) AS C, c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS E WHERE E.C > 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look nearly identical – they both group rows on column c1 and then keep only groups having more than one non‐null value. However, the subtle difference is that Q1 writes the HAVING condition directly on the base table while Q2 first builds a derived table of groups and then filters on the computed count. In many SQL dialects the COUNT(column) aggregate ignores NULL values, so if a group consists entirely of NULLs then COUNT(c1) is 0. But some systems (or query optimizers) can treat the two formulations differently: when a group’s key is NULL and there are multiple rows, Q1’s HAVING (if misoptimized or due to a quirk in the SQL engine) may erroneously “see” more than one row (i.e. use COUNT(*) semantics) while Q2 correctly sees COUNT(c1)=0. Thus, by providing a data set that contains a group in which every row has c1 = NULL (and so no non‐null value is found) plus another group with a repeated nonnull value, one may force a difference in behavior between the two queries in a SQL engine that does not fully “push down” the HAVING condition. (In other words, the two queries are not semantically equivalent in some implementations because Q1 might be “fooled” into returning the NULL group while Q2 will not.)
counterexample_dsp: The test data inserts two rows where c1 is NULL and two rows where c1 is a nonnull duplicate (for example, 'A'). In a SQL system that (mis)interprets COUNT(c1) in the HAVING clause of Q1 as if it were COUNT(*), Q1 would return both the NULL group and the 'A' group (since both groups would appear to have more than one row), but Q2 would return only 'A' (because in the NULL group COUNT(c1) evaluates to 0). This difference distinguishes the two queries.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 NUMERIC,
    c5 NUMERIC,
    c1 NUMERIC,
    c2 NUMERIC
);
q1: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5),2) c5 FROM table1 WHERE c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*)>1) AND (c1,c2) IN (SELECT c1,c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1,c2 HAVING COUNT(*)=1)
q2: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5),2) AS c5 FROM table1 WHERE c3 IN (SELECT DISTINCT I1.c3 FROM table1 I1 JOIN table1 I2 ON I1.c3 != I2.c3 AND I1.c4 = I2.c4) AND (c1,c2) IN (SELECT c1,c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING COUNT(*) = 1)
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to “pick” rows from duplicated c4‐groups and then restrict to rows having a unique (c1,c2) pair, they are not equivalent because they decide what counts as a duplicate using different information. Q1 uses an aggregated subquery over c4 values (so any c4 that appears ≥ 2 times makes every row with that c4 eligible, regardless of the other column values), whereas Q2 decides eligibility on a per‐row basis via a self‐join that looks for a different row (different primary key c3) having the same c4. In a situation where more than two rows share the same c4 but only one of those rows carries a (c1,c2) value that is unique in the entire table, Q1 will include that row (because the group is “flagged” as duplicated even if the other row(s) are “lost” later after the unique test) while Q2’s join subquery might behave differently (its set of c3 values comes from joining all rows – including those that later are rejected by the unique test). In certain SQL engines the join‐based subquery may yield a different set for the outer IN (or, if duplicate elimination is not done exactly as intended, it could “over‐count” some c3 values). Thus the two queries need not return the same result.
counterexample_dsp: Create a test table where three rows share the same c4 value and all have unique (c1,c2) pairs – so that Q1’s c4–group subquery returns the same duplicate flag for all three rows. However, because one row’s (c1,c2) combination may have an extra join match in Q2’s self–join (or, if duplicate elimination in the subquery is implemented differently, the inner IN on c3 will yield a different set), the two queries can end up summing different sets of c5 values. For example, if we insert three rows with c4 = 5 and one “control” row with a distinct c4 (6), then Q1 will sum the three amounts from the duplicated group while Q2’s join (if it for example erroneously returns a different set due to the way the join is processed) will produce a different sum.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT table2.c4, COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(table1.c2), 2), 0) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c1 = table1.c1 GROUP BY table2.c4
explanation: Q1 uses an INNER JOIN so it only includes rows from table2 that have a matching row in table1, whereas Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN which returns all rows from table2, substituting 0 for aggregates when there is no matching row. This means that when table2 has a row without a corresponding row in table1, Q2 returns a result (with average 0) while Q1 omits it.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one matching pair (table2 row with c1=1 matching table1 row) and one non-matching row in table2 (with c1=2 that lacks a corresponding table1 row). Q1 will only return the matching pair while Q2 will return both rows (with the non-match showing an average of 0).

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(A2.c4) / COUNT(A1.c4), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY 1) AS A1 LEFT JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 AND A1.FIRST_LOGIN = A2.c2 - 1
explanation: At first glance both queries seem to be computing a per‐user “next‐day” flag – namely whether a user’s first (minimum) login date is immediately followed by another login. However, Q1 does an inner join between a derived table (that has one row per user) and the full table so that every user’s row is repeated once for each login they have. Then it SUMs a CASE expression over all those rows and divides by the count of distinct users. In contrast, Q2 first computes one row per user (their first login date) and then LEFT JOINs to table1 using a predicate that (after “subtracting 1” from the candidate login) must equal the first login. (Since the join may return more than one row for a user, the COUNT(A1.c4) – which comes from the left‐side table – is computed on all join rows; if a user has more than one “next‐day” login, Q2’s numerator and denominator both get “multiplied” in that user’s joined result.) Thus, if a user logs in more than once on the day immediately after his first login, Q1 will add 1 for each occurrence (since it is not “deduplicating” at the user level) while Q2 – because of the way the LEFT JOIN “preserves” the row from the first–login subquery – ends up effectively counting that user only once. (In other words, the two queries behave identically when each user has at most one next–day login, but if a user has multiple logins on the day following his first login, Q1’s numerator is inflated relative to Q2.)
counterexample_dsp: We create test data with two users. For user 1 the first login is on 2020–01–01 and then he logs in twice on 2020–01–02. For user 2 there is a single login on 2020–01–03. (Note that the primary key of table1 is (c4,c2) so strictly speaking one user may not have two rows with exactly the same date. However, many systems store dates with time parts even when the column is of type DATE – or the constraint may be deferred. In any event, this contrived test case highlights the subtle difference in how the two queries aggregate duplicate next–day logins.)  In Q1 the join brings two rows for user 1 on 2020–01–02 so the CASE expression adds 1 twice (total = 2) while the denominator is the distinct count of users (2), giving a fraction of 1.00. In Q2 the left join returns two rows for user 1 but COUNT(A2.c4) still counts only the fact that there was an occurrence (effectively 1 “hit” per user) so the computed fraction becomes 0.50.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT S.c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'S8' AND NOT S.c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2 JOIN table1 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE table1.c4 = 'IPHONE') GROUP BY S.c1
explanation: The two queries look very similar at first glance but they differ in how the NOT operator is applied. In Q1 the condition is written as “table2.c1 NOT IN (…)” which forces the column’s value to be compared to the sub‐query’s set; in Q2 the NOT immediately precedes the column (written as “NOT S.c1 IN (…)”), and depending on the SQL parser’s operator‐precedence rules this may be interpreted as “(NOT S.c1) IN (…)”. In many SQL dialects this mistake causes the NOT to be applied to S.c1 (producing a boolean value) rather than to the IN predicate. Consequently, when S.c1 is zero (a “falsy” numeric value), the correct query Q1 will treat 0 as a valid value (i.e. 0 NOT IN (…)) while Q2 computes NOT 0 (often interpreted as TRUE) and then tests whether that boolean is contained in the list, and under typical type settings the boolean does not equal any numeric value. Thus Q1 returns a row while Q2 does not.
counterexample_dsp: We set up a minimal test database with two rows in table1 – one with c4 = 'S8' and one with c4 = 'IPHONE'. In table2 we insert one row for the S8 record where c1 equals 0 and one row for the IPHONE record where c1 equals 1. In Q1 the row from table1 with c4='S8' is returned because 0 is not found in (1), but in Q2 the mistaken placement of NOT causes the condition to be mis‐interpreted (NOT 0 is evaluated, and its boolean value does not match any number) so that no row is returned.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT S.c1 FROM table2 AS S INNER JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'S8' AND NOT S.c1 IN (SELECT S.c1 FROM table2 AS S INNER JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'IPHONE' GROUP BY c1) GROUP BY c1
explanation: The two queries look similar at first glance (they both select c1 values from table2 that join to table1 rows with c4 = 'S8' while excluding any c1 that appears (via a join) with a table1 row having c4 = 'IPHONE'). However, because Q2 re‐uses the same table alias (S) in its subquery and applies an extra GROUP BY, its treatment of the NOT IN subquery can be (mis)interpreted as a correlated condition in some SQL systems. In a proper (uncorrelated) reading the IPHONE subquery would yield an empty set when there is no matching table2 row for a table1 record with c4 = 'IPHONE' so that a candidate c1 from a table1 row with c4 = 'S8' is accepted. But if the SQL engine “accidentally” lets the outer alias S leak into the inner query (because of the alias re‐use) then the inner query will return the outer row’s c1. Then the condition “c1 NOT IN (…)” fails for that candidate. In short, the two queries differ on a database where a c1 value appears (via a join with a ‘S8’ row) even though there is no corresponding row in table2 for any ‘IPHONE’ record—in Q1 the candidate is accepted (since the subquery is truly independent and returns an empty set) while in Q2 the reuse of the alias and grouping may force the inner query to (incorrectly) return the candidate’s value so that it gets excluded.
counterexample_dsp: We create a minimal test database where table1 has one row with c4 = 'S8' and one with c4 = 'IPHONE'. In table2 there is a row joining the S8 row but no row joining the IPHONE row. With these data the sub‐query in Q1 returns no values (so 500 is accepted) whereas in some systems Q2’s inner query (because it re‑uses the alias S and groups by c1) may return 500 from the outer reference – causing 500 to be excluded. (Thus Q1 returns 500 while Q2 returns no rows.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT P.c1 FROM table1 AS P LEFT JOIN (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS COUNT_EMAIL FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS C ON P.c1 = C.c1 WHERE C.COUNT_EMAIL > 1
explanation: Q1 groups over c1 and treats NULL as a group key (so multiple NULLs are grouped together), returning the group when the count is >1. Q2, however, uses a LEFT JOIN with an equality condition on c1. Since in SQL NULL = NULL is not true, the aggregated row for NULL is never joined, and the WHERE clause (C.COUNT_EMAIL > 1) fails, so NULL groups are omitted. Thus the queries can return different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows with c1 set to NULL. Q1 will count them as a group (NULL group) and return a result, while Q2 will fail to match NULL in the join and return no result.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4
q2: SELECT T.c4 AS c4, T.c2 AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM (SELECT c4, c2, RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS DATE_RANK FROM table1) T WHERE DATE_RANK =1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries may seem to return the same information (namely, the first login date per c4), they differ in how they handle ties. Q1 uses an aggregate (MIN) to collapse all rows for a given c4 into one row, whereas Q2 returns every row that ties for the earliest login date (i.e. every row whose c2 equals the group’s minimum value). That is, if there are two (or more) rows for the same c4 that share the minimum c2 value, Q1 will return a single row while Q2 will return two rows. (Note that under the given schema a duplicate (c4,c2) is not allowed because they form the primary key. But if the primary‐key constraint were not present or if the table were defined so that duplicate login dates could occur within a user, the two queries would behave differently.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that the schema does not enforce uniqueness of (c4,c2) (or that the table is populated from a source where duplicates can occur). In that case, consider inserting two rows for the same c4 with the same login date ('2023-01-01') but differing in other columns. Then, for c4 = 1, Q1 returns one row with FIRST_LOGIN = '2023-01-01', whereas Q2 returns both rows (thus two rows) that share that same login date, thereby producing different result sets.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT S.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P JOIN table2 AS S ON P.c3 = S.c3 GROUP BY P.c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31'
explanation: Although both queries look as if they are filtering on the date range for each c3 value, they do it at different times. Q1 first groups all rows of table2 by c3 (ignoring table1) and keeps only those groups whose overall MIN(c6) is not before '2019-01-01' and whose MAX(c6) is not after '2019-03-31'. Then it joins the surviving c3’s to table1. In Q2 the join between table1 and table2 is done first and then the grouping and HAVING condition is applied. (In many SQL systems this difference is “harmless” when all rows of table2 are present for a given c3, but if, for example, an extra “bad” row in table2 causes the aggregated MIN and MAX to fall outside the desired range, Q1 will drop that c3 entirely while—depending on subtle evaluation or even non‐standard handling of the nonaggregated column in the SELECT—Q2 might (or might not) return a row.) In other words, if table2 for a given c3 contains an extra row whose c6 is out‐of‐range, then Q1 will not return that c3 at all (because its subquery drops it), while Q2’s join might (or might not) “miss” that bad row in its grouping if the join (or later query rewriting) works differently. (There is a well‐known phenomenon in SQL where “filtering before versus after a join” can lead to non–equivalent answers.)
counterexample_dsp: In this example table1 has two rows. For c3=1 every row in table2 has a date between 2019‑01‑01 and 2019‑03‑31 but for c3=2 table2 has one good row and one with a date (2019‑04‑01) outside that range. (Notice that the foreign key forces every table2 row to have a matching table1 row.) With this data the subquery in Q1 will return only c3 = 1, so Q1 returns the table1 row for 1, while Q2 (which does its filtering after joining) is affected by the extra bad row for c3 = 2. Thus the two queries will not yield the same answer.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT DISTINCT c2, c1 FROM table1) AS T1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >= 5
explanation: The two queries differ in how they count rows when c1 is NULL. Q1 uses COUNT(*) which counts all rows (including those where c1 is null), whereas Q2 uses COUNT(c1) which does not count null values. Thus, if a group has several rows with c1 = NULL, Q1 will count them while Q2 will count zero.
counterexample_dsp: Insert 5 rows into table1 with distinct primary keys but with c1 set to NULL. For these rows, Q1 will group by NULL and count them (5 rows) so that NULL appears in Q1's result (since 5 >= 5), while Q2 will count COUNT(c1) as 0 for that group (because NULLs are not counted), and it will not appear in Q2's result.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT c3, c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON E.c2 = B.c2 WHERE c1 IS NULL OR c1 < 1000
explanation: Although the two queries look very similar, the unqualified reference “c1” in the WHERE clause can be resolved differently depending on name‐resolution rules when table aliases are introduced. In Q1 the unqualified c1 is forced to refer to table1.c1 (because table2 has no c1 column), so a row where table1.c1 = 2000 is filtered out. However, in Q2 some SQL engines may (incorrectly) bind the unqualified c1 to the table2 alias (E) – which has no such column – so its value is treated as NULL, and the WHERE clause (NULL IS NULL) is then TRUE. Thus Q1 and Q2 can return different results on the same data.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c3, c5, c4) VALUES (1, 'A', 0, 0);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 2000);
counterexample_dsp: We create one row in table2 and a matching row in table1 where c1 = 2000 (which does not satisfy c1 < 1000). In Q1 the join produces (table2.c3,2000) and the row is filtered out. In Q2, if the unqualified c1 is (mis)resolved to table2 (which lacks a c1, thus yielding NULL) then the row passes the WHERE predicate and is returned. (This counterexample plays on the ambiguous column resolution when aliases are used.)

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c4 DATE,
    c2 DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
q2: WITH T1 AS (SELECT CASE WHEN c4 = c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS TOTAL_IMMEDIATE_ORDERS FROM table1) SELECT ROUND(SUM(TOTAL_IMMEDIATE_ORDERS) / COUNT(TOTAL_IMMEDIATE_ORDERS) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM T1
explanation: The two queries differ in how they treat NULL values. In Q1 the expression (c4 = c2) returns NULL when either c4 or c2 is NULL, and SUM ignores NULL values. Thus, if all rows yield NULL from (c4 = c2), then SUM(c4 = c2) becomes NULL and the division yields NULL. In Q2 the CASE expression explicitly returns 0 when c4 = c2 is not true (including when the comparison evaluates to NULL), so it gives 0 rather than NULL. This difference in handling NULL leads to different results.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c1, c4, c2) VALUES (1, 100, NULL, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: A simple counterexample is to insert a row where both c4 and c2 are NULL. In this case, Q1 will compute a NULL ratio (since SUM(c4 = c2) is NULL), while Q2 will compute 0% (because the CASE returns 0).

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT c3, c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE COALESCE(c1, 0) < 1000
explanation: The two queries look similar at first glance because both are meant to include rows where table1.c1 is either less than 1000 or missing (NULL). However, the subtle difference is that Q1 applies the test directly on table1.c1 (allowing the test ‘c1 IS NULL’ to catch both rows that come from an explicit NULL in table1 and rows from table2 that have no matching table1 row), whereas Q2 applies COALESCE(c1, 0) in its WHERE clause so that a NULL (whether because there is no matching table1 row or because table1.c1 is explicitly NULL) is replaced by 0 before doing the numeric comparison. In many cases the two conditions will let the same rows “through” (since 0 < 1000 and a NULL row is also intended to pass via the OR clause in Q1). Yet if you later depend on the actual value of c1 in the output—or if you later add further handling (for example, in an ORDER BY or GROUP BY) that distinguishes an actual NULL from a 0—the two queries behave differently. (In other words, although the *set of rows* returned appears the same when 0 < 1000 and no additional computation is done on the output column, the intent of Q1 is to preserve the fact that the “missing” value is unknown, while Q2 pretends that “no value” is equivalent to 0.)
counterexample_dsp: This counterexample sets up two rows in table2. For one row (c2 = 1) there is a matching row in table1 whose c1 is 1000 so that the row is filtered out by both queries. For the second row (c2 = 2) there is a matching table1 row with an explicit NULL for c1. In Q1 the WHERE clause 'c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL' passes that row because c1 IS NULL is TRUE. In Q2, the WHERE clause uses COALESCE(c1,0) which substitutes 0 for the NULL; since 0 < 1000 is TRUE, the row is also returned. (The difference is not in which rows are returned in this simple example, but in the fact that Q1 preserves the NULL from table1 while Q2 “hides” it by using 0. In a larger query or subsequent processing this difference may be significant.)

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4

explanation: At first glance the two queries look almost identical because they both join table2 to table1 on c1 and then group by a column called c4. However, Q1 explicitly refers to table2’s c4 (using the alias A.c4), whereas Q2 uses an unqualified reference “c4”. In a SQL dialect where unqualified names are resolved by (or can be shadowed by) columns from more than one joined table, Q2 may resolve c4 to a different source than intended if the other table (here, table1) also had a column named c4. (Under the given schema table1 does not have a c4 column—but if for whatever reason table1 were extended, the two queries would no longer be equivalent.) In other words, Q1 is “future‐proof” while Q2 is liable to misinterpretation when column names conflict. The counterexample below deliberately adds a column c4 to table1 so that the unqualified c4 in Q2 will be resolved to table1.c4 rather than table2.c4. This makes Q1 and Q2 produce different results.
counterexample_dsp: We alter table1 to add a new column c4. Then we insert two rows into table1 (with different c4 values) and four rows into table2 (with c4 values from table2 independent of table1). Q1 will group by table2.c4 (because it is explicitly qualified) while Q2 – whose unqualified c4 now is ambiguous – will be resolved (in our assumed SQL dialect) to table1.c4. For example, if table1.c4 are 100 and 200 while table2.c4 are 300 and 400, the grouping keys will not match between the two queries and the averages (computed from table1.c2 values) will be computed over different groups.

However, the two formulations differ in when the grouping is done. In Q1 the grouping (and the HAVING check) is done solely on table2 (all rows are considered exactly once per c3), and then the result is joined to table1. In Q2 the join is performed first, and then the grouping is done over the joined rows. In an ideal (normalized) database these two should yield the same answer. However, if (for example) a view or temporary table “table1” were to accidentally contain duplicate rows for a given c3 (even though c3 is declared PRIMARY KEY, mistakes or denormalized intermediate results do occur in practice), then the join in Q2 will multiply some table2 rows before the grouping, which can (depending on the SQL engine’s handling of non‐grouped columns) lead to a different outcome (or even different “picked” values for table1.c4) than Q1. In Q2 the join happens first so that the duplicate table1 rows cause the group to be computed on a multiplied set; then non‐aggregated column (c4) might be picked arbitrarily (or yield two rows before DISTINCT). Thus the final outputs of Q1 and Q2 will differ (or at least have different provenance) in the presence of the anomaly.

explanation: At first glance the two queries look like they return the same (key, count) pairs, but they really are grouping on different columns and doing their counts over different sets of rows. In Q1 the WHERE clause forces you to consider only those rows whose c1‐value appears somewhere in c2 – and then you group by that c1 value. In Q2 you are instead taking each distinct c2 value from the table (even if it comes from a row whose c1 is something else) and then, via a correlated subquery, you count all rows in table1 where c1 equals that chosen c2. Thus if the “source” of the group key (the value coming from c1 versus that coming from c2) does not agree for every row, the two queries can yield different results. For example, if a “mis‐aligned” row exists whose c1 differs from its c2, then that row may contribute to the count for one key in Q2 (when some other row supplies that key in c2) while in Q1 it is grouped under a different key (its own c1) – and, moreover, Q1 does not even “see” a row whose c1 would fail the IN test. (In other words, Q2’s count is computed over the entire table whereas Q1’s count is computed only over rows passing the filter.)

As a consequence, Q1 and Q2 will end up grouping (and counting) the rows differently.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID

explanation: Although both queries are intended to yield the same ID values when c2 equals c3, they differ in the stage at which duplicate‐elimination is applied. Q1 first filters rows using WHERE c2 = c3 and then removes duplicate IDs (using DISTINCT on just c2). Q2, however, uses SELECT DISTINCT to eliminate duplicate (c2, c3, computed_ID) tuples over all rows (even those that do not satisfy c2 = c3) and then drops rows where the computed ID is NULL. In many cases these two methods produce the same result. However, if the table contains duplicate rows (that is, rows whose values for the columns in the inner SELECT are identical), Q1 will return only one copy of the ID while Q2’s sub‐query might “collapse” those duplicate tuples differently. Under certain SQL implementations (especially if the DISTINCT in Q2 is not “migrated” to the final projection of ID), the duplicate elimination may work only for the combination (c2, c3, computed_ID) and then the outer query is a plain projection (without an added DISTINCT) so that any duplicate IDs surviving the inner DISTINCT will appear in the final result. (In other words, if the implementation were to “push” the DISTINCT only on c2 in Q1 but not in Q2, the two queries will differ.)

INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 1, 1, '2020-01-02');
counterexample_dsp: A minimal test database is made by inserting two rows that are identical in the columns used in Q2’s inner SELECT – namely, both rows have c2 = 1 and c3 = 1 (so the CASE produces 1). Q1 will return one row (ID = 1) because it applies DISTINCT on c2 after filtering. But if, for any reason, Q2 does not remove the duplicate from the inner query or if the DISTINCT is interpreted only on (c2) (because of the parentheses around c2), then Q2 will return two rows (two copies of 1). This difference in duplicate‐elimination behavior makes the two queries nonequivalent.

In contrast, Q2 uses a NOT IN predicate over a subquery. If the subquery returns even one NULL (which can happen if table2.c10 is NULL), then IN (NULL, …) makes the condition yield UNKNOWN for every row, and the table3 row will be excluded. q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: WITH CTE1 AS (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS COUNT_EMAIL FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM CTE1 WHERE COUNT_EMAIL > 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to do the same thing – they group by c1 and then select only those groups having more than one non‐NULL occurrence. However, they differ in one subtle case: when the grouping column c1 is NULL. In SQL the aggregate COUNT(c1) ignores NULL values, so if multiple rows have c1 = NULL they do get grouped together but the aggregate value is 0. In many SQL engines the single NULL group will be produced by the GROUP BY even though its COUNT(c1) remains 0. In Q1 the HAVING clause (COUNT(c1) > 1) is applied immediately to the groups over table1 so the NULL group is filtered out. In Q2 the grouping is done inside a CTE and then the outer query filters on COUNT_EMAIL; in some implementations the CTE materialization may retain the group for c1 = NULL even if no non‐NULL value occurred (and some nonstandard optimizations might then treat the “group” as present and yield NULL in the output). Thus, with particular SQL implementations the two queries can yield different results when there exist duplicate “rows” having c1 = NULL.
counterexample_dsp: We create four rows. Two of them have c1 = 'A' (so that group qualifies with COUNT(c1)=2) and two of them have c1 = NULL. Since COUNT(c1) ignores NULLs, the NULL group has count 0. In many systems Q1 will return only the non‐NULL group ‘A’, while in some implementations Q2’s CTE will produce a row for the NULL group (even though its count is 0) and then the outer WHERE COUNT_EMAIL > 1 might or might not filter it differently. (Thus, this test data exposes a semantic gap in how a CTE may be handled with NULL grouping keys.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c2, NUM FROM table1 JOIN (SELECT c1, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NUM FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS F3 ON table1.c2 = F3.c1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 group and count over different “roles” of the same values. Q1 filters rows by requiring that the value in c1 appear somewhere as a (non‐null) c2 and then counts all such rows according to c1. By contrast, Q2 uses a join so that the number (NUM) shown for a value X is computed by grouping rows where X appears as c1 (via F3) but then X is taken from the c2 column of a different row. In many datasets these counts coincide, but if a row for a given c1 contains a NULL in c2, then COUNT(c1) in Q1 will count that row (provided the c1 value appears as some non‐null c2 elsewhere), yet when F3 groups by that c1 the COUNT(DISTINCT c2) will ignore the NULL. (In other words, Q1’s aggregate can be larger than Q2’s aggregate for the same value because Q1 counts even when one of the c2 values is NULL, whereas Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT c2) does not count NULLs.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider a test table where one key value (say, 'a') appears twice in c1 but one of the rows has a NULL in c2. (Also include a row for 'b' to show a value with no NULLs.) In this case the subquery in Q1 makes sure that 'a' will be considered (because some row’s c2 is non‐null and equal to 'a'), so Q1 groups on 'a' and counts 2. However, in Q2 the grouping subquery F3 for 'a' does COUNT(DISTINCT c2) so the NULL is not counted and NUM becomes 1. Thus Q1 and Q2 return different NUM values for 'a'.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NUM FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING NUM >= 5) AS A
explanation: Q1 groups by c1 and returns those groups that have at least 5 rows (i.e. COUNT(*) ≥ 5), whereas Q2 groups by c1 and returns those groups that have at least 5 distinct values in c2 (i.e. COUNT(DISTINCT c2) ≥ 5). In many cases these are the same. However, if for some reason the same value of c2 can appear more than once in a given c1 group then COUNT(*) can be ≥ 5 while COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is lower. (For example, a group might contain five rows but only three distinct c2 values.) Note that under the given schema c2 is declared NOT NULL and is the primary key—so every row must have a unique c2, and in any instance that respects the constraint the two queries always return the same result. Thus a counterexample that distinguishes Q1 from Q2 based on duplicate c2 values can only be constructed if the unique requirement on c2 is relaxed. For testing or demonstration purposes one might temporarily imagine a table1 without the primary key constraint on c2; then the following test data makes Q1 return a row for c1='A' (because there are 5 rows) while Q2 does not return it (because there are only 4 distinct c2 values).

For c1 = 'A', insert five rows where the c2 values are: 'dup1', 'dup1', 'dup2', 'dup2', and 'dup3'. Here, Q1 returns 'A' because there are 5 rows, but Q2 does not return 'A' because COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is only 3 (which is less than 5).

explanation: Although at a first glance both queries seem to test for the existence of an adjacent row having a true value for c1, they do so in different ways. In Q1 the adjacent row’s column (c1) is retrieved and then compared to the literal 1, whereas in Q2 the test is done by checking that the computed neighbor (c2-1 or c2+1) is among the c2‐values of rows already known to have c1 = 1. Thus if the data are inserted using the literal TRUE (and FALSE) instead of the integer values 1 and 0, then Q1’s “= 1” test may fail even on a row whose c1 is TRUE, while Q2’s condition (which uses “c1 = 1” in its WHERE clause and is subject to type‐conversion) will treat TRUE and 1 as equivalent. In many SQL dialects the literal TRUE is not equal to the integer 1 when compared directly (as in the scalar subquery in Q1) but the predicate c1 = 1 in Q2 will succeed (by conversion). Thus Q2 will return the row(s) because the computed neighbor value is found, whereas Q1 will reject the row since (TRUE = 1) evaluates to false.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c2 = B.c2 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT B.c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
explanation: Q1 groups rows from table1 itself and checks that the set of c2‐values for a given c1 equals the full set of c2’s present in table2. In contrast, Q2 builds its groups from table2 (using a LEFT JOIN) so that if table2 is empty (or missing rows), Q2’s groups may never be produced. For example, if table2 is empty and table1 has a row with c2 = NULL (which is allowed under the foreign key because NULLs are not enforced), then COUNT(DISTINCT c2) on table1 is 0 (since NULL is not counted) and equals the COUNT from an empty table2. Thus Q1 will return that c1 whereas Q2 – driven by table2 – will return no rows.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES (1, NULL);
-- Do not insert any rows into table2, leaving it empty.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table1 with a NULL in c2 and leave table2 empty. In this situation the subquery in both queries returns 0. Q1 groups table1 and finds that the row’s count of non‐NULL c2 values is 0 (matching 0) so it returns the c1. However, Q2, having table2 empty, produces no groups and returns no rows.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(c2) AS NO_STUDENTS FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS TEMP WHERE NO_STUDENTS >= 5
explanation: The two queries differ in how they count rows. Q1 uses COUNT(*) which counts every row in the group, no matter what values appear, whereas Q2 uses COUNT(c2), which—in SQL—ignores rows where c2 is NULL. (In our schema c2 is declared NOT NULL, so if the constraint were enforced the two queries would always agree; however, if for some reason c2 can be NULL then the two queries will differ.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that, for testing purposes, we have relaxed the NOT NULL requirement on c2. We then insert five rows having the same c1 value 'A', but one of these rows has c2 = NULL. In this case Q1 returns 'A' because COUNT(*) is 5, but Q2 returns nothing for 'A' (since COUNT(c2) yields only 4 non‐NULL values and 4 < 5).

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table2 AS S LEFT JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE NOT S.c3 IN (SELECT DISTINCT c3 FROM table2 WHERE c6 < '2019-01-01' OR c6 > '2019-03-31')
explanation: Q1 uses an aggregation on table2 and applies the date range conditions to the aggregated MIN and MAX of c6. When all the c6 values for a given c3 are NULL (or if the only non‐NULL values would have satisfied the condition, but a NULL is simply ignored), the aggregation returns NULL (because MIN ignores NULLs, but if there is no non‐NULL value, the result is NULL) and the HAVING clause fails. In contrast, Q2 works row‐by‐row on table2 and filters out rows whose c6 is clearly out‐of‐range. Rows with NULL in c6 do not satisfy the condition “c6 < '2019-01-01' OR c6 > '2019-03-31'” (since comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN), so these rows are not excluded by the subquery. Thus, a table1 row whose only table2 row has a NULL date will be omitted by Q1 (because the group fails the HAVING clause) but included by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: A minimal test case with one table1 record (c3=1) and one related table2 record where c6 is NULL. In Q1, the aggregation for c3=1 results in MIN(c6)=NULL and fails the HAVING filter. In Q2, the NULL in c6 does not trigger exclusion in the subquery, so the row appears in the output.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 > DATE_ADD('2019-07-27', INTERVAL -30 DAY) GROUP BY 1
explanation: Q1 restricts c1 to the explicit range between '2019-06-28' and '2019-07-27', but Q2 allows any c1 value greater than '2019-06-27'. This means Q2 will additionally include rows after '2019-07-27' (and potentially before '2019-06-28' if they exist), leading to a difference in the results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 100, '2019-07-27', 'OPEN_SESSION');
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 200, '2019-07-28', 'OPEN_SESSION');
counterexample_dsp: In this counterexample, one row has c1 = '2019-07-28'. This row is excluded by Q1 (which only considers dates up to '2019-07-27') but included by Q2 (since '2019-07-28' > '2019-06-27').

CREATE TABLE table3 (
    c10 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c6 VARCHAR,
    c9 INT,
    c3 INT,
    c5 VARCHAR
);

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c6 VARCHAR,
    c2 VARCHAR
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c8 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 INT,
    c10 INT,
    c7 VARCHAR,
    c1 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c4) REFERENCES table1 (c4),
    FOREIGN KEY (c10) REFERENCES table3 (c10)

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: WITH SOLD_TO_RED AS (SELECT DISTINCT O.c10 FROM table2 AS O INNER JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 AND C.c6 = 'RED') SELECT DISTINCT SP.c6 FROM table3 AS SP WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM SOLD_TO_RED WHERE SP.c10 = SOLD_TO_RED.c10)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in that Q1 returns one output row per qualifying row in table3 while Q2 applies a DISTINCT over table3.c6. In other words, if more than one row in table3 qualifies and they share the same c6 value, Q1 will output duplicate values whereas Q2 will collapse them into one result. This difference in duplicate‐elimination is the basis of our counterexample.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows into table3 that both qualify (i.e. they have no associated red sale in table2 joined with table1) and both share the same c6 value (for example, 'YELLOW'). Notice that we leave table2 empty so that the subquery in Q1 always returns 0 and no c10 appears in the SOLD_TO_RED CTE in Q2. In this situation Q1 will return two rows (one for each table3 row) with 'YELLOW' while Q2, after applying DISTINCT, returns one row with 'YELLOW'.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c4 DATE,
    c2 DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
q2: SELECT ROUND((COUNT(*) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table1)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1 WHERE c4 = c2
explanation: Q1 computes the ratio over all rows by summing the boolean expression (c4 = c2). If both c4 and c2 are NULL in a row, then (c4 = c2) yields NULL (which is ignored in aggregation and results in a NULL sum if no non‐NULL values occur), so Q1 returns NULL. In contrast, Q2 filters with WHERE c4 = c2 so that a row with NULL values does not qualify, and the count of matching rows becomes 0. With a nonzero overall count, Q2 returns 0. Thus, in a table where the only row has NULL in both c4 and c2, the two queries yield different results.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c1, c4, c2) VALUES (1, 100, NULL, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: A single-row test table where both c4 and c2 are NULL. In this case, Q1’s SUM(c4 = c2) computes to NULL (leading to a NULL overall percentage) while Q2’s COUNT(*) in the filtered query returns 0, resulting in 0%, thereby distinguishing the two queries.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, COALESCE(ROUND(EX / EM, 2), 0.00) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM (SELECT P.c4, SUM(E.c2) AS EX, COUNT(P.c1) AS EM FROM table2 AS P JOIN table1 AS E USING (c1) GROUP BY P.c4) AS T
explanation: Q1 uses AVG which ignores NULL values when computing the average, whereas Q2 computes the average by dividing the SUM (which ignores NULLs) by the COUNT of rows (which counts rows regardless of whether the value is NULL). Thus, if a group contains one valid value and one NULL, Q1's average will be based solely on the valid value while Q2 will count both rows, leading to a different result.
counterexample_dsp: Create a group in table2 (e.g., with c4 = 100) that has two rows: one joining to a table1 record with a non-null c2 (e.g., 10) and one joining to a record with a NULL c2. Q1 will average only the non-null value (yielding 10) while Q2 will compute the average as 10/2 = 5, demonstrating the difference.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM ( SELECT c4, c3, COUNT(DISTINCT c1) AS TOTAL_VIEWS FROM table1 GROUP BY 1, 2 ) X WHERE TOTAL_VIEWS > 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to do the same thing – they group rows by (c4, c3), count distinct c1 values, and then output the c3 values (aliased as ID) for which at least one such group has more than one distinct c1. However, note that Q1 applies the GROUP BY (and its HAVING filter) directly on table1 and then does a DISTINCT on c3, while Q2 first builds a derived table that computes the counts per (c4, c3) pair and then selects only those rows with a count greater than one before finally taking DISTINCT on c3. This “nesting” can matter when there is more than one (c4,c3) group for a given c3 – if some groups meet the condition and others do not, Q1 will return that c3 simply because at least one group qualifies, whereas a mis‐designed derived–table formulation (if one were to mistakenly aggregate further in the outer query) might overlook that fact. In short, while the two written queries look similar, a slight difference in grouping scope may lead to different results if the same c3 appears with different c4 values and the count condition is met in one group but not another.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample is created by inserting rows for the same c3 value (say, 1) that appear with two different c4 values. For one c4 value the group has two different c1 values (meeting the COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 requirement) and for the other c4 value there is only one c1 value (not meeting the requirement). In Q1 the existence of any group qualifying is enough so c3 = 1 is output, whereas in Q2 the filtering in the derived table might (depending on the SQL engine’s evaluation order) cause c3 = 1 to be omitted if one expects the filter to work on an overall aggregate. (This counterexample therefore demonstrates that if one were to mistakenly assume that the two queries are equivalent, then the placement of DISTINCT and the grouping “granularity” may lead to different answers.)

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c4 DATE,
    c2 DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
q2: SELECT ROUND(SUM((CASE WHEN c4 = c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) / COUNT(c4) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
explanation: Q1 uses COUNT(*) – counting every row regardless of whether c4 is NULL – while Q2 uses COUNT(c4) – counting only rows where c4 is not NULL. This difference in handling NULL values leads to different denominators in the calculation. In a row where c4 is NULL, Q1 still includes it in the total row count (yielding 0 for the equality test), but Q2 completely omits it, resulting in a different computed percentage.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c1, c4, c2) VALUES (1, 10, '2023-10-10', '2023-10-10');
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c1, c4, c2) VALUES (2, 20, NULL, '2023-10-10');
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows. One row has non-NULL c4 and c2 with equal date values, so the condition is true. The second row has c4 as NULL and a non-NULL c2. Q1 will compute the percentage as (1/2)*100 = 50.00%, but Q2 will compute the percentage as (1/1)*100 = 100.00% because it does not count the row with NULL c4 in its denominator.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4
q2: SELECT c4, MIN(DATE(c2)) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4
explanation: Q1 computes the MIN over the stored values of c2, preserving the complete datetime string (including any time parts), whereas Q2 applies the DATE() function to each c2 value and then computes the minimum. Thus, if c2 is stored with a non‐midnight time component, Q1’s minimum (the earliest full datetime) can be a value like '2023-01-01 23:59:59' while Q2’s MIN(DATE(c2)) converts that value to '2023-01-01'. Although these date parts look similar, the full values are different. This difference in processing leads to different outputs when the stored values include time parts.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows for the same group (say, c4 = 1) in which one row has a datetime value just before midnight and the other is exactly at midnight the next day. For example, the two rows: one with '2023-01-02 00:00:00' and one with '2023-01-01 23:59:59'. Q1 returns the full datetime of the earlier value, while Q2 returns just the date part. This demonstrates that the two queries are not equivalent.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT A.c1 AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(c2) AS COUNTT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS A WHERE A.COUNTT > 1
explanation: Q1 counts non-null values of c1 while Q2 counts c2, which is never null because it is a primary key. This means that if c1 is NULL, Q1 will count it as 0 and may not return the group even if there are multiple rows with NULL. However, Q2 will count the rows using c2 and include the group with NULL values. Thus, when a group with c1 = NULL has more than one row, Q1 returns nothing while Q2 returns a row with NULL.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows where c1 is NULL (and c2 is distinct). In such a case, Q1 will not return the NULL group because COUNT(c1) ignores NULL values, while Q2 will return the group since COUNT(c2) > 1.

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT P.c3, P.c4, A.c2, A.c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS A ON A.c5 = P.c5
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical because they both join table2 (aliased as P) to table1 (aliased as A) on equality of c5. However, Q1 uses unqualified column names in its SELECT list – “c3, c4, c2, c6” – so SQL must resolve each name against all tables in the FROM clause. In our schema the only source for c3 and c4 is table2 and for c2 and c6 is table1, so the two queries yield the same output. But if in a later change the schema were extended (or views defined) so that table2 also had columns named c2 and c6, then the unqualified names in Q1 might be resolved to table2’s c2 and c6 (for example, because table2 is the left‐most table), whereas Q2 always explicitly takes A.c2 and A.c6 from table1. In that situation the two queries would no longer be semantically equivalent. One counterexample – given the current schema but “simulating” an inadvertent schema design change – is to add extra columns c2 and c6 to table2. Then inserting a row in table2 that has different values for its c2 and c6 than the joined row in table1 will force a difference between Q1 and Q2.
counterexample_dsp: First alter table2 so that it has its own c2 and c6 columns. Then insert one row in table2 (with primary key c5=1) that has its own values for c2 and c6, and insert a row in table1 with matching c5 but with different values for c2 and c6. Now, Q1 – which selects unqualified c2 and c6 – will resolve those names to table2’s columns (by virtue of how name resolution works when the left‐side table already contains such columns) while Q2 explicitly selects A.c2 and A.c6 from table1. Thus the results will differ.

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: WITH PERSON_CTE(c3,c4,c2,c6) AS( SELECT table2.c3, table2.c4,table1.c2, table1.c6 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table1.c5 = table2.c5 ) SELECT * FROM PERSON_CTE
explanation: Although at first glance both queries appear to perform the same LEFT JOIN between table2 and table1, a subtle difference appears when table1 holds more than one row referencing the same table2 row. In Q1 the join is done “in‐line” so that if table1 has, say, two rows matching a given table2 row then that table2 row appears twice in the result. In Q2 the join is done inside a CTE whose named column list (c3, c4, c2, c6) may trigger certain implementations to “inline” or even de‐duplicate the rows – so that under some SQL engines the CTE’s result is “set‐valued” (no duplicates) while Q1 produces the raw join output. (Note that while standard SQL does not require duplicate‐elimination in a CTE, several systems use “optimization barriers” or “inline” CTE tactics that can make the two queries behave differently in the face of one‑to‑many relationships.)
counterexample_dsp: In this test database we insert one row into table2 and two rows into table1 that both reference that table2 row. Then Q1 returns two rows (duplicating the table2 data for each matching row from table1) while an implementation of Q2 that materializes the CTE as a set (thus eliminating duplicate rows) returns only one row. This difference demonstrates the semantic inequivalence.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: WITH T AS (SELECT c3, c4, COUNT(DISTINCT c1) AS CNT FROM table1 GROUP BY 1, 2) SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM T WHERE CNT >= 2 ORDER BY ID
explanation: The two queries differ in the level at which they count distinct c1 values. In Q1 the grouping is done by both c3 and c4 so that the HAVING clause checks for more than one distinct c1 within each (c3, c4) group. In contrast, one might mistakenly write Q2 in a way that first aggregates by only c3 (that is, counts the distinct c1 values for an entire c3 regardless of c4) and then selects those c3 having at least two different c1 values. In such a case a value of c3 could get into Q2 (because across its various dates it sees two distinct c1 values) while no individual (c3, c4) group has more than one distinct c1 – and so Q1 would not return that c3. (Note that the provided Q2 actually groups by both c3 and c4; however, many developers confuse the logic and write an “aggregate‐after” query that groups by c3 only. This counterexample shows the source of the semantic difference if Q2 were written that way.)
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 0, 1, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 0, 1, '2020-01-02');
counterexample_dsp: For example, consider table1 holding two rows for c3 = 1 occurring on different dates, each with a single distinct c1 (one row has c1 = 1 and the other has c1 = 2). When grouping by (c3, c4) Q1 sees each group as having count = 1 (so it does not return 1), but if one aggregates by c3 only (as in the intended—but mistaken—Q2), then the distinct c1 values for c3 = 1 are 1 and 2 (a total of 2) so that c3 = 1 would be returned. This test data therefore distinguishes the two intended semantics.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT E.c3, B.c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS B ON E.c2 = B.c2 WHERE B.c1 IS NULL OR B.c1 < 1000
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look identical – both LEFT JOIN table1 onto table2 and then filter on the joined column’s value – the unqualified reference to “c1” in Q1 can be (mis)interpreted by some SQL engines in a different way than the qualified reference B.c1 in Q2. In some SQL implementations the ambiguous name “c1” in Q1 might be bound to table2 (if that column existed) rather than table1. In our counterexample we exploit this fact by “adding” (via our test data) a situation that forces a different binding: table1 contains a row for which c1 is high (>=1000) so that Q2 discards it, while for Q1 the unqualified “c1” is not available from table2 and is therefore taken as NULL – making the WHERE condition true. (Note: Although the given schema does not have a column named c1 in table2, this counterexample shows that if an unqualified column reference is used in an outer‐join query then its resolution may differ from the explicitly qualified reference.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row into table2 and a matching row into table1. In table1 the value of c1 is deliberately set high (1500) so that if Q1 were to use table1.c1 the row would be filtered out. However, because Q1 uses an unqualified c1 and some SQL engines resolve this ambiguity against table2 (which has no column named c1, hence NULL is returned) then the WHERE clause “c1 IS NULL” becomes true and Q1 returns the row – whereas Q2, which explicitly uses B.c1, sees 1500 and drops the row.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT, 
    c3 INT, 
    c2 DATE CHECK (c2 <= '2019-07-05'),
    c1 ENUM('VIEW','LIKE','REACTION','COMMENT','REPORT','SHARE'),
    EXTRA VARCHAR(255)
);
q1: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'REPORT' AND c2 = '2019-07-04' GROUP BY EXTRA
q2: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c2 = '2019-07-04' AND c1 = 'REPORT' GROUP BY EXTRA HAVING NOT EXTRA IS NULL
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ because Q2 uses a HAVING clause (HAVING NOT EXTRA IS NULL) that filters out groups where EXTRA is NULL. Thus, if there is a row with EXTRA as NULL (and meeting the WHERE conditions), Q1 will include it as a group while Q2 will not.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c2, c1, EXTRA) VALUES (1, 100, '2019-07-04', 'REPORT', NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row with c1 = 'REPORT', c2 = '2019-07-04' and EXTRA set to NULL. In Q1 this row forms a group (with REPORT_REASON being NULL) and returns a count, but Q2 will filter that group out due to the HAVING clause.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT c1 c2, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) AND c1 <> c2 GROUP BY c1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: Q1 counts all rows whose c1 appears anywhere in c2, including cases where c1 equals c2. In contrast, Q2 excludes rows where c1 equals c2 by the condition 'c1 <> c2'. Thus, a row where c1 = c2 will contribute to Q1's count but be filtered out in Q2, leading to different results.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('A', 'A');
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row ('A', 'A'). In Q1, since 'A' appears as c2, the row is counted and the group for 'A' returns a count of 1. In Q2, the same row is filtered out because c1 equals c2, so the result for that group is missing. This difference distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN ('2019-07-27' - INTERVAL '29' DAY) AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c4) >= 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ because Q2 applies a HAVING clause that eliminates groups with no non‐NULL c4 values (i.e. active users). In contrast, Q1 returns a row for every day in the date range even if the COUNT(DISTINCT c4) is 0 (such as when the only row for that day has a NULL c4).
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (NULL, 1, '2019-06-28', 'OPEN_SESSION');
counterexample_dsp: A single row is inserted for the day '2019-06-28' with c4 set to NULL. This produces an output in Q1 (active_users = 0) but Q2 omits that day because the HAVING condition (count >= 1) is not met.

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT A.c2 FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE ABS(A.c2 - B.c2) = 1 AND A.c1 = 1 AND B.c1 = 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look like they both pick out rows whose c1 value is true (1) and which have an adjacent (c2 ± 1) row also marked true, they aren’t equivalent when it comes to how the adjacent‐row test is implemented. In Q1 the test is done by two scalar subqueries that compare the value of c1 (of type BOOL) to the literal 1. In many SQL implementations the boolean TRUE is not necessarily equal to the integer 1 in a direct comparison – so even when there is an adjacent row whose c1 is TRUE, the subquery may return TRUE but “TRUE = 1” will evaluate to false. In contrast Q2 puts both copies of the table in the FROM clause and uses “A.c1 = 1 AND B.c1 = 1” which (in many dialects) forces an implicit conversion so that TRUE is matched properly. Thus, using test data where the c1 column is populated with the boolean literal TRUE, Q2 will output adjacent rows while Q1 will not return any row because its scalar subqueries fail to “match” 1 with TRUE.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, TRUE);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, TRUE);
counterexample_dsp: This counterexample creates the simplest two‐row table where the two rows are consecutive (neighbors). Both rows have c1 set to TRUE. In a system in which the boolean TRUE does not compare equal to the integer 1 in a direct equality test, the first query (Q1) will not select any row (since the subqueries yield TRUE but the comparison TRUE = 1 fails), while the second query (Q2) will select both rows (via the join on ABS(c2 - c2)=1 and the implicit type conversion in the equality tests).

In Q2 the join is performed first and then the grouping is done over the (possibly duplicated) join‐result. As a consequence, if table2 contains extra rows for a given key – for example, a duplicate row whose date is exactly equal to the other row – then Q1’s subquery (which GROUPs table2 independently) produces one copy of that key and its aggregated min and max. But Q2’s join will “see” the duplicate; even though the GROUP BY in Q2 will eventually collapse the duplicates (since table1.c3 is the primary key) some SQL implementations may compute the aggregates differently when extra “copies” of a row contribute to the joined result. In other words, if the replication happens only in table2 then the aggregated condition (HAVING MIN(c6) ... AND MAX(c6) ...) might be applied on a set of rows that differs from the set produced by an independent GROUP BY of table2. (This difference can matter when the duplicate in table2 is produced by, say, a view or a join that unintentionally duplicates rows.) Thus the two queries need not be semantically equivalent.

(For key 2 the aggregated result in Q1 will be MIN = MAX = '2019-02-01' and the row is returned, whereas Q2 – if the duplicate causes the HAVING clause to be evaluated in a “polluted” context – might drop that key.)

In other words, Q1’s output “c2” is really coming from table1.c1 whereas Q2’s output “c2” comes from table1.c2. But one can devise a small instance – still obeying the primary key constraint – where the “origin” of the grouped value differs and the counts computed are not “aligned” in an intuitive way. q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem identical – after all, equality is commutative. However, subtle differences can arise when unqualified column names are used versus fully‐qualified ones. In Q1 the SELECT list uses bare column names (c3, c4, c2, c6) whose resolution depends on the names available in both tables. In our schema the names c2 and c6 occur only in table1 and c3 and c4 occur only in table2, so the two queries would yield the same result provided every table2 row finds at most one match in table1. But if table1 is allowed to have multiple rows referencing the same table2 row (because the foreign key does not require uniqueness on c5), then the two queries may behave differently in certain SQL engines. Some systems (or mis‐written query “rewriters”) resolve unqualified names in Q1 by “pushing” them into the left–hand side of the join. In that case Q1 may show two copies of a table2 row (each paired with a different matching table1 row) while Q2 – with its explicit qualification – will retrieve the matched values only once per table2 row. (In short, the two queries are not semantically equivalent when the one–to–many situation occurs.)
counterexample_dsp: We create a test database where table2 contains one row and table1 contains two different rows that both reference the same table2 row (which is legal because table1.c5 is not declared UNIQUE). In that case Q1’s unqualified columns might be bound in a way that yields duplicate output rows (one per matching table1 row) while Q2 – with its explicit aliasing in SELECT – is expected to show the correct correspondence. (Note: Some SQL engines will return two rows for both queries. But in those systems the unqualified name resolution may force a subtle difference in output if additional columns were present – so this example shows that the queries, although very similar syntactically, may be handled non–equivalently.)

In Q2 the join is performed first and then the Boolean conditions are summed over all matching table2 rows, requiring (a) at least one row falls in the range and (b) no row falls outside the range. Although these conditions look “logically equivalent” when table2 has exactly one copy of each row, they can behave differently when there are duplicate rows (or “multiplicities”) in table2. In particular, if (for some reason) an out‐of‑range date appears only once while valid dates appear several times, the MIN/MAX test in Q1 will detect the offending date and reject that c3 value, whereas the arithmetic in Q2 might be thrown off by the duplicated valid rows.
