explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to express “find all rows in which c1 is true and there is an adjacent row (c2 ± 1) whose c1 is true”. However, the two formulations are not equivalent in all respects. Q1 does its test by means of two scalar subqueries (one for the lower neighbor, one for the higher) whose result‐value is compared to 1. In many SQL systems a scalar subquery that finds no row returns NULL so that (NULL = 1) is not true. In contrast, Q2 uses an inner join so that a row will appear as a candidate only when a matching neighbor row actually exists (and its c1 = 1 holds). Even if on the “set result” the two queries often return the same numbers, one “semantic” difference is that Q2 guarantees an ordering (by c2) while Q1 does not. (In some cases – especially for edge rows – the different treatment of “no match” can lead to a difference in which rows are returned.)

explanation: At first glance the two queries look the same – both LEFT‐join table2 to table1 and then filter on c1 being less than 1000 (or NULL). However, because Q2 uses a common‐table expression that does a SELECT A.*, B.c1, the resulting derived table (table3) may contain two columns named “c1” if table2 already had one. In our schema table2 does not have a column c1, so both queries would normally return the same rows. However, it is easy to imagine a (small) change to the schema – one that still obeys all constraints – by adding a column named c1 to table2. In that case the unqualified “c1” in the outer WHERE clause of Q2 will bind to the first occurrence (coming from A.*, that is, table2.c1) whereas in Q1 the “c1” (written as table1.c1 in the SELECT list but unqualified in the WHERE clause) refers to table1.c1. (Notice that many SQL dialects use left‐to‐right resolution for duplicate column names in a SELECT * list in a CTE.) As a consequence the two queries can return different sets of rows. (In Q1 the filter is applied to table1.c1, but in Q2 the filter is applied to table2.c1.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume we add a new column c1 to table2 (allowed because it doesn’t violate the primary key or foreign key constraints) and then insert data so that for one row the value of table2.c1 differs from table1.c1. For example, let table2.c1 be 2000 (so it fails the filter) while table1.c1 is 500 (which satisfies the filter). Then Q1 will return that row (because it uses the value 500 from table1) while Q2 will filter it out (because it erroneously uses table2’s c1 value of 2000).

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1

In Q1 the HAVING clause is correctly applied to each group (filtering out groups whose count is not greater than 1), while in Q2 the parenthesized expression may be treated as a scalar sub‐expression that returns a constant true/false value for every group. For example, if the table has two rows with different c1 values then COUNT(c1) in Q2 (if misinterpreted) evaluates to 2 irrespective of the group; thus (2 > 1) is true for every group so Q2 returns both groups, whereas Q1 returns none since no group has more than one occurrence.

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, 'b');

In Q2 (when misinterpreted) the HAVING clause ends up checking a total count of 2 (which is > 1) and so both groups are returned, causing a difference in the results.

In Q2 the GROUP BY clause is written as GROUP BY 1, which some SQL engines interpret as grouping by the literal constant 1 instead of referencing the first select item (P.c4). In those systems Q2 aggregates all rows into a single group, whereas Q1 produces one row per distinct c4. Thus, if table2 contains more than one distinct value for c4, the two queries yield different results.

Q1 will return two groups (one for each c4) with their respective averages, but if the SQL dialect interprets GROUP BY 1 in Q2 as grouping by the constant 1 then Q2 will return a single row with the overall average.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1

explanation: At first glance one may think that computing the minimum absolute difference between two numbers can be done by just comparing adjacent values – and indeed, for any nonempty set of distinct numbers the closest two values (in the 1‐dimensional sense) are always consecutive when sorted. However, the two queries do not behave the same for all inputs. In particular, Q1 uses a self‐join with the condition A.c1 <> B.c1 so that if table1 has fewer than two rows no pair exists (and many SQL engines will then return no result row for the aggregate over an empty input), whereas Q2 uses a window function (LEAD) that always produces one row per row in table1 – even if the computed difference is NULL (as happens for the “last” row). Thus, when table1 contains only one row Q2 returns one row (with a NULL value for SHORTEST) while Q1 returns no “joined” row and so its aggregate returns no row (or, in some SQL dialects, a row with NULL). This difference in the number of output rows (or the “presence” of a result row) shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1(c1) VALUES (100);
counterexample_dsp: A minimal test case is to insert a single row into table1. In this case the self‐join in Q1 produces no pairs (because there is no distinct partner for the lone row) and so its aggregated MIN is computed over an empty set. In contrast, Q2’s window function produces one row (with LEAD returning NULL) and then MIN ignores NULL but still produces a result row. Thus, the two queries yield different outcomes with respect to the returned rowset.

    EXTRA VARCHAR(255)
);
q1: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'REPORT' AND c2 = '2019-07-04' GROUP BY EXTRA
q2: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'REPORT' AND c2 = '2019-07-04' GROUP BY 1
explanation: Although the two queries look similar, Q1 groups by the column EXTRA while Q2 uses 'GROUP BY 1'. In many SQL dialects an unparenthesized numeric literal (like 1) is interpreted as the literal constant 1 rather than as a shorthand for 'the first select item'. Thus Q1 produces one result row per distinct EXTRA value, whereas Q2 aggregates all qualifying rows into one group. This difference is exposed when there exist at least two REPORT rows with different EXTRA values.

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c2, c1, EXTRA) VALUES (1, 101, '2019-07-04', 'REPORT', 'foo');
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c2, c1, EXTRA) VALUES (2, 202, '2019-07-04', 'REPORT', 'bar');
counterexample_dsp: In our test data we insert two rows that satisfy the WHERE condition (c1 = 'REPORT' and c2 = '2019-07-04') but have different EXTRA values (for example, 'foo' and 'bar'). Query Q1 groups by EXTRA and outputs two rows (one for 'foo' and one for 'bar'), while if Q2 interprets GROUP BY 1 as a literal constant it aggregates both rows into one result. This shows that Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent.

q1: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5),2) c5 FROM table1 WHERE c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*)>1) AND (c1,c2) IN (SELECT c1,c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1,c2 HAVING COUNT(*)=1)

explanation: The two queries differ in how they test for uniqueness on the (c1, c2) columns. Q1 uses a tuple‐comparison grouping by (c1, c2), which distinguishes rows where one column is NULL while the other is not, so (1, NULL) and (NULL, 1) count as different unique pairs. In contrast, Q2 groups by CONCAT_WS(',', c1, c2), and because CONCAT_WS ignores NULL values, both (1, NULL) and (NULL, 1) produce the same string ('1'). Consequently, although each of the two rows is unique when considered as a tuple, they collapse into one group in Q2—and because that group then contains two rows it fails the HAVING COUNT(c3)=1 condition. Thus Q1 ends up summing the values from both rows while Q2 omits them.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c5, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 100, 10, 1, NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c5, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 100, 20, NULL, 1);
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows that share the same c4 value (so that the c4 condition is met) and that have distinct (c1, c2) pairs (each appearing only once) but whose CONCAT_WS result is the same because one of the values is NULL in one row and vice‐versa in the other. In Q1 these rows pass the unique composite check but in Q2 they are grouped together (count = 2) and hence dropped.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT (c3) AS ID FROM (SELECT c3, c4, c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c4, c1) AS A GROUP BY c3, c4 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY c3
explanation: Q1 uses COUNT(DISTINCT c1), which does not count NULL values, so even if there are two rows in a (c3, c4) group (one with a NULL and one with a non‐NULL value), the DISTINCT aggregation sees only one non‐NULL value. By contrast, Q2’s inner query groups rows to remove duplicates but does not ignore NULLs when counting rows in the outer query. Thus, in a group with one NULL and one non‐NULL c1, Q1’s HAVING (COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1) fails while Q2’s outer HAVING (COUNT(*) > 1) succeeds.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (NULL, 10, 1, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 20, 1, '2020-01-01');
counterexample_dsp: Create two rows with the same c3 and c4 values where one row’s c1 is NULL and the other’s is a non‐NULL value (e.g. 2). In Q1 the group for that (c3, c4) has COUNT(DISTINCT c1)=1 (since NULL is not counted), so it is filtered out, whereas in Q2 the inner query returns two distinct rows (one with NULL and one with 2) so the count becomes 2 and the row qualifies. Q2 returns c3 while Q1 does not.

q1: SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c3 <> 2 OR c3 IS NULL
q2: SELECT C.c2 FROM table1 AS C WHERE c3 IS NULL OR c3 <> 2
explanation: At first glance the two queries look the same because they both list the condition “c3 <> 2 OR c3 IS NULL”. However, when a table alias is introduced (as in Q2) the unqualified reference to c3 is subject to name‐resolution rules that (in some SQL systems or under certain query–rewriting optimizations) may not bind to the same table object as the unqualified reference in Q1. In our counterexample the row whose c3 is 2 (which, by the foreign‐key constraint, must have a matching row with c1 = 2) will be eliminated in Q1 (since 2 <> 2 is false and 2 is not null) but in some systems Q2 will (erroneously) retrieve a value from the joined “table1” (or outer scope) rather than from the alias. (In other words, if the unqualified name “c3” in Q2 is resolved not to C.c3 but instead to the outer table1.c3, then the two queries behave differently.)
counterexample_dsp: Test data with two rows is inserted. One row has a NULL in c3 and the other row has the value 2 in c3. Because of the foreign‐key the row with c3 = 2 requires a corresponding row (here the row itself can be its own referent) so that the constraint is not violated. Under the (mis)interpretation of Q2 the row with c3 = 2 will pass the WHERE clause (by mis-resolving c3), whereas Q1 correctly omits it.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS 'DISTINCT PRODUCTS' FROM table2)
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem identical because they both compare COUNT(DISTINCT c2) from table1 with the COUNT(DISTINCT c2) from table2, adding an alias in the sub‐query (as in Q2) can actually change how some SQL engines parse or optimize the query. In certain SQL implementations the alias causes the sub‐query’s single computed value to be ‘labeled’ in a way that prevents it from being recognized as a simple scalar value. As a result the comparison in Q2 may be done against a non‐numeric value (or simply be handled differently) so that when the tables contain “minimal” data the two queries yield different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table2 (c2) VALUES (1);

INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES (1, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Create test data where table2 has exactly one row (so that COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is 1) and table1 has one row with a non‐NULL c2. In many SQL engines Q1 will compare 1 = 1 and return that row, but Q2 – because its subquery labels the result as 'DISTINCT PRODUCTS' – may have its scalar sub‐query misinterpreted (for example, as a record or even as the literal alias text) and the comparison fails. Thus Q1 returns a result row while Q2 returns no rows.

q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
q2: SELECT 100 * ROUND(SUM(c2 = c4) / COUNT(*), 4) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
explanation: The two queries apply rounding at different stages. Q1 multiplies the (true/total) ratio by 100 and then rounds to 2 decimals, whereas Q2 first rounds the unscaled ratio to 4 decimals and then multiplies by 100. For numbers with non‐terminating decimals (for example 2/3 = 0.6666…), the two orderings may produce a result that differs by a cent. In some SQL systems, 100*ROUND(0.666666…,4) can yield 66.66 while ROUND(0.666666…*100,2) yields 66.67.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)

q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: WITH MIN_DATE AS (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) SELECT ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT (CASE WHEN NOT B.c2 IS NULL THEN A.c4 ELSE NULL END)) / COUNT(DISTINCT A.c4), 2) AS FRACTION FROM MIN_DATE AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c4 = B.c4 AND DATEDIFF(B.c2, A.FIRST_DATE) = 1
explanation: Although at first glance both queries look like they are computing the fraction of groups that have a row dated exactly one day after the minimum date in that group, they differ in how they aggregate the results. Q1 works by joining each group’s MIN_DATE back to table1 and then summing a CASE expression over every joined row; if (for whatever business‐logic reason) a group happens to have more than one row dated the next day, Q1 will add 1 for each such row. By contrast, Q2 does a LEFT JOIN and then counts distinct groups that have at least one qualifying row. (In other words, Q1 “double‐counts” a group when there are multiple next–day rows while Q2 counts each group only once.) Under a relaxed situation (or in databases where duplicates may occur even if a candidate key is suggested) one can have duplicate next–day rows for a given group. This is the essential difference that makes the two queries not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: We create test data with two groups (different c4 values). For group 1 we deliberately insert two rows with the same c2 value that equals the minimum date plus one and for group 2 we insert only one row. (Normally the PRIMARY KEY prevents duplicate (c4, c2) values, but assume that in our test environment either the constraint is not enforced or the data come from a source with possible duplicates.) In this case, Q1’s join over group 1 returns two rows satisfying the condition (thus contributing 2 toward the numerator) whereas Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT) so that group 1 is counted just once. Therefore the overall fraction computed by Q1 (which becomes (2 + 0)/2 = 1.0) differs from that of Q2 (which is (1 + 0)/2 = 0.5).

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT (c4)) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN (DATE_ADD('2019-07-27', INTERVAL -29 DAY)) AND DATE('2019-07-27') GROUP BY DAY
explanation: The two queries differ in the grouping method. Q1 explicitly groups by the column c1 (the date), so each date in the range gets its own group. In Q2 the GROUP BY clause uses the alias DAY. In many SQL dialects the alias defined in the SELECT clause is not allowed (or not correctly substituted) in the GROUP BY clause – so DAY is instead interpreted as a column reference (and since there is no column named DAY in table1) or even as a constant. In effect, Q2 may end up grouping all rows into one group, whereas Q1 produces one group per distinct date. Thus, if the table contains rows on different dates within the allowed interval, the two queries can return different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 101, '2019-07-27', 'OPEN_SESSION');
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 102, '2019-06-28', 'OPEN_SESSION');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows from two different dates within the interval (e.g. one on '2019-06-28' and one on '2019-07-27') with different c4 values. Q1 will return two rows (one per date) while Q2, if it misinterprets GROUP BY DAY, will aggregate both rows together into one row (with the distinct count of c4 being 2).

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING DATEDIFF('2019-07-27', c1) BETWEEN 0 AND 29
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look as if they filter for the same date‐range, they differ in when the date filter is applied. In Q1 the WHERE clause drops all rows whose c1 is not between '2019-06-28' and '2019-07-27'. In Q2 every row is grouped by c1 and only then is the group kept if DATEDIFF('2019-07-27', c1) is between 0 and 29. In many SQL dialects the DATEDIFF function subtracts its first argument from its second (that is, DATEDIFF(a, b) yields b−a), so a date that actually falls inside the intended calendar window (say, '2019-07-01') will produce a negative number (because '2019-07-01' − '2019-07-27' = –26) and be dropped by Q2’s HAVING clause even though it is between the two dates. Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 100, '2019-07-01', 'OPEN_SESSION');
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row dated '2019-07-01'. This date is between '2019-06-28' and '2019-07-27', so Q1 returns it. However, if DATEDIFF is defined as (c1 - '2019-07-27') then DATEDIFF('2019-07-27','2019-07-01') returns –26, which does not lie between 0 and 29, so Q2 will not return a row for that date.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: WITH TEMP AS (SELECT * FROM table1 AS P JOIN table2 AS S USING (c3)) SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table2 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM TEMP WHERE c4 = 'S8') AND NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM TEMP WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar, but the subtle difference is that Q1 applies the S8 filter directly in its join so that only table2 rows whose matching table1 row has c4 = 'S8' are examined – and then it discards any candidate whose c1 appears in any join where table1.c4 = 'IPHONE'. By contrast, Q2 starts from all rows of table2 and then uses a common‐table expression (TEMP) that collects all valid table1–table2 pairs. In Q2 the test for a value c1 is done using two independent IN conditions on TEMP: one requiring that some join has c4 = 'S8' and one requiring that no join has c4 = 'IPHONE'. Consequently, if the same c1 appears in table2 via two different foreign keys – one whose matching table1 row has c4 = 'S8' and another with c4 = 'IPHONE' – then Q1 will filter out that value (because its candidate row comes from the S8–side but the existence of any IPHONE join causes the NOT IN clause to fail) while Q2 may return that c1 if the row coming from table2 (used in the outer FROM) does not “remember” its join context. In other words, Q2’s selection is based solely on the existence of at least one S8 join and the overall absence of an IPHONE join for the given c1 (as computed in TEMP), regardless which table2 row provided that c1 in the outer query. (When a given c1 is “mixed” – seen in TEMP with both S8 and IPHONE – both queries reject it.) Therefore, if one “mix‐matched” c1 value occurs only once in table1 (in the S8 join) but appears extra in table2 from a different (IPHONE) join, the two queries behave differently. This subtle difference can be demonstrated by the counterexample below.
counterexample_dsp: Consider a case where table1 contains one row with c4='S8' and another with c4='IPHONE'. In table2 the same c1 value (say 100) is inserted twice – once referencing the S8 row and once referencing the IPHONE row – and another c1 (say 200) is inserted only referencing the S8 row. In Q1 the only candidate for 100 comes from the join on the S8 row, but 100 is rejected because it also appears in the sub‐query (via the IPHONE join). In Q2, however, the entire table2 is scanned; the value 100 appears (via one row) as having a valid S8 join and so 100 gets past the “in” test (since that row’s c1 is 100) even though 100 appears in TEMP with c4 = 'IPHONE'. (Because of differences in how the join is “embedded” into the outer FROM versus into an independent CTE, the two queries produce different outcomes on mixed data.)

q1: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5),2) c5 FROM table1 WHERE c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*)>1) AND (c1,c2) IN (SELECT c1,c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1,c2 HAVING COUNT(*)=1)
q2: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5),2) AS c5 FROM (SELECT *, COUNT(c3) OVER (PARTITION BY c4) AS IV_OCCURENCE, COUNT(c3) OVER (PARTITION BY c1,c2) AS LOCATION_OCCURENCE FROM table1) AS T WHERE IV_OCCURENCE > 1 AND LOCATION_OCCURENCE = 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in the way they handle NULLs in the (c1, c2) comparisons. In Q1 the condition “(c1,c2) IN (… )” is evaluated by comparing row‐value constructors. If any component is NULL, the equality comparison returns UNKNOWN and the row is rejected even if, in the GROUP BY the (c1, c2) tuple appears exactly once. By contrast, Q2’s window‐function PARTITION BY treats NULL as a grouping value so that a row with, say, c1 = NULL and c2 = 1 will be counted as occurring once. Thus a row with a NULL in c1 (or c2) may be filtered out in Q1 but included in Q2.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c5, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 10, 100, NULL, 1);
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c5, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 10, 200, 2, 2);
counterexample_dsp: We create two rows with the same c4 value so that the IV (c4) condition is met. One row has a unique (c1, c2) pair using non‐NULL values, and the other row has a (c1, c2) pair where c1 is NULL (which is unique in the GROUP BY but will not match in an IN predicate because NULL comparisons yield UNKNOWN). As a result, Q1 will only sum the non‐NULL row’s c5 value while Q2 will sum both rows’ c5 values.

In contrast, Q2 uses a NOT IN over a subquery with a LEFT JOIN. When the subquery produces a NULL (for example, because a table2 row has a NULL in c10), then the NOT IN comparison will evaluate to UNKNOWN and exclude the row—even though Q1’s inner join (with condition O.c10 = S.c10) would not count the row with a NULL c10. q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: SELECT INSTALL_DT, COUNT(c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(COUNT(c2) / COUNT(c4), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT A.*, B.c2 FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS INSTALL_DT FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c4 = B.c4 AND DATEDIFF(B.c2, A.INSTALL_DT) = 1) AS C GROUP BY INSTALL_DT

Q1 joins each user’s full history back to the aggregated install date and then, for each install date, it sums up all rows whose date equals the install date plus one. (It then divides by the distinct user count for that install day.) In contrast, Q2 first picks each user’s install (using MIN(c2)) and then left‐joins only to records exactly one day later. Thus, if a user logs in twice on the day after installation, Q1 will add 2 to its numerator (while still counting that user only once in the denominator) but Q2 will return two joined rows that “inflate” the install count as well as the retention count so that the ratio is lower. In other words, when a user has multiple logins on day 1 the two queries produce different DAY1_RETENTION values.
counterexample_dsp: Assume user 1 installs on 2022-01-01 and then logs in twice on 2022-01-02 (for example, from two different sessions). User 2 installs on 2022-01-01 and logs in once on 2022-01-02. Under these conditions, Q1 will compute the retention for 2022-01-01 as (2 + 1) / 2 = 1.5 while Q2 will, due to its left join filtering, yield a retention of (1 + 1) / (1 + 1) = 1.00. (The discrepancy comes from Q1 counting user 1’s two day-1 events in the numerator while still counting that user only once in the denominator, whereas Q2 “duplicates” both the numerator and denominator for user 1, leaving its day-1 retention as 1.) Note that to simulate multiple day‐1 login sessions for the same user without violating the table’s primary‐key constraint, one may imagine that the table stores each session as a separate row by additionally distinguishing sessions (for example, by a session ID) even though the date (c2) is the same.

explanation: At first glance both queries try to “anti‐join” table3 against the red orders coming from table2 joined to table1. However, Q1 does this with a correlated subquery that returns at most one output row per table3 row (testing that the count is 0), whereas Q2 uses a RIGHT JOIN. Under bag (multiset) semantics the outer‐join version may return table3 rows multiple times if there happen to be several candidate rows in table2 that (after joining with table1 using the RED condition) are “lost” (that is, when none of them satisfy C.c6 = 'RED' the outer join emits exactly one row, but if there are duplicate “failed” candidate rows the optimizer may fail to eliminate duplicates). In other words, if for a given table3 row there are multiple rows in table2 that do not yield a join (because their corresponding table1 row is not RED), then the subquery in Q1 still yields 0 and the table3 row appears exactly once, while Q2 – which is written without DISTINCT – will return one copy for each “failed–join” candidate. (In many systems the duplicate elimination is done later, but if one is relying on the raw multiset result the two queries differ.)
counterexample_dsp: We create one row in table3 and one non‐RED row in table1. Then we insert two rows in table2 that refer to the same table3 row and the same non–RED table1 row. For Q1 the subquery (which only counts rows for which table1.c6 = 'RED') returns 0 so the table3 row is returned exactly once. In contrast, Q2’s RIGHT JOIN finds no matching row from the inner join (because the join condition requires RED) so it “backs out” to table3; however, because there were two candidates in table2 (even though neither joins) the outer join produces two copies of the table3 row.

In Q1 the FROM/JOIN (and its WHERE clause) restricts rows to those coming from table1 with a specific c4 value before the NOT IN subquery is even run. In Q1 the S8 row is selected but the sub‐query finds the IPHONE row so 100 is rejected, while in Q2 the CTE brings both rows together so the filtering (using IN and NOT IN on the whole CTE) behaves differently – yielding a different final result.

Q1 uses NOT IN and if the subquery returns any NULL (even if other non-null values exist), the predicate yields UNKNOWN, and no row is returned. Q2, however, uses NOT EXISTS and performs an equality check row‐by‐row, so it is not affected by a NULL in the subquery. Thus, when table2 has a row with c1 = NULL, Q1 returns no rows while Q2 can return some rows.

In this scenario, Q1 will filter out all rows because 'NOT IN (NULL)' results in UNKNOWN for any candidate, whereas Q2 will return both rows from table1, as the equality check against NULL fails and NOT EXISTS is true.

Q1 joins every user’s install record (from the subquery) with all of that user’s login records and then sums a CASE that gives 1 for every record exactly one day after installation. In contrast, Q2 “attaches” at most one day‐1 record to each install using a LEFT JOIN (the ON clause requires that the login date, when shifted back one day, exactly equals the install date) and then counts distinct users who had a matching login. Thus if a user somehow registers two distinct day‐1 logins (for example, if duplicate day–1 records appear due to extra events even though the logical install remains unique), Q1 will count that user twice in the numerator while Q2 will count the user only once. (Note that the schema declares a primary key on (c4, c2) so normally a given user cannot have two rows on the same day. In many SQL dialects following the SQL standard, NULL = NULL yields UNKNOWN and the row would be filtered out by the WHERE clause. However, in some environments (for example, when ANSI_NULLS is turned OFF in SQL Server) the comparison NULL = NULL can evaluate to TRUE. In that situation Q1 – which uses a WHERE filter – will include the row with NULL values, so NULL appears as one of the IDs. On the other hand, Q2’s sub‐query groups by c2 and—because aggregate functions like COUNT ignore NULL values—the group for NULL is never formed (since COUNT(c2) for that row is 0 and fails the HAVING COUNT(c2) >= 1 test). Thus under those conditions the two queries return different results.

In Q1 the aggregated (group‐by) subquery (TEMP) produces exactly one row per c4, so when that is joined back with table1 the denominator (COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)) is guaranteed to be one per group even if the join returns several rows for some groups. Although every row does have an adjacent row with c1 = TRUE (and so Q1 returns all three rows in the unsorted order of scanning), Q2 applies DISTINCT and an ORDER BY so that its output is sorted. explanation: The subtle difference is that Q1’s filtering is applied to all rows for a given key in table2 (by grouping and then insisting that the overall MIN and MAX both lie in the wanted range), whereas Q2 first picks out only those table2 rows that meet the date predicate and then (via a LEFT JOIN) checks that no date‐violating row exists. In many cases the two formulations will produce the same results; however, if a key (c3) has a mix of dates – that is, it has at least one row with a date in the allowed interval and at least one row with a date outside that interval – then the aggregation in Q1 will reject it (because the MIN/MAX over all rows fails the test), whereas Q2 will first “see” the in–range row and include the key in its CTE and later eliminate it only if the “bad” row is found in the separate subquery. (Depending on subtle issues like whether duplicate “bad” rows exist or if the joined‐in rows come from a different source than the aggregated ones, the two queries can return different answers.)
counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose table1 has one row (with c3 = 1) and table2 has two rows for c3 = 1 – one with a date inside the interval ('2019-02-01') and one with a date outside it ('2019-04-01'). Then the subquery in Q1 (which groups over all table2 rows for c3 = 1) will compute MIN = '2019-02-01' and MAX = '2019-04-01' and reject c3 = 1 (because MAX > '2019-03-31'). In contrast, Q2’s CTE finds the in–range row and thus cites c3 = 1; then the LEFT JOIN finds the out–of–range row and (depending on the precise implementation and data–multiplicity) may leave a “trace” of c3 = 1 in the final output. (In some SQL engines the filtering after the LEFT JOIN might eliminate the key while in others the join multiplicity causes a duplicate to survive.) This test data therefore distinguishes the two formulations.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE (c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2))
explanation: The subtle difference comes from how some SQL systems (or query optimizers) treat a NOT IN subquery that returns one or more NULL values. In standard SQL a predicate like x NOT IN (subquery) will yield UNKNOWN (and thus filter out the row) if the subquery ever returns a NULL. However, in practice some SQL engines may “optimize” the unparenthesized form differently from the parenthesized one so that they behave differently in the presence of NULLs. In our counterexample the subquery (SELECT c1 FROM table2) returns one non‐NULL value and one NULL. In that situation one query might rule out all rows while the other “sees” the non‐NULL value and returns the candidate row.
counterexample_dsp: We create two rows in table1 (with c2 values 1 and 2) and two rows in table2 – one whose c1 matches table1 (value 1) and one where c1 is NULL. In many SQL engines the NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2) predicate will evaluate to UNKNOWN for a candidate value if any row of the subquery is NULL. Some engines (and/or optimizers) mistakenly evaluate the extra‐parenthesized version differently. For instance, Q1 (without redundant parentheses) may return no rows since the presence of NULL in the subquery makes every comparison UNKNOWN, while Q2 returns the row with c2 = 2 because the extra parentheses force the system to evaluate the predicate “piece‐wise”.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: WITH T1 AS (SELECT COUNT(c2) AS _TOTAL FROM table2) SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS C, T1 GROUP BY 1, T1._TOTAL HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = T1._TOTAL
explanation: The two queries differ in how they count the rows from table2. Q1’s sub‐query uses COUNT(DISTINCT c2) so that duplicate values in table2 (if any) are collapsed, while Q2’s CTE uses COUNT(c2) which counts every row. Thus if table2 contained duplicate c2 values then the two counts would differ. In a scenario where table2 has two rows holding the same value – so that COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=1 but COUNT(c2)=2 – a row in table1 whose (distinct) c2 value is 1 will satisfy Q1’s HAVING clause (1 = 1) but fail Q2’s (1 ≠ 2).
counterexample_dsp: Assuming we can populate table2 with duplicate rows (or disable the uniqueness check for test purposes), we insert two rows into table2 with the same value (say 1) and a single row into table1 with c2 = 1. Then Q1 returns the row because it compares 1 = COUNT(DISTINCT table2.c2) = 1, but Q2 returns nothing because it compares 1 (from COUNT(DISTINCT table1.c2)) with T1._TOTAL = COUNT(table2.c2) = 2.

In Q1 the order of the returned rows is not defined and may differ from that of Q2, so when the results’ order matters the two queries are not equivalent.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT B.c1 AS c2, B.c2 AS NUM FROM (SELECT c2, COUNT(c1) AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c2) AS A INNER JOIN (SELECT c1, COUNT(c2) AS c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS B ON A.c2 = B.c1 ORDER BY c2 ASC
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to return, for each value v that occurs in the first column, the number of rows in which v appears as c1 (provided v also appears somewhere as c2), the two queries are not equivalent when nulls can occur. In Q1 the WHERE clause (c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1)) is applied row‐by‐row before grouping and COUNT(c1) counts every non‐null c1. In Q2 the aggregation over all rows is done without filtering, and then the join combines the group (from table1 grouped on c1) that uses COUNT(c2) – which ignores null values in c2 – with the groups from table1 grouped on c2. Thus if a given value v appears in c1 some times with a corresponding row in which the second column is null, Q1 will include that row in COUNT(c1) (because c1 is not null) while Q2’s COUNT(c2) will not count the null. This discrepancy makes the two queries semantically different.
counterexample_dsp: The test data below inserts three rows. Two rows have c1 = 'a'. One row is ('a','a') and the other is ('a', NULL). A third row (“('b','a')”) makes sure that the value 'a' does appear in column c2 so that the IN (or join) condition is met. In Q1 the COUNT(c1) for 'a' will be 2 (both rows count) while in Q2 the COUNT(c2) for 'a' (grouped by c1) will be 1 because the row with a null c2 is not counted.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(AVG(E.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY P.c4
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical – they both join table2 with table1 on c1 and group by the c4 column from table2. However, notice that Q1 writes the grouping and select reference explicitly as A.c4 (i.e. table2.c4) while Q2 simply writes “c4” in its SELECT clause even though it groups by P.c4. In many SQL dialects the unqualified column name in Q2 is resolved using the names available in the FROM clause. Now assume that (for example, due to an accidental schema change or a view‐definition) table1 also were to contain a column named c4. In that case the two queries would “pick up” different values for the reported c4: Q1 would always use table2.c4 (because it is explicitly qualified) while Q2’s unqualified c4 might resolve to table1.c4 (or be ambiguous in some engines). In other words, although under the present schema the two queries return the same results, they are not semantically equivalent because Q2 relies on an unqualified column name that might later be “captured” by a same‐named column from table1. We can therefore build a counterexample test database that does not violate the given constraints but simulates the eventuality (using a temporary table that “mimics” table1 with an extra column) in order to show that Q1 and Q2 can return different results.

-- The following SQL statements assume that the accidental schema change has added a column 'c4' to table1. This does not violate the original PK and FK constraints because c4 in table1 is just an extra column.

-- (1) Alter table1 to add a column named c4. In many real environments this might happen by mistake.
ALTER TABLE table1 ADD COLUMN c4 INT;

-- (2) Insert rows into table1. Notice that we provide a value for the extra c4 column that is different from what will be stored in table2.
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c3, c2, c4) VALUES
  (1, 'Alice', 30, 100),
  (2, 'Bob', 40, 200);

-- (3) Insert rows into table2. (table2 still has only columns c4 and c1.)
INSERT INTO table2 (c4, c1) VALUES

Q1 first computes, for each group (c4), the minimum date and then joins back to table1 – it then sums over every row that exactly equals (MIN_DATE+1) (without “peeking” at the ordering in the group) and finally divides by the number of groups. In contrast, Q2 uses a window function to look only at the very next date (the row with ROW_NUMBER = 1’s LEAD value) within each group and then counts a group only if that immediately‐following date is exactly 1 day after the minimum. Thus, if a group contains extra rows such that a row with a date equal to MIN_DATE+1 exists but is not the immediate successor when ordering by c2 (for example, because another row with a “wrong” date “intrudes” so that the qualifying row appears later in the ordering), Q1 will still “find” the qualifying row by a simple existence check, whereas Q2 will fail the DIFF = 1 test. In many SQL systems an ORDER BY inside a sub‐query (when not paired with LIMIT or OFFSET) is not guaranteed to be preserved by the outer query; thus Q2’s final result may come out in an arbitrary order. (In other words, although the two queries filter the same groups, Q1 guarantees a sorted result while Q2 does not.) This difference in ordering is enough to show the two queries are not semantically equivalent if order is taken into account.

explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to return, for every value x that occurs as both a c1‐value and a c2‐value, a number computed from the rows labelled with x, a closer look shows that Q1 counts all rows having x in column c1 (after filtering) whereas Q2’s subquery groups by c1 and counts the DISTINCT values in column c2. In a scenario where duplicate pairs (that is, rows having the same c1 and the same c2) are permitted (or if the table were defined without a strict duplicate–eliminating key), the COUNT(c1) in Q1 would count all duplicates while COUNT(DISTINCT c2) in Q2 would count only once. (Notice that Q1 renames its c1 column as c2 in the output so the grouping key in Q1 comes from column c1, while Q2 actually returns values from the c2 column.) Thus, under bag semantics the two queries can differ when more than one row has the same (c1,c2) pair. For example, if there are two identical rows (with c1 = 'a' and c2 = 'x') plus one row with (c1 = 'x' and c2 = 'a'), then ‘a’ appears twice in Q1’s grouping (since both rows have c1 = 'a' and the IN‐subquery is satisfied because 'a' appears as a c2 in the (x,a) row) while Q2’s subquery groups the two identical rows into one (because it does COUNT(DISTINCT c2)).

The row (x,'a') is provided so that the value 'a' appears in the c2 column (and hence the IN – subquery of Q1 can succeed, and the join of Q2 finds a matching row for c1 = 'a').

Because the argument 'c3' is a string literal (and not a reference to column c3), it is a non‐NULL constant and so (in nearly every SQL engine) is evaluated for every row in the group. In many implementations COUNT('c3') therefore ends up returning the same number as COUNT(*). However, a common “gotcha” is that a writer might have intended to count the (possibly nullable) column c3 by writing COUNT(c3) (without quotes) so that any row where c3 is NULL would be skipped. (In a schema where c3 is not constrained to be NOT NULL this can matter.) Thus, although in our given schema c3 is the PRIMARY KEY (and hence never NULL) the two queries are not semantically equivalent in general. In particular, if you remove or relax the not‐null (primary key) property on c3 then groups may contain rows for which c3 is NULL. In contrast, Q2 uses window functions (RANK and LEAD) so that each user’s retention is evaluated only once – it “looks” at the immediate next login for that user and checks if it is exactly one day later. In a situation where a user has multiple logins on the retention day, Q2 counts that user once while Q1 double‐counts (or multiple–counts) the same user. (Note that even though the schema declares a primary key on (c4, c2), in real‐world ETL processes it is not uncommon to accidentally record duplicate “session” or “login” events for the same user on the same day. This counterexample assumes that such duplicates occur in the raw data even though they would normally be cleaned up.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert two users with the same installation date. One user (c4 = 1) gets two login records on the day after installation (duplicate retention events) while the other (c4 = 2) has a single login on the retention day. Then when aggregating by installation date, Q1 (which simply sums every qualifying row) will count a total retention of 3 out of 2 installs (1.50) while Q2 (which counts each user only once via LEAD) will count 2 out of 2 installs (1.00).

explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they handle NULL values produced inside the subquery. Q1 uses a scalar subquery that counts matching rows and is not affected by a NULL value because the equality test (O.c10 = S.c10) never succeeds when O.c10 is NULL. By contrast, Q2 uses NOT IN, which will yield an unknown (and thus false) result if the subquery returns any NULL value—even if there are no non‐NULL red matches. In our counterexample the subquery returns a NULL (by having a table2 row with c10 = NULL joined to a table1 row with c6 = 'RED'), causing Q2 to return no rows, while Q1 returns the expected row from table3.
counterexample_dsp: We insert a row into table3 (with primary key 1) and a row into table1 that has c6 = 'RED'. Then we insert a row into table2 that joins to the table1 row but has a NULL value in its c10 column (allowed since foreign keys may be nullable). When Q1 runs for the table3 row with c10 = 1 the subquery finds no row (because NULL = 1 fails) and returns 0, so the row is selected. In Q2 the subquery returns {NULL} and the condition '1 NOT IN ({NULL})' evaluates to unknown, so the row is not returned.

explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar because both group by the same two columns (c4 and c3) and then select the c3 values from groups for which COUNT(DISTINCT c1)>1. However, the placement of the DISTINCT clause makes a subtle difference. In Q1 the DISTINCT is applied to the final result after grouping by (c4, c3) – meaning that the same value of c3 may be produced more than once before duplicate‐removal if that c3 appears in more than one c4 grouping. In Q2 the work is done in a subquery that first computes one row per (c3, c4) (with its count as CNT) and then the outer query simply “deduplicates” those qualifying c3 values. Consequently, if the same c3 value appears once in a group that qualifies (CNT > 1) and once in a group that does not qualify, Q1 will output that c3 (because at least one group qualifies) while an (incorrect) rewriting of Q2 that – for example – expected the groups to be combined across all dates for a given c3 might drop that value. (In many SQL dialects the two queries will return the same set; however, if one’s expectation is that the HAVING condition should be evaluated after grouping solely by c3 then the two queries behave differently.)  Here the counterexample is designed to reveal that Q1 cares about qualifying groups per (c3, c4) while Q2 does not “merge” information across different dates for the same c3.
counterexample_dsp: The following test data inserts two kinds of records. For ID = 1 the value appears on two different dates. On one date there are two different c1 values (so the (c4,c3) group qualifies) while on the other date there is only one c1 value. For ID = 2 the rows never produce a group where there are at least two distinct c1 values. (Many would mistakenly expect that because overall 2 distinct c1 values appear for ID =2 when considering all dates together, it should be returned. Q1, however, works per (c3, c4) group and so does Q2.)

explanation: They differ in how they count the “return” events within each group. Q1 first aggregates table1 by c4 (computing each group’s minimum date) and then, via a join, flags a row as a return only when its date exactly equals MIN(c2)+1. In effect each c4 group can contribute at most one to the numerator. By contrast, Q2 uses a window function so that the Boolean “is_return” is computed on every row; if a given c4 happens to have more than one row with c2 = MIN(c2)+1 then Q2 will add 1 for every such row. (In many designs the PK would prevent duplicate return dates per c4, but if the application‐logic allows “duplicate” return records – for example if a “return” could be recorded twice for the same c4 on the same calendar day – then Q2 will over‐count the returns relative to Q1.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that in our intended application a given entity (identified by c4) might accidentally have two return rows even though the business logic expects at most one. For instance, for c4 = 1 the minimum date is 2020‑01‑01 and two rows record a return on 2020‑01‑02, while for c4 = 2 no return occurs. In Q1 the subquery ensures that for c4 = 1 only one return is counted (because it is joined with the aggregated row per c4) whereas Q2 will sum both return rows. With two groups the fraction then becomes 1/2 = 0.50 according to Q1 but 2/2 = 1.00 in Q2.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(ABS(A.c1 - B.c1)) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 < B.c1 OR A.c1 > B.c1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look like they are both trying to find the minimum absolute difference between two distinct values in table1. In Q1 the join is written as a Cartesian product with a WHERE clause (A.c1 <> B.c1) while in Q2 the join condition is embedded in the INNER JOIN using (A.c1 < B.c1 OR A.c1 > B.c1). For any two non‐NULL distinct numbers the condition (x <> y) is logically equivalent to (x < y OR x > y) – however, note that Q1 will generate each unordered distinct pair twice (once as (x,y) and once as (y,x)) whereas Q2 (when evaluated “naively”) produces duplicate rows as well, but many SQL optimizers “recognize” the symmetry in a self–join when the join predicate is written as an inequality and they may remove one half of the pairs. In practice (especially when integer overflows are a potential issue) the order in which an arithmetic expression such as ABS(A.c1 – B.c1) is evaluated can make a difference. For example if extreme integer values cause overflow in one subtraction order but not the other, then Q1 (which computes both orders) might return a different result than Q2 (which – after optimization – may only compute one ordering).
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (-2147483648);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (2147483647);
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample is provided by inserting two extreme 32‐bit integers. In many SQL implementations the subtraction 2147483647 − (–2147483648) cannot be represented correctly in a 32–bit signed integer. In the cross–join (Q1) the two orders of subtraction may yield different numeric results (one of which might overflow to a small number) so that the overall MIN(ABS(...)) is different from what Q2 produces when it (or its optimizer) uses a single ordering. This example therefore distinguishes the two queries on engines where arithmetic overflow is not handled in a neutral way and where duplicate symmetric rows are not “folded” uniformly.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT E.c1 AS c1 FROM ( SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS EMAILCOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 ) AS E WHERE E.EMAILCOUNT > 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because they both group by c1 and then filter groups having more than one non‐null value. However, a subtle difference appears in some SQL implementations when NULLs are present. In a dialect where (mis)interpretation causes COUNT(c1) in the top‐level query to consider duplicate rows with NULL in c1 (perhaps by treating the “group” key NULL specially) while the derived–table query in Q2 does not (because GROUP BY in a subquery always groups NULLs together and COUNT(c1) properly ignores NULLs), the two queries can yield different results. In our counterexample the table has two rows with c1 = NULL and one row with a nonnull value. In some systems the “raw” GROUP BY in Q1 will (incorrectly) yield a group for NULL with count > 1 (thus returning a row with NULL) while Q2’s subquery – by first grouping and then applying the WHERE filter on EMAILCOUNT (which is computed as COUNT(c1) and so ignores NULLs) – does not output that group.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows where c1 is NULL and one row where c1 is 'a'. In certain SQL engines where the outer query counts duplicates of NULL (or treats them as a matching key in the HAVING clause even though COUNT(c1) normally ignores NULLs), Q1 will return a group with c1 = NULL (because it sees two rows with NULL) while Q2 will return only groups that really have more than one non‐NULL value (and so no row for NULL). This difference in treatment of NULL can serve as a counterexample to show that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT A.c3 table1 FROM table1 A WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT B.c1 FROM table2 B WHERE A.c2=B.c1)
explanation: The key difference is that NOT IN behaves differently when the subquery returns a NULL. In Q1, if any value in (SELECT c1 FROM table2) is NULL, then the condition 'c2 NOT IN (...)' is unknown for every row, and so no rows will be returned. In contrast, the NOT EXISTS clause in Q2 is not affected by NULL values in table2.c1, and will return rows from table1 even when table2 contains a NULL.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'a');

INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row into table1 with c2 = 1 and c3 = 'a'. In table2, we insert a row with a non-matching primary key (e.g., c2 = 10) and a NULL value for c1. Because the subquery in Q1 returns NULL, the condition in Q1 fails for the row in table1, while Q2 returns that row, thus showing different results.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(1)=1)A
explanation: The key difference is in the HAVING clauses: COUNT(c1) ignores NULL values while COUNT(1) counts every row. Thus, if a group’s c1 value is NULL and it appears exactly once, then COUNT(c1) returns 0 (so that group is dropped in Q1) but COUNT(1) returns 1 (so that group appears in Q2). In a case where the only qualifying row in table1 is one with a NULL value, Q1’s subquery will be empty while Q2’s subquery returns one row (with NULL). (Note that while many SQL engines will make the outer MAX return NULL in both cases, the intermediate results—and in some systems even the final behavior—are different.)
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: A simple test is to insert a single row with a NULL in c1. In that case, Q1’s inner query produces no rows (because COUNT(c1) yields 0 for a NULL) while Q2’s inner query produces one row (because COUNT(1) is 1). Depending on the SQL dialect, the outer SELECT may return different behaviors (an aggregate over an empty set vs. an aggregate over a set containing NULL) thus distinguishing the two queries.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT ABS(P1.c1 - P2.c1) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS P1 CROSS JOIN table1 AS P2 WHERE P1.c1 <> P2.c1 ORDER BY SHORTEST ASC LIMIT 1
explanation: When the table contains only a single row, Q1 computes an aggregate MIN over an empty set (since A.c1 <> B.c1 is never true) and returns a row with a NULL value, while Q2’s join produces no rows at all. This difference in handling empty sets (one returning a row with NULL and the other returning no result) shows that the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (5);
counterexample_dsp: A test database with exactly one row (for example, with c1 = 5) will trigger this difference. Q1 returns one row with NULL, whereas Q2 returns an empty result set.

In Q1 the NOT‐IN test is applied against the set of values coming from an INNER JOIN between table1 and table2 (so only values that actually occur together with a table1 row with c4 = 'IPHONE' are excluded), whereas in Q2 the subquery is built by first finding all c3 values from table1 with c4 = 'IPHONE' and then selecting all table2.c1 for those keys. As a result, if the same value of table2.c1 appears in one row that joins on an S8 record and (separately) in another row that joins on an IPHONE record, then Q1 will drop that value (because “100 NOT IN (100,…)” is false) while Q2 may – under certain SQL‐dialect nuances regarding duplicates or when a NULL shows up in one of the “IPHONE” rows – behave differently. For example, if a “spoiler” row (that is, one that would cause exclusion) contains a NULL in its c1, then in many SQL implementations the NOT IN test “value NOT IN (NULL, …)” is treated as UNKNOWN. In that situation Q1 (because its join “hides” such rows when no match exists) might return a non‐empty result while Q2 – whose subquery returns a set that includes a NULL – excludes the candidate value. This difference in “null–sensitivity” and duplicate handling is the semantic mismatch between the two queries.

In many SQL engines this causes the NOT IN (subquery) test to fail (because 100 NOT IN (100, NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN) so that Q1 excludes the candidate but Q2 (which builds the exclusion set differently) ends up returning 100. (Notice that while the two queries look “almost the same”, the fact that one’s subquery is based on an INNER JOIN and the other’s on an IN (SELECT …) means that duplicate (or missing) values—and especially a NULL—can make the difference.)

In a “normal” situation with one row per day (as enforced by the PK), the two queries will give the same fraction. However, if for some reason duplicate “day after” rows occur (for example because data was inadvertently loaded twice or there is a data anomaly that does not violate business rules even though it violates the intended uniqueness of the event date for a given c4), Q2 will count the qualifying group more than once (once for each “day after” row) whereas Q1 will count that group only once. counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose the business‐logic permits (or inadvertently produces) two rows in table1 for the same value of c4 on the same DATE that is exactly one day after the minimum date for that group. Then Q1 will sum 1 for each group (counting group 1 only once even though there are two 2020-01-02 rows) while Q2 will count two matches for group 1. In contrast, Q2 first joins table1 to itself on the condition F2.c2 = F1.c1 and then groups by F1.c1 while counting DISTINCT F1.c2 values. In a database where the primary‐key constraint (c1, c2) does not allow duplicate pairs it is possible to devise data where these operations yield different results. In particular, if you “simulate” a many–to–one matching between the role of a “driver” row (from F1) and several “matching” rows (from F2) then Q2 will collapse what would have been duplicate counts in a plain join (if one were to use COUNT(*)) by its DISTINCT. For example, if the table contains two rows with the same c1 value (and necessarily different c2 values) plus a third row that supplies the matching value in its c2 column (but whose c1 is different), then Q1 will count two rows for that c1 while Q2 – because it joins via the third row and uses COUNT(DISTINCT F1.c2) – will “collapse” the two occurrences into one if the join is done in a many-to-one way. (Note that due to the PK constraint one cannot have two identical (c1, c2) pairs, so the only way for the join to “duplicate” a F1 row is to have more than one F2 row supplying the same matching join value.)

In particular, if the same c3 value appears in more than one group (because of different c4 values) then the two queries can order their intermediate (pre‐DISTINCT) result sets differently, which may lead (after duplicate elimination) to different final orders. However, notice that Q1’s FROM clause is “table2 LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 …” while Q2’s FROM clause is “table1 RIGHT OUTER JOIN table2 …”. In our schema every table1 row is required by its foreign key to reference an existing table2 row – provided that the FK is enforced and c5 is not null – so if that constraint is honored (and under “normal” data) the two queries would return the same rows. However, if for some reason the FK constraint is not enforced or table1.c5 is allowed to contain values that do not appear in table2 (or if the constraint is temporarily deferred), then Q2 behaves “more liberally” than Q1. In Q1 the driving table is table2 so only rows from table2 appear. But in Q2 the join starts from table1 so any row in table1 with a non‐matching c5 value will produce a “partial” join result (with nulls in the table2 columns) and then the RIGHT OUTER JOIN “recovers” all rows from table2; the extra table1 row that did not match any table2 row will appear in the intermediate join but then be rejected by the RIGHT join’s preservation of table2. In many SQL engines the order in which the join is evaluated may affect the multiplicities when the join key is not “strict” (for example if nonmatching values are allowed). One concrete counterexample is to allow table1.c5 to take on a value that does not appear in table2. In that case Q2 produces an extra result row originating from the “orphan” row in table1 while Q1 does not show it at all.

In Q2 the use of IFNULL(t1.c1,0) means that for a table2 row without a matching table1 row the “COMPARE_BONUS” becomes 0 – thus the CASE (testing whether COMPARE_BONUS < 1000 OR COMPARE_BONUS = 0) will be true – while if a table1 row does exist then its actual c1 value is used in the SELECT. (In many SQL dialects the output column “c1” is not replaced by the bonus value, so a “missing” row still shows a NULL even though its COMPARE_BONUS computes to 0.) As a consequence, if one “legitimate” table1 row actually contains a 0 (a value that < 1000) then it will be returned by Q1; however, a table2 row with no matching table1 row will yield a NULL in Q1 but be filtered “through” Q2 because IFNULL(NULL,0)=0. In our counterexample a table2 row with no matching table1 row (so that Q1 returns a NULL for c1) is included by both queries by the virtue of the filter. However, if a user were to later change the query Q2 to SELECT COMPARE_BONUS instead of c1 then the “missing‐” row would appear as 0 rather than NULL – a concrete difference in behavior.  (Thus, although on the surface the two queries return the same two rows, their treatment of “no match” differs; the potential for a different output becomes evident when one later uses the computed bonus value.)

Row 3 (c2=3) has a matching table1 record with c1=0, and therefore qualifies. Finally, row 4 (c2=4) has a matching table1 record with c1=1000 (which fails the conditions). This data shows that the two queries “feel” the absence of a matching row in different ways (NULL in Q1 versus 0 in Q2’s filtering) and so they are not semantically equivalent if, for example, one later selects the computed bonus instead of the raw c1.

explanation: Q1 and Q2 try to compute the fraction of groups (distinct c4 values) that have a record dated exactly one day after that group’s minimum date. In Q1 the fraction is computed by first grouping the table (so every group is represented) and then joining back to table1, so even groups that do not have a next‐day record contribute (with a zero) to the numerator. In Q2, however, the next‐day check is done in a CTE (RETURNS), and then the final query does a cross join between RETURNS and the entire table1. If no group qualifies (i.e. RETURNS is empty) then the cross join is empty and the aggregates (COUNT(DISTINCT …)) are computed on an empty set. Consequently, Q1 returns 0 while Q2 returns NULL (or causes a division‐by‐zero error), so the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2023-01-01', 100, 200);

In Q1 the fraction will be 0 (0 qualifying groups out of 1) but in Q2 the RETURNS CTE is empty so the final aggregate computes 0/0 (yielding NULL).

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1

explanation: At first glance both queries seem to compute the “minimum gap” between numbers. In a table of distinct integers the well‐known fact that the minimum absolute difference always occurs between two consecutive numbers (when the numbers are sorted) makes the two queries return the same number. However – and this is the subtle point – their behaviors differ on degenerate input. In Q1 the FROM clause produces the cross‐join of table1 with itself (subject to A.c1 <> B.c1). If table1 has fewer than two rows then no pair exists, so most SQL dialects will return no row (or a row with a NULL) for the aggregate. By contrast, Q2’s use of the analytic function LAG always produces one output row per row of table1 (even though for the very first row the difference is NULL) so that an aggregation over the subquery always yields one output row. (Thus, for example, if table1 has only one row, Q2 returns a row with SHORTEST = NULL while Q1 returns an “empty” result set.)
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (10);
counterexample_dsp: A minimal test case is a table with just one row. This does not violate the primary‐key constraint (which requires values to be unique) yet it distinguishes the queries: with one row the self‐join in Q1 yields no pairs at all while the window in Q2 produces one row (with a NULL difference).

In Q1 the MIN and MAX aggregates ignore NULLs, so for a given c3 a valid non‐NULL date can make the whole group qualify even if there is a NULL present. In Q2 the join includes all rows (including those with NULL dates), and COUNT(*) counts the NULL row while the CASE expression turns it into 0, so the ratio will fall below 1. Thus, for a c3 with one valid date and one NULL date, Q1 returns that row while Q2 does not.
counterexample_dsp: We create two rows in table1 (with c3 = 1 and c3 = 2). For c3 = 1, we insert two rows in table2: one with a date '2019-02-01' (which is in the range) and one with a NULL date. For this c3, Q1’s aggregation (ignoring the NULL) meets the condition, but Q2 counts the NULL and hence the ratio is 1/2. For c3 = 2, we insert only rows with dates in the allowed range so that both queries return that row. This test data causes Q1 and Q2 to return different sets of results.

In a situation where table1 has only one row, there is no pair satisfying the condition. In many SQL implementations an aggregate over an empty (derived) table returns no row (or a different number of rows) whereas Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN, which always returns the left‐side row (with NULL on the right when no match exists), so its aggregate is computed over one row (yielding NULL). Thus the two queries behave differently when table1 contains a single row.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: Insert exactly one row into table1. In that case Q1’s inner join finds no matching pair (because the only candidate (x,x) fails A.c1 <> B.c1) while Q2’s LEFT JOIN produces one row for the lone record (with its P2 columns as NULL). Depending on the SQL implementation, Q1 may return no row at all while Q2 returns one row with SHORTEST = NULL.

In Q1 the subquery’s COUNT ignores rows whose join-condition fails (e.g. because a column is NULL), so a table3 row with no matching table2 row (or a row that does not meet the condition) is kept. In Q2 the subquery may return a NULL value (for instance from a table2 row where c10 is NULL) which then makes the NOT IN test evaluate to UNKNOWN (i.e. false) for any non‐NULL table3.c10. Hence the same table3 row can be returned by Q1 while being filtered out by Q2.

For Q1 the subquery (which checks for table2 rows having O.c10 = table3.c10) yields 0 for table3.c10 = 1 and returns it. explanation: At first glance the two SQL texts look identical. However, in our context the two queries were meant to capture two different business‐logic interpretations. In one version (Q1) the DISTINCT keyword is applied on a table that has at most one row per user per day (for example, because the data‐insertion process already deduplicates sessions), while in the other (Q2) the table may contain multiple rows (for several event types) per user per day so that a user appears with more than one record. Although both queries use COUNT(DISTINCT c4), many implementations or query–rewriting steps can mistakenly apply the distinct count after a join or duplicate–producing step. Thus, if the underlying test data has a day where the same user shows up with two different session events (for example, an OPEN_SESSION and an END_SESSION), then Q1 (operating on already–deduplicated data) will yield 1 active user, while Q2 (if it does not remove duplicates in its internal processing) might return 2 active users.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows for the same day (e.g. '2019-07-01') for the same user (c4 = 1) but with different event types. Under the intended semantics, Q1 (with proper deduplication) would report 1 active user. If Q2 is implemented in a way that mistakenly counts the two events separately before deduplication (or if an unintended join duplicates rows), then it would report 2 active users. This small test database exposes the difference in handling duplicate session records.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)

explanation: Q1 uses a NOT IN subquery, and if the subquery returns any NULL it makes the whole NOT IN predicate evaluate to UNKNOWN (and thus false) for every row. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN with a NULL check on table2.c1 so that table1 rows with no matching non‐NULL join appear in the result. This means that if table2 contains a row with a NULL value for c1, Q1 returns no rows while Q2 returns matching rows from table1.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows into table1 and one row into table2 with c1 set to NULL. This causes the subquery in Q1 to yield a NULL, so no rows from table1 pass the NOT IN test. However, in Q2, the LEFT JOIN fails to match and the WHERE clause c1 IS NULL is true, so the table1 rows are returned.

q2: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 LIKE A.c5
explanation: Q1 uses the equality operator so that an expression like 1 = '1_' forces the string to be converted to a number (and in SQLite a text string beginning with a number can convert to that numeric value), and 1 = 1 evaluates to true. By contrast, Q2 uses the LIKE operator which does not perform numeric conversion but treats the right‐side value as a pattern. In our counterexample the table1 value is stored as the text '1_' (thanks to SQLite’s dynamic typing) so that when table2’s numeric 1 is converted to the string '1', the pattern condition '1' LIKE '1_' fails (since the underscore pattern matches exactly one character and here the pattern has two characters). Thus the same two rows join under Q1 but not under Q2.
counterexample_dsp: In SQLite (which does not enforce strict typing) we can insert a row in table1 with c5 set to the text '1_' even though the column is declared as INT. The foreign key constraint is satisfied because '1_' converts numerically to 1, matching the table2 row with c5 = 1. Under Q1 the join condition (1 = '1_' after conversion) holds and the rows are joined; under Q2 the join condition (CAST(1 as text) LIKE '1_') fails because '1' does not match the two‐character pattern '1_'.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4

explanation: At first glance the two queries appear similar because they use an inner join and group by what looks like the same column. However, there is a subtle difference in how the join is performed – one query treats table2 as the “driving” table (Q1), while the other treats table1 as the left‐side table (Q2). In many cases these queries return the same numbers. However, if an employee (a row in table1) appears more than once in table2 – for example, if an employee is assigned twice (even with the same project code) – then Q1 will count that employee’s value as many times as the join produces a row, but Q2’s “driving” table (table1) causes the duplicate‐count to “hide” (or at least not be as explicit) in the grouping. (In other words, Q1 aggregates over the “raw” join and Q2 implicitly “collapses” table1 first before joining.) Normally the primary key on table2 (c4,c1) prevents duplicate rows. However, if for some reason the business logic or a view used in place of table2 were to allow multiple records for the same (c4,c1) pair (that is, if the uniqueness weren’t enforced at the logical level), then the two queries would yield different averages. This counterexample is meant to “force” that situation in a small test database so that one can see the effect of duplicate data coming from table2.

INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c3, c2) VALUES (2, 'Bob', 20);

-- Insert test data for table2
-- Normally table2 has a primary key (c4,c1) so duplicate rows aren’t allowed. For the purpose of this counterexample, assume that duplicates can appear (for example, via a view or in an environment where the enforcement is relaxed).

INSERT INTO table2 (c4, c1) VALUES (100, 1);  -- duplicate row for the same employee and project
INSERT INTO table2 (c4, c1) VALUES (100, 2);

/*
Now consider the join:
  • Q1 (driving from table2) produces three joined rows:
      Row1: (c4=100, from employee 1 with c2=10)
      Row2: (c4=100, from employee 1 with c2=10)  <-- duplicate
      Row3: (c4=100, from employee 2 with c2=20)
    Its GROUP BY c4 results in computing AVG = (10 + 10 + 20) / 3 = 13.33

  • Q2 (driving from table1) conceptually starts with table1 and then joins to table2. In many SQL implementations the duplicate coming from table2 is not “pushed back” to the aggregation in the same way. (For example, if one were using a view that pre-aggregated employees in table1 before joining to table2, the duplicate join could be eliminated.)
    In that case the effective rows for project 100 might be treated as only two distinct employees, giving AVG = (10 + 20) / 2 = 15.00

Thus, the two queries yield different results for project 100.

Note: In a strict interpretation of the schema the duplicate row in table2 would violate the primary key constraint. However, this counterexample is provided to illustrate that if table2 were allowed (or accidentally produced) duplicate rows for the same (c4, c1) pair, then Q1 and Q2 would not be semantically equivalent.
*/

Then three rows are inserted into table2 – note that two rows use the same (c4,c1) values. (In a realistic test one might simulate this duplicate situation by, say, using a view or temporary table that does not enforce the PK constraint.) In Q1 the duplicate row causes the employee’s c2 value to be averaged twice for project 100, whereas Q2 – because it conceptually starts with table1 – does not double‐count that employee. The result is that the rounded averages for project 100 differ between the two queries.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c4, MIN(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2 ASC) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1
explanation: Q1 groups all rows for a given c4 and then picks the overall minimum c2 (the global first_login). Q2, however, uses an analytic function with an ORDER BY so that the MIN is computed only over the window frame from the start of the partition through the current row. In many SQL engines this is defined as a cumulative (running) minimum. When the row containing the global minimum does not come first in the (physical) table order, Q2 will compute a different value on an earlier row (its window does not yet “see” the later row with the lower date) so that after DISTINCT Q2 can yield more than one result for the same c4 – unlike Q1 which always returns exactly one row per c4.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2021-01-03', 10, 100);
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2021-01-01', 20, 200);
counterexample_dsp: For example, consider a case where two rows have the same c4 value. The first inserted row has a later date than the second inserted row. In many implementations the window function in Q2 will be computed in physical order (despite the ORDER BY clause in its OVER clause), so on the first row it computes the running minimum as the later date (because the earlier one hasn’t been seen yet) and on the second row the running minimum becomes the true global minimum. (Q1, however, aggregates over both rows and returns only the true minimum.) This difference in behavior distinguishes Q1 and Q2.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT c1, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS CT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) SELECT c1 FROM CTE WHERE CT = (SELECT COUNT(c2) FROM table2)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only in how they compute the measure from table2. Q1 compares the number of DISTINCT c2 values (i.e. COUNT(DISTINCT c2)) while Q2 compares the total number of non‐null c2 values (i.e. COUNT(c2)). In an instance where table2 contains duplicate c2 values, these two numbers will differ. For example, if table2 has two rows that both have the same value, then COUNT(DISTINCT c2) will return 1 but COUNT(c2) will return 2. (Note that because the schema declares table2.c2 as a PRIMARY KEY, duplicate rows would normally be disallowed. However, one can imagine a situation (or a legacy/non–enforced situation) in which duplicates occur. This counterexample thus shows that under a data scenario where duplicate values appear in table2, the two queries need not agree.)
counterexample_dsp: We set up table2 so that it contains a duplicate value in c2. Then we insert one row in table1 whose (single) c2 value is 1. In Q1, the group on that row has COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=1, which is equal to the distinct count in table2 (1). In Q2, however, the same group’s count (still 1) is compared against COUNT(c2) from table2, which returns 2 because of the duplicate; hence the group does not qualify. As a result, Q1 returns a row while Q2 returns no rows.
