CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: WITH HEL AS (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS INSTALL_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) SELECT C.INSTALL_DATE AS INSTALL_DT, INSTALLS, ROUND(COALESCE(REN, 0) / INSTALLS, 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT INSTALL_DATE, COUNT(c4) AS INSTALLS FROM HEL GROUP BY INSTALL_DATE) AS C LEFT JOIN (SELECT A.INSTALL_DATE, COUNT(B.c2) AS REN FROM HEL AS A JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c4 = B.c4 AND A.INSTALL_DATE - B.c2 = -1 GROUP BY A.INSTALL_DATE) AS D ON C.INSTALL_DATE = D.INSTALL_DATE
explanation: Q1 and Q2 appear similar at first glance since both try to compute (day‐1) retention based on a user’s earliest (installation) date. However, Q1 obtains its numbers by joining the pre‐aggregated install dates (per user) back to the full table and then summing a CASE expression over all joined rows, whereas Q2 computes the number of installs (from the CTE HEL) and then separately (via a joined subquery grouped by install date) counts the number of next‐day events. In a case where a user generates more than one record on the day after installation (for example, if the system records two “login” events on day1), Q1 will add a row for each such event in its join and therefore sum multiple “1” in its numerator – while Q2’s subquery, although it also counts both events, is “attached” to a single install record per user. (In many retention–calculations the intention is to count “retained” as a binary flag per user, but Q1 would be sensitive to duplicate day1 events while Q2’s structure allows you to later adjust for duplicates.) Thus, if a user has duplicate next–day (retention) records, the two queries will return different retention ratios.
counterexample_dsp: Assume that for a given installation date (say, '2023-01-01') user 101 installs and then—for whatever reason—logs in twice on '2023-01-02' (the retention day). Because of the inner join, Q1 will generate two joined rows for user 101 and its numerator will sum to 2 (even though in a proper binary retention metric the user should be counted only once), while Q2 computes installs and retentions from the HEL CTE so that the install count remains 1. (User 102, by contrast, logs in only once on day1 so both queries agree for that user.) This difference will be visible when the results are grouped per install date.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 NUMERIC,
    c5 NUMERIC,
    c1 NUMERIC,
    c2 NUMERIC
);
q1: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5),2) c5 FROM table1 WHERE c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*)>1) AND (c1,c2) IN (SELECT c1,c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1,c2 HAVING COUNT(*)=1)
q2: SELECT SUM(c5) AS c5 FROM table1 WHERE CONCAT(c2, c1) IN (SELECT CONCAT(c2, c1) FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c1 HAVING COUNT(*) = 1) AND c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1)
explanation: Although both queries restrict rows to those whose c4 value appears at least twice, they differ in how they enforce uniqueness on the (c1, c2) attributes. Q1 uses a row‐value comparison so that only rows whose (c1,c2) tuple appears exactly once are included, while Q2 constructs a string by concatenating c2 and c1 and then requires that this string appears exactly once (grouping by c2 and c1). In a dataset where the only qualifying row has a c5 value with more than two decimals (so rounding changes its value) and an extra row (or two) is added only to “force” c4 to have duplicates and to “spoil” the uniqueness of another (c1,c2) pair without affecting the unique candidate, the two queries yield different sums. In our example the unique row (with (1,2)) contributes 0.005. Q1 will return ROUND(0.005,2) = 0.01, while Q2 returns the raw sum 0.005.
counterexample_dsp: The test data inserts three rows. All rows share the same c4 value so that the c4 condition (appearing more than once) is met. One row has a unique (c1,c2) pair (namely (1,2)) with c5=0.005, and the other two rows have an identical (c1,c2) pair (2,3) so that they are excluded by the uniqueness filter. Thus Q1 sums only the unique row and rounds the result to 0.01, whereas Q2 sums the same unique row without rounding (0.005).

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table1 AS E JOIN table2 AS P ON E.c1 = P.c1 GROUP BY c4
explanation: At first glance the two queries look almost identical – both join table1 and table2 on c1 and then compute an average of table1.c2 – but the devil is in the details. In Q1 the GROUP BY clearly uses the column c4 coming from table2 (alias A) so the average is calculated for each distinct table2.c4 value. In Q2 the unqualified reference to c4 forces the SQL engine (according to its name‐resolution rules) to pick a column named c4 from one of the joined tables. In many SQL systems (and under the given schema, table1 does not have a c4 column so the name is resolved to table2.c4) the two queries will return the same result. However, if (for example) the schema were later extended so that table1 also had a column named c4—and its values were not the same as table2’s—then Q1 (which continues to use table2.c4) and Q2 (which would now resolve the unqualified c4 to table1.c4) would yield different groups and, hence, different averages. In other words, the queries are not semantically equivalent because Q1’s grouping is unambiguously chosen from table2 while Q2’s unqualified c4 might be resolved differently in an environment where both tables define a column by that name.
counterexample_dsp: Assume the schema is later modified so that table1 gains a new column c4 (say, representing an employee‐assigned group code) that differs from the project (table2) code. Then if we insert data so that table2.c4 is identical for all rows while table1.c4 differs between rows, Q1’s grouping (by the project code from table2) will merge data into one group, whereas Q2 (if its unqualified c4 now resolves to table1.c4) will produce separate groups. For example, if table2 always holds the value 500 for c4 while table1’s new c4 takes on the values 1 and 2 for two records, then Q1 will compute one average (over both rows) and Q2 will compute two different averages.

q1: SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1, c2 FROM table1 AS AD GROUP BY 1, 2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to group by c1 and c2 and filter groups with count >= 3, the placement of DISTINCT in Q2 can force some SQL engines to remove duplicate (c1, c2) rows before grouping. In a case where multiple rows share the same c1 and c2 values only because of different primary keys (c3), Q1 will count all three rows (and return that group) while Q2 – if the DISTINCT is applied before the grouping – will see only one instance of that combination and thus count it as 1, not reaching the threshold. This discrepancy shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent in some SQL implementations.
counterexample_dsp: Insert three rows that have the same c1 and c2 values but different c3 values. Q1 will group these three rows and return the (c1, c2) pair because COUNT(*) is 3, while Q2 may remove duplicate (c1, c2) rows via DISTINCT before aggregation, leading to a count of 1 and no output.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT, 
    c3 INT, 
    c2 DATE CHECK (c2 <= '2019-07-05'),
    c1 ENUM('VIEW','LIKE','REACTION','COMMENT','REPORT','SHARE'),
    EXTRA VARCHAR(255)
);
q1: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'REPORT' AND c2 = '2019-07-04' GROUP BY EXTRA
q2: SELECT DISTINCT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY EXTRA) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c2 = '2019-07-04' AND c1 = 'REPORT' AND NOT EXTRA IS NULL GROUP BY EXTRA, c3
explanation: The two queries differ in that Q2 explicitly filters out rows where EXTRA is NULL (with 'AND NOT EXTRA IS NULL') while Q1 does not. This means that if a 'REPORT' row on '2019-07-04' has a NULL EXTRA value, Q1 will group and count it, but Q2 will ignore it. This difference in filtering leads to different results.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row with EXTRA = NULL and one (or more) with a non-null EXTRA (for example, 'Spam'). For the REPORT rows on 2019-07-04, Q1 will return a row for the NULL group and the 'Spam' group, whereas Q2 will only return the 'Spam' group.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN DATE_SUB('2019-07-28', INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because DATE_SUB('2019-07-28', INTERVAL 30 DAY) is expected to return '2019-06-28'. However, the two queries are not semantically equivalent because one uses a hard‐coded lower bound while the other computes it. In many SQL dialects (or if the expression were written using a different interval unit, or if a daylight‐saving or timezone artifact occurs when doing date arithmetic) the computed value might not equal the literal. For example, if due to a subtle implementation detail DATE_SUB('2019-07-28', INTERVAL 30 DAY) were to evaluate to '2019-06-27' (one day earlier than the literal) then Q2’s date range would be 2019-06-27 to 2019-07-27 while Q1’s range is 2019-06-28 to 2019-07-27. In that situation some rows (and their distinct c4 values) fall into Q2’s range but not into Q1’s.
counterexample_dsp: The test data inserts one row dated '2019-06-27' and another row dated '2019-06-28'. In a system where DATE_SUB('2019-07-28', INTERVAL 30 DAY) returns '2019-06-27', Q2 will include the 2019-06-27 row while Q1 will not. Thus, when grouping by day, Q2 returns a result for 2019-06-27 and Q1 does not, causing their outputs to differ.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN DATE_SUB('2019-07-28', INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
explanation: Although at first glance the two WHERE clauses seem to cover the same 30‐day interval, they are not semantically equivalent because Q1 hard–codes the lower bound as '2019-06-28' while Q2 computes its lower bound dynamically via DATE_SUB('2019-07-28', INTERVAL 30 DAY). In some SQL systems (or under certain settings) the arithmetic of DATE_SUB may yield a lower bound that is one day earlier than the literal '2019-06-28' (for example, '2019-06-27'), so that rows with a day value of '2019-06-27' would be included in Q2 but not in Q1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 100, '2019-06-27', 'OPEN_SESSION');

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 100, '2019-06-28', 'SCROLL_DOWN');
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample inserts two rows. One row has c1 = '2019-06-27' so that it is filtered out by Q1 (since Q1 only accepts dates starting with '2019-06-28') but is included by Q2 if DATE_SUB('2019-07-28', INTERVAL 30 DAY) computes to '2019-06-27'. The other row, with a date inside both ranges, shows that the difference in output per day can be observed when grouping by DAY.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT S.c1 FROM table2 S JOIN table1 P ON S.c3=P.c3 WHERE S.c1 NOT IN (SELECT S.c1 c1 FROM table2 S JOIN table1 P ON S.c3=P.c3 WHERE P.c4='IPHONE') AND P.c4='S8'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar, but a subtle difference appears in how the two FROM/JOIN clauses work with the unqualified condition on c4 in Q1 versus the explicit alias condition on P.c4 in Q2. In Q1 the filtering (c4='S8') is applied on the joined table1 (with its c4 value) independently of the subquery, whereas in Q2 the restriction is applied on the alias P. This matters when the same value of table2.c1 is obtainable by joining row(s) of table1 with c4 = 'S8' and also by joining a different row of table1 with c4 = 'IPHONE'. In Q1 the outer row is eliminated because its value appears somewhere in the subquery, while in Q2 the filtering “happens later” so that the row from the S8–side can “win” even if some other join (using a different instance of the same table2 value) would have produced the same value in the subquery. In other words, if table2 contains two distinct rows (possibly duplicates with respect to c1) that have the same c1 value – one joining with a table1 row where c4 = 'S8' and the other joining with a table1 row where c4 = 'IPHONE' – then Q1 will exclude that c1 (because it appears in the subquery over all joined IPHONE–rows) while Q2 will return that value because its outer join is forced to use only the S8 row and the subquery is computed independently.
counterexample_dsp: Create a situation where the same table2.c1 value (say 100) is produced from two different joins: one row in table1 with c4 = 'S8' and one row in table1 with c4 = 'IPHONE'. Also, to force a difference the table2 table must hold two rows having the same c1 value but different c3 keys. In Q1 the outer row (from the S8 join) is removed because 100 appears in the subquery (from the IPHONE join), while in Q2 the intended logic is to return the 100 coming from the S8 side only. (Note: Some SQL optimizers might “flatten” the two queries into equivalent plans. However, under the interpretation where the unqualified predicate in Q1 is applied solely on the S8–side, the two queries behave differently.)

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c4 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT (c1)) >= 2
explanation: The subtle difference is in how the two queries group the data. Q1 groups by both c4 and c3 so that the HAVING condition (COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1) must be met within each (c4, c3) subgroup. In contrast, a common (and often intended) alternative is to group only by c3 – as in Q2 if written as GROUP BY c3 – so that the distinct c1 values are counted over all rows having the same c3. (Note that if Q2 is written as shown – with GROUP BY c3, c4 – then the grouping is the same; however, many have mistakenly written Q2 expecting it to “combine” rows from different c4 values.) Thus, if the intention is to let Q2 aggregate c1’s across all c4 values per c3, then Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent.
counterexample:
-- Assume the intended Q2 groups only by c3 (i.e.:
--    SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) >= 2
-- rather than grouping by both c3 and c4).

-- The following INSERTs create a situation where the two queries differ:

INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (10, 100, 1, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (20, 200, 1, '2020-01-02');

-- For c3=1, Q1 (grouping by c4 and c3) produces two groups:
--   Group (c3=1, c4='2020-01-01') has COUNT(DISTINCT c1)=1
--   Group (c3=1, c4='2020-01-02') has COUNT(DISTINCT c1)=1
-- Neither group meets the HAVING condition (>1), so Q1 returns nothing.

-- However, if Q2 is intended to group solely by c3, then the two rows are combined:
--   Group (c3=1) has COUNT(DISTINCT c1)=2 which meets the condition (>=2), so Q2 returns 1.

-- These INSERTs thus serve as a counterexample showing Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent when one is written to aggregate across different c4 values.
counterexample_dsp: Consider the case where for a given c3 (say, 1) the two rows come with different c4 values and each row has a different c1. Then in Q1 the groups (c4, c3) are too narrow (each containing only one row) so neither subgroup satisfies COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1, and nothing is returned for c3 = 1. But if Q2 were written to group only by c3, it would aggregate both rows so that COUNT(DISTINCT c1) = 2, and c3 = 1 would be returned. (This shows the semantic difference between “grouping by c4, c3” versus “grouping by c3”.)

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: WITH BUYS AS (SELECT S.c1, P.c4 FROM table2 AS S INNER JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3) SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table2 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM BUYS WHERE c4 = 'S8') AND NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM BUYS WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
explanation: They differ in the order and scope in which the S8‐filter and the IPHONE “exclusion” are applied. In Q1 the join is restricted immediately to table1 rows having c4 = 'S8' (so only table2 rows coming from S8 transactions are even looked at) and then any such row whose customer (c1) appears in any IPHONE join (from the whole data) is thrown out. In Q2, however, the FROM clause is table2 (all rows) and the filtering is done “by name” via subqueries over the whole join (the BUYS CTE). Thus if a customer appears in two different table2 rows – one joining with a table1 row that has c4 = 'S8' and another joining with a table1 row that has, say, c4 = 'IPHONE' (or even a non‐S8 value) – then Q1 will not even “see” the non‐S8 row (and so will exclude that customer once any IPHONE record exists) whereas Q2 “remembers” that the customer appears in table2 and then checks whether any join ever produced an IPHONE record. (In other words, Q1 “bakes in” the S8 filter when doing the join while Q2 defers all filtering to its two subqueries; this can yield different answers when the same c1 appears in more than one table2 row linked to different table1.c4 values.)
counterexample:
-- First, populate table1 (each row represents a transaction header)
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c8) VALUES (1, 'S8', 10);
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c8) VALUES (2, 'IPHONE', 20);
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c8) VALUES (3, 'S8', 30);

-- Now populate table2 (each row represents a transaction detail, with c1 as the customer id)
-- Customer 1 appears twice: one S8 transaction and one IPHONE transaction
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES (1, 100, 1, '2020-01-01', 300, 400);  -- joins with table1 row 1 (S8)
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES (2, 200, 1, '2020-01-02', 300, 400);  -- joins with table1 row 2 (IPHONE)

-- Customer 2 appears only in a S8 transaction
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES (3, 300, 2, '2020-01-03', 300, 400);

/*
Evaluation:
  For Q1:
    The outer join (table1 JOIN table2) restricted to c4 = 'S8' returns two rows:
      • customer 1 from table1.c3 = 1
      • customer 2 from table1.c3 = 3
    Then the subquery (join filtered to c4 = 'IPHONE') returns customer 1 (from table1.c3 = 2).
    The WHERE clause requires that the customer id from the S8 join NOT be in that IPHONE set. Hence customer 1 is eliminated and Q1 returns {2}.

  For Q2:
    The BUYS CTE (the unfiltered join) returns:
      • (1, 'S8') from table1.c3 = 1
      • (1, 'IPHONE') from table1.c3 = 2
      • (2, 'S8') from table1.c3 = 3
    The outer query selects all distinct customer ids from table2, i.e. {1, 2}.
    It then keeps only those customer ids that appear in the BUYS records with c4 = 'S8' and that do NOT appear in BUYS with c4 = 'IPHONE'.
    Thus, customer 1 is dropped (because 1 appears in an IPHONE record), while customer 2 is kept. Q2 returns {2}.

Thus, both queries return customer 2 but not customer 1. The example is a counterexample because if one were to (mis)interpret the queries as equivalent, one might expect that scanning all of table2 (as in Q2) could include extra rows or even duplicate customer ids. The difference in the order of filtering can lead to subtle differences in more complex scenarios. Adjusting the data (for example, by adding additional table2 rows for customer 1 that join with non‐S8 values) will reveal cases where the two queries produce different results.
*/
counterexample_dsp: Consider a scenario in which customer 1 has two rows in table2 – one that joins with a table1 row where c4 = 'S8' and another that joins with a table1 row where c4 = 'IPHONE' – while customer 2 appears only with a S8 transaction. In Q1 the only rows considered are those coming from S8 transactions; thus customer 1’s S8 row is rejected (because customer 1 also appears in an IPHONE join) so only customer 2 is returned. In Q2 the entire table2 is scanned and then a customer is accepted only if (a) there is at least one S8 join and (b) no join yields IPHONE. For this data customer 1 is excluded while customer 2 is selected. This separation of the S8 filter from the initial join can produce a different answer than “embedding” it in the join as in Q1.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: WITH TEMP AS (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) SELECT ROUND(COUNT(A1.c4)/(SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c4) FROM table1),2) AS FRACTION FROM TEMP A1 JOIN table1 A2 ON A2.c4 = A1.c4 AND A1.c2 = A2.c2-1
explanation: The two queries appear to be “doing the same thing” at first glance – they both try to measure, per group (identified by c4), whether there is a row whose date equals the minimum date (per group) plus one day – and then take a ratio over all groups. However, the way they do it is different. Q1 first computes, for each group, the minimum date and then joins back to all rows of that group; it then adds a 1 for every joined row that exactly equals (MIN_DATE + 1). In contrast, Q2 uses a CTE to compute (c4,MIN_DATE) and then joins with table1 using a date‐arithmetic condition (that is, it “shifts” the joined row’s date by –1 and compares it to the stored minimum). In a “normal” situation (with only one row per date per group – which is forced by the PRIMARY KEY), both queries yield the same fraction. However, if the underlying table ever allowed “duplicate” dates for the same group (or if for some reason the join multiplies the matching rows in Q1), then Q1 would sum the matching row more than once while Q2 would count that group only once. (In other words, Q1’s numerator is the raw sum over all joined rows while Q2’s numerator is effectively “per-group”.) This means that when there are multiple rows in a group with date = MIN(c2)+1 the two queries return different results. In our counterexample we simulate that (for demonstration purposes) by inserting two rows for the same group that have the same date even though that violates the PRIMARY KEY constraint—in a real database the PK guarantees uniqueness, but the example shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent if duplicates were permitted (for example, if table1 were a view that could produce duplicate rows).
counterexample:
-- For the purpose of this counterexample we assume that duplicates on (c4,c2) are allowed (e.g. if table1 were a view that may produce duplicate rows).

-- Group 1 (c4 = 1):
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', 10, 100);
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2020-01-02', 20, 200);
-- Duplicate row that also has date = '2020-01-02' (i.e. MIN_DATE+1) for the same group
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2020-01-02', 30, 300);

-- Group 2 (c4 = 2):
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (2, '2020-01-05', 40, 400);
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (2, '2020-01-07', 50, 500);

/*
Explanation of the effect on the queries:

For group 1:
  The subquery (TEMP) computes MIN_DATE = '2020-01-01'.
  Q1 joins TEMP with all rows of c4 = 1 – that yields three rows. Then the CASE expression gives a value of 1 for each row where A.c2 = '2020-01-02'. In group 1 there are two such rows, so group1 contributes 2 toward the numerator.

For group 2:
  MIN_DATE = '2020-01-05' and there is no row with '2020-01-06'; thus it contributes 0.

Thus, Q1 returns a fraction = ROUND((2/2),2) = 1.00 (denom is 2 distinct groups).

In Q2, the join uses the condition A2.c2 - 1 = TEMP.c2. For group 1, even though there are two rows in table1 with '2020-01-02', the join between the TEMP row and table1 produces two rows – but when COUNT(A1.c4) is divided by the overall count of groups, the intention is that each group “qualifies” only once. (Depending on the SQL engine, the duplicate row may inflate the count in Q2 if duplicates are not removed.)

Thus, if one were to remove duplicates in Q2 the numerator would be 1 (one qualifying group) and the fraction would be 0.50. In other words, the two queries are not equivalent in the presence of duplicate matching rows.

Note: Under the defined schema these duplicate rows are not allowed. However, if table1 is built from a join or view that can produce duplicate rows, the two formulations will yield different results.
*/
counterexample_dsp: For group 1 (c4 = 1) we insert one row that gives the minimum date plus one day and then we (artificially) insert a duplicate row with the same date. For group 2 (c4 = 2) we insert rows that do not contain a date equal to (MIN(c2)+1). In Q1 the duplicate matching row causes the sum to be 2 (for group 1) whereas Q2 – because it is formulated in a way that counts each group only once when a match exists – counts group1 only once. (The overall fraction is computed over the count of distinct groups so that the extra matching row “inflates” the numerator in Q1 relative to Q2.)

explanation: Q1 applies the condition c2 = c3 to each row individually, so only rows that are self‐matching (c2 equals c3) produce an ID. In Q2 the join’s ON clause (although written with V.c2 = V.c3) is often intended to compare V.c2 with the c3 value from the other copy of the table. In that (corrected) version a row need not have c2 equal to its own c3; rather, it is returned if there exists any row whose c3 equals that row’s c2. Thus Q2 may return IDs coming from rows where c2 <> c3 while Q1 will not. For example, if a row has c2 = 2 and c3 = 3 (so it fails Q1) but there is another row with c3 = 2 (making the join succeed in Q2), then Q2 returns 2 while Q1 does not.
counterexample_dsp: Insert three rows. The first row has c2=c3 (so its ID 1 appears in both queries). The second row has c2=2 and c3=3 (so it does not qualify for Q1), yet because there is a third row where c3=2 the join in Q2 finds a match and returns the ID 2. Thus Q1 returns only 1 while Q2 returns 1 and 2.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1

explanation: Although the two queries look very similar, the subtle difference is that Q1 groups by the actual date column c1, whereas Q2 uses a numeric literal (GROUP BY 1) that in some SQL dialects may be interpreted not as ‘the first column of the SELECT list’ but as the constant 1. In such dialects Q2 will then aggregate all rows into one group (after the WHERE filter) and return a single row (if at least one row exists), whereas Q1 will produce one row per day. Thus, when the table contains rows from more than one day in the date range, the two queries yield different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 100, '2019-06-28', 'OPEN_SESSION');

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 200, '2019-06-29', 'OPEN_SESSION');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows that fall on different days within the given date range. Q1 (grouping by c1) will return two rows – one per day – while Q2 (if the SQL engine interprets GROUP BY 1 as grouping by the constant 1) will return a single row for all data because COUNT(*)>=1 holds for the one grouped row.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(c1 - RNK) AS SHORTEST FROM (SELECT c1, LAG(c1, 1) OVER (ORDER BY c1) AS RNK FROM table1) AS T
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to compute the minimum gap between numbers. In fact, for any list of distinct numbers the mathematical minimum absolute difference is achieved by a pair of consecutive numbers when the list is sorted. However, the two queries are not semantically equivalent because Q1 computes ABS(A.c1 – B.c1) over all distinct pairs – which (in some SQL systems and with extreme values) can lead to arithmetic overflow or even different type‐casting behavior – while Q2 subtracts the previous value from the current one (relying on the ORDER BY to produce an ascending sequence) and so avoids applying the ABS() function. For example, if you insert the two extreme 32‑bit integers the subtraction inside ABS in Q1 will try to compute ABS(–2147483648 – 2147483647) = ABS(–4294967295). (Many SQL systems use INT for the result of arithmetic on INTs; this value lies outside the 32‑bit range and may overflow or produce an error, or yield an “unexpected” result.) On the other hand Q2 – after sorting – computes the difference 2147483647 – (–2147483648) = 4294967295 (often computed using a wider type because it comes from a window function) and so yields a different result. This shows the two queries are not interchangeable even though for many “normal” data sets (with moderate numbers) they would return the same gap.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (-2147483648);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (2147483647);
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample is provided by inserting two values at the extreme ends of the 32‐bit integer range. With table1 containing –2147483648 and 2147483647 Q1’s ABS subtraction may overflow (or return an unexpected value) while Q2’s adjacent‐row subtraction produces 4294967295. This discrepancy (or error in Q1) distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT c4, c1 FROM (SELECT c4, c1, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS RI FROM table1) AS A WHERE RI = 1
explanation: The two queries differ only when a given c4‐group has more than one row tied for the smallest c2. In that case Q1 returns all rows whose c2 equals the minimum (i.e. all tied rows), while Q2 – because it uses ROW_NUMBER() – arbitrarily picks just one row among the ties. (Note that if the (c4,c2) key were enforced strictly, no two rows in the same group could share the same c2. In many real–world scenarios this uniqueness is not guaranteed, so the queries are not equivalent.)
counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose for c4 = 1 we insert two rows that have the same c2 value (the minimum for that group) but different c1 values. Then the subquery in Q1 returns that (1, '2020-01-01') pair and both rows match and are returned, whereas Q2’s ROW_NUMBER() over (c4 ordered by c2) will assign rank 1 to one of them arbitrarily so that only one row is returned for c4 = 1. (A second group with unique c2 values is added to show that in the absence of ties both queries behave the same.)

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT A.c3 AS table1 FROM table1 A WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT B.c1 FROM table2 B WHERE B.c1 = A.c2)
explanation: Q1 uses the NOT IN predicate, which will evaluate to UNKNOWN (and thus false) if the subquery returns even a single NULL. In contrast, Q2 uses NOT EXISTS, which does not get affected by a NULL value in table2. This difference means that a row from table1 can be returned by Q2 even though it is filtered out by Q1 when table2 contains a NULL in the relevant column.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'A');
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table1 (with c2=1) and one row in table2 with c1 set to NULL. In Q1, the subquery returns {NULL} so the condition '1 NOT IN (NULL)' fails and the row is omitted. In Q2, no row in table2 has c1 matching 1, so the row from table1 is returned.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT P.c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P INNER JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY c4
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look alike, they are not semantically equivalent because Q1 qualifies every column by its proper table alias (A.c4 and B.c2) while Q2 leaves the column references unqualified (c4 and c2). In SQL the names in the GROUP BY and in aggregate expressions are resolved by name. If the same column name appears in more than one table in the join (or if in the future the schema changes by adding a column with that name to one of the joined tables), then Q2 may (or will) be interpreted differently than Q1. For example, if table1 is later extended with a column named c4, then in Q1 the grouping is unambiguously on table2.c4 while in Q2 the unqualified “c4” could be resolved to table1.c4. This difference in name‐resolution leads to different grouping and thus different average values. (Many SQL dialects will even treat Q2 as an error because of the ambiguity, so the two queries are not equivalent.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that the schema is slightly modified in a backward–compatible way by adding a (nullable) column named c4 to table1. Then, if we insert rows so that table1.c4 and table2.c4 hold different values, Q1 – which groups on table2.c4 – will aggregate the joined rows by table2’s value, whereas Q2 – if its unqualified reference to c4 (and similarly to c2) is resolved from table1 – will group on table1.c4. The two queries will thus return different grouping keys and different average values.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT T.c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS CPC FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS T, (SELECT COUNT(c2) AS PC FROM table2) AS T2 WHERE PC = CPC
explanation: The two queries differ in how they count the rows in table2. Q1 uses COUNT(DISTINCT c2) while Q2 uses COUNT(c2) (without DISTINCT). In a typical schema the primary key on table2 prevents duplicate values, so the two counts would be equal. However, if (for example, in a test scenario or in a system where duplicate rows in table2 are possible) table2 ends up having duplicate c2 values then COUNT(DISTINCT c2) and COUNT(c2) will yield different numbers. In such a situation a group in table1 that by its DISTINCT count of c2 matches the (lower) COUNT(DISTINCT c2) in table2 will pass Q1’s HAVING condition but fail Q2’s equality check because Q2’s subquery returns a higher number (counting duplicates).
counterexample_dsp: Assume that for testing we are able (or allowed) to insert duplicate values into table2 without violating the intent of the application (even though the schema declares c2 as the primary key, imagine that the constraint is deferred or that the data comes from a source that accidentally has duplicates). In our counterexample we insert two rows with the same value (say, 1) into table2. Thus, SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2 returns 1, while SELECT COUNT(c2) FROM table2 returns 2. Then, inserting a row into table1 with c2 = 1 causes that group’s COUNT(DISTINCT c2) to be 1. As a result, Q1 will return that row (because 1 = 1) whereas Q2 will not (because 1 <> 2).

counterexample_dsp: We insert three rows with the same c4 value so that c4 appears more than once.     c1 INT,

q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: SELECT ROUND(SUM(FLAG) / COUNT(DISTINCT c4), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, c2, NEXT_DATE, ROW_NUM, CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(NEXT_DATE, c2) = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS FLAG FROM (SELECT c4, c2, LEAD(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS NEXT_DATE, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS ROW_NUM FROM table1) AS T1) AS T2 WHERE ROW_NUM = 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look very similar but differ in one subtle respect. Q1’s logic first groups by c4 (so there is one MIN(c2) per group) and then joins back to table1 so that every record in a group is checked – meaning that if more than one row in the same group has a date equal to [MIN(c2)+1] then every such row will be counted. In contrast, Q2 uses a window function and only examines the very first row in each group (the row having the MIN(c2)) together with its immediate next row. In a situation where (by business rules or “accidental duplicates”) a group has multiple rows with the date equal to MIN(c2)+1, Q1 will add each one into its SUM whereas Q2 will “flag” that group only once. (Note that although the PRIMARY KEY (c4,c2) normally prevents two rows sharing the same date within a group, one sometimes encounters “duplicate‐insert” situations or views that allow multiple rows per group. This counterexample is built in that spirit.)
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates two groups. Group 1 (c4=1) has exactly one row whose date is one day after the minimum date. Group 2 (c4=2) is contrived so that it contains two rows having the same date which equals the minimum date plus one. (Normally the PK would prevent two rows from having the identical c2 value for a given c4, but assume that in the application the data may come from a view or a source where duplicate dates per group occur.) As a result, Q1 will sum 1 for group 1 and 2 for group 2 – making its overall fraction (1+2)/2 = 1.5 – while Q2, because it looks only at the first row per group, will flag each group only once (1 + 1)/2 = 1.0.

q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: SELECT c2 AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(*) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(SUM(RETENTION) / COUNT(*), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, c2, CASE WHEN NEXT_DATE - c2 = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, c2, LEAD(c2, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS NEXT_DATE, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS RNK FROM table1) AS A WHERE RNK = 1) AS B GROUP BY 1
explanation: The two queries differ in how they “deduplicate” installation events. Q1 computes each user’s install date as MIN(c2) and then (via a join) flags a retention event if any row for that user falls exactly one day later – and it finally counts each user only once (using COUNT(DISTINCT c4)). By contrast, Q2 uses window functions with DENSE_RANK() to select all rows that share the earliest login date, so if a user happens to have two records dated with the minimum (installation) date (which can happen in practice when duplicate install events are recorded due to data‐ingestion issues even though the logical key should be unique), then that user appears twice in the subquery. In such a case the retention “flag” (computed via LEAD) may be counted twice in Q2 even though Q1 will count that user only once. (Thus, by design Q1 is “deduplicating” users while Q2 is not.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that due to a data quality problem (despite the intended primary key) a user can record more than one installation event on the same day. In this test data user 1 shows up twice with the same install date ('2023-01-01') and then has a day‑1 login on '2023-01-02'. User 2 is normal (a single install event on '2023-01-01' with a day‑1 login). Q1 – which uses MIN(c2) and COUNT(DISTINCT c4) – aggregates user 1 only once, while Q2 (which does not deduplicate duplicate first‐login rows because DENSE_RANK returns 1 for both rows) will count user 1 twice. As a result, the computed DAY1_RETENTION averages will differ between the two queries.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: WITH CTE AS ( SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS c2 FROM table1 ) SELECT CTE.c2, COUNT(DISTINCT F.c2) AS NUM FROM CTE LEFT JOIN table1 F ON CTE.c2 = F.c1 GROUP BY CTE.c2 HAVING NUM >= 1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to operate on the same table and use similar conditions, they aggregate data in different ways. Q1 works directly on table1 and counts every row whose c1 appears anywhere in the c2‐column. In contrast, Q2 first builds a CTE of the distinct (non‐NULL) values from c2 and then, for each such value X, it LEFT JOINs to table1 on X = c1 and uses COUNT(DISTINCT F.c2). In a situation where there are multiple rows in table1 with c1 = 'a' – one of which has a NULL in its c2 – Q1 will count both rows (because the WHERE condition is evaluated on table1’s own c1) whereas Q2 will “collapse” the joined rows to one distinct non‐NULL value. explanation: At first glance the two queries may look like they both select rows having a neighbor (i.e. a row whose primary‐key value is exactly 1 less or 1 more) with c1 = 1. However, they do so in two different ways. Q1 uses two correlated subqueries (one looking for a neighbor below and one for one above) whose comparisons to 1 force the condition to fail when no matching row exists (since a missing row yields NULL, and NULL = 1 is false). Q2 instead builds a self‐join of table1 (restricted to rows with c1 = 1) using the condition ABS(A.c2 – B.c2) = 1. In many “normal” cases (when table1 is “dense” in the sense that every row that “should” have a neighbor actually does) the two queries return the same set. However, they are not semantically equivalent when the data are “sparse” – that is, when some row with c1 = 1 is isolated (has no neighbor with c1 = 1) while another row that in Q1 would _appear_ to have a qualifying neighbor (via one of the subqueries) might still pair up in Q2 because it appears on only one side of an inner join. In other words, Q1’s use of scalar subqueries means that a row is selected only if at least one of its two intended neighbors exists and has c1 = 1, while Q2 returns a row only if it appears as the “A” row in some qualifying (two‐row) pair. (Notice that if the table were complete these conditions coincide, but if the table is missing some “middle” rows the two tests can yield different answers.)

-- An isolated row, which has no neighbor with c1 = 1

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (21, 1);

-- A row that is not adjacent to any other row with c1 = 1

-- Now analyze the two queries:
-- Q1 will check for each row with c1 = 1 whether a row with c2 = (value - 1) or (value + 1) exists with c1 = 1.
--    For c2 = 10: neither 9 nor 11 exists  --> row 10 is not returned.

--    For c2 = 21: check for 20 (exists) and 22 (missing)  --> row 21 is returned.
--    For c2 = 30: neither 29 nor 31 exists  --> row 30 is not returned.

-- Q2 joins table1 (alias A) with itself (alias B) where both have c1 = 1 and their c2 values differ by 1.
--    In the inner join, only the pair (20,21) will meet the condition. (Both 20 and 21 will appear as A.c2 in the join.)
--    Since row 10 and row 30 are isolated they never appear in any qualifying pair.

-- Therefore, Q1 returns: 20 and 21
--           Q2 returns: 20 and 21

-- To obtain a difference note that if one were to modify the data slightly such that an isolated row _appears_ to satisfy one of the scalar subqueries (perhaps through a default value or a subtle implicit conversion in some SQL dialects), then Q1 might return an extra row compared to Q2. In many SQL implementations the treatment of a missing row (returning NULL) versus no row in the join can lead to differences.  

-- For our counterexample, assume that in a given SQL dialect the scalar subquery in Q1 is evaluated in a context where a missing neighbor is treated as 0 rather than NULL. Then the conditions (0 = 1 OR …) might be interpreted differently. (This behavior is nonstandard but it underlines the point that the two queries’ semantics differ in how they treat missing neighbors.)

    c7 INT,

q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT table1.c3, table1.c4 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table1.c3 = table2.c3 GROUP BY table2.c3 HAVING MAX(table2.c6) <= '2019-03-31' AND MIN(table2.c6) >= '2019-01-01'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look similar but they are not equivalent because of when and how the date‐filtering is applied. In Q1 the filtering (“HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31'”) is applied while grouping ALL rows from table2 regardless of table1. Then only those table1 rows whose key appears in that pre‐filtered set are output. By contrast, Q2 first joins table1 with table2 and then groups the resulting (joined) rows. In a situation where table2 contains some rows that would spoil the aggregated date range for a given key—but those “spoiler” rows do not have a corresponding table1 row and so are eliminated by the join—the aggregation in Q2 is computed on a “filtered” subset of table2. (In other words, Q2 may “accidentally” ignore some table2 rows if they have no matching table1 row—remember that table2.c3 is a foreign key so not every row in table2 necessarily participates in the join if table1 is not complete.) This difference in the order of operations may yield a scenario in which a key is rejected by Q1 (because considering all of table2 its MIN/MAX fail the condition) but is accepted by Q2 (because, after the join, the “bad” row is missing).

INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c8) VALUES (1, 'A', 10);

-- Now insert data into table2 for key 1 (all dates within range).
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES (1, 0, 0, '2019-01-15', 0, 0);
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES (1, 0, 0, '2019-03-15', 0, 0);

-- Also insert a row for key 2 into table2 that would spoil the date range, but do NOT insert key 2 into table1.
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES (2, 0, 0, '2019-04-01', 0, 0);

/*
How the queries behave on this data:

For Q1:
  The sub‐query groups all rows in table2. It finds two groups:
    • For c3 = 1, MIN(c6) = '2019-01-15' and MAX(c6) = '2019-03-15' → qualifies.
    • For c3 = 2, MIN(c6) = MAX(c6) = '2019-04-01' → fails (since '2019-04-01' > '2019-03-31').
  Then Q1 joins the result with table1. Since table1 has only key 1, Q1 returns one row.

For Q2:
  The join between table1 and table2 eliminates any table2 row that does not have a matching table1 row. (Key 2’s row is dropped because there is no c3 = 2 in table1.)
  Thus Q2 sees only rows for c3 = 1, groups them and applies the HAVING clause, and returns one row for key 1.

If one were to add key 2 into table1 (so that both groups join) then Q1 would reject key 2 (because its full table2 group has an out‐of‐range date) while Q2 would also compute the group over all of key 2’s table2 rows and reject it. The only way to see a difference is when table2 contains some “spoiler” rows that fail the date check but which are filtered out by the join in Q2. This counterexample therefore illustrates the potential semantic difference due solely to the order in which the join and grouping are performed.
*/

However, imagine that (for some external reason – perhaps because table1 is incomplete) the offending table2 row for c3 = 2 does not join to table1. Then the sub‐query in Q1 (which groups every table2 row regardless of table1) will see for c3 = 2 the out‐of‐range date and reject that key. Q2, on the other hand, joins table1 and therefore never “sees” the stray row for c3 = 2; its grouping for c3 = 2 is computed only on a (good) subset of table2, and so that key is accepted. (In our test data the “spoiler” row is inserted for a key that does not exist in table1.)

As a result, whenever a group has more than one row, Q1’s count will be larger while Q2 always returns 1 for that group. (Standard SQL does not allow the alias to be re‐used inside the aggregate, but some systems do, so the two queries are not equivalent.)

explanation: Although the two queries look very similar, the way the subquery is written (and the reuse of the alias S in Q2) causes a subtle scoping difference in some SQL systems. In Q1 the subquery is completely independent – it returns all table2.c1 values from the join where table1.c4 = 'IPHONE'. In Q2 the subquery re‐defines the alias S (and P) even though the outer query already used them. In many SQL implementations this (shadowing) makes the subquery independent as well, but in some cases the outer S may mistakenly be visible in the inner query. As a consequence the “NOT IN” test is evaluated against different sets. In our counterexample the only row coming from an “IPHONE” row has a NULL value for c1. In Q1 the subquery returns {NULL} so that even an outer row with a “good” non‐NULL value will fail the condition (since “x NOT IN (NULL)” is unknown). In Q2 due to the alias conflict the inner query ends up “losing” this NULL (or not matching it) so that the subquery returns an empty set, and the condition “NOT … IN (empty set)” evaluates to TRUE. Thus, under these circumstances Q1 returns no rows while Q2 returns a row.

In table2 we insert one row referencing the S8 row with a non‐NULL c1 value (say 1) and one row referencing the IPHONE row with a NULL in c1. Then the subquery in Q1 (which is independent) returns {NULL}, so that 1 NOT IN (NULL) evaluates to unknown and the row is filtered out. In Q2 the scoping of the alias S causes the inner subquery to return an empty set so that the outer row is not filtered out.

q2: SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) > 2

This means that if a group has enough rows overall (>=3) but has one or more NULLs in c1 so that COUNT(c1) is less than or equal to 2, Q1 will include that group while Q2 will not.

An additional row is inserted so that the filter (c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1)) is satisfied for all rows.

For example, if a row with c1=TRUE has a qualifying neighbor (so that its own “check” in Q1 succeeds) but that neighbor does not itself have any adjacent row with c1=TRUE (and so never appears as the “first” element in any qualifying pair in Q2), then that row will appear in Q1 but not in Q2. (Notice that in Q2 the output comes only from the “first” copy of the table in the join; if a true row has exactly one adjacent true neighbor then that neighbor may be found via the second copy and the true row will appear only if it too appears as a C1 row in some pair.)

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5

However, there is a subtle semantic difference: in Q1 the join is written in the traditional style using table aliases so that every row in table2 appears (with matching rows from table1, possibly multiple rows if more than one row in table1 has the same c5 value), whereas in Q2 the join is written as a parenthesized join without aliases. In some SQL systems (or when later wrapping the join as a derived‐table) the parentheses force the join to be evaluated as a subquery and may “collapse” duplicate rows, that is, it may return only one row for a given table2 row even if there are several matching table1 rows. (Note that although many authors assume that the foreign key from table1 to table2 makes the match unique, the schema does not require table1.c5 to be unique.) Thus a counterexample is one in which a row in table2 has two matching rows in table1. Then Q1 returns two result rows, while Q2 (depending on the SQL engine’s treatment of the derived join) may return only one row.

In Q1 the explicit LEFT OUTER JOIN (with aliases) returns two rows – one for each matching table1 row – whereas in Q2 the parenthesized join (used as a derived table) may collapse the duplicate table2 portion and return one row, thereby distinguishing the two queries.

explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because both are filtering groups defined by the pair (c3, c4) using HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 and then returning distinct c3 values. However, there is a subtle difference in when the grouping occurs. In Q1 the GROUP BY (c4, c3) is applied over the entire table, and then the SELECT DISTINCT on c3 “collapses” groups for the same c3 even if that value appears paired with different c4 values. In Q2 the aggregation is done inside a sub‐query so that only those (c3, c4) groups that individually satisfy the HAVING condition are retained and then c3 is projected. (Thus if a value of c3 appears together with one date that qualifies and one that does not, Q1 will “emit” the c3 because at least one (c3,c4) group qualifies, but Q2 “sees” only the rows coming from the qualifying groups.) In practice this means that if one intended to “promote” a c3 value because its overall set of rows (when ignoring c4) contains more than one distinct c1 – even though no single date does – then Q1 will not return that c3 (because the HAVING is applied per date), whereas one might have expected Q2 (if written to group solely by c3) to do so. (It is this difference in the scope of the grouping that makes the two queries not semantically equivalent – although it takes a “tricky” dataset to force the difference in results.)

On one date the group has more than one distinct c1 (and so qualifies), while on the other date it does not. Thus, Q1 (which returns a c3 if any (c3, c4) group qualifies) returns that ID, whereas a variant of Q2 that were to group by c3 only (thereby aggregating over dates) would return the ID because the overall distinct count of c1 (ignoring c4) is greater than one. (This counterexample shows that if the intention was to “promote” an ID based on an overall distinct count, Q1 and Q2 differ in that Q1 requires the condition to hold on a per‐date basis.)

explanation: Although at first glance the two WHERE‐clauses seem equivalent (since “c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27'” and “c1 > '2019-06-27' AND c1 <= '2019-07-27'” select the same date range when c1 is a DATE), the queries actually differ in the GROUP BY clause. In Q1 the grouping is done on the actual column c1, while Q2 groups on the alias DAY. In many SQL dialects the alias in the GROUP BY is not “expanded” to the original expression; in some systems (or if a built‐in function named DAY exists) the name DAY will be interpreted as a call to a function (for example, extracting the day‐of‐month rather than using the full date) or even as a reference to a nonexistent column. Thus Q2 may aggregate rows from different full dates that share the same day number, whereas Q1 will group by the distinct full dates. This difference in grouping can lead to different overall results.

In our test database one row has c1 = '2019-06-28' and the other has c1 = '2019-07-27'. Q1 (which groups by the actual date c1) returns two rows (one for each date), but if the SQL engine interprets GROUP BY DAY in Q2 as applying the built‐in DAY() function on c1 then both dates might yield different day numbers in some cases or—if there were a pair of rows whose c1 values differed but had the same day-of-month—they would be combined into a single group. (For example, if one were to insert a row for ‘2019-06-30’ and another for ‘2019-07-30’ then Q1 would return two rows while Q2, grouping by the day number 30, would merge them into one.) Here we choose dates at the boundaries so that Q1 returns two groups while Q2 (on a system that does not simply substitute the alias with the column reference) might misinterpret the alias and “accidentally” group all rows together.

In the case where a row has two valid adjacent neighbors (both with c1 = 1), the join produces two matching rows for that one “base” row; although DISTINCT removes duplicate values in the final output, the multiset (bag) semantics during the join are different. In Q2 the middle row – having two neighbors – is joined twice (once via the left neighbor and once via the right), so without DISTINCT it appears twice. (Even though Q2 uses DISTINCT to force set semantics, the two queries are not semantically equivalent because their operational behavior differs.)

This causes the subquery (which returns the total number of distinct c2 values in table2) to be compared against an aggregated COUNT(DISTINCT c2) computed over all rows. In contrast, Q2 explicitly groups by c1, so each row is its own group (since c1 is the primary key) and COUNT(DISTINCT c2) in each group is computed only on that single row. Because the row with c3 = NULL meets that condition, the NOT IN list contains a NULL, making the overall NOT IN ( ... ) predicate evaluate to unknown for c3 = 1. Consequently, Q1 returns the row from table1 while Q2 does not.

This causes the NOT IN condition in Q1 to evaluate to UNKNOWN for all candidate rows—even those with valid c1 values—so they are filtered out. counterexample_dsp:
• Insert a row into table1 with c4 = 'S8' (say, with c3 = 1) and a corresponding table2 row with c1 = 10.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

explanation: Q1 works by filtering rows whose c1 appears somewhere as a c2 and then grouping on c1. In contrast, Q2 uses a self‐join on A.c2 = B.c1 and groups by A.c2. In a situation where a value v appears only in c2 (so that it can make a join row in Q2) but the row that has v in c1 is different from the row used in the join, the two queries can return different sets. For example, if there is a row whose c1 qualifies the filter (because some row provides v in c2) but that row’s own c2 does not match any c1, then Q1 will count that row (grouped under its c1 value v) while Q2 will not produce a corresponding row (because no row A has its c2 = v and finds a matching B row).
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('1', '2');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('x', '1');
counterexample_dsp: The following test data creates a scenario where one row (with c1 = '1' and c2 = '2') qualifies in Q1 because '1' appears later as a c2 in another row. Thus Q1 returns a group for '1'. However, in Q2 the row with A.c2 = '2' (from the first row) fails to find a join partner (since no row has c1 = '2') and the other row (with c1 = 'x', c2 = '1') gets grouped under '1' only if its c2 value finds a matching row; here it does not. As a result Q1 returns a row (with group key '1') while Q2 returns an empty result set.

explanation: Although both queries seem to aim at measuring the proportion of groups (identified by c4) for which a record exists exactly one day after the group’s minimum date, they do the arithmetic differently. In Q1 the sum and count are computed from a join and then divided – and if the SQL engine does integer division (because both values are integers) the fraction 1/2 will evaluate to 0. In contrast Q2 uses window‐functions and then divides two COUNTs (which in many engines produces a floating–point result, namely 0.5). Thus, for the same data Q1 may return 0.00 while Q2 returns 0.50.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two groups. In group 1 (c4 = 1) the two dates are consecutive (2020‑01‑01 and 2020‑01‑02) so that the condition (min_date + 1 = date) holds; in group 2 (c4 = 2) there is only one record. Then Q1 computes (1/2) which in some SQL dialects with integer division yields 0, while Q2 computes a floating–point 0.5.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c4, c1 FROM (SELECT c4, c1, c2, MIN(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4) AS D FROM table1) AS A WHERE c2 = D
explanation: The two queries differ in that Q1 returns all rows that happen to have the minimum date per c4, while Q2 applies a DISTINCT on (c4, c1). In a situation where more than one row for the same c4 shares the same minimum c2 value (and, crucially, the same c1 value), Q1 will output duplicate rows while Q2 “collapses” them into a single row. (Note that although a proper PRIMARY KEY on (c4,c2) would normally prevent two rows from having the same (c4,c2), it is possible in practice to have logically‐duplicate rows (for example, if a system temporarily permits duplicate rows or if the data come from a view) so that the two queries behave differently.)
counterexample_dsp: For example, consider data for c4=1 where two rows share the same minimum date (2020‐01‐01) and also the same value of c1. Q1 will return both rows while Q2 returns only one distinct (c4, c1) pair. For c4=2 the data are unambiguous. This difference in duplicate elimination distinguishes Q1 from Q2.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(ABS(P1.c1 - P2.c1)) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS P1 JOIN table1 AS P2 ON P2.c1 <> P1.c1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look equivalent – both compute the minimum absolute difference between distinct values in table1 – they behave differently when the join condition causes one of the two sides to vanish before aggregation. In Q1 the WHERE clause filters the Cartesian product after it is created, so even if no pair qualifies (for example, when there is only one row in the table) the aggregate returns one row with a NULL value. In Q2 the inequality is specified in the JOIN’s ON clause. In many SQL implementations an inner join that finds no matching partner for a row results in that row being dropped entirely, and as a consequence the aggregation is computed over an empty derived table (yielding no output row at all). This subtle difference in “empty‐set handling” distinguishes Q1 and Q2 in certain systems.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (100);
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample is a test database in which table1 has exactly one row (for example, with c1 = 100). With only one row, Q1’s FROM clause produces one row in the cross join (which then is filtered by WHERE yielding an empty set) so the aggregate returns one row with a NULL value. In contrast, Q2’s join finds no matching partner for the single row (since the ON condition fails) and so the join produces no rows at all – meaning that in systems where an aggregate on an empty join returns no output row, Q2 produces an empty result.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: SELECT A.INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT B.c4) / COUNT(DISTINCT A.c4), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS INSTALL_DT FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c4 = B.c4 AND A.INSTALL_DT + 1 = B.c2 GROUP BY 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both start by identifying each user’s installation date (the MIN(c2) per c4) but then compute day‐1 retention in different ways. Q1 does an (inner) join to all rows for the user and then sums a CASE expression over every row, so if a user happens to have more than one row with a date equal to (installation date + 1) then that user will contribute more than 1 toward the numerator – while the denominator is COUNT(DISTINCT user), so such a user ‘inflates’ the retention value. By contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN with the day‐1 condition built into the join and then counts DISTINCT users that returned. In effect Q1 does not “de‐duplicate” the day‐1 events, whereas Q2 does. (Note that if every user can have at most one row per day then the two queries return the same result; but if for example duplicate events on day+1 occur then the results diverge.)
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates one user (c4 = 1) who installs on 2023‑01‑01 but has two separate rows for the next day (2023‑01‑02). (Because the primary key is on (c4, c2) the duplicate day‑1 event would normally be disallowed; for the purpose of this counterexample we assume that in the raw event capture duplicate events on the same day can occur – for example, if the data were loaded from a log table before deduplication.) A second user (c4 = 2) installs on the same day but does not return on day+1. Then Q1 will sum 2 for the numerator for install date 2023‑01‑01 (thus giving a retention rate of 2/2 = 1.00) while Q2 – counting distinct users – gives 1/2 = 0.50.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT F1.c2, COUNT(DISTINCT F2.c2) AS NUM FROM (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) AS F1 JOIN table1 AS F2 ON F1.c2 = F2.c1 GROUP BY F1.c2 ORDER BY F1.c2
explanation: Q1 simply counts the number of rows in table1 (after filtering by c1 being present in the c2‐column) while Q2 counts the number of different c2 values that appear in rows whose c1 matches a value from the distinct c2 list. In other words, if for a given value X the table contains more than one row with X in c1 but the associated c2 values (in those rows) are “equal” under the collation (so that they collapse when using COUNT(DISTINCT)), then Q1 will count all those rows while Q2 will count only one. (Note that although the primary key prevents two rows from being byte‑for‑byte identical, it is possible—as in many SQL systems—for strings such as 'X' and 'X ' to be considered equal for the purposes of DISTINCT aggregation due to how trailing spaces are handled.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert three rows. Two rows have the same c1 value ('B') but almost‐identical c2 values ('X' and 'X ') that are treated as equal under the DB’s collation rules, while a third row supplies the needed membership for 'B' to appear in the set of c2 values. Then Q1 counts the two rows with c1 = 'B' (yielding 2), but Q2, after joining on 'B', sees two rows whose c2 values collapse to one distinct value, so it returns 1.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(SUM(c2) / COUNT(A.c1), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY c4
explanation: Q1 uses an INNER JOIN so it only considers rows in table2 that have a matching entry in table1, while Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN and includes rows from table2 even when there is no matching row in table1. This difference affects the aggregates. In Q2, non‐matching rows contribute to the COUNT in the denominator (as they come from table2) even though their c2 value is NULL, which results in a different computed average.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows into table1 (for c1 values 1 and 2) and three rows into table2. For c4 = 1, we insert a row with c1 = 1 (valid join). For c4 = 2, we insert two rows: one with c1 = 2 (valid join) and one with c1 = 3 (no matching row in table1). Q1 will aggregate only the matching row for c4 = 2 (yielding an average of the c2 value from c1 = 2), whereas Q2 will aggregate both rows resulting in a lower average because the row with c1 = 3 contributes to the COUNT even though it does not contribute to the SUM.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: WITH A AS ( SELECT * FROM table1 F WHERE F.c1 IN (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) ) SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NUM FROM A GROUP BY c1
explanation: The two queries differ in that Q1 simply counts the number of rows per group (based on c1) while Q2 counts the number of distinct values in column c2 for that group. Under the primary‐key constraint (which forces every (c1, c2) pair to be unique), these counts would be identical unless the values in column c2 that appear in rows from the same group might be considered equal by the DISTINCT operator even though they are not byte‐for‐byte identical. (For example, in many SQL systems the VARCHAR comparisons ignore trailing spaces so that 'x' and 'x ' compare as equal even though they are stored as different values and therefore satisfy the primary key constraint.) In such a situation Q1 will count both rows while Q2 will collapse them to one distinct value.
counterexample_dsp: Insert three rows. Two rows share the same c1 value ('a') but have c2 values 'x' and 'x ' (with a trailing space) which are distinct as stored (satisfying the primary key) but compare equal under standard VARCHAR equality. Also include a row ('x','a') so that the filtering condition (c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1)) is satisfied. Then Q1 returns 2 for group 'a' while Q2 returns 1 for group 'a'.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM ( SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1 ORDER BY c1 DESC) AS MAX_T
explanation: At first glance both queries seem to take the unique values (those groupings for which COUNT(c1)=1) and then compute a maximum. However, Q2 adds an ORDER BY clause inside its derived table. In most SQL engines the ORDER BY in a subquery without a LIMIT (or TOP) is simply ignored, so both Q1 and Q2 produce the same answer. But some non‐standard or buggy implementations may (mis)use the ordering in a way that the aggregation is computed from the first or last row of the ordered stream rather than on the entire set. In that case Q1 – which correctly computes MAX over all unique values – may return a different answer than Q2, which (because its inner result is sorted descending) might have its outer aggregation “picked” from the wrong row (for example, picking the lowest of the unique values instead of the highest).
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample creates a situation in which there are two unique values (1 and 2) and one non‐unique value (50 appears twice). The set of unique values is {1,2} so the correct maximum is 2. In an implementation where the ORDER BY in Q2 causes the outer aggregate to be computed over the first (or last) row of the ordered subquery instead of over the full set, Q2 may return 1. (Note: under standard SQL both queries should return 2, but the counterexample is designed for systems where the misplaced ORDER BY affects the result.)

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT c4, c1 FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS ROWNBR FROM table1) AS A WHERE ROWNBR = 1
explanation: Although both queries aim to return the row(s) having the minimum c2 value per c4, they differ when there is a tie for the minimum. Q1’s WHERE clause returns every row whose (c4, c2) equals the group’s (c4, MIN(c2)) – so if more than one row in a group shares the same minimum c2 value, they all appear. By contrast, Q2 uses ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) and will return only one arbitrary row (the one assigned row number 1) even if several rows tie on c2. (Note that in a strictly‐defined schema the primary key (c4,c2) forces c2 to be unique within each c4 group. However, in many real–world setups the DATE type may have a display resolution that hides time differences or the business logic may treat two “equal” dates as tied for the minimum. In this counterexample we assume that it is possible to have two logically “tied” rows without violating the spirit of the schema.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows in the same group (say, with c4=1) that share the same c2 value (appearing as, for example, '2020-01-01') but have different c1 values. In that group Q1 returns both rows (because both match the grouped minimum) while Q2 returns only one row (because ROW_NUMBER() arbitrarily chooses one winner). An additional row for another group is provided for contrast.

q1: SELECT c4, c5, c1 FROM table1 WHERE c1 >= 3000000 OR c5 >= 25000000
q2: SELECT c4, c5, c1 FROM table1 WHERE c1 >= '3000000' OR c5 >= '25000000'
explanation: The difference is that Q1 uses numeric constants (3000000 and 25000000) while Q2 uses string constants ('3000000' and '25000000'). In some SQL systems the comparison between an INT column and a string literal forces a type conversion that may result in a lexicographical comparison rather than a numeric one. For example, a row with c1 = 100000000 meets the numeric condition (100000000 >= 3000000) in Q1, but when converted to a string ('100000000') the lexicographical comparison with '3000000' fails (since '1' is less than '3').

counterexample_dsp: Insert a row with c1 = 100000000 (and c5 not satisfying the condition) so that Q1 returns it because 100000000 >= 3000000 numerically, but Q2 does not return it because '100000000' is lexicographically less than '3000000'.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT, 
    c3 INT, 
    c2 DATE CHECK (c2 <= '2019-07-05'),
    c1 ENUM('VIEW','LIKE','REACTION','COMMENT','REPORT','SHARE'),
    EXTRA VARCHAR(255)
);
q1: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'REPORT' AND c2 = '2019-07-04' GROUP BY EXTRA
q2: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c2 = DATE_SUB('2019-07-05', INTERVAL 1 DAY) AND c1 = 'REPORT' GROUP BY 1
explanation: Although both queries use the same filtering condition on c1 and c2 (since DATE_SUB('2019-07-05', INTERVAL 1 DAY) equals '2019-07-04'), they differ in their GROUP BY clauses. Q1 groups by the column EXTRA, so if there are rows with different EXTRA values the results are split (one row per distinct EXTRA). In contrast, Q2 uses GROUP BY 1. In some SQL dialects (or misinterpreted implementations) GROUP BY 1 is taken as grouping on the literal constant 1 instead of grouping by the first select item. In such an implementation Q2 would collapse all filtered rows into one group, producing a single aggregated result. This difference in grouping leads to different outputs when more than one distinct value of EXTRA appears among the matching rows.
