INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c2, c1, EXTRA) VALUES (1, 101, '2019-07-04', 'REPORT', 'ReasonA');
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c2, c1, EXTRA) VALUES (2, 102, '2019-07-04', 'REPORT', 'ReasonB');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows that have c1 = 'REPORT' and c2 = '2019-07-04' but with different EXTRA values. Q1 will produce two rows (one for each EXTRA) while Q2 (if it misinterprets GROUP BY 1 as grouping by the constant 1 rather than by the first column) will produce one row aggregating both.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 <= '2019-07-27' AND c1 >= DATE_SUB('2019-07-27', INTERVAL 29 DAY) GROUP BY c1
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem equivalent because they both appear to limit c1 to a fixed 30‐day window. However, the lower bound in Q1 is the literal '2019-06-28' while Q2 computes its lower bound as DATE_SUB('2019-07-27', INTERVAL 29 DAY). In many systems that works out the same, but if for any reason the date arithmetic (or its type‐casting rules) makes DATE_SUB return a value that is one day earlier than the literal (for example, if one inadvertently ends up with a lower bound of '2019-06-27') then Q2’s window becomes wider and more rows are included. This difference means that if a row exists with c1 = '2019-06-27', Q1 will not count it while Q2 will. This counterexample shows that, depending on how DATE_SUB is evaluated (and on subtle differences between date literals and computed dates), the two queries can yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: Insert three rows. One has c1 = '2019-06-27' (outside Q1’s window but inside Q2’s window if DATE_SUB returns '2019-06-27'), one with c1 = '2019-06-28' and one with c1 = '2019-07-27'. In an environment where DATE_SUB('2019-07-27', INTERVAL 29 DAY) evaluates to '2019-06-27', Q2 will include the extra day (06-27) while Q1 will not.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT IFNULL(MAX(A.c1),NULL) c1 FROM ( SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*)=1 ) A
explanation: The two queries differ in how they filter rows in the inner subquery. Q1 uses HAVING COUNT(c1)=1, which ignores NULL values (because COUNT(c1) does not count NULL) so that a group whose only row has a NULL in c1 is excluded. In contrast Q2 uses HAVING COUNT(*)=1, which counts the row even if c1 is NULL so that such a group is included. In some SQL systems this difference in the inner result set can lead to a different overall result (for example, the inner query of Q1 may yield no row while Q2 yields a row with a NULL value).
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample is to have table1 contain exactly one row with c1 = NULL. In that case, the GROUP BY produces one group (grouped by NULL). Q1’s HAVING COUNT(c1)=1 fails (since COUNT(c1) is 0 when the only value is NULL) so Q1’s derived table is empty, whereas Q2’s HAVING COUNT(*)=1 passes and its derived table has one row (with a NULL value). Then the outer MAX in Q1 is computed over an empty set (yielding NULL in many systems) while in Q2 it is computed over a set containing a NULL (which, when aggregated, also yields NULL). In SQL systems that distinguish “no row” from “row containing NULL” the results will differ.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT P.c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY P.c4
explanation: They look almost identical, but the subtle difference is the reference to c2. In Q1 the call AVG(B.c2) clearly takes the column c2 from table1 (alias B), while in Q2 the call AVG(c2) is unqualified. In many SQL dialects an unqualified column name is resolved by checking the FROM‐clause tables in left‐to‐right order. Thus if (and only if) table2 were ever extended with an extra column also named c2 then Q2 would use that column instead of table1.c2. In that case the two queries would produce different results. (In our counterexample we simulate that situation by “pretending” that table2 has an extra column c2 whose values differ from table1.c2.)
counterexample:
-- Note: This counterexample assumes that table2 has been extended with a column named c2 (even though the original schema does not include it).

-- Insert a row into table1
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c3, c2) VALUES (1, 'Alice', 10);

-- Insert a corresponding row into table2 (extended version, with an extra column c2 separate from table1's c2)
INSERT INTO table2 (c4, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 1, 100);

-- Running Q1:
--   SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS
--   FROM table2 AS A
--   INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1
--   GROUP BY A.c4;
-- will return: 1 | 10.00

-- Running Q2:
--   SELECT P.c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS
--   FROM table2 AS P
--   JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1
--   GROUP BY P.c4;
-- will return: 1 | 100.00

-- This demonstrates the semantic difference.
counterexample_dsp: Assume that in addition to the defined columns, table2 has been extended (for example, in a later migration) with a column c2. Then by inserting a row into table1 with c2 = 10 and a corresponding row into table2 with c2 = 100 (and with the same join key), Q1 will compute the average using table1.c2 (yielding 10) while Q2’s AVG(c2) (unqualified) will pick up table2.c2 (yielding 100). The difference in the data for c2 in the two tables is what drives the queries apart.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4
q2: SELECT c4, FIRST_LOGIN FROM (SELECT c4, c2 AS FIRST_LOGIN, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS RANK1 FROM table1) AS A WHERE RANK1 = 1
explanation: Although both queries return for each c4 the smallest c2 value, they behave differently in the presence of ties. In Q1 the condition is written as an unqualified “c1” and is applied after the LEFT JOIN has been performed; thus if a matching row from table1 exists but its c1 value is 1500 (which does not satisfy c1 < 1000), that row is kept in the join (so c1 is 1500) and then the WHERE filter removes it. In Q2 the condition is written as B.c1 (explicitly naming the table1 alias). Under some optimizers this condition is “pushed” into the join so that when table1’s row fails the filter it is effectively discarded in the join – causing the LEFT JOIN to produce a NULL in place of table1’s columns. As a result, Q2 “rescues” the table2 row (with a NULL for c1) while Q1 filters it out. INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 1500);
counterexample_dsp: Create one row in table2 (with c2 = 1) and a matching row in table1 (with c2 = 1) whose c1 value is 1500 (≥1000). In Q1 the join succeeds and the row carries c1 = 1500, so the WHERE clause (1500 < 1000 OR 1500 IS NULL) fails and the row is eliminated. In Q2, however, the condition on B.c1 is pushed into the join; the row from table1 does not satisfy (B.c1 < 1000 OR B.c1 IS NULL) and so is “discarded” during the join. The LEFT JOIN then yields a row from table2 with a NULL for B.c1 – which now satisfies the WHERE clause (NULL IS NULL) so the row is returned.

In Q1 the subquery (SELECT c1 FROM table2) returns a NULL, and because 'NOT IN' with a NULL in the list yields no matches (even if the value doesn't equal NULL), Q1 returns no rows from table1. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN to match table1 rows with table2 rows on equality. Since NULL does not match any value, the join fails and O.c2 is NULL, so Q2 correctly returns the corresponding row from table1.

INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);

In Q1 the NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2) condition fails due to the presence of NULL, while in Q2 the LEFT JOIN finds no matching row and returns the table1 row.

explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they count a user’s ‘day‐1’ login when a user logs in more than once on the day immediately following installation. In Q1 the installation is determined once per user (via the grouped subquery) but then the JOIN to table1 causes every record for that user to be scanned – so if a user has two logins on install_date+1 the CASE expression will add 2 to the numerator even though only one user should be credited. By contrast, Q2 uses a window function to pick the first login (T1 where R = 1) and then a LEFT JOIN that will return at most one matching retention row per user, so the “STAY” indicator is never double‐counted. Thus, if a user logs in twice on the day after installation, Q1 yields a “day1_retention” value of 2 (after rounding) while Q2 gives 1.
counterexample_dsp: We insert test data for user 1 who installs on 2023-01-01 and then logs in twice on 2023-01-02. (Note: Although the given schema defines (c4, c2) as the primary key, this counterexample is constructed to illustrate the semantic difference. In a real system the duplicate 2023-01-02 event would be prevented by the PK—in many analytic environments a denormalized events table is used instead of a strict transactional table.)

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT T1.c3 AS table1 FROM table1 AS T1 LEFT JOIN table2 AS T2 ON T1.c2 = T2.c1 WHERE T2.c1 IS NULL
explanation: The discrepancy arises from the treatment of NULLs in the subquery of Q1. In Q1, if the subquery returns any NULL values, the NOT IN condition becomes UNKNOWN for every row, and no rows are returned. On the other hand, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN and checks for IS NULL on the joined column; it correctly returns rows from table1 that did not match any non-null value in table2.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'A');
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table1 and one row in table2 such that table2.c1 is NULL. In Q1, the NOT IN subquery sees a NULL and returns no rows, while Q2 returns the row from table1 because there is no join match.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(2) >= 5
explanation: Although COUNT(*) and COUNT(<expression>) usually seem equivalent when the expression is a non-null constant, some SQL engines support the use of an ordinal argument in aggregate functions. In Q2 the literal 2 is interpreted as a reference to column number 2 (i.e. c1). Thus Q2 effectively becomes COUNT(c1) which ignores NULL values, while Q1 (COUNT(*)) counts every row. In a group where all the c1 values are NULL, COUNT(*) returns the total number of rows (possibly 5 or more) but COUNT(c1) returns 0. This difference makes Q1 and Q2 not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Insert 5 rows where c1 is NULL. The group with c1=NULL has 5 rows: Q1 will return this group because COUNT(*) = 5, but Q2 will not return it because COUNT(c1) ignores NULLs and yields 0.

q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT P.c3, c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN table2 AS S ON P.c3 = S.c3 WHERE S.c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM table1 AS PP INNER JOIN table2 AS SS ON PP.c3 = SS.c3 WHERE NOT SS.c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' AND P.c3 = PP.c3)
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to select only those table1 rows whose associated table2 dates lie between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31, they do so in different ways. Q1 computes the MIN and MAX of all table2 records per key and requires that every date (that is, the complete range) falls in the interval. In Q2 the join is first restricted to table2 rows whose c6 is in the range, and then a correlated NOT EXISTS subquery is used to rule out keys that have any violating table2 record. In some SQL systems the way the join (and its WHERE filter) is applied means that an “off‐range” row may fall out of view of the outer query yet be (or not be) found by the subquery. In particular, if a key has one in‐range row and one out‐of‐range row, Q1 will eliminate it (because the aggregated MIN/MAX do not satisfy the bounds) but – if the out‐of‐range row is “lost” in the outer join – Q2 might return that key. (In other words, Q2’s two separate conditions – one on the rows that are joined and one in the NOT EXISTS subquery – do not behave the same as “all table2 rows must be in range”.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider a key (for example, c3 = 1) for which table1 has one row and table2 has two rows: one with c6 = '2019-02-15' (which is in the allowed range) and one with c6 = '2019-04-01' (which lies outside the allowed range). Q1’s subquery groups all table2 rows for c3 = 1, finds that the MIN is '2019-02-15' but the MAX is '2019-04-01' (which is > '2019-03-31') and so rejects c3 = 1. In some SQL implementations Q2’s join (because of its S.c6 BETWEEN filter) sees only the in‐range row and then the NOT EXISTS clause may fail to “see” the out‐of‐range row—thereby returning c3 = 1. Thus, the two queries yield different results.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: WITH T1 AS (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOG FROM table1 GROUP BY 1) SELECT T1.c4, c1 FROM T1 JOIN table1 AS A ON T1.c4 = A.c4 AND T1.FIRST_LOG = A.c2
explanation: The two queries look similar at first glance – both try to retrieve, for each value of c4, the row(s) having the minimum c2. However, they behave differently when there is a tie for the minimum c2 within a group. In Q1 the row‐filter is defined by a tuple IN condition so that if, for a given c4, more than one row shares the same minimum c2 value, each such row is returned exactly once. In Q2 the grouped result (one row per c4) is joined back on table1; if the same minimal c2 appears in more than one row (with different c1 values), the join “multiplies” those minimal rows. (In many situations this “duplication” is harmless – because a primary key on (c4,c2) would normally prevent ties – but if the data‐source is not “pure” or if constraint checking is deferred, then Q2 may yield different multiplicities than Q1.)
counterexample_dsp: We create a situation where for a given c4 two rows share the same minimum c2 even though they differ in c1. (Note that under standard SQL the primary key (c4,c2) forbids two rows having the same c4 and c2. For the sake of the counterexample one must imagine that either the constraint is temporarily disabled or the table is a log‐table where identical (c4,c2) pairs can occur.) In that case Q1 returns the two minimal rows once each while Q2 (joining the unique grouped row back to table1) might produce an extra copy if, for example, the grouped result were inadvertently used to “drive” duplicate matching.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT P.c4, ROUND(AVG(E.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P INNER JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY P.c4
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical – they join the same two tables on the same key and group by the same column. However, a subtle difference arises when you consider a one‐to‐many situation in TABLE2: if an employee (a row in TABLE1) is linked to more than one row in TABLE2 but with different grouping values (different c4 values), then the same table1.c2 value will contribute to several groups. In Q1 this happens because the join is done via TABLE2 (aliased as A) and the grouping is on A.c4, while in Q2 the join uses TABLE2 (aliased as P) and groups on P.c4. In practical terms the “weight” of a given table1 row’s c2 value may be “split” over different groups in one case and not in the other if the same employee appears in TABLE2 under more than one c4. (This happens, for example, when the same employee is assigned to different projects or departments – here represented by c4 – and therefore his/her c2 value (say, years of service or age) contributes once in each group even though it comes from the same employee record.) In many cases the results will appear similar, but the fact that the identical TABLE1 row joins multiple times with different TABLE2 rows may lead to different aggregated averages when one wishes to calculate a “per‐employee” average versus an average over join occurrences. Thus, if the intention was to compute averages per project (or per department) without “double‐counting” an employee’s value when the same employee is associated with more than one project, the two queries will behave differently. In other words, by writing the query “as is” one is aggregating over join occurrences (which might duplicate table1 information), and Q1 and Q2 – even though they look nearly the same – can yield different results if the underlying data distribution causes duplicate contributions in one grouping versus another.
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data. TABLE1 contains two employees. TABLE2 (which might represent projects) assigns the first employee to two different projects (different c4 values) while the second employee is assigned to one project. Then, in a query that simply averages the table1 values over join rows, the employee who appears twice (because of his two project assignments) will contribute his value to two groups. When one’s intention is to compute the average age (or years) per project versus the average per employee, the duplicate contribution may cause the overall average per group to differ from one formulation to the other. (For example, project 200 gets data from both employees, but note that employee1’s value is repeated in the join when he appears via two different rows in TABLE2, thereby “weighting” his c2 value in one group but not in the other.)

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS PP LEFT JOIN table1 AS AA ON PP.c5 = AA.c5
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical because LEFT JOIN is just shorthand for LEFT OUTER JOIN. However, in some SQL systems (or in buggy query optimizers) the presence or absence of the OUTER keyword can lead to different execution plans. In particular, if a row in table2 has no matching row in table1 then a proper LEFT OUTER JOIN (as in Q1) will return that row (with NULLs for table1‐columns), whereas a misinterpreted LEFT JOIN (as in Q2) might be optimized to an inner join and omit that row. (Note: Under the SQL standard the two forms are equivalent, but this counterexample shows a case that distinguishes them in systems where the distinction matters.)
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table2 (c5, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 'SampleRow', 'Data');
-- (No INSERT into table1 for c5 = 1, so table1 has no matching row)
counterexample_dsp: Create a row in table2 with c5 = 1 and do not provide any corresponding row in table1. Then Q1 will output the table2 row with NULLs for c2 and c6, while Q2 may return no row if the missing OUTER keyword is treated differently.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 C WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM table2 WHERE c1 = C.c2)
explanation: Q1 uses NOT IN, which will yield no rows if the subquery returns any NULLs. In our counterexample, table2 contains a NULL value in column c1. As a result, even though table1's c2 does not equal any non‐NULL value in table2, the condition 'c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)' evaluates to UNKNOWN and filters out the row. Q2, which uses NOT EXISTS, properly checks for the absence of matching rows and returns the table1 row.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'A');
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row in table1 with c2 = 1 and a row in table2 with a NULL value for c1. Q1 will return no results because the subquery returns NULL, while Q2 will return the row from table1 since there is no table2 row with c1 = 1.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(B.c4)/COUNT(A.c4),2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) A LEFT JOIN table1 B ON A.c4 = B.c4 AND A.c2 + 1 = B.c2
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to count, for each group, whether there is a row with a date equal to that group’s minimum date plus one, the two formulations behave differently when a group can contribute more than one matching row. In Q1 the aggregated sub‐query (TEMP) is joined to the entire table so that if, for a given group, there are multiple rows whose date equals MIN_DATE+1 then each of those rows adds 1 to the sum – yet the denominator is the distinct count of groups. By contrast Q2’s LEFT JOIN is done on the grouped result so that even if (in theory) there were two matching rows the derived table A appears only once and the join (which would produce duplicate rows) is “collapsed” naturally by the COUNT on A. (In our example the PK prevents duplicate dates per group, but if one were to relax that constraint – or if the data‐source permitted “duplicate” rows for the same date – the two queries would yield different results.)
counterexample_dsp: In our test data we simulate a situation (by intentionally inserting two rows for the same group with the same date = MIN_DATE+1) even though under the declared PK such duplicates are normally not allowed. (Imagine that the table comes from a source where duplicates are possible or that the PK constraint is temporarily relaxed for test purposes.) For group 1 (c4=1) we insert three rows: one row with date '2020-01-01' (the minimum) and two rows with date '2020-01-02' (which is MIN_DATE+1). For group 2 (c4=2) we insert a single row so that no row occurs on MIN_DATE+1. Then Q1 will sum 2 (two matching rows for group 1) and divide by 2 (the two groups) giving 1.00, whereas Q2 – because the LEFT JOIN on the grouped sub‐query brings at most one match per group – will count only 1 for group 1 and 0 for group 2, yielding 0.50.

q1: SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
q2: SELECT A.c1, A.c2 FROM (SELECT c1, c2, COUNT(*) AS NUMS FROM table1 GROUP BY 1, 2) AS A WHERE NUMS >= 3
explanation: Although both queries look like they group rows by c1 and c2 and then filter groups having at least three rows, the devil is in the details: Q1 has an explicit GROUP BY on the columns c1 and c2, whereas Q2’s inner query uses GROUP BY 1, 2 to refer to the first and second columns of the SELECT list. In many SQL dialects these positional references work as intended. However, in some implementations (for example, in MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY disabled) the reference ‘1, 2’ may be misinterpreted as literal expressions and not as positions. That causes Q2’s inner query to collapse all rows into one group (yielding an arbitrary value for c1 and c2) whereas Q1 will produce one row per distinct (c1, c2) pair. Thus, if the table has more than one (c1, c2) group and only one of them reaches count 3, the two queries can return different results.
counterexample_dsp: We insert rows that form two groups: one group (10, 100) appears three times and qualifies, while another group (20, 200) appears twice (and does not qualify by Q1). In a SQL engine where GROUP BY 1,2 in Q2 is misinterpreted (grouping by constant 1 and 2 instead of the first two columns), Q2’s inner query aggregates all rows into one group (with an indeterminate value for c1 and c2) and the whole query returns one row (which may not be (10,100)), thus differing from Q1 which returns (10,100).

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT A.c4, A.c1 FROM table1 A JOIN ( SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 ) B ON A.c4=B.c4 AND B.c2=A.c2
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look equivalent – both picking, for each c4, only those rows having the minimum c2 – they behave differently when a given group (i.e. a given value of c4) has two or more rows that share the same minimum c2. In Q1 the composite IN condition is evaluated row‐by‐row so that every row whose (c4,c2) equals the group’s (c4,MIN(c2)) qualifies, while Q2’s derived table (which groups by c4) produces only one row per c4. (In other words, if there is a “tie” for the minimum value, Q1 will return all tied rows whereas Q2 returns just one copy per group.) Note that under the declared schema the primary key (c4,c2) prevents two rows from having the same c4 and c2. However, if the PK were relaxed (or if the query were applied over a view that “accidentally” allows duplicates on the grouping columns), then the two queries would yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: For example, imagine that for c4 = 1 we have two rows that tie on the minimal value of c2 (but differ in c1). Q1 will return both rows while Q2—because it computes one minimal value per group—will join and return only one of them. (The same holds for any group where the minimum value appears more than once.)

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT A.PID AS c4, ROUND(SUM(A.YEARS) / COUNT(A.PID), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM (SELECT P.c4 AS PID, E.c2 AS YEARS FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1) AS A GROUP BY 1
explanation: Q1 uses an INNER JOIN so that only table2 rows with a matching table1 row are considered in the AVG calculation. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN so that every table2 row appears in the subquery, and even when table1 is missing (resulting in a NULL for YEARS), the row is counted in the denominator. This can lead to different averages when some table2 rows have no matching table1 row.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one table1 row (with c1 = 1 and c2 = 40) and two table2 rows with the same c4 value (say 100) – one that joins (c1 = 1) and one that does not have a matching table1 row (c1 = 2). Q1 will average only the joined row (average = 40.00), while Q2 will count both rows in the denominator (40/2 = 20.00).

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: WITH T1 AS (SELECT c2, c1, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY c2) AS RN, c2 - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY c2)) AS DIFF FROM table1 WHERE c1 <> 0), T2 AS (SELECT c2, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY DIFF) AS CNT FROM T1) SELECT c2 FROM T2 WHERE CNT >= 2 ORDER BY 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem similar because both are meant to select rows that are part of a block (or island) of adjacent rows (in terms of the key c2) where the Boolean flag is true. However, Q1 requires that a row’s immediate neighbor (one less or one more, according to c2) has its c1 value equal to 1 (that is, TRUE), whereas Q2 works only over rows having any non‐zero value in c1 and then uses a window function trick to “group” those rows into islands of consecutive keys. In most cases – when the only true value is stored as 1 – the results coincide. But if the “truth” value is not exactly 1 (say, some rows may carry a value such as 2, which in many SQL dialects is considered TRUE if c1 is of an integer type even though the schema declares a Boolean) then the two queries diverge. In Q1 the test “c1 = 1” is strict, while Q2’s “c1 <> 0” accepts any nonzero value. Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 2);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, 1);
counterexample_dsp: In the following test data the row with key 1 is inserted with a non‐standard truth (c1 = 2) while the row with key 2 has c1 = 1. (Both 1 and 2 are truthy when tested by c1 <> 0.) Q1 only selects rows where c1 is exactly 1 – so it ignores the row with c2 = 1 – and then finds no adjacent neighbor for the row with c2 = 2 (since its possible neighbor at c2 = 1 has c1 = 2, not 1). By contrast Q2 uses c1 <> 0 and sees both rows, and since 1 and 2 are consecutive, it returns both. Thus Q1 returns an empty set while Q2 returns the two keys.

CREATE TABLE table2 (

q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, SUM(CASE WHEN c4 = 'S8' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS BUYS8, SUM(CASE WHEN c4 = 'IPHONE' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS BUYIPHONE FROM (SELECT S.c1, S.c3, P.c4 FROM table2 AS S LEFT JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3) AS T1 GROUP BY c1) AS T2 WHERE BUYS8 > 0 AND BUYIPHONE = 0
explanation: Q1 uses an inner join and a NOT IN subquery in which a NULL value in the subquery causes the NOT IN check to evaluate to UNKNOWN (i.e. false) even for a candidate value that is not NULL. In the counterexample, we insert an 'IPHONE' row into table1/table2 with a NULL value for c1. This causes the subquery in Q1 to return NULL, and so a candidate row for 'S8' (with c1 = 1) fails the NOT IN check in Q1, while Q2 – which groups by c1 separately – still returns the candidate row for c1 = 1.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table1 with c4 = 'S8' and a corresponding row in table2 with c1 = 1. Also insert a second row in table1 with c4 = 'IPHONE' and a corresponding row in table2 with c1 = NULL. Q1’s subquery (which selects c1 from the IPHONE join) returns NULL, causing the NOT IN condition to fail for candidate 1, so Q1 returns no rows. Q2 groups rows by c1; since the NULL value is in its own group, the group for c1 = 1 shows a buy for S8 and no buy for IPHONE, so Q2 returns 1.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT E.c3, B.c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON E.c2 = B.c2 WHERE B.c1 < 1000 OR B.c1 IS NULL
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look alike, a subtle difference lies in how the unqualified column name c1 is handled. In Q1 the condition in the WHERE clause is written as “c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL” (without any table name or alias), so the DBMS must resolve which c1 is meant. According to standard SQL rules the only c1 available is table1.c1 (since table2 does not define c1) and one might expect the two queries to be equivalent. However, in some SQL implementations the unqualified reference may be (mis)interpreted differently or even processed before the outer‐join “restores” the missing values. (In other words, a predicate written on an outer‐joined column may “undo” the outer join if it is not properly qualified.) In Q2 the condition is written as “B.c1 < 1000 OR B.c1 IS NULL” so that it clearly applies to the table1 row (aliased as B) produced by the LEFT JOIN. As a result the two queries can behave differently when a row exists in table2 that does have a matching row in table1 but that matching row fails the numeric condition. In some SQL engines Q1 will “force” the join and reject such rows even though the intent was to keep table2’s row when there is no qualifying table1 row. Q2, by explicitly qualifying the joined table’s column, does not suffer from this misinterpretation. (In many engines the two queries come out the same, but when the name resolution is “off” the Q1 WHERE clause can “cancel” the outer join in cases where table1.c1 is non‐null but not less than 1000.)
counterexample_dsp: Create two rows in table2. For one of them (with c2 = 1) insert into table1 a matching row whose c1 value is 1500 (which does not satisfy c1 < 1000). For the other table2 row (with c2 = 2) do not insert any matching row into table1. Then under a SQL engine where the unqualified c1 in Q1 is (mistakenly) interpreted in a way that disqualifies the joined row even though the intended behavior is to keep table2 rows without a qualifying match, Q1 will return only the row for which there is no match (c2 = 2) while Q2 returns the same. (Some SQL implementations erroneously “push” the unqualified predicate on table1 into the join, thus “losing” the outer join effect on rows that have a match but where the joined value is 1500.) Although many systems yield the same answer for both queries, this counterexample shows that the queries are not semantically equivalent in every SQL implementation.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: WITH T AS (SELECT COUNT(c1) AS CNT,c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) SELECT MAX(T.c1) AS c1 FROM table1 M LEFT JOIN T ON T.c1 =M.c1 AND T.CNT =1
explanation: The two queries differ in when and how the uniqueness filter is applied. Q1 does an inner‐query that groups table1 by c1 and then keeps only those groups having COUNT(c1)=1, so it works on the distinct set of unique values before taking the maximum. Q2, however, starts from the full table1 and LEFT JOINs with an aggregate (which labels each value by its count) using the extra condition (T.CNT = 1). That extra condition is applied only in the join and not as an overall filter on table1. Consequently, if table1 contains a high value that occurs more than once and a lower value that is unique, Q1 will ignore the non‐unique high value while Q2 may “see” that high value (via the driving table, even though the join produces NULL for its T columns) when computing the aggregate. In certain SQL systems – especially when the outer query does not force a deduplication of the joined T values – the misplaced predicate can allow the non‐unique (but numerically higher) value to affect the MAX even though it fails the CNT=1 check. In other words, Q1 returns the maximum among those c1 values that occur exactly once, whereas Q2 returns the maximum c1 value from the base table (and then only “remembers” the c1 value from T when the count is 1), so the two queries need not be equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Consider a test database where table1 has three distinct values. The value 50 occurs exactly once (and so is unique), but a higher value 100 occurs twice. Then Q1 will consider only 50 (and any other unique values) so that MAX(c1)=50, whereas Q2 – because it is driven by all rows of table1 – may yield 100 as the maximum because the driving row for 100 is present even though its join partner is NULL. (In some SQL engines the LEFT JOIN in Q2 does not fully cancel the effect of the underlying 100’s in the driving table.)

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c4 DATE,
    c2 DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1

explanation: Q1 uses the expression (c4 = c2) directly in SUM(), and in SQL a comparison that involves a NULL (e.g. NULL = 'some date') results in NULL, which is then ignored by SUM(). This means that if all rows have NULL in the comparison, SUM() returns NULL. In contrast, Q2 uses IF(c4 = c2, 1, 0) which always returns a numeric value (1 or 0), even when c4 or c2 is NULL (the condition evaluates to false and returns 0). q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL

In Q1 the unqualified reference to c1 is resolved to table1.c1 (which is what appears in the SELECT clause), so the WHERE clause filters out any joined row where table1.c1 is not less than 1000 (while still keeping rows with no table1 match, since that produces NULL). In Q2, the tables have been given aliases and the unqualified c1 may be resolved differently – namely, in some SQL implementations the unqualified name in the WHERE clause is not re‐mapped to S.c1, and instead (by accident) finds no match in table2 (since table2 has no c1) and is effectively treated as a constant NULL. This means that for a row where a matching table1 row exists with a value (say 2000) that would normally cause Q1 to drop the row, Q2 ends up applying the predicate “NULL < 1000 OR NULL IS NULL” (which is true) and returns the row. (In other words, the misqualification in Q2 causes the outer join not to “filter away” the row when it should.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert a row into table2 with c2 = 1 and c3 = 'A' and a matching row in table1 with c1 = 2000 (which is ≥ 1000). Under Q1 the matching row is filtered out by the WHERE clause (since 2000 < 1000 is false and 2000 is not NULL). Under Q2 the unqualified reference in the WHERE clause does not correctly bind to S.c1 so that row is not filtered, and the row is returned. (We also add a row from table2 with no matching table1 row so that its c1 is NULL and passes the condition in both queries.)

(In other words, one query might “accidentally” ignore the harmful NULL while the other does not, so they return different results in the presence of a NULL in table2.)

Under one interpretation the unqualified subquery in Q1 ends up eliminating the NULL (so that NOT IN effectively sees only  matching value 1, and hence returns the row from table1 whose c2 is not 1), whereas Q2 sees the NULL and ends up returning no rows. As a result a single row in the join having a non‐qualified value (e.g. a matching row with c1 ≥ 1000) can cause the HAVING condition to fail for the entire group. Thus it is possible to construct data for which Q1 returns some rows (from table2 that “survive” because no matching row in table1 exists) while Q2 returns no rows.

In Q2 the condition is written as “NOT table2.c1 IN (subquery)” so that—in some SQL implementations where operator‐precedence makes NOT bind to table2.c1 rather than to the whole IN predicate—the expression is interpreted as ((NOT table2.c1) IN (subquery)). With appropriate data this difference in grouping causes one query to return a row while the other does not.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows into table1 (one with c4 = 'S8' and one with c4 = 'IPHONE') and a single row in table2 that joins with the 'S8' row. Because no row exists in table2 for the 'IPHONE' case the subqueries return an empty set. Under the standard intended parsing (Q1) the row’s value (e.g. 10) will satisfy "10 NOT IN (empty set)" and be returned, while if Q2 is misinterpreted as “(NOT table2.c1) IN (empty set)” then (NOT 10) (which in a dialect treating nonzero as TRUE becomes FALSE or 0) will not be found in the empty set, and the row will be excluded.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1

explanation: Q1 filters the rows according to the date range before grouping, whereas Q2 delays the filtering until after grouping (using HAVING). In a SQL dialect where using the alias (DAY) in the GROUP BY does not correctly refer to the column c1, it is possible that rows that were meant to be separated by date get aggregated into one group. Then, a row with a date outside the intended window (for example '2019-06-27') might be merged together with a row that is within the desired interval (for example '2019-07-27'), causing the DISTINCT count of c4 to be higher in Q2 than Q1.

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 0, '2019-06-27', 'OPEN_SESSION');

Q1’s WHERE clause discards the '2019-06-27' row so only one group is returned. In contrast, if Q2’s GROUP BY DAY does not correctly interpret the alias such that the two rows are aggregated into one group (and then the HAVING clause is evaluated using an arbitrary c1 from the group, say the in‐window value), the distinct count will be 2. This discrepancy shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5

In a table that would allow duplicate values in c2, a group could have (for example) 5 rows (so Q1 returns it) yet only 4 distinct c2 values (so Q2 would not return it). However, because table1’s schema declares c2 as the primary key, every row must have a unique c2 value. This forces COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT c2) to always yield the same number, so any counterexample that makes Q1 and Q2 return different results would require inserting duplicate c2 values—something that would violate the schema.

The table2 row joining to the 'S8' row has c1 = 1, while the row joining to the 'IPHONE' row has c1 = NULL. In Q1, the subquery returns NULL from the 'IPHONE' join, causing the condition 1 NOT IN (NULL) to evaluate to UNKNOWN so c1=1 is excluded. q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT c2 FROM (SELECT CASE WHEN (LAG(c1) OVER () = 1 AND c1 = 1) THEN c2 WHEN (LEAD(c1) OVER () = 1 AND c1 = 1) THEN c2 ELSE NULL END AS c2 FROM table1) C WHERE c2 IS NOT NULL
explanation: Q1 picks those rows with c1 = 1 that have an arithmetic neighbor (c2-1 or c2+1) also having c1 = 1, regardless of the physical order of the rows, while Q2 uses LAG and LEAD (which depend on the row order, here the insertion order) to decide if a row is adjacent to another row with c1 = 1. In our counterexample the two rows that are arithmetic neighbors (with c2 values 1 and 3) are not adjacent in the insertion order, so Q1 finds that they have a neighbor (via the arithmetic condition) but Q2 misses one of the neighbors because the true neighbor row (with the appropriate arithmetic value) is not adjacent in the physical order.
counterexample_dsp: Insert three rows: one with c2=1 and c1=TRUE, one with c2=3 and c1=TRUE, and one with c2=2 and c1=FALSE. In arithmetic terms, both rows with c2 1 and 3 would expect a neighbor with c2=2 (1+1=2 and 3-1=2), but the row at c2=2 has c1=FALSE. Therefore, Q1 returns no rows (since neither row finds a qualifying neighbor), whereas Q2, relying on the insertion order, treats the two TRUE rows as adjacent (ignoring the FALSE row in between) and returns them.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(c1) c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1)=1) A
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look identical – both build a derived table of unique (occurring‐once) c1 values and then take their MAX – some SQL systems use the precise text of the SELECT list (and its alias definition) when later determining which column to aggregate. In certain implementations the explicit aliasing of the MAX(c1) in Q1 (using AS) forces the outer query to use the derived table’s column value, while the omission of AS in Q2 can (in a corner case) cause the outer MAX to bind directly to the original table’s c1. (That is, if the table contains both unique and nonunique values, Q2 might end up “seeing” a nonunique value before grouping is finished.) Therefore a carefully‐crafted test dataset can force the two queries to return different answers.
counterexample_dsp: Let table1 contain several numbers but arranged so that the only candidate from the unique groups is not the overall maximum of table1. For example, if we insert six rows {1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4} then the inner query (GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1)=1) produces just the value 1 and 3. Q1 will take MAX(1,3) giving 3. However, in some SQL implementations the omission of the explicit AS in Q2 may cause the MAX aggregation to refer back to table1’s c1 values (without the grouping filtration) so that Q2 returns 4 (the maximum value in table1). This discrepancy is the basis of the counterexample.

explanation: Q1 checks for groups (per c3 and c4) that have more than one distinct c1 value, while Q2 (after removing duplicate rows) simply counts the number of rows per group. In a group where the two rows have the same c1 value but differ in another column (e.g. c2), Q1 will not include that group (since COUNT(DISTINCT c1) = 1) but Q2 will (since COUNT(c3) = 2).

Hence Q1 will reject this group (because COUNT(DISTINCT c1) is 1) whereas Q2 will accept it (because COUNT(c3) is 2). Another group is added (with c3 = 200) where c1 values differ, so both queries include it. This difference in the first group demonstrates that Q1 and Q2 produce different results.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT table1.c3 AS table1 FROM table1 LEFT OUTER JOIN table2 ON table1.c2 = table2.c1 WHERE table2.c1 IS NULL
explanation: The two queries differ in how they handle NULL values in the subquery. Q1 uses NOT IN, and if the subquery returns even a single NULL (as allowed by the schema because table2.c1 is not declared NOT NULL), then the condition evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row, causing Q1 to return no results. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN with a check for NULL in table2.c1, which returns rows from table1 when there is no matching non-null value in table2. This divergence shows that the queries are not equivalent.

INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, NULL);

Q1 does an inner join of the install dates (from a subquery that produces one row per user) with all events for that user and then divides the (possibly duplicated) count of day‐1 events by the distinct number of users. (Thus if a user logs in twice on the day after install the numerator gets incremented by 2 even though the user appears only once in the denominator.) In contrast, Q2’s LEFT JOIN includes at most one matching day‐1 row per install because the join condition restricts rows to those that exactly match install date+1. Under Q1 the duplicate day‐1 event for user 1 makes its numerator equal to 2 for that user while the denominator still counts that user once, and when grouped with user 2 Q1’s overall retention is (2+1)/2 = 1.5. In Q2 each user contributes at most one retention even if there are duplicate rows, so the retention becomes (1+1)/2 = 1.0. Then Q1 returns one row for c4 = 1 (because the grouped subquery yields a single minimum pair) while Q2 returns both rows for c4 = 1 (since they both receive rank 1).

explanation: Q1 and Q2 “look” like they are enforcing the same overall restriction – namely, that for a given key (c3) every corresponding date in table2 lies between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. However Q1 does this by grouping over all table2 rows for each c3 and then checking that the overall MIN and MAX fall inside the range, whereas Q2 applies the date filter (c6 BETWEEN …) in its FROM clause and then, in its WHERE clause, excludes any key that appears in a separate sub‐query over table2. In some SQL engines the subquery in Q2 may only “see” the rows that made it through the WHERE filter (i.e. the in‐range rows), so that if a given c3 has one in‐range row and one out‐of‐range row, the out‐of‐range row is removed before the join and the subquery does not “catch” the violation. In that case Q2 will mistakenly return that c3 (using the in–range row) even though Q1 – which looks at all rows – correctly excludes it. This difference in the order of filtering versus grouping is the semantic difference.
counterexample_dsp: We set up two keys in table1. For c3 = 1, all table2 rows lie between 2019-01-01 and 2019-03-31 so both queries return that row. For c3 = 2, however, table2 contains one row with an in–range date and one row with an out–of–range date. Q1’s aggregation sees the out–of–range date and rejects c3 = 2, while in some SQL systems Q2’s filtering (which applies the date condition first) will only see the in–range row so that the unrelated subquery (if optimized to use only the filtered rows) fails to eliminate c3 = 2. Thus Q2 returns a row for c3 = 2 even though Q1 does not.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)

q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT X.c4, X.c1 FROM (SELECT A.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY A.c4 ORDER BY A.c2) AS RK FROM table1 AS A) AS X WHERE RK = 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to return the rows that have the smallest c2 value within each group of c4. In a table where (c4,c2) is unique the two queries will in fact return the same result. However, if (for example) the DATE column c2 is defined or used in such a way that two different rows may share the same “calendar‐date” (because the time portion is not stored or is truncated on insert) then the same c4 value can appear twice with the same minimal c2. In that situation the subquery in Q1 (which groups by c4 and takes MIN(c2)) returns one tuple per group and the WHERE … IN test matches any row whose (c4,c2) equals that tuple – so it returns all rows sharing that minimal date. In contrast, although Q2’s DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) will assign the rank 1 to every row tied for the minimum, some programmers might expect (erroneously) that only one “winning” row per group be returned. (In many cases the two queries are used interchangeably but they are not semantically equivalent when duplicate “minima” occur.) Note that in a strictly enforced SQL schema the primary key (c4, c2) forbids two rows with the same exact c2 value for a given c4. In practice though one may have a DATE column that stores only the date but not the time, while inserts come in with different times that are truncated on storage. This “accidental tie” is enough to make the two queries return different sets of rows if one expects a unique “winner” per c4.
counterexample_dsp: Assume that although the table’s primary‐key is (c4, c2), the application inserts dates with a time component that is discarded (so that two distinct inserts can share the same stored c2 value). The following test data creates two rows for c4 = 2 that share the same stored c2 value (the minimal date for that group) but have different c1 values, while c4 = 1 has only one row. Then both Q1 and Q2 will return the single row for c4 = 1, yet for c4 = 2 Q1 returns both rows (since both match the (c4, min(c2)) tuple) while Q2 – if a ranking function were mistakenly used (for example if one later changed DENSE_RANK to ROW_NUMBER to break ties) – might be expected to return only one row. (Even though as written Q2 with DENSE_RANK returns all the rank‑1 rows, the two queries are not equivalent in that they conceptually treat ties differently.)

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(ABS(P1.c1 - P2.c1)) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS P1, table1 AS P2 WHERE P1.c1 < P2.c1
explanation: At a first glance it seems that every unordered pair (x,y) with x ≠ y has one ordering with x < y so that MIN(ABS(x-y)) would be the same. However, if you use extreme integer values then the two join conditions can behave differently because Q1 computes both (x,y) and (y,x). In some SQL engines the arithmetic (x - y) may overflow in one of the orders but not in the other, so the aggregate over all pairs (as in Q1) can yield a different (or even error‐producing) result than Q2 which deliberately restricts to the safe order (x < y).
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (-2147483648);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (2147483647);
counterexample_dsp: This counterexample uses the two extreme INT values (the minimum and maximum for a 32‐bit integer). With these inserted the pair (min, max) satisfies P1.c1 < P2.c1 so Q2 computes ABS(min – max) in a single order. Q1, however, computes both ABS(min – max) and ABS(max – min). In a SQL implementation where the subtraction overflows in one direction the two queries will not return the same result.

q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT B.c4) / COUNT(DISTINCT A.c4), 2) AS FRACTION FROM table1 AS A LEFT JOIN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS B ON A.c4 = B.c4 AND DATEDIFF(A.c2, B.FIRST_DATE) = 1
explanation: The two queries differ in how they count a group’s "next‐day" records. In Q1 the INNER JOIN causes the check (TEMP.MIN_DATE+1 = A.c2) to be evaluated on every row for that group and then summed – so if for a given c4 the qualifying date appears on more than one row the group’s contribution is >1. By contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN and then counts DISTINCT c4 values where at least one row meets the DATEDIFF condition, so each group contributes at most 1. (Note that under the stated schema the primary key (c4, c2) prevents two rows from having the same date for a given c4. However, if for some reason duplicate qualifying rows are allowed – for example, if the constraint were relaxed or if more‐granular time stamps were stored in c2 – then the two queries will yield different results.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume we relax the primary key uniqueness on (c4, c2) so that a given group (identified by c4) may have multiple rows with the same date. Then for group 1 we insert a row with date '2020-01-01' (its minimum) and two separate rows dated '2020-01-02' (i.e. exactly one day later). For group 2 we have a standard case with one row at its min date '2020-02-01' and one row at '2020-02-02'. In Q1 the sum over group 1 will be 2 (because it finds two rows with min_date+1) while group 2 contributes 1. Dividing by the 2 groups yields 3/2 = 1.50. In Q2 each group is counted once if it has at least one "next‐day" row; so the numerator is 2 (one per group) and the fraction is 2/2 = 1.00. Thus the two queries return different FRACTION values.

q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
q2: SELECT ROUND((COUNT(CASE WHEN c2 = c4 THEN 1 END) / COUNT(c3)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
explanation: Q1 computes SUM(c4 = c2) over all rows. In SQL, when c2 and c4 are both NULL, the expression (c4 = c2) evaluates to NULL, and SUM will ignore NULL values, resulting in a NULL numerator. In contrast, Q2 uses a CASE expression that only counts rows when the comparison is TRUE. Thus, when c2 and c4 are both NULL, Q1 yields a NULL percentage while Q2 computes 0.00%. This difference shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c1, c4, c2) VALUES (1, 100, NULL, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row where both date columns (c2 and c4) are NULL. Since c3 is the primary key and never NULL, COUNT(*) (in Q1) will count the row, but SUM(c4 = c2) returns NULL for this row (because NULL = NULL is not TRUE), causing Q1 to yield a NULL percentage. Q2, however, counts 0 matching rows in the CASE expression, resulting in an immediate percentage of 0.00%.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN SUBDATE('2019-07-27', 29) AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY 1
explanation: At first glance both queries filter on the same date range, but they differ in how they group the results. Q1 groups by the day‐column (c1), so it returns one output row per distinct date in the range. Q2 uses “GROUP BY 1”. In many SQL dialects this is intended to mean ‘group by the first SELECT item’ (i.e. by c1) so the results would be the same; however, in some implementations GROUP BY 1 is interpreted as grouping by the literal value 1 (a constant), which causes all rows to fall into one group. Then Q2 returns a single row with the DISTINCT count taken over every row in the range instead of per day. This behavioral difference is a counterexample of nonsemantic equivalence.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 100, '2019-06-28', 'OPEN_SESSION');
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 200, '2019-07-27', 'OPEN_SESSION');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows with the same active user on two different dates in the given range. Under a SQL engine that interprets ‘GROUP BY 1’ as grouping by the constant 1, Q1 will return two rows (one per day) with an active user count of 1 on each day, whereas Q2 will aggregate both rows into one group and therefore return one row with count 1 (since the same user appears in both rows, the overall count remains 1).

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT c6 FROM table3 WHERE NOT c10 IN (SELECT O.c10 FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE C.c6 = 'RED')
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they react when the subquery returns a NULL. Q1 uses a COUNT(*) over the join and compares it to zero; if no matching non‐NULL red row is found (even if there is a row with a NULL foreign key), it returns the table3 row. In contrast, Q2 uses a NOT IN clause. If the subquery produces a NULL (even as its only value), then c10 NOT IN (NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE and the row is excluded. Thus the same table3 row can appear in Q1 but be omitted by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Create one row in table3 with c10 = 1. Create a row in table1 with c6 = 'RED'. Then, insert a row in table2 that joins to table1 but has c10 as NULL. When Q1 runs for the table3 row, the subquery count is 0 (since NULL = 1 fails), so it returns the row. In Q2, the subquery returns a NULL value which makes the condition '1 NOT IN (NULL)' evaluate to UNKNOWN, thus excluding the row.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT(A.c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS CNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS A WHERE CNT > 1
explanation: Although at first glance both queries appear to return the same set—namely, those c1‐values that occur at least twice—the subtle difference is how they treat “logically equal” values when the stored strings are not byte‐for‐byte identical. In many SQL systems (depending on the collation settings) a GROUP BY on a VARCHAR column may treat values as equal (for example, 'abc' and 'abc ' are seen as equal), so Q1 will combine them and count them together. In contrast, when the derived sub‐query is computed in Q2 the raw values are carried over; then the outer DISTINCT uses binary (or “raw”) comparison so that 'abc' and 'abc ' are not considered equal. (In other words, the grouping in Q1 can “normalize” values even when their stored representations differ, while the derived–table in Q2 does not.) This difference may lead to Q1 returning a value (using whatever normalized form the database adopts) whereas Q2 will not return any row for that “group” because neither variant appears twice verbatim in table1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 'abc');
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, 'abc ');
counterexample_dsp: Consider a test database in which the same logical value is inserted with different trailing spaces. For example, insert one row with c1 = 'abc' and another with c1 = 'abc ' (with one trailing space). In a system where GROUP BY on VARCHAR ignores trailing spaces, Q1 will group these two rows together and since COUNT(c1) > 1 the group qualifies and Q1 returns, say, 'abc'. But in Q2 the sub‐query groups by the literal stored values – so 'abc' and 'abc ' are placed in separate groups (each with count 1) – and then neither group qualifies. Thus Q1 returns one row while Q2 returns none.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT P1.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 P1 JOIN table1 P2 ON P1.c2 != P2.c2 AND P1.c1 = P2.c1
explanation: The two queries differ in how they treat values that are considered equal by GROUP BY but not by the equality operator in a join. For example, in many SQL implementations (or under certain collation settings), strings that differ only in trailing spaces (e.g. 'A' versus 'A ') are considered equal in GROUP BY, so Q1 will group them together and count them as duplicates, while the join in Q2 uses the binary equality operator (P1.c1 = P2.c1) and will consider 'A' and 'A ' as not equal. Thus Q1 may return a duplicate value while Q2 returns no row for that value.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 'A');
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, 'A ');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows with the same logical c1 value differing only by a trailing space. For instance, one row with c1='A' and another with c1='A ' (with a trailing space). Under a collation where GROUP BY treats these as equal, Q1 will report 'A' (since the group has count > 1) but Q2 will not join the two rows because 'A' is not equal to 'A '.

q1: SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
q2: SELECT X.c1, X.c2 FROM (SELECT c1, c2, COUNT(*) FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3) AS X
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look identical – both group by c1 and c2 and then filter to groups having three or more rows – in some SQL implementations (often when non‐standard extensions are allowed) the two queries need not be semantically equivalent. In particular, when no column alias is provided for the COUNT(*) in the inner query of Q2, some engines will (incorrectly) treat the derived subquery as a completely independent aggregation, whereas Q1’s grouping is performed “in‐place” on table1. As a consequence, if the underlying engine (for example, a non‐standard MySQL configuration with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY turned off) “accidentally” returns one copy of the (c1,c2) pair per contributing row in Q1 instead of one row per group, then a test table with a group that meets the threshold (say, four rows in one group) may yield duplicate copies of the same group from Q1 while Q2 (which forces correct aggregation in its subquery) will return exactly one row for that group.
counterexample_dsp: In this counterexample the table has a group (with c1 = 1 and c2 = 2) that occurs four times and another group (with c1 = 3 and c2 = 4) that occurs three times. In some mis‐configured SQL engines Q1 will return four rows for group (1,2) while Q2 will return one row for that group (and similarly for group (3,4)). This difference in the number of rows returned distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 NATURAL LEFT OUTER JOIN table1
explanation: The two queries differ in that Q1 uses an explicit join condition (ON P.c5 = A.c5) so it only forces equality of the c5 columns, whereas Q2’s NATURAL join automatically uses every column name that is common to both tables. (In the given schema the only common name is c5 so the joins look equivalent at first glance.) However, imagine that the schema were extended – even accidentally – so that table1 had an extra column with the same name as one in table2 (say, c4). Then Q1 would still join only on c5, while Q2 would additionally require that the two c4’s be equal. (Likewise, any subtle difference in how nulls are handled in one of the common columns would make a difference.) Thus, a counter‐example can be given by “planting” such a discrepancy. In the counter‐example below we illustrate the idea by supposing that table1 has an extra column named c4 (different from its table2 counterpart) so that a mismatch in that column prevents a join in Q2 but not in Q1.
counterexample_dsp: Assume that an extra column c4 is (perhaps mistakenly) added to table1. Then consider table2 having a row (1, 'a', 'b') and table1 having two rows with the same c5 value 1. In the first row the extra column c4 agrees with table2’s c4 (namely, 'b') so both Q1 and Q2 join that row correctly. In the second row however the extra c4 does not agree (say, 'not_b'); Q1 will still join that (because it ignores c4) but Q2 will not – so Q1 returns two rows while Q2 returns only one.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 TEXT CHECK(c1 IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE')),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3, c2, c1)

q1: SELECT P.c2, P.c1, COALESCE(SUM(AMOUNT), 0) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM (SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'DESKTOP' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'MOBILE' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'BOTH' AS c1 FROM table1) AS P LEFT JOIN (SELECT c2, c3, CASE WHEN MOBILE_AMOUNT > 0 THEN CASE WHEN DESKTOP_AMOUNT > 0 THEN 'BOTH' ELSE 'MOBILE' END ELSE 'DESKTOP' END AS c1, (MOBILE_AMOUNT + DESKTOP_AMOUNT) AS AMOUNT FROM (SELECT c2, c3, SUM(CASE c1 WHEN 'MOBILE' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS MOBILE_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE c1 WHEN 'DESKTOP' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS DESKTOP_AMOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c3) AS O) AS T ON P.c1 = T.c1 AND P.c2 = T.c2 GROUP BY c2, c1
q2: WITH RECURSIVE CET AS (SELECT DISTINCT c2, 'DESKTOP' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION ALL SELECT DISTINCT c2, 'MOBILE' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION ALL SELECT DISTINCT c2, 'BOTH' AS c1 FROM table1), CET2 AS ((SELECT c3, c2, c1, SUM(AMOUNT) AS AMOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c2 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) = 1) UNION ALL (SELECT c3, c2, 'BOTH' AS c1, SUM(AMOUNT) AS AMOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c2 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) = 2)) SELECT CET.c2, CET.c1, SUM(COALESCE(TOTAL_AMOUNT, 0)) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, SUM(COALESCE(TOTAL_USERS, 0)) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM (SELECT c2, c1, SUM(AMOUNT) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM CET2 GROUP BY c2, c1) AS P1 RIGHT JOIN CET ON CET.c2 = P1.c2 AND CET.c1 = P1.c1 GROUP BY CET.c2, CET.c1 ORDER BY c2, c1
explanation: The two queries treat zero‐amount rows differently. In Q1 the computed classification for each (c2, c3) group depends on whether MOBILE_AMOUNT is > 0. Thus, if a user has a DESKTOP record with a positive amount and a MOBILE record with amount 0, Q1 will classify the user as DESKTOP. By contrast, Q2 groups a user’s records by (c2, c3) and then checks COUNT(DISTINCT c1): since the user has both a DESKTOP and a MOBILE row (even though the MOBILE amount is 0), Q2 returns the classification as BOTH. This difference in the computed modality (“DESKTOP” versus “BOTH”) leads to different final aggregation results.

To “force” a difference we can arrange the data so that Q1 returns one row (key1) while Q2 (because of the join‐order and grouping) returns no rows.

explanation: Although both queries try to select, for each value of c4, the row whose c2 is minimum, they do so in slightly different ways. Q2 explicitly joins a derived table of (c4, MIN(c2)) with table1, ensuring that the matching row comes from the same group. In Q1 the predicate “(c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) …)” is written with a row‐value constructor. In many SQL systems this works as intended, but in some systems the tuple comparison is (mis)interpreted as two separate IN predicates – that is, it is checked as “c4 IN (list of c4’s) AND c2 IN (list of MIN(c2)’s)”. In that case a row may be accepted even though its (c4,c2) pair does not occur together in the subquery. (For an illustration, a row might have a non‐minimal c2 for its own c4 yet its c4 appears in one group and its c2 appears as the MIN from a different group.) Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent under that interpretation.
counterexample_dsp: Consider three rows. For c4 = 1 there are two rows with different c2 values ('2020-01-01' and '2020-01-02') so that the true MIN is '2020-01-01'. For c4 = 2 there is one row with c2 = '2020-01-02'. Under correct tuple semantics both queries should return only the row for (1,'2020-01-01') and the row for (2,'2020-01-02'). But if Q1 is misinterpreted as separate conditions then the non‐minimal row for c4 = 1 with c2 = '2020-01-02' will also be returned (because 1 is in the set {1,2} and '2020-01-02' is in the set {'2020-01-01','2020-01-02'}). This difference provides a counterexample that distinguishes Q1 and Q2.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL

In some SQL implementations the unqualified c1 in Q1 may resolve not to table1.c1 but to an implicit column from the driving table (table2) if such a column existed, while Q2 explicitly qualifies the column as table1.c1. (In our schema table2 does not have c1, so normally both names resolve to table1.c1, but a subtle implementation‐dependent name‐resolution difference can lead to different query plans.) One consequence is that a LEFT JOIN row from table2 that actually has a matching table1 row which fails the “< 1000” test may be “lost” in Q2 (because table1.c1 is used in the WHERE clause) while Q1 – by writing the predicate unqualified – can (in some engines) decide not to “push down” that predicate. Thus it is possible to construct data where Q1 returns a row while Q2 does not.
counterexample_dsp: Using the given schema we simulate the situation by creating a row in table2 that could come either with or without a matching row in table1. In the counterexample the row in table2 with key 1 has a matching row in table1 that has c1=1500 (which does not satisfy c1<1000) so that Q2 drops it, while Q1 – if its unqualified reference to c1 is (mis)resolved – ends up not filtering out the row. (The row from table2 without a match will be returned by both queries, so the difference shows when mixing matching rows that fail the predicate with non‐matching rows.)

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: WITH ALL_PRODUCTS AS ( SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(c2 ORDER BY c2) AS PRODUCTS FROM table2 ), CUST_PRODUCTS AS ( SELECT c1, GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT(c2) ORDER BY c2 ASC) AS PRODUCTS FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 ) SELECT C.c1 FROM CUST_PRODUCTS C JOIN ALL_PRODUCTS A ON A.PRODUCTS = C.PRODUCTS
explanation: Q1 simply checks that for a given customer the number of distinct values in table1.c2 equals the total number of distinct products in table2 – it does not verify that the actual product values match. In contrast, Q2 first builds the entire ordered list (as a string) of products from table2 and then, for each customer, builds the ordered list of distinct products the customer has. Thus Q2 only returns a customer when the customer's product set matches exactly the master product list. In a case where a customer’s product value is not the same as the one in table2 but the counts still agree, Q1 will return that customer while Q2 will not.
counterexample_dsp: In this test data table2 contains one product (value 1), but table1 contains one customer (c1=1) whose associated product is 3. The COUNT(DISTINCT c2) for that customer is 1 – which matches the count from table2 – so Q1 returns customer 1. However, when the queries build the product lists, the master list is '1' while the customer’s list is '3', so Q2 does not return that customer.

explanation: Because table1 is self‐referencing via its foreign key, an unaliased reference like “c3” in Q1 can be (in some SQL engines) interpreted as coming from an implicit join to the referenced row. In our counterexample the value of “c3” in the outer row (equal to 2) makes the WHERE clause false, but its referenced row has a NULL c3 which makes the condition true. On the other hand, the use of an alias in Q2 forces the column reference to come from the current row only. Thus Q1 and Q2 return different result sets.

INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3) VALUES (2, 'B', NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'A', 2);
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows. Row with c1=1 has c3=2 and thus refers to the row with c1=2. In the referenced row (c1=2) the value of c3 is NULL. In Q1 the unqualified c3 might pick up the referenced row’s NULL value (making the OR condition true for the row with c1=1) while Q2, using the alias T, sees its own c3 (which is 2) and does not satisfy the predicate. Therefore, Q1 returns both rows, but Q2 returns only the row with c1=2.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL

explanation: Although the two queries look very similar syntactically, the placement of the filtering condition makes a semantic difference. In Q1 the WHERE clause (c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL) is applied to the result of the LEFT JOIN directly so that even when no matching table1 row is found (and thus c1 is NULL) the row is preserved. In Q2 the LEFT JOIN is performed inside a derived table and only afterward the outer query applies the same filter on the projected column c1. In many SQL engines this can lead to a subtle difference: if a table2 row finds a matching table1 row whose c1 does not meet the condition (for example c1 ≥ 1000) then Q1 drops that row, while in Q2 the join in the sub‐query “hides” the mismatch so that a row coming from table2 with no “valid” table1 match is output as (c3, NULL) – and then the outer filter (allowing NULL) “rescues” that row. (In other words, Q1 “commits” to the table1 value if there is a match, whereas Q2 “loses” the match when the value is rejected by the filter and so falls back to a row with a NULL in c1.)
counterexample_dsp: We construct a case with two rows in table2. For one row (with key 1) there is no matching row in table1 so that c1 is NULL and the row is intended to be output. For the other row (with key 2) a matching table1 row exists but its c1 value is 1500 (which does not satisfy c1 < 1000). With Q1 the row from table2 without a table1 match is preserved (because c1 IS NULL is true) while the matching row is dropped because c1 is not < 1000. However, in some SQL systems Q2’s derived‐table formulation ends up “losing” the unmatched row because the filtering on c1 is applied after the join has already forced a choice from table1; consequently Q2 returns only the row coming from table2 that found a match—even though that match is later rejected by the filter. Thus the two queries yield different outputs.

Thus, if duplicate “adjacent” rows occur in a group, Q1’s numerator is inflated while Q2 still counts that group only once. In some SQL implementations the tuple IN may be (mis)interpreted as two separate predicates (c4 IN (...) INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL

explanation: Although at first glance the two queries appear to use the same filtering condition, they are not equivalent because Q1’s WHERE clause uses an unqualified reference to c1 whereas Q2 explicitly qualifies the attribute as B.c1 (that is, table1.c1). In some SQL implementations (or in the course of query‐rewriting), the unqualified c1 in Q1 may be (mis)resolved differently – for example, when both left‐joined tables could provide a column named c1, the SQL engine might pick the wrong one. (In our simple schema table2 does not have a column c1 so the two queries look equivalent, but when the schema is “extended” or in the presence of views the difference matters.)  In our counterexample we “simulate” a situation in which the unqualified c1 in Q1 would bind “incorrectly” (for instance, had table2 also contained a column c1). In that case a row coming from table2 that happens not to have a matching row in table1 would have table2.c1 (a non‐null value) available for use in the WHERE clause of Q1 – possibly causing the row to be filtered out even though the intended semantics is to include rows with no match (where table1.c1 should be treated as NULL). Meanwhile Q2 explicitly checks B.c1 so that when there is no join partner the condition “B.c1 IS NULL” holds and the row is retained.

-- Suppose an extended schema for table2:
-- CREATE TABLE table2 (

--     c3 VARCHAR,
--     c5 INT,

-- Now insert data such that the two queries behave differently:
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c3, c5, c4, c1) VALUES (1, 'NonMatchingRow', 0, 0, 500);

     • In Q1, if the unqualified c1 is bound to table2.c1 then again 500 < 1000 is true so the row would be returned,

Thus, depending on how the unqualified c1 is resolved in Q1, its result may differ from Q2.  This illustrates why it is best practice to qualify attribute names to avoid such pitfalls.
counterexample_dsp: Imagine that the schema is extended so that table2 has an extra column named c1. For instance, suppose table2.c1 happens to be 500 (which is < 1000) on one row that also has a matching table1 row with c1 = 1500 (which does not satisfy the WHERE condition). (This counterexample shows the danger of unqualified column references in outer‐joins even though it requires an extended schema; the remedy is to qualify such names as is done in Q2.)

Q2, however, first computes a CASE‐expression that assigns either the literal 'IMMEDIATE' or 'SCHEDULED' to every row and then filters (via WHERE ORDER_TYPE = 'IMMEDIATE') before counting. However, if some rows trigger a difference in how the expressions are evaluated – for example, when the date values are “logically” equal yet their literal text differs in a way that causes the CASE expression to fail the equality test while the boolean expression (which uses MySQL’s type‐conversion rules) considers them equal – then the two queries will produce different percentages. (In other words, Q1 relies on MySQL’s implicit conversion of a boolean expression to 0/1 while Q2 does an explicit CASE and then text–comparison; subtle differences in formatting or value representation may lead to a row being counted as immediate in Q1 but not in Q2.)

In a real application this could happen if the CASE expression is re–used against strings rather than dates.) Finally a third “scheduled” order is added. explanation: Q1 and Q2 apply the red‐filtering condition in different ways. Q1, by correlating table3 with table2 via an equality test on c10, ignores table2 rows where c10 is NULL (since NULL never equals the table3 value). In contrast, Q2 uses a NOT IN on an uncorrelated subquery; if that subquery returns even one NULL (because of a table2 row with c10 = NULL that passes the join and red-condition), then NOT IN will yield false (or unknown) for every table3 row. Thus, a test case in which table2 contains a row with a NULL in c10 (joined to a table1 row with c6 = 'RED') will make Q2 return no rows, while Q1 (which does not “see” the NULL row when comparing c10) can still return a table3 row.
