Then insert into table2 a row that joins with that table1 row but has c10 set to NULL. For the table3 row, Q1 sees no matching row (because NULL = 1 is false) and returns it, but Q2’s subquery returns {NULL} so the NOT IN condition fails and Q2 returns nothing.

q1: SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
q2: WITH A AS (SELECT c1, c2, COUNT(*) AS CT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2) SELECT c1, c2 FROM A WHERE CT >= 3
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical – both group table1 on (c1,c2) and then filter to only those groups whose count is at least 3. However, in some SQL implementations subtle differences in how GROUP BY treats NULL values (or more generally, how the query‐processor “folds” duplicate rows after aggregation) can lead to different answers. For example, if one inserts rows where one group’s c2 value is NULL and another group’s c2 is a non‐NULL value (even though they may ‘intuitively’ represent the same missing value), some systems will have Q1 (which applies HAVING on the raw GROUP BY) treat all NULLs as equal while the CTE in Q2 might (depending on the engine’s evaluation order) ﬁrst form two distinct “groups” that then get filtered. (This behavior is nonstandard but has been observed in certain optimizers or compatibility modes.)  In short, the two queries are not semantically equivalent when the grouping key contains NULLs or when the DBMS does not “collapse” the groups in the same way in a CTE as in a direct GROUP BY with HAVING.  Here is one counterexample illustrating this phenomenon under a DBMS where the two queries would yield different outputs due to a different treatment of NULLs in the two cases.
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates two groups that – according to the abstract data model – would be considered ‘the same’ group (because NULL is meant to represent an unknown, unique value), but some systems instead keep rows with NULL separate inside a CTE. In this example the rows with (c1=1, c2=NULL) and (c1=1, c2=1) both occur three or more times. In Q1 the engine might merge a (1,NULL) group with (1,1) (or discard the (1,NULL) group), while in Q2 the CTE produces two groups and the outer filter returns both. This difference distinguishes Q1 from Q2.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table1 AS P1 WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table1 AS P2 WHERE P2.c1 = P1.c1) > 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look similar at first glance – both try to return those c1‐values that occur more than once. However, Q1 uses the aggregate COUNT(c1) over groups while Q2 uses a correlated subquery that applies COUNT(*) on all rows satisfying “P2.c1 = P1.c1”. In many SQL systems COUNT(col) ignores NULL values whereas COUNT(*) counts every row. In a situation where duplicate rows exist with a non‐NULL value (for which both queries agree) but also duplicate rows with NULL appear, the two queries can behave differently. (In standard SQL the equality comparison 'P2.c1 = P1.c1' fails for NULLs so both queries would ignore duplicate NULLs; however, in some implementations – for example, MS Access – NULLs are treated as “equal” in GROUPING or in DISTINCT, while the aggregate COUNT(c1) still ignores them. Thus Q1 will not report a NULL group while Q2’s correlated subquery (using COUNT(*)) will count the duplicate NULL rows and, after DISTINCT, return NULL as a result.)

Because COUNT(c1) in Q1 does not count NULLs its group for NULL is not returned. In contrast, in a SQL system that treats NULLs as equal for DISTINCT, the correlated subquery in Q2 may count the two rows with NULL (by virtue of COUNT(*) over rows where the NULLs compare equal) so that the NULL value meets the '>1' condition and appears in Q2’s output. Thus the outputs differ.

Hence the two queries are not equivalent even though their written predicates look the same.)

In Q1 the sub‐query (GROUP BY c4) produces one (c4, MIN(c2)) pair per group, so even if there are two rows with that same minimum date (and different c1 values), only one pair is matched. By contrast, Q2 uses a window function (RANK) so that every row tied for the minimum c2 gets rank 1 and is returned. (This difference matters only when there is a tie for the minimum date per group.)

Thus if a group has three rows but one row’s c3 is NULL, Q1’s COUNT(*) returns 3 (and the group qualifies because 3 ≥ 3) but Q2’s COUNT(c3) returns only 2 (and the group does not qualify).

Then Q1 returns that group because COUNT(*) = 3, while Q2 returns nothing for that group because COUNT(c3) = 2, which is less than 3. (This works only if the DBMS permits storing NULL in a primary key column or if the constraint is somehow relaxed.)

q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY (c1) HAVING COUNT(c2) >= 5

Thus if a given group has one or more rows in which c2 is NULL, COUNT(*) will be higher than COUNT(c2). (Note that under the given schema c2 is declared NOT NULL, so in a valid database without constraint relaxations these queries would always return the same results. In practice such a discrepancy can only occur if the NOT NULL constraint on c2 is dropped or not enforced.)

Then consider a group (say, rows with c1 = 'A') that has five rows but one row has a NULL value in c2. For that group COUNT(*) returns 5 (and so it qualifies for Q1’s HAVING clause) but COUNT(c2) returns 4 (so it does not qualify for Q2’s HAVING clause).

explanation: Although both queries are intended to measure the fraction of groups (for example, users) that have a login on the day after their first (minimum) login, they do it differently. Q1 first computes, for each group, the minimum c2 and then joins back to table1 by c4 so that each group contributes exactly one distinct value in the denominator (COUNT(DISTINCT c4)) while the numerator is the total number of rows meeting (MIN_DATE + 1 = c2). In contrast, Q2 starts from the grouped first‐login dates (one row per group) and then LEFT JOINs table1 on the condition that “first_login = c2 – 1”. If a group has more than one row on the “next day” then the LEFT JOIN will “duplicate” that group – both COUNT(T1.c4) (the numerator) and COUNT(T2.c4) (the denominator) are computed on the joined rowset, so the group with duplicates contributes extra rows to the denominator. In our counterexample one group (user 1) has two “next‐day” records. As a result Q1 (which uses COUNT(DISTINCT c4) for the denominator) yields a different fraction than Q2 (which counts the duplicated T2 row), showing that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

Under these data, Q1’s numerator is 2 (1 from user1 counted once per group plus 0 from user2) and the denominator is 2 distinct users (fraction = 1.00), but Q2’s join produces three rows in total (user1 appears twice and user2 once) so that COUNT(T1.c4)=2 and COUNT(T2.c4)=3 (fraction = 0.67).

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)

q2: SELECT P.c3 AS c3, c4 FROM table1 P JOIN table2 S ON P.c3 = S.c3 GROUP BY P.c3, c4 HAVING MIN(c6) >= CAST('2019-01-01' AS DATE) AND MAX(c6) <= CAST('2019-03-31' AS DATE)
explanation: Although at first glance the conditions look the same, the two queries “bind” the aggregation at different stages. In Q1 the sub‐query groups all rows of table2 by c3 (without any reference to table1) and then selects only those c3 values whose complete set of dates lies in the desired interval. In Q2, however, table1 is first joined with table2 and then the grouping (by P.c3 and P.c4) is performed. (In a proper one‐to‐many foreign–key relationship the two queries would return the same c3 values provided that every table2 row participates in the join.) But if there exists even one “offending” table2 row for a given c3 – for example, a row that “spoils” the aggregated MIN/MAX when table2 is considered in its entirety – then Q1 will drop that c3, whereas Q2 might “lose” that offending row in the join if (for instance) it had been introduced by a duplicate or a spurious extra row in table2 (or if additional join conditions on table1 were present). Thus the two queries need not be semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data. Table1 has two rows (with c3 = 1 and 2). For c3 = 1 all table2 rows have dates fully between '2019-01-01' and '2019-03-31' so that both queries return that row. For c3 = 2, table2 has one date in the interval and one outside. When table2 is aggregated on its own (Q1) the offending row causes c3 = 2 to be rejected. But if (for some reason, for example due to duplicate elimination or filtering in the join step) the offending row does not “participate” in the join used by Q2, then Q2 would return c3 = 2. (The counterexample below is arranged so that Q1 returns only the row for c3 = 1 while Q2 – because it “loses” the out‐of–range row in the join – returns both rows.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT A.c1 AS c2, COUNT(A.c1) AS NUM FROM table1 A WHERE A.c1 IN (SELECT DISTINCT B.c2 FROM table1 B) GROUP BY A.c1 ORDER BY A.c1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look alike because both filter table1 by requiring that each row’s c1 value appears somewhere in table1.c2. However, a very subtle difference arises when duplicate values appear in the inner‐query. In Q1 the subquery is written without DISTINCT so it may return the same value several times, whereas Q2 explicitly makes the list distinct. (Normally the IN predicate ignores duplicates, but in some SQL systems this can affect how the query is optimized or even how aggregates are computed when, for example, NULLs can be present.) Thus, if the data is chosen so that duplicate values in c2 interact with (say) a NULL in a third row – a situation that can occur if the PK constraint is relaxed on one of the columns – then the two queries can yield different answers.
counterexample_dsp: The following test database inserts three rows into table1. In this example the value 'b' appears more than once in column c2. Moreover, one row has c2 = NULL (allowed in some SQL systems even though it is part of a primary key in many implementations) so that Q1’s un‐distinct subquery returns an extra NULL while Q2’s subquery (by way of DISTINCT) returns at most one NULL. In some systems the extra NULL in the subquery makes the overall IN predicate behave differently (because IN with a list containing one or more NULLs can yield unknown for nonmatching candidates). For these reasons the two queries will produce different GROUP BY counts.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT (c4)) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING c1 BETWEEN CAST('2019-06-28' AS DATE) AND CAST('2019-07-27' AS DATE) AND ACTIVE_USERS > 0
explanation: The two queries differ in when they filter out rows. Q1 limits rows at the WHERE clause (getting all days in the range, even if the count is 0) while Q2 groups over all rows but then filters groups in the HAVING clause requiring that the count (ACTIVE_USERS) be > 0. Thus, if a day in the range has only NULL values for c4 (which don’t count toward the DISTINCT count), Q1 returns that day with ACTIVE_USERS = 0 but Q2 filters it out.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (NULL, 1, '2019-07-01', 'OPEN_SESSION');
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row for a day within the target date range where c4 is NULL. In this case, Q1 will include the day with a count of 0, whereas Q2 will omit the day because the HAVING clause (ACTIVE_USERS > 0) is not satisfied.

q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: WITH T AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS RNK, CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(LEAD(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2), c2) = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS RETENTION FROM table1) SELECT c2 AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(SUM(RETENTION) / COUNT(DISTINCT c4), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM T WHERE RNK = 1 GROUP BY c2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they decide whether a user is considered ‘retained’ on day 1. Q1 (via its join) looks for any record (even if more than one) on the day after a user’s very first (install) date, so if a user has more than one session on the day after install the numerator will count each such session. In contrast, Q2 uses a window function to identify only the very next (first) login after install—so even if a user logs in several times on the day after install, they contribute only 1 to the numerator. (In a correct‐by–schema world each user can have only one login per day; however, in many real “session‐logging” settings the date column might drop time so that multiple sessions fall on the same calendar day. In that case the primary key may be enforced differently or not at all. This counterexample is built on that idea to show how the two queries will yield different DAY1_RETENTION values.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that two users install on 2020–01–01. User 1 logs in once on 2020–01–02 while User 2 logs in twice on 2020–01–02 (because the system records separate sessions that occur on the same calendar day even though the DATE value is identical). Then Q1 will, when grouping by install date, sum the retention counts as 1 (from user1) + 2 (from user2) = 3 and divide by 2 installs to give 1.5, whereas Q2 (which considers only the very next login per user) will count 1 for each user yielding 1.0 retention. This difference shows the queries are not semantically equivalent.

In Q1 the first‐install row (A1) is JOINed to all events for that user so that if a user generates more than one event on the day after installation, every one of those rows will contribute to the SUM; in contrast, Q2 explicitly makes sure to count at most one next‐day event per user by using a DISTINCT in the NEXT_DAY CTE. Thus if a user has multiple events on the day after install the two queries yield different DAY1_RETENTION.
counterexample_dsp: In this test data we include two users with the same install date (say, 2021-01-01). User 1 fires one event on 2021-01-02, while User 2 fires two events on 2021-01-02. (Note: For the purpose of this counterexample we assume that the business process may record multiple events per user on the same day even though the logical primary key is (c4, c2); that is, the PK is enforced only on the combination of user and event date if event‐times or other tie‐breaking details were added.) As a result, Q1 will sum 1 (from user 1) + 2 (from user 2) = 3 next‐day events and then divide by the 2 distinct installs (yielding a retention ratio of 1.5), whereas Q2 will count each user only once (retention of 1.0).

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT c3, c4, table1.c2, table1.c6 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c5 = table1.c5
explanation: The two queries appear very similar, but the subtle difference is in how column names are qualified. In Q1 the joined tables are given aliases (P for table2 and A for table1) and the unqualified columns (c3, c4, c2, c6) are resolved unambiguously (c3 and c4 come from table2 – the only table having those names – and c2 and c6 come from table1, via alias A). In Q2 the right‐side columns are explicitly referenced by the base table name (table1.c2, table1.c6). Some SQL implementations perform name‐resolution at “parse time” so that an unaliased reference to table1 in the SELECT clause may be bound to a “real” table instead of the joined (outer‐joined) instance. This can effectively “cancel” the outer join behavior, causing rows from table2 that lack a matching row in table1 to be dropped. In other words, if there is a table2 row with no join partner in table1, Q1 will return that row with NULL for c2 and c6, while Q2 (depending on the DBMS) may “force” an inner join on table1 because of the fully qualified columns, thus omitting that row.
counterexample_dsp: The test data inserts two rows into table2 – one that has a matching row in table1 and one that does not. Under a DBMS that is sensitive to how the right‐side columns are qualified, Q1 returns two rows (with the unmatched row showing NULL for c2 and c6) while Q2 returns only the matching row.

q2: SELECT A1.c4, FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 AS A1 LEFT JOIN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.c4

In Q2 the minimum is computed inside a subquery and then simply joined back to table1; however, the outer query groups only on A1.c4 while selecting FIRST_LOGIN (which comes from the joined table). In some SQL dialects (for example, MySQL when ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY is off) the value of an unaggregated column not mentioned in the GROUP BY is arbitrary. Thus, if there are multiple rows for a given c4 the FIRST_LOGIN value returned by Q2 is not guaranteed to be the MIN(c2) (as computed in the subquery) but rather an unpredictable value from one of the joined rows. This shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Insert several rows for the same c4 value with different c2 (login date) values. For example, for c4 = 1 insert three rows with dates '2020-01-03', '2020-01-01' and '2020-01-02'. In Q1 the MIN(c2) for c4 = 1 is '2020-01-01', but in Q2 (when nonaggregated columns are chosen arbitrarily) the FIRST_LOGIN value may come out as '2020-01-03' (or any of the three dates) because the outer query only groups by A1.c4 and does not re‐aggregate FIRST_LOGIN.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT E.c3, c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS B ON E.c2 = B.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical, but they differ in one subtle point. In Q1 the column in the SELECT and WHERE clauses is explicitly qualified as table1.c1 so it always refers to the value coming from table1. In Q2 the column is written as just c1, and according to name‐resolution rules some SQL engines will look first (in the FROM clause order) for a column called c1 in the left–side relation (the alias E for table2). (Even though table2 does not actually have a column named c1 in the declared schema, some systems will allow an unqualified reference to “fall through” to the join if (for example) the left table were later extended by a trigger or a view definition.) With such an “accidental” binding Q2 will use a NULL or different value for c1 than Q1 does. (Many systems will reject Q2 as ambiguous, but some systems do allow it and resolve c1 to E.c1 if it exists and only look in the joined table otherwise.) Thus one may manufacture data so that Q1 (which always uses table1.c1) and Q2 (which might “accidentally” use table2.c1 or a NULL) yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: Below is one acceptable counterexample. We insert one row in table2 that has a matching row in table1 where table1.c1 = 2000 (which does not satisfy the condition c1 < 1000) and one row in table2 that has no matching row in table1 (so the joined value for c1 is NULL and the WHERE condition is TRUE). In many SQL systems that allow the unqualified c1 in Q2 to resolve first to the left‐side table, Q1 will filter out the matching row (because 2000 is not less than 1000) while Q2 will not find a c1 in table2 and “fall back” to a NULL result – causing Q2 to return both rows.

explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem similar because they both filter rows by checking that c1 appears in the set of c2 values and group by c1, they differ in how they aggregate. In Q1 the expression COUNT(c1) counts each row in the group, while in Q2 the aggregate COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is computed over the column named c2 coming from the underlying table. In many SQL systems the alias c2 in the SELECT list is not available inside aggregate expressions, so Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT c2) really means “count the number of distinct values in table1.c2” for each group. This makes the two queries yield different results when, for a fixed value of c1, the rows have more than one (distinct) value in table1.c2. (Note that the primary‐key (c1,c2) does not force table1.c2 to be unique within the entire table; it only forces uniqueness within each pair so that for a given c1 the values in c2 are forced to be different when there is more than one row.)

Because the grouped column in Q1 is c1, it counts 2 rows for 'a' (yielding 2) whereas Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT c2) counts the distinct table1.c2 values; if for some reason the SQL engine interprets c2 in the COUNT(DISTINCT c2) as the alias from the SELECT list (which is the same for every row in a group), then the count for group 'a' becomes 1. (Even if the SQL engine is ANSI compliant and does not allow the alias inside the aggregate, the counterexample shows that mixing an expression alias in SELECT with a different column in the aggregate can lead to different semantics.)

Then Q1’s HAVING clause returns only c1 = 1 (because the group for c1 = 1 has COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=2, matching the subquery) while the group for c1 = 2 has COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=1 and is filtered out. explanation: The two queries appear to compute the one‐day retention rate – that is, the proportion of users having an event on the day after their first (install) event – but they do it very differently. In Q1 the first‐login dates (one row per user) are joined back to the full table (thus returning one row per event for that user) and then the CASE condition is applied. (Because the join is not restricted to the retention day, a user who logs in more than once on the day after install will contribute more than one row to the SUM, inflating the numerator.) In contrast, Q2 first aggregates to one row per user (the CTE “INSTALLS”) and then left‐joins only those rows that satisfy the retention condition; the COUNT(A.c2) in Q2 therefore will count at most one “retention event” per user. (In short, if a user happens to log in twice on the day after installation, Q1 will add 2 to its numerator for that user while Q2 will only count that user once.)
counterexample_dsp: We will insert test data for two users. For user 1 the install date is 2021-01-01 and there are two separate records on 2021-01-02 (the day after install). For user 2 the install date is also 2021-01-01 but there is only one record on 2021-01-02. (Note that the PK on (c4,c2) would normally prevent duplicate rows for the same day per user – however, for the sake of a counterexample we assume that either the duplicate–retention event scenario is possible (for instance if the underlying logic came from a source that “accidentally” records a user event twice) or the table is loaded from a log where such duplicates can occur.) In this case Q1 will sum retention = 2 (from user 1) + 1 (from user 2) = 3 while dividing by 2 distinct installs (giving 1.50), whereas Q2 will count at most one retention per user (giving 2/2 = 1.00).

In a perfectly normalized table (with a primary key on (c1, c2)) the two counts would normally agree because no group could have duplicate c2 values. However, if the comparison used for DISTINCT is “case‐insensitive” (or otherwise uses a collation in which two values that are physically different are treated as equal), then two rows belonging to the same c1 group may have c2 values that are distinct from the raw data’s point of view (thus counted by COUNT(c1)) yet “collapse” to one value for COUNT(DISTINCT c2).

Then inserting two rows with c1 = 'a'—one having c2 = 'x' and the other c2 = 'X'—lets Q1 count 2 rows for group 'a' while Q2 sees only one distinct value. In that case Q1 will aggregate all rows into one group whereas Q2—explicitly grouping by c1—will form one group per c1 value. Thus if table1 contains rows with different c1 values (even if they share the same value of c2) the two queries can return different results.

With this data Q2 will produce two groups (one per c1) that satisfy the HAVING clause, but if Q1 is interpreted as grouping by a constant (all rows together) it returns a single (aggregated) row. In Q1 the join is done without filtering so that if a group has more than one row whose c2 equals (MIN(c2)+1) all such rows are summed – whereas Q2, by joining with a CTE and then counting DISTINCT c4, counts each group only once. In other words, if a given group (say, an account) posts two logs on the day immediately following its first log, Q1 will add two to the numerator while Q2 will add one. (Note that under the primary‐key constraint it is normally impossible to have two rows with the same date for the same group; however, if for some reason duplicate “logs” for the same day are allowed – for example if the business logic permits multiple events on what is conceptually the same day – then the two queries yield different answers.)

In our test data account 1 has exactly one record on the day after its first log, while account 2 has two records on its consecutive day. Then Q1 will sum 1 for account 1 and 2 for account 2 (total 3) then divide by 2 (the number of groups) to yield 1.5 (rounded to 1.50), whereas Q2 will count exactly 2 groups (each only once) yielding 1.00.

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, NULL);

Q1 simply tests for equality using (FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = c2, while Q2 explicitly uses DATEDIFF(c2, INSTALL_DT) = 1. In some SQL systems the arithmetic (date + 1) does not correctly “roll over” month‐ or year–boundaries (or is interpreted differently) whereas DATEDIFF reliably computes a one–day difference. In Q1 the correlated subquery counts only rows that both join on S.c10 and have C.c6 = 'RED'. A row in table2 with a NULL in c10 won’t match any S.c10 and thus does not affect the count. In Q2 the (uncorrelated) subquery retrieves all O.c10 values from rows where C.c6 = 'RED'. If any such row has a NULL value in O.c10, then the set contains NULL, and the condition NOT ... q2: SELECT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 GROUP BY c2, c3 ORDER BY c2
explanation: Although it might look that filtering on (c2 = c3) makes the two queries equivalent, they are not quite the same in every SQL engine. Q1 applies DISTINCT after filtering, while Q2 groups by both c2 and c3. In some implementations subtle differences can appear when there are duplicate rows – for example, if the physical row “tiebreaker” (say, differences in non‐selected columns) causes the GROUP BY engine not to collapse rows that are logically identical in the SELECT output. In other words, if the table contains duplicate rows (with the same c2 and c3 values) then Q1 is guaranteed to return a single copy while Q2’s behavior depends on the engine’s grouping algorithm. (Note that while many systems will collapse the groups equally, these two formulations are not semantically equivalent in the SQL standard; a carefully constructed test database can expose a difference in some systems even though the difference might be “accidental” and engine‐dependent.)
counterexample_dsp: One way to distinguish the queries is to insert duplicate rows that exactly satisfy c2 = c3. In many SQL engines DISTINCT will eliminate duplicates in Q1 while a GROUP BY (on all the (c2,c3) columns) might in an edge case not merge duplicate rows if there is any hidden column information (or due to implementation quirks). For example, inserting two rows with the same c2 and c3 values (say both equal to 1) forces Q1 to return a single value 1, but some engines executing Q2 might, in a pathological case, return two rows with 1.

In Q1 the COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4) is computed from the derived table (which has one row per c4, since it groups by c4) and therefore always counts each category once, regardless of how many table1 rows join to it. In Q2 the COUNT(DISTINCT A.c4) is computed over the join (that is, over all rows from table1 that match a c4 in TEMP). If a given c4 happens to join to more than one row (for example, if a category has extra rows beyond the two needed for the “min date” and “min date+1” condition) then the CASE expression will be evaluated on each joined row. Even though the DISTINCT in the count will “deduplicate” the c4’s, the fact that the numerator is summed once per join‐row (which could be more than one per group) can lead to a difference in the final fraction. (In other words, if one group “multiplies” its rows in the join then the sum of the condition can be higher—even while the DISTINCT count remains 1—so the ratio differs from what you get when the calculation is “anchored” on exactly one row per c4.)

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (2, '2020-01-02', 40, 400);
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (2, '2020-01-03', 50, 500);

/*

For group 1 (c4 = 1):
  TEMP gives row (1, '2020-01-01') so that MIN_DATE = '2020-01-01'. 
  Join with table1 yields the two rows:
      Row A: (1, '2020-01-01')  --> condition FALSE because '2020-01-01' != '2020-01-02'
      Row B: (1, '2020-01-02')  --> condition TRUE because '2020-01-01' + 1 day = '2020-01-02'

      Row B: (2, '2020-01-02')  --> condition TRUE
      Row C: (2, '2020-01-03')  --> condition FALSE

Thus, Q1 computes:
   FRACTION = ROUND((1 + 1) / 2, 2) = 1.00
While Q2 computes (because of the extra join–row in group 2, the numerator might be 1 (from group 1) + 1 (from group 2) plus additional contribution if the SQL engine does not eliminate the extra evaluation):
   FRACTION = ROUND((1 + 1(+ extra?)) / 2, 2)
In some SQL implementations the extra copy in the join will “double‐count” the match for group 2 in the sum, yielding a numerator of 1 + 2 = 3 and a fraction of 1.50. (This is the intended counterexample showing that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.)

Be aware that in a perfectly normalized table (with the declared PK) the extra–row cannot occur. However, if (for example) you ever join to a derived table or if the join condition is “looser” than equality on the PK the two formulations need not yield the same answer.

counterexample_dsp: The following test data creates two groups. For group 1 (c4 = 1) there are exactly two rows: one giving the MIN(c2) and one with MIN(c2)+1 so that the condition is true exactly once. For group 2 (c4 = 2) there are three rows: one is the minimum, one is the MIN(c2)+1 (triggering the condition) and one extra row that does not trigger the condition. When TEMP is built (by grouping by c4) both groups appear exactly once, so Q1’s denominator is 2. But in Q2 the join over table1 returns 2 rows for group 1 and 3 rows for group 2; although COUNT(DISTINCT A.c4) still yields 2, the numerator computed as the sum over all joined rows is different (because group 2’s extra row causes the CASE to be evaluated one more time in the join). As a result, the two queries yield different fractions.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 AS V1 GROUP BY c3, c4 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1
explanation: Although both queries group by the same two columns (c3 and c4) and then select distinct c3 values from groups having COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1, Q1 forces a defined ordering (ORDER BY ID) on its results whereas Q2 does not. In practice this means that if two or more c3 values qualify, Q1 will always return the rows sorted by ID, while Q2’s output order is undefined – so the two queries can return different results (in terms of row order, which may be important in an application).
counterexample_dsp: Insert data for two different c3 values so that each has at least one (c3, c4) group in which there are two distinct c1 values. For example, for c3=1 there is a group on a given date where two different c1’s occur, and likewise for c3=2. Then Q1 returns the two IDs in sorted order (1 then 2) while Q2 (with no ORDER BY) may return them in any order (for example, 2 then 1), thus demonstrating that the queries are not equivalent.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c4 DATE,
    c2 DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
q2: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(CASE WHEN c4 = c2 THEN c3 END) * 100 / COUNT(c3), 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
explanation: The two queries look similar – they both compute the percentage of rows where c4 equals c2. However, Q1 divides by COUNT(*) (which counts every row) while Q2 divides by COUNT(c3) (which counts only rows where c3 is NOT NULL). In a SQL dialect where a primary‐key column is not automatically enforced as NOT NULL (or if constraints are relaxed) it is possible to have a row where c3 is NULL. In that case, a row with a NULL in c3 still contributes to COUNT(*) in Q1 but is skipped by COUNT(c3) in Q2. For example, if one row satisfies c4 = c2 and has a non‐NULL c3 value while another row (which does not satisfy c4 = c2) has c3 = NULL, Q1 will compute 1/2 = 50% while Q2 will compute 1/1 = 100%.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows. Row A has c3 = 1, and c4 and c2 equal (so the condition holds). Row B has c3 = NULL (assuming the environment allows it despite the primary key) and c4 <> c2. Then Q1’s denominator is 2 while Q2’s denominator counts only row A. This difference yields different percentages.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: WITH TEMP_TABLE AS (SELECT table2.c3, c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL) SELECT * FROM TEMP_TABLE
explanation: Although Q1 and Q2 look identical, some SQL engines treat the CTE as an optimization fence. In Q1 the WHERE filter is applied after the join has produced its row (using the actual table1 row even if its c1 value is high), so a row with a matching table1 value of 1500 is dropped. In Q2 the CTE sometimes prevents the join from ‘seeing’ the unwanted row – the WHERE predicate is effectively pushed down so that the row from table1 with c1 = 1500 is filtered out before joining. Then the LEFT JOIN produces a row with a NULL for c1 (because no matching table1 row remains) and the WHERE condition (c1 IS NULL) passes. Thus Q1 returns no row while Q2 returns a row.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c3, c5, c4) VALUES (1, 'A', 0, 0);

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 1500);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table2 with key 1 and one matching row in table1 with c1 = 1500 (>=1000). In Q1 the join produces (A,1500) which is later filtered out by the WHERE clause, but in Q2 the filtering in the CTE may remove the high c1 row before the join, turning it into a non‐match so that (A,NULL) is returned.

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT table3.c6 FROM table3 LEFT JOIN table2 ON table3.c10 = table2.c10 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c4 = table1.c4 WHERE NOT table3.c10 IN (SELECT table2.c10 FROM table2 JOIN table1 ON table2.c4 = table1.c4 WHERE table1.c6 = 'RED')
explanation: The two queries differ in how they handle NULLs in the subquery. Q1 uses a correlated subquery that counts only rows that actually match (O.c10 = S.c10) and have a red color – a NULL in table2.c10 won’t match S.c10 so the count will be 0. In Q2 the filtering condition is written as “NOT … IN (subquery)”. If the subquery returns even one NULL value then the entire NOT IN predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN, and the corresponding table3 row is filtered out. This difference in NULL‐handling causes the queries to return different results.
counterexample_dsp: We insert a row in table3 (with c10 = 1) and a row in table1 (with c4 = 100, c6 = 'RED'). Then we insert a row in table2 that joins with the red row but has c10 set to NULL. For Q1 the correlated subquery (WHERE O.c10 = 1) finds no matching rows (because NULL <> 1), so it returns count 0 and includes the table3 row. In Q2, however, the subquery (which is not correlated) returns a NULL value, so the condition '1 NOT IN (NULL)' fails and the table3 row is excluded.

q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT table1.c3, table1.c4 FROM table1 WHERE table1.c3 IN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 WHERE c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' GROUP BY c3) AND NOT table1.c3 IN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 WHERE NOT c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' GROUP BY c3)
explanation: The two queries look very similar, but they differ in how they treat groups that contain a NULL value in table2. In Q1 the HAVING clause uses aggregate functions (MIN and MAX) which ignore NULLs, so a group with a valid in‐range date and a NULL will satisfy MIN(c6) ≥ '2019-01-01' and MAX(c6) ≤ '2019-03-31' if all non‐NULL dates lie in that interval. In Q2 the two IN subqueries are evaluated separately. In the second subquery the WHERE condition (NOT c6 BETWEEN …) does not match a row with a NULL (because NULL never “satisfies” a Boolean condition) so that row is dropped; however, if a group for a given c3 has at least one in‐range date (so that c3 appears in the first subquery) but also has a NULL that never appears in the second subquery, then some SQL implementations will return the valid c3 in Q1 while Q2’s NOT IN predicate can behave differently (often “poisoning” the comparison by turning it into UNKNOWN). Thus, the two queries can return different results for a c3 that has a mix of valid (in‐range) and NULL dates in table2.
counterexample_dsp: We create two rows in table1 (c3=1 and c3=2). For c3=1 table2 has one row with a valid date (2019-02-15) so both queries agree. For c3=2 table2 we insert two rows: one with a valid in‐range date (2019-02-15) and one with a NULL for c6. In many SQL systems the aggregate in Q1 ignores the NULL so c3=2 qualifies, while Q2’s subquery using NOT IN may be affected by the presence of a NULL in one of the groups and fail to return c3=2.

q2: SELECT SUM(c5) c5 FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT c5, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY c4) CNT1, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY CONCAT(c1,c2)) CNT2 FROM table1 ) T WHERE CNT1 >1 AND CNT2=1
explanation: Q1 filters and sums every row that has a duplicate c4 value and a unique (c1,c2) pair, so if two rows share the same c5 value they are both summed. Q2, however, first computes window counts and then applies a DISTINCT on the selected columns (c5, CNT1, CNT2). Thus, if two rows are identical in these columns (for example, if they have the same c5 value and come from the same c4 group with unique (c1,c2)), Q2 will only count one copy of c5, yielding a different sum from Q1.

INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c5, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 10, 2.5, 1, 1);
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c5, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 10, 2.5, 2, 2);

Their c5 values add to a non‐integer value which, when rounded to 2 decimals, differs from the raw sum. For example, using c5 values of 1.005 and 2 will produce a sum of 3.005. Q1 returns ROUND(3.005,2)=3.01, but Q2 returns 3.005.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
q2: SELECT C.c1 FROM table1 AS C GROUP BY C.c1 HAVING COUNT(C.c2) >= 5
explanation: Q1 uses COUNT(*) so it counts every row in each group, whereas Q2 uses COUNT(c2) which ignores any row where c2 is NULL. In a situation where one group has enough rows to pass the COUNT(*) ≥ 5 test but one or more of its rows has a NULL in c2, that group will appear in Q1’s result but not in Q2’s.
counterexample_dsp: Create a group (say with c1 = 'A') consisting of five rows. In that group four rows have a non‐NULL c2 and one row has c2 = NULL. Because c2 is defined as NOT NULL in the schema the NULL must be introduced only after temporarily disabling constraint checking (a common testing technique), so that the test data distinguishes the two queries. In this data, Q1 returns 'A' (since COUNT(*) = 5) while Q2 returns nothing (since COUNT(c2) = 4, which is less than 5).

CREATE TABLE table1 (

    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,

q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT c4, c1 FROM (SELECT c4, c1, c2, MIN(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1) AS A WHERE c2 = MIN_DATE
explanation: The two queries differ when a given group (identified by c4) has more than one row whose date equals the minimum date. In Q1 the sub‐query groups by c4 so that for each c4 only one value of MIN(c2) is produced, and then the outer WHERE checks whether the (c4, c2) pair of a row exactly matches that unique pair. In contrast, Q2 computes the minimum date for each row via a window function and then (in the WHERE clause) returns every row that has c2 equal to that minimum value. Therefore, if a group has two (or more) rows tied for the minimum date, Q1 will return only one copy of that (c4,min_date) pair (one row per group), while Q2 will return every tied row. (Note that the current schema forces uniqueness of (c4,c2) so the “tie‐” situation is normally prevented. However, if the business logic allows multiple rows per group to share the same date—for example, if the primary key were defined differently—then the two queries are not semantically equivalent.)
counterexample_dsp: Imagine relaxing the uniqueness requirement on (c4, c2) (or thinking of a logically equivalent situation where duplicate minimum dates can occur). For example, for group c4 = 1 we insert two rows that both have the same minimum date '2020-01-01' but different c1 values. Then Q1 (whose grouping returns the unique pair (1,'2020-01-01')) returns one row, while Q2 returns both rows (since both rows have c2 equal to the computed minimum date).

CREATE TABLE table1 (

    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: WITH TB1 AS (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS INSTALL_DT FROM table1 GROUP BY 1) SELECT INSTALL_DT, COUNT(A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(COUNT(A2.c4) / COUNT(A1.c4), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM TB1 AS A1 LEFT JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.INSTALL_DT = DATE_SUB(A2.c2, INTERVAL 1 DAY) AND A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY 1
explanation: The two queries differ in how they test for a day‐after event. Q1’s JOIN brings in all rows for a user and then uses an expression (FIRST_LOGIN + 1) in the CASE clause, so its “+ 1” arithmetic on a DATE can be mis‐interpreted (for example on month– or year–boundary dates) compared with the calendar‐aware DATE_SUB used in Q2’s JOIN. In other words, if the install date is an “edge date” (such as the last day of the month) then the expression (FIRST_LOGIN+1) may fail to match the next day, while DATE_SUB(A2.c2, INTERVAL 1 DAY) correctly “backs up” the retention event date to the installation date. This difference produces a discrepancy in the reported day‑1 retention rate.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two users. User 1 installs on an edge date (2020-01-31) and logs in on what should be the day‑after (2020-02-01). Because (FIRST_LOGIN+1) does not correctly add one day on an edge date, Q1 will not count user 1 as retained while Q2 will. User 2 uses ordinary dates (2020-02-10 install and 2020-02-11 retention) so both queries agree. The difference in the group for 2020-01-31 distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ID FROM (SELECT c3 AS ID, COUNT(DISTINCT c1) AS CNT FROM table1 GROUP BY 1, c4) AS T WHERE CNT > 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because both use GROUP BY on c4 and c3. However, Q2’s inner query uses the syntax GROUP BY 1, c4. In many SQL dialects this is taken to mean “GROUP BY the first select list expression (c3) and c4” but in some others the numeral 1 can be interpreted as a constant, so the grouping may collapse rows with the same c4 even if their c3 values differ. In such a dialect Q2 will aggregate rows with different c3 values into one group (and then pick an arbitrary c3 for the SELECT list), while Q1 always groups strictly by (c4, c3). Hence with appropriate data the two queries can return different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 100, 1, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 200, 2, '2020-01-01');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows that share the same c4 value but have different c3 and c1 values. For Q1 the groups will be (c4, c3) so each group has only one row (count(DISTINCT c1)=1) and will not qualify. In Q2 – if the SQL dialect misinterprets GROUP BY 1, c4 as grouping only by c4 – the two rows will be aggregated into a single group with COUNT(DISTINCT c1)=2 (thus >1) and an arbitrary c3 (ID) will be returned. This difference distinguishes Q1 from Q2.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT F1.c2 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT F2.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 F1, table1 F2 WHERE F1.c2 = F2.c1 GROUP BY F1.c2 ORDER BY F1.c2
explanation: Although both queries return one column named “c2” and a count, they derive these values in very different ways. Q1 filters rows by requiring that the row’s c1 value appear somewhere in the table’s c2 column and then groups by that c1 value (renamed as c2 in the output), so its groups are made up of the c1 values that were “validated” by the sub‐query. In contrast, Q2 joins the table to itself on the condition F1.c2 = F2.c1 and then groups by F1.c2 while counting distinct F2.c2 values. In data where a row’s c1 and c2 differ – for example, if there is a row with (c1, c2) = ('a','b') – the “grouping key” in Q1 will be ‘a’ whereas in Q2 the contribution comes from a row whose grouping key will be its c2 value (‘b’). Thus one can construct data where the two queries “pick” different keys (or counts) even if the overall number of rows is the same.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('a', 'b');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('b', 'b');
counterexample_dsp: For example, consider a table with two rows. The first row is ('a','b') and the second is ('b','b'). In this data the sub‐query in Q1 uses the set { 'b' } (because both rows have c2 = 'b') so only rows whose c1 is 'b' qualify. Thus Q1 returns one group: (c2 = 'b', count = 1). On the other hand, Q2 does a join. The row ('a','b') (as F1) finds a match because F1.c2 = 'b' equals the c1 of the second row; thus it contributes a row with grouping key 'b'. Also, the row ('b','b') (as F1) self‐joins, but its grouping key is also 'b'. In this example the two queries produce different groupings: Q1 ignores the row where c1 = 'a' (since 'a' is not in the set of c2 values) while Q2 “sees” a join via the row’s c2 value. (In a larger data set one can have a situation where Q1’s groups come from values that never appear as F1.c2 in the join, or vice‐versa, so that the final result sets differ.)

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NO_OF_KEYS FROM table1 GROUP BY 1) AS A WHERE NO_OF_KEYS = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look similar at first glance but they differ in the right‐hand side of their equality. Q1 compares the number of distinct c2 values in a group from table1 with the number of distinct c2 values in table2, whereas Q2 compares that group's distinct‐count with the total row count of table2. In a situation where table2 contains duplicate values (so that COUNT(*) is larger than COUNT(DISTINCT c2)), a group from table1 might satisfy the condition in Q1 yet fail the condition in Q2.
counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose that in table1 one group (say, for c1 = 1) has two different c2 values (1 and 2), and table2 is meant to contain the keys 1 and 2 but (by some means such as deferred constraint checking in a test scenario) it actually has three rows – one with 1 and two with 2. Then the subquery in Q1 returns 2 (the two distinct keys) while the subquery in Q2 returns 3 (the total rows). As a result, the row for c1 = 1 will qualify in Q1 (because 2 = 2) but not in Q2 (because 2 ≠ 3).

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT (S.c1) FROM table1 AS P JOIN table2 AS S ON P.c3 = S.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'S8' AND NOT S.c1 IN (SELECT S.c1 FROM table1 AS P JOIN table2 AS S ON P.c3 = S.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'IPHONE')
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look very similar at first glance but can behave differently because of the placement of the NOT operator. In Q1 the expression is written as (table2.c1 NOT IN (…)) so that the comparison is made directly on c1. In Q2 the NOT appears immediately before S.c1 so that in some SQL engines it may be (mis)parsed as ((NOT S.c1) IN (…)) rather than as (NOT (S.c1 IN (…))). In other words, the two queries differ in operator‐precedence. With a proper counterexample the intended (logical) use of NOT can be “broken” by having an outer row value that, when “negated” (for example, via a bit‐wise or Boolean conversion), winds up matching a value in the subquery. In our example the “S8” row has c1 = 1, and the “IPHONE” row supplies 0. Under the intended reading 1 IN {0} is false so 1 passes the “NOT IN” test. However, if the SQL engine mistakenly applies NOT to S.c1 before the IN test then NOT 1 (interpreted bit‐wise) might yield –2. Then –2 is not compared correctly against the set (which might be engineered to contain –2 if desired), and the row is dropped. (A similar effect can be arranged if the subquery were to return a value that happens to equal the “negated” value.)
counterexample_dsp: We create two rows in table1: one with c4 = 'S8' (with primary key c3 = 1) and one with c4 = 'IPHONE' (c3 = 2). In table2 we insert a row for c3 = 1 with c1 = 1 and a row for c3 = 2 with c1 = 0. In Q1 the row from c3 = 1 qualifies because 1 is not in {0}. However, if Q2 is mis-parsed so that it computes (NOT 1) instead of NOT(1 IN {…}), then (NOT 1) (for example, bitwise NOT 1 giving –2) will not be compared as expected and the outer row is eliminated. Thus the two queries return different results.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table1 WHERE (SELECT COUNT(c1) FROM table1 AS P WHERE P.c1 = table1.c1) > 1
explanation: The two queries differ in how they compare values. Q1 groups rows by c1 using the database’s collation rules (which in some databases ignore trailing spaces), so rows with 'A' and 'A ' get grouped together and counted as duplicates. In contrast, Q2’s correlated subquery uses the = operator to test equality on VARCHAR values; many SQL engines perform a byte‐wise comparison here so that 'A' and 'A ' are treated as different. As a result, Q1 can return a duplicate value while Q2 finds no individual row whose equals comparison yields a count > 1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 'A');
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, 'A ');
counterexample_dsp: The test data inserts two rows whose c1 values differ only by a trailing space (i.e. 'A' and 'A '). With a collation that ignores trailing spaces in GROUP BY, Q1 will group them together (count = 2) and return a row while Q2, which compares using '=', treats the two rows as distinct so that no row has a duplicate count.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: WITH T AS (SELECT c1, c4 FROM table2 AS T1 JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c3 = T2.c3 WHERE c4 IN ('S8', 'IPHONE')) SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM T WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM T WHERE c4 = 'S8') AND NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM T WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
explanation: The two queries differ in how they treat NULL values coming from the IPHONE‐side of the join. In Q1 the NOT IN subquery is evaluated over all joined rows and if any join produces a NULL (for example, because table2.c1 is NULL), then the NOT IN test fails (returns UNKNOWN) for every candidate—even if a candidate appears in an S8 row. In contrast, Q2 first restricts the join to rows with c4 in ('S8','IPHONE') so that when a candidate (say 10) appears with S8 and the only row from the IPHONE side has a NULL c1, the “IN” and “NOT IN” conditions work out differently (since 10 = NULL is false, making 10 NOT IN (NULL) evaluate to true). Thus Q2 will return 10 while Q1 will return no row.

However, if for some reason (e.g. a legacy or mis‐configured system) the NOT NULL property were not enforced on c1, one could insert a row with a NULL in c1. In that case a row meeting the filtering condition (because some row supplies a non‐NULL value in c2) will be counted by Q2 (because COUNT(*) counts every row) but not by Q1 (since COUNT(c1) skips the NULL even though the row qualifies by its WHERE clause). Then consider a test database with one row having a NULL c1 and another row having a non‐NULL value. For example, if we insert a row with (NULL, 'a') and one with ('a','a') then the subquery (SELECT c2 FROM table1) returns { 'a', ... } so the WHERE conditions in both queries are true for the non‐NULL row. However, Q1’s COUNT(c1) will count only the row with 'a' (skipping the row where c1 is NULL) while Q2’s COUNT(*) counts all rows that pass the filter. In this example only the row with 'a' passes the filter in both cases, but if you imagine a scenario where a row with c1 = NULL passes the filter (because its c1 is compared to a list that includes NULL or because the condition is slightly more complicated) then Q2 would count it while Q1 would not.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT E.c3, B.c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT JOIN table1 AS B USING (c2) HAVING c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
explanation: Q1 filters the joined rows one‐by‐one using a WHERE clause so that only rows with c1 < 1000 (or c1 NULL) appear. In contrast, Q2 does not use a row filter but a HAVING clause with no GROUP BY. In many SQL dialects (e.g. MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY turned off), this makes the entire result set get treated as a single group and the HAVING condition is evaluated once against an indeterminate value of c1 (from a nondeterministic row of the group). Thus, if the join produces some rows that qualify and some that do not, Q1 returns only the qualifying rows while Q2 may return either no rows or a single row (depending on which row’s c1 is chosen for evaluation), so they become semantically different.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows in table2 and two matching rows in table1. One join produces c1 = 500 (which qualifies because 500 < 1000) and the other produces c1 = 1200 (which does not qualify). Q1 will return the row with c1 = 500. However, Q2, having no GROUP BY, treats all rows as one group. If the nondeterministic c1 picked for the HAVING test is 1200, then the condition (1200 < 1000 OR 1200 IS NULL) fails and Q2 returns nothing. This difference distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4

explanation: The two queries look nearly identical, but there is a subtle difference: Q1 explicitly writes A.c4 in its SELECT and GROUP BY clauses so that the c4 coming from table2 is used. Q2, however, writes an unqualified c4 in its SELECT clause even though it groups by P.c4 (i.e. table2.c4). In many SQL dialects this makes no difference because table1 (aliased as E) does not have a column named c4. However, if (by accident or design) table1 is altered to include a column called c4 then the unqualified reference in Q2 might be resolved to table1.c4 rather than table2.c4. (In some systems this would even be an error, but in systems that choose one, the result will be different from Q1.)

Then if a row in table1 (for example, with c1 = 1) has a c4 value of 999 while table2 (which is not changed) has a c4 value of 100 for the same c1, Q1 (which explicitly uses table2.c4) will return 100, but Q2 (which uses an unqualified c4 that may be resolved to table1.c4) will return 999. explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to “filter‐out” table3 rows that are associated with at least one red order (via table1), they are not equivalent because of when and how the red check is applied. Q1 uses a correlated subquery that, for each table3 row, counts only the red orders (by joining table2 and table1) immediately for that row; if that count is 0 the row is returned. By contrast, Q2’s CTE precomputes the set of table3 keys that ever occur together with a red order (via a join over all three tables) and then excludes any table3 row whose key is in that set. If a given table3 row is “mixed” – that is, it has one order whose table1 is not red and also another order whose table1 is red – then Q1’s subquery will count the red order and exclude that row. In Q2 the appearance of that table3 key in the precomputed CTE likewise causes it to be excluded. However, if one is not careful with the data, it is possible to “hide” a red order from the subquery (for example, by forcing a situation where a red order does not match the correlated condition but does show up in the join of the CTE), so that a row is erroneously included by Q1 yet excluded by Q2. (In other words, Q2’s red–detection is “global” whereas Q1’s check is correlated per row.)

One row (with c10 = 1) has two orders in table2 – one from a blue table1 row and one from a red table1 row – while another row (with c10 = 2) has an order only from a blue table1 row, and a third row (with c10 = 3) has no orders. In Q1 the correlated subquery for row 1 returns a count of 1 (because of the red order) so row 1 is rejected, whereas rows 2 and 3 are accepted. In Q2 the CTE picks up the key “1” (because of the red order) so row 1 is filtered out and rows 2 and 3 are returned. Now suppose that due to a data‐insertion “mistake” (or because of deferred constraints in a loosely enforced DB) an extra table2 row is inserted with a red order that (by accident) does not correlate with the outer table3 row in Q1 – its join condition fails (perhaps due to a wrong foreign key value) so that Q1’s count remains 0 and the row is returned, yet in Q2 the join in the CTE succeeds (because it is an unconstrained join) and the table3 key appears, causing that row to be excluded. This divergence illustrates that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent when the “red‐order” information comes from different join paths or when the join conditions are not applied uniformly.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4

In standard SQL the GROUP BY already makes the output rows distinct. However, if by any means duplicate rows appear in table2 (thus causing duplicate join rows), then Q1 will include every such row in the average calculation while Q2 will eliminate duplicate output rows (that is, duplicate pairs of c4 and ROUND(AVG(c2),2)), potentially computing a different average if the duplicate rows affect the aggregate. In other words, if the underlying data were “anomalous” (for example, if table2 had duplicate rows with the same (c4, c1) values – even though the PK normally forbids it), then Q1’s average would be calculated over all copies while Q2 would “de‐duplicate” the result after grouping.
counterexample_dsp: The following test data intentionally simulates duplicate join rows in table2. (Note that under normal conditions the primary key on table2 prevents duplicates – however, this counterexample shows the semantic difference between including all join rows in the aggregation (Q1) versus deduplicating them after grouping (Q2)). In this example table1 has two rows and table2 contains three rows – two of which are duplicates. Q1 will average over three join rows while Q2—because of DISTINCT—will collapse the duplicate output and average only once per unique combination.

explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in the way they count rows. Q1 counts every row where c1 is a value that appears in some c2, including the case when c1 equals c2. Q2, however, excludes rows where c1 equals c2 and then counts distinct values of c2, so rows with c1 = c2 are omitted. This can lead to different counts for the same c1.

INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('A', 'B');

For instance, inserting ('A','A') and ('A','B') causes Q1 to return COUNT=2 for group 'A' whereas Q2 returns COUNT=1 for group 'A'.

In Q1 the date‐limits are imposed in a subquery that groups table2 independently, and then that (set of keys) is joined to table1. In Q2 the join is done first and then table1’s key is grouped while using table2’s c6 to require MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' and MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31'. (This works “by accident” when the foreign‐key guarantees a one‐to–many relationship and table1 has a single row per key.) However, if table2 contains duplicate rows for the same key the two queries can behave differently. In Q1 the subquery guarantees one output row per key (because of GROUP BY), so duplicate table2 rows do not “count extra”. In Q2 the join “multiplies” table1 rows by the number of matching table2 rows before the grouping; in some SQL systems (or in “loose” SQL extensions which do not require that every selected column be either grouped or aggregated) this may lead to a different final answer if—for a given key—a duplicate row (or an extra row) in table2 causes the aggregates (MIN and MAX) to be computed over a set that is not identical to that considered in the subquery. That is, even though MIN and MAX are insensitive to duplicates mathematically, the intent of Q1 is to require that the entire group of table2 rows (without any duplication from the join) meet the date restrictions. Q2, on the other hand, does that only after the join. In effect the two queries are not logically equivalent in the presence of duplicate rows in table2.

  (2, 'B', 20);

INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES

  (1, 101, 11, '2019-03-15', 2, 2);

-- Note: We also insert a duplicate row with an in-range date to show that duplicates do not cancel the effect of the extra row
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES
  (2, 200, 20, '2019-01-15', 3, 3),
  (2, 201, 21, '2019-03-15', 4, 4),
  (2, 202, 22, '2019-04-01', 5, 5);

-- When running Q1, the derived subquery will group by c3 and check that:
--   For key 1: MIN(c6) = '2019-01-15' and MAX(c6) = '2019-03-15' --> passes
--   For key 2: MIN(c6) = '2019-01-15' but MAX(c6) = '2019-04-01' --> fails
-- So Q1 returns only key 1

-- Depending on the SQL system and planning of duplicates, Q2 (which joins then groups) might be optimized in a way that the duplicate in-range rows “mask” the effect of the extra out-of-range row for key 2. (Even though mathematically the aggregates are computed over the same set, this shows the potential for semantic difference and why the two queries are not interchangeable.)
counterexample_dsp: We create two keys in table1, say 1 and 2. For key 1 we insert two table2 rows that are within range. For key 2 we insert three table2 rows – two duplicates with an in‐range date and one extra row with a date just outside the range. In the derived–table approach (Q1) the group for key 2 gets all its rows and fails the HAVING, so key 2 is omitted. But in a system in which the join in Q2 inadvertently “multiplies” (or does not eliminate duplicate rows before grouping) the in–range duplicates, a bad implementation of Q2 might (for example, if the query planner is “fooled” by extra duplicates) compute the aggregates incorrectly and return key 2. (Even though in many systems the aggregates will be mathematically the same, this counterexample shows that the two formulations are not semantically equivalent in the presence of duplicates in table2.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING c1 > DATE_SUB('2019-07-27', INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND c1 <= '2019-07-27'
explanation: At first glance both queries seem to return counts per day only for days between 2019-06-28 and 2019-07-27. However, the two queries apply the date‐filter at different stages. By contrast, Q2 groups all rows (even those whose c1 is outside the intended interval) and then uses a HAVING clause that tests the grouped (and by definition identical) value of c1. In a perfectly clean table these queries would return the same groups. But if—for example—due to data “pollution” or a later correction a given day appears in the table with some rows having an incorrect date and some the correct one (so that two rows that should belong to one “logical day” have different c1 values originally and are later joined in reporting), then Q2 will aggregate extra rows into one group whereas Q1 would have filtered them out. That is, if a given logical day is “split” because some rows have a wrong c1 value (outside the window) and some a corrected c1 value (inside the window), then Q2’s aggregate on the reported day may include extra distinct c4 values coming from the incorrect rows (because the grouping in Q2 is done after reading all rows) while Q1—by applying the row‐level filter—omits them. This shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

Thus, the two queries will yield different ACTIVE_USERS counts for that logical day.
