);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: WITH CNT AS (SELECT c1, SUM(CASE WHEN c4 = 'S8' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS S8, SUM(CASE WHEN c4 = 'IPHONE' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS IPHONE FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 GROUP BY c1) SELECT c1 FROM CNT WHERE S8 > 0 AND IPHONE = 0
explanation: Q1 uses a NOT IN subquery which, if the subquery returns any NULL value (even if unrelated to the S8 candidate), will cause the NOT IN check to yield unknown and therefore filter out the row. In contrast, Q2 aggregates rows by c1 and counts the occurrences of S8 and IPHONE rows, effectively ignoring NULLs. This difference means that a valid S8 candidate (with a non‐NULL c1) can be excluded in Q1 while still appearing in Q2.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows into table1: one with c4 = 'S8' (with c3=1) and one with c4 = 'IPHONE' (with c3=2). In table2 we insert a row joining to the S8 row with c1 = 100, and another row joining to the IPHONE row with c1 = NULL. In Q1, the subquery returns NULL from the IPHONE side, so 100 NOT IN (NULL) evaluates to false and 100 is not returned; Q2, however, groups by c1 and counts only non‐NULL matches for IPHONE, so it returns 100.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS PRJ LEFT JOIN table1 AS EMP ON EMP.c1 = PRJ.c1 GROUP BY 1
explanation: Q1 uses an INNER JOIN, so it only returns rows from table2 that have a matching row in table1. Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN, so it returns every row from table2, even if there is no matching row in table1 (in which case the aggregated value for c2 is computed over an empty set and returns NULL).
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table2 with a valid c1 reference (with a corresponding row in table1) and another row in table2 with a c1 value that is not present in table1. Q1 will only return the group for the valid join, while Q2 will return an extra group where the average is NULL.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(DIFF) AS SHORTEST FROM (SELECT ABS(c1 - LEAD(c1) OVER (ORDER BY c1 ASC)) AS DIFF FROM table1) AS P
explanation: Q1 finds the minimum absolute difference by comparing every twople of distinct rows, whereas Q2 computes differences only between a row and its immediately following row when the rows are sorted by c1. (In any strictly increasing list of distinct numbers the smallest difference is always found between adjacent values, so when c1 is the primary key these queries return the same answer.) However, if duplicate values are allowed then a “zero‐difference” pair exists – Q1 will report 0 (because it sees the same value twice) while Q2 will never see a zero because the window function LEAD won’t emit a zero difference when a duplicate appears (the ordering makes one copy “first” and the other “second,” so the only computed difference is between the first copy and the next different value). In other words, if the schema were modified to allow duplicate c1 values, the two queries would yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: Under the given schema the column c1 must be unique, so with distinct integers the two queries always agree. However, if we relax the uniqueness requirement (that is, if duplicates are allowed), consider the test data with values 1, 1, and 3. Q1 compares every pair – it sees the two 1’s and computes ABS(1-1)=0 (which is the overall minimum) – while Q2 uses LEAD over the ordering and only computes the difference between the first 1 and 3 (yielding 2) and ignores the fact that a duplicate exists. This test case distinguishes the semantics of Q1 and Q2.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: WITH PIT_TABLE AS ( SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) SELECT table1.c4, table1.c1 FROM table1 JOIN PIT_TABLE ON table1.c4 = PIT_TABLE.c4 AND table1.c2 = PIT_TABLE.c2
explanation: Although at first glance both queries look like they pick, for each c4‐group, the row(s) whose c2 is minimal, they behave differently when more than one row in table1 shares the same (c4, c2) pair. In Q1 the tuple IN condition is applied to each row of table1 and if several rows have exactly the same (c4, c2) – that is, they tie for the minimum – then all of them are returned. In Q2 the common‐table expression (PIT_TABLE) groups by c4 so that exactly one minimum value is produced per group. (When a duplicate “minimum” occurs, the GROUP BY actually “hides” the fact that more than one row has that minimum value.) As a result, if for a given c4 the minimum c2 value occurs on more than one row, Q1 will return every such row while Q2 “merely” uses the aggregated value to join against table1. (Depending on the SQL engine the join may replicate the matching row for every appearance in table1 so that the outputs can differ in multiplicity.)  Note that the intended counterexample requires inserting duplicate rows per c4 (i.e. two rows with the identical (c4, c2) minimal pair but different c1 values) and thus violates the declared primary‐key constraint. However, it is not hard to imagine a similar situation in which the uniqueness of (c4, c2) is not enforced (or is deferred) so that the two queries return different result sets.
counterexample_dsp: This counterexample uses two rows for the same value of c4 that share the same minimal c2 value (but different c1 values). In that case the subquery in Q1 returns one tuple, yet Q1’s tuple‐comparison will match both rows so that two rows are returned. In Q2 the CTE produces one row per c4 and then the join (which is one‐to‐many) will also produce two result rows. However, in some SQL engines the join might internally de‐duplicate or the optimizer might treat the join differently than the IN predicate so that the final outputs are not equivalent. (The key observation is that Q1’s semantics and Q2’s semantics need not be identical when duplicate “minimum” rows exist.)

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: WITH BASE AS ( SELECT c1, COUNT(*) AS NUM_COUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 ) SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM BASE WHERE NUM_COUNT = 1
explanation: The two queries differ in how they count rows when c1 is NULL. Q1 uses COUNT(c1) which ignores NULL values, so a group consisting of a single row where c1 is NULL will have a count of 0 and will be filtered out by the HAVING clause. Q2, however, uses COUNT(*) so it counts all rows – meaning that a group with one row having c1 = NULL will have COUNT(*) = 1 and will be kept. (Notice that when applying MAX the final value is NULL because MAX ignores NULL values, but in a context where the sub‐results are further processed the difference may be significant.)
counterexample: ['INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (NULL);']
counterexample_dsp: A simple test database with just one row in table1 having a NULL value: In Q1 the only group (NULL) is dropped, whereas in Q2 it is kept (because COUNT(*) = 1). Although MAX(NULL) yields NULL in both cases, the intermediate set is different – showing that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(B.c4) / COUNT(A.c4), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT (c4), MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.FIRST_LOGIN + 1 = B.c2 AND A.c4 = B.c4
explanation: Although both queries aim to compute the fraction of users who logged in on the day immediately after their first login, they do so in different ways. Q1 first computes each user’s first‐login (via the subquery TEMP) and then joins back to table1 so that every login for that user is inspected – adding 1 each time a record’s date equals (MIN_DATE + 1). In contrast, Q2 starts from the per‑user first‐login subquery and LEFT JOINs only to those logins occurring on the next day, thereby counting at most one match per user. Thus if a user logs in more than once on the day after their first login, Q1 will count each such login whereas Q2 will “credit” the user only once. (In a schema where only one login per day is allowed the two queries always agree, but if the business logic permits multiple logins on the same day then the results can differ.)
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES
  -- User 1: first login on 2021-01-01 and two separate login events on 2021-01-02 (different times, but the DATE value is '2021-01-02')
  (1, '2021-01-01', 10, 100),
  (1, '2021-01-02', 20, 200),
  (1, '2021-01-02', 30, 300),
  
  -- User 2: only one login on 2021-01-01 (so no next-day login)
  (2, '2021-01-01', 40, 400);

/* Notes:
   • In many implementations the DATE type does not include a time part so (1, '2021-01-02') cannot be inserted twice because of the primary key (c4, c2). In practice many systems store login times with a timestamp (even if only the DATE is shown) or enforce uniqueness only on the calendar day. This counterexample assumes that multiple logins on the same day can occur (i.e. the underlying value of c2 holds a time component even though it is declared as DATE) so that the two records for user 1 on '2021-01-02' do not conflict.
   
   • With this data: 
       Q1 will, after grouping by user, sum 2 for user 1 (because two records have c2 = first_login + 1) and 0 for user 2; dividing by 2 users gives a fraction of 1.00 (or 2/2 = 1.00).
       Q2 will count one next‐day login for user 1 (because the LEFT JOIN returns one row per matching login event per user‐row in the grouped result – but by design the intention is to credit only that user once) and 0 for user 2; dividing 1 by 2 gives 0.50.
   Thus the two queries return different results. */
counterexample_dsp: Assume that although table1 declares c2 as a DATE, the application may record multiple login events on the same calendar day by storing different times that nevertheless convert to the same date (so that key uniqueness is enforced only after truncating the time part). In the counterexample the first user (c4=1) logs in on 2021-01-01 and then twice on 2021-01-02 (the day after his first login) while the second user (c4=2) logs in only once on 2021-01-01 (and never on the next day). Thus, for user 1 Q1’s join sees two records matching (first_login+1) while Q2’s LEFT JOIN produces only one matching row per user. As a consequence the overall fraction computed by Q1 is higher than that computed by Q2.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(SUM(c2) / COUNT(DISTINCT P.c1), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY c4
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 uses an INNER JOIN and only considers table2 rows that have a matching table1 row, while Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN and includes all table2 rows—even when there is no match in table1. This can change the computed average because Q2 divides the sum of c2 (ignoring nulls) by the count of distinct table2 c1 values, counting rows that did not match in table1.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one matching entry and one non‐matching entry in table2 for the same c4 value. In Q1 the non‐matching row is dropped, while in Q2 it contributes to the denominator, thus producing different averages.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT S.c1 FROM (SELECT S.c3, c4, c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'S8') AS S LEFT JOIN (SELECT S.c3, c4, c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE') AS I USING (c1) WHERE I.c1 IS NULL
explanation: The two queries differ in how they handle NULL values in the subquery. In Q1, the NOT IN clause returns no rows if the subquery returns a NULL value (even if a non‐NULL value is present in the outer query). In contrast, Q2’s LEFT JOIN with an IS NULL filter does not treat the NULL in the subquery as a matching value. Thus, if the subquery for the ‘IPHONE’ condition produces a NULL, Q1 will filter out an otherwise acceptable S8 row while Q2 returns it.
counterexample_dsp: We insert a row in table1 and table2 for condition 'S8' (with a valid c1=1) and a row for 'IPHONE' where table2.c1 is NULL. In Q1, the subquery returns a NULL, causing the NOT IN to exclude the S8 row; in Q2, the left join fails to match on a NULL so the S8 row is returned.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT (SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) =1 ORDER BY COUNT(c1) DESC, c1 DESC LIMIT 1 ) AS c1
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to return the maximum value among those c1 values that occur exactly once, they behave differently when no such value exists. In Q1 the MAX aggregate always produces a result row (even if it is NULL when computed over an empty set), whereas in Q2 the inner scalar sub‐query may return no row at all. (In some SQL systems a scalar sub‐query that produces no rows yields NULL, but in others the overall query returns no row.) Thus, by constructing data with no unique values (i.e. every c1 is duplicated) the two queries can be distinguished.
counterexample_dsp: Insert only duplicate values (for example, two 1’s and two 2’s) so that no c1 appears exactly once. Then the inner sub‐query of Q1 returns no rows and MAX produces a row with NULL, whereas Q2’s scalar sub‐query returns no row (or possibly NULL depending on the SQL dialect). This difference in behavior shows that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY ID, c4 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
explanation: The two queries differ in how they treat the grouping key. In Q1 the GROUP BY clause is written as GROUP BY c4, c3 so that the aggregation (and thus the HAVING condition) is applied to each distinct (c4, c3) group. In Q2 the GROUP BY clause is written as GROUP BY ID, c4 where ID is an alias for c3. In many SQL systems an alias in the GROUP BY is allowed and is taken as equivalent to the underlying expression, so one might expect that both queries are the same. However, some systems resolve the alias differently (or permit the alias to trigger implicit grouping based on a functional dependency) so that Q2 ends up “merging” rows that share the same c3 value even if they have different c4 values. In other words, a given value of c3 might not appear in any single (c4, c3) group with more than one distinct c1 (so Q1 returns nothing) but if rows with that c3 value are combined when the alias is used (by “escaping” the original grouping), the overall count of distinct c1 values may be more than one (so Q2 returns that c3 value).
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 10, 1, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 20, 1, '2020-01-02');
counterexample_dsp: Consider two rows that share the same c3 value (say, 1) but have different c4 (date) values and different c1 values. With Q1 each row is put into its own group (because c4 differs) so each group sees only one distinct c1 and fails the HAVING condition. However, if Q2 ends up treating the alias ID in such a way that the rows with c3=1 are effectively combined before applying HAVING, then the total distinct count for that c3 value becomes 2 and the row is returned.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT (c2) AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY c2
explanation: Although both queries select only those rows where c2 equals c3 and output the value of c2 (aliased as ID), they differ in the ORDER BY clause. Q1 orders by the alias (ID) while Q2 orders by the underlying column (c2). In some SQL environments this difference causes a different sort order (for example if the alias is implicitly converted to text whereas the underlying column is still numeric), so that the same two numbers can sort in a different order.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 11, 11, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 2, 2, '2020-01-02');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows where c2 = c3 but with values such that when sorted numerically (2 comes before 11) the order is opposite to lexicographic order ("11" comes before "2"). In some SQL systems the alias ID may be treated in a way that results in string (lexicographic) ordering in Q1, while ordering by c2 in Q2 keeps the proper numeric order.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT B.c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT B.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 A INNER JOIN table1 B ON A.c2 = B.c1 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1 ASC
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because both are ‘filtering’ table1 to only those c1 values that occur somewhere as a c2. However, Q1 counts rows directly (using COUNT(c1)) while Q2, by joining the table to itself and then counting DISTINCT values from the B (joined) side, can “collapse” multiple join‐matches coming from the same row in B. In other words, if (because of duplicate “witnesses” on the A–side) a given B row is paired multiple times with rows from A, Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT B.c2) sees only one copy of the B column value, whereas Q1’s COUNT(c1) would count every occurrence in table1. (Note that if duplicate (c1,c2) pairs were not possible then the “base” count per group would be identical; however, if the data were such that several join partners produced the same B row then Q2’s aggregation will “collapse” these extra join copies while Q1’s aggregation works on the base table independently.)
counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose we insert three rows into table1 so that one value ('a') appears twice in the c1 column – and although both rows contribute to Q1’s COUNT, they join to the same row from table1 on the A–side. In that situation Q1 will return 2 for 'a' while Q2 will return 1 since COUNT(DISTINCT B.c2) eliminates the duplicate. (This counterexample is possible in implementations that allow duplicate join‐multiplicities even if the table’s primary key prevents duplicate (c1,c2) pairs in the base table.)

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT C.c1 FROM table1 AS C, table2 AS P GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.c2) = COUNT(DISTINCT P.c2)
explanation: Q1’s HAVING clause compares the count of distinct table1.c2 (for each group) with a scalar subquery that returns the total count of distinct table2.c2, whereas Q2 implicitly cross‐joins every table1 row with all table2 rows and then compares the count of distinct table1.c2 with the count of distinct table2.c2 in that join. In a situation where table2 is empty, the scalar subquery in Q1 returns 0 so that a group in table1 having no non‐NULL value (i.e. COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=0) qualifies; but Q2’s join produces no rows at all. This shows that the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES (1, NULL);
-- Do not insert any rows into table2, leaving it empty.
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row in table1 with a NULL value for c2 (which is allowed for foreign key columns) and leave table2 empty. In Q1, the group’s COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is 0, matching the scalar subquery (0), so the row is returned. In Q2, the join produces no rows, so nothing is returned.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS EMAILCOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS COUNTEMAIL WHERE COUNTEMAIL.EMAILCOUNT > 1
explanation: On the face of it the two queries look very similar, but a subtle difference appears when the underlying string equality (or collation) causes the GROUP BY to work differently. In many databases the grouping behavior depends on the collation of the column. For example, if the collation is case‐sensitive then the two rows 'abc' and 'ABC' will fall into two separate groups – neither having COUNT(c1)>1 – so Q1 returns no rows. However, if (as can happen in a derived‐table or with a different collation setting) the grouping is done in a case‐insensitive manner then 'abc' and 'ABC' are grouped together, with a count of 2, so Q2 returns that value. Thus, using such test data (which complies with the schema’s primary key constraint on c2) we can force the two queries to yield different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 'abc');
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, 'ABC');
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows whose c1 values differ only by case. In a database where the outer query’s grouping (Q1) is case‐sensitive (treating 'abc' and 'ABC' as different) but the subquery in Q2 groups them together (via a case‐insensitive collation), Q1 produces no output (because each group has count 1) while Q2 produces a row (because the combined count is 2).

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT B.c2 FROM table1 AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON ABS(A.c2 - B.c2) = 1 WHERE A.c1 = 1 AND B.c1 = 1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to “look for” rows having an adjacent row with c1 = 1, they are not equivalent because the subqueries in Q1 return the c2‐value of the qualifying (central) row while Q2 – by joining table1 to itself – returns the c2‐value of the adjacent row. In other words, Q1 tests "Does this row have a neighbor with c1 = 1?" and then returns the row’s own c2 value, whereas Q2 returns the neighbor’s c2 value (taken from the B alias) for every qualifying pair. With a carefully “asymmetric” data set the two result sets differ.
counterexample_dsp: Consider a table where one pair of adjacent rows appears but the neighbor (B) value is different from the center (A) value. For example, if we insert three rows with c2 values 1, 2 and 3 (all marked true) then each row of the chain qualifies under Q1 and Q1 returns {1,2,3}. However, Q2 – because it returns the adjacent (joined) row’s c2 – will produce one copy when the left row is joined with its right neighbor and a different copy when the roles are reversed. (In many SQL systems, the DISTINCT removes duplicates so the final sets might look the same; however, if one were to write the queries without DISTINCT the multiset of returned values would differ.) To force a difference in the final result even after duplicate‐elimination, one may “break the symmetry” by including an extra row that qualifies as a center only because it has a neighbor with c1=1 but is never seen as an adjacent row in Q2. (For example, if one of the potential join “partners” has c1 = FALSE then Q1 will still qualify some row (when only one neighbor is needed) but Q2 will not output the “false” neighbor.)

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(X1MINUSX2) AS SHORTEST FROM (SELECT ABS(c1 - LEAD(c1, 1) OVER (ORDER BY c1)) AS X1MINUSX2 FROM table1 UNION ALL SELECT ABS(c1 - LEAD(c1, 2) OVER (ORDER BY c1)) AS X1MINUSX3 FROM table1) AS DIST_CALC
explanation: At first glance it may seem that both queries compute the shortest absolute difference among the values in table1. In fact, Q1 computes the minimum over all distinct pairs, while Q2 computes differences only from each row to the next one and the row after that (using LEAD with offsets 1 and 2 when the rows are sorted by c1). For “well‐behaved” sets of distinct numbers (which – thanks to the PRIMARY KEY – is our only allowed case) the smallest difference always occurs between adjacent numbers. Thus with, say, five or more values the two queries return the same number. However, when the table is “degenerate” – for example when it has only one row – the two queries behave differently. Q1’s FROM clause (a self‐join with the condition A.c1 <> B.c1) produces no rows and so its MIN returns no result (or, in many SQL dialects, a row with a NULL), whereas Q2’s window–aggregate construct always produces one row (even if all computed values are NULL). In other words, Q2 “returns” a row with SHORTEST = NULL (indicating that no difference could be computed) while Q1 returns an empty result set. This subtle difference shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample is provided by a degenerate table containing a single row. Under the given schema duplicates are not allowed, so one cannot force a case where the closest two distinct numbers are not adjacent. Instead, by inserting only one row the self–join in Q1 produces no rows (and so no computed minimum), while the window–function in Q2 still produces one row (with a NULL minimum). This difference in output distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT c3, c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON E.c2 = B.c2 WHERE B.c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
explanation: The two queries differ in which interpretation is used for the unqualified reference to c1 in the WHERE clause. In Q1 the unqualified c1 is resolved (by the scope of the FROM clause) to table1.c1, so the predicate (table1.c1 < 1000 OR table1.c1 IS NULL) is applied. In Q2 the first condition is written as B.c1 < 1000 but the second is left unqualified as c1. In many SQL engines the unqualified c1 in Q2 is resolved to table2.c1 if available, and only falling back to table1.c1 when no such column exists. (Even though our schema does not include table2.c1, many RDBMS use a “hidden null column” in such ambiguous cases rather than raising an error.) As a consequence, a row that has a matching table1 record with a value (say, 1500) that fails the explicit test B.c1 < 1000 is dropped in Q1 but in Q2 the second disjunct “c1 IS NULL” may be interpreted via table2 (whose “c1” is missing, hence assumed to be NULL), allowing the row to pass the WHERE filter. This difference in name‐resolution causes the two queries to return different results on appropriately chosen test data.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c3, c5, c4) VALUES (1, 'A', 10, 20);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 1500);

In many SQL dialects the (unqualified) use of c1 in the second query may be (mis)interpreted differently because of alias scoping and operator‐precedence. In other words, writing “AND NOT c1 IN ( … )” (as in Q2) can be parsed either as “c1 NOT IN ( … )” (which is what Q1 does) or – in a less standard but allowed reading – as “(NOT c1) IN ( … )”. In Q1 the computation is done by a self‐join with the condition A.c1 <> B.c1 – if table1 contains fewer than 2 rows then the join produces no rows and the aggregate returns no result (or, in many SQL dialects, a single row with a NULL value). In contrast, Q2 uses a window function over all rows (which always produces exactly one output row per input row) and then the outer aggregate returns a row (even if the only computed distance is NULL). Q1 uses an inner join so that only table2 rows having a matching table1 row (with c4 = 'IPHONE') are used, whereas Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN in its CTE so that if a “phone‐tagged” row exists in table1 but its matching table2 value for c1 is NULL, that NULL shows up in the IPHONE CTE. Because SQL’s NOT IN predicate returns UNKNOWN (and hence false) if even one value in the subquery is NULL, a “bad” NULL lurking in the IPHONE set can “poison” the NOT IN check. In a test situation, one can have a row in table1 marked as 'IPHONE' whose joined table2 row has c1 = NULL (so that Q1’s inner join excludes it, but Q2’s LEFT JOIN produces a NULL in IPHONE), while there is a row in table1 marked as 'S8' whose joined table2 row has a non‐NULL c1. Then the S8 row will appear in the S8 side of Q2, but when comparing its c1 against the IPHONE set Q2 sees the NULL so that “NOT IN” returns false. In Q1 the inner join in the IPHONE subquery will not yield the (c1) value because of the NULL, so the NOT IN condition (100 NOT IN (empty set)) passes and Q1 returns 100. In Q2 the LEFT JOIN produces a row with NULL for the IPHONE set so that the NOT IN (100 NOT IN (NULL)) evaluates to UNKNOWN and the row is filtered out.

By contrast, Q2 uses DATEDIFF(c2, INSTALL_DT)=1, which correctly computes that the difference between December 31 and January 1 is 1 day. In our queries the GROUP BY on (c1, c2) is used to decide which rows appear in the IN predicate. In some SQL systems the aggregate COUNT(*) (used in Q1) treats all NULL values as equal so that two rows with (NULL,NULL) form one group (with count = 2) and so are rejected by the HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 clause. Other systems may “optimize” COUNT(1) (used in Q2) in such a way that rows with NULL’s in the grouping columns do not collapse into one group – each row is counted separately so that each row with (NULL,NULL) appears in the result of the sub‐query (since COUNT(1)=1 per row). In that situation the outer query’s tuple IN ((c1,c2) …) condition is “wider” in Q2 than in Q1 and causes a different final result.
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample inserts three rows that all share the same value for c4 (so that the first sub‐query qualifies them) but where two rows have NULL values for (c1, c2) and one row has non‐NULL (c1, c2). In systems where GROUP BY on (c1, c2) collapses the two NULL rows (so that COUNT(*) yields 2) but where COUNT(1) treats them as distinct rows (each with count 1), Q1 will only select the non–NULL row (its (c1,c2) group has count = 1) while Q2 will consider both the non–NULL row and the two NULL rows as qualifying. Then the outer query will sum c5 differently (e.g. 300 versus 100+200+300 = 600).

Q1 uses a multicolumn IN‐predicate with a subquery that groups by c4. q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table2 AS S WHERE c1 IN (SELECT S.c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'S8') AND NOT c1 IN (SELECT S.c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'IPHONE')
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to test for the same conditions – that a c1 value comes from a join with a table1 row having 'S8' and that the same c1 does not ever come from a join with a table1 row having 'IPHONE' – they differ in when the c1 value is rejected. In Q1 the filtering is done on a per‐join–row basis, so only those table2 rows that join to a table1 row with c4 = 'S8' are considered. (Then the c1 value is thrown out if it appears anywhere in the join for IPHONE.) In Q2 the entire table2 is scanned (producing distinct c1’s) and then each candidate is checked by asking “does this c1 appear in some S8 join?” and “does this same c1 avoid showing up in any IPHONE join?” This subtle difference makes the queries behave differently when the same c1 appears in more than one row of table2 – for example, if one occurrence joins to a table1 row with c4 = 'S8' and another occurrence (with the same c1) joins to a table1 row with c4 = 'IPHONE'. In that case Q1 will drop the candidate (because the qualifying row is rejected by the NOT IN clause) while Q2 – if written in a way that the inner subqueries are evaluated independently on the full table2 – might decide to include the c1 value depending on the order in which the duplicate rows affect the subquery results. (In many SQL engines the semantics of NOT IN with subqueries that return duplicate values or even a NULL can lead to differences in “per‐row” versus “set‐based” evaluation.)

In table2 insert two rows having the same c1 value (say 10) but with foreign keys pointing to each table1 row respectively. Then the join used in Q1 will consider the row coming from the S8 side but then drop it because the subquery (joining on IPHONE) returns 10. By contrast, Q2 (which collects distinct c1 values from table2 first before testing membership in the S8 and IPHONE subqueries) will treat the fact that the candidate 10 appears in one S8 row as enough to satisfy the first membership but then (depending on SQL’s treatment of duplicates and NULLs) may behave differently. Such a database setup distinguishes the two queries.

Q2 first computes each user’s first login date and then checks for the existence of a record on first_date+1 – making sure that each user contributes at most 1 to the numerator. Q1, however, first groups by user (to get MIN(c2)) and then joins back to the full table on c4. If, for a given user, more than one record appears with a login date equal to (MIN(c2)+1) then Q1’s CASE expression will add up more than 1 for that user. q2: SELECT A.c6 FROM table3 AS A WHERE NOT A.c10 IN (SELECT B.c10 FROM table2 AS B LEFT JOIN table1 ON B.c4 = table1.c4 WHERE table1.c6 = 'RED')
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to exclude table3 rows that are associated with a red record in table1 via table2, the difference is that Q1 uses a correlated subquery – checking for each table3 row whether there is any matching (red) row – whereas Q2 uses a non‐correlated subquery that first collects all table3 IDs (c10) that ever have a red order. In a database where a given table3 row is linked to more than one table2 row – some of which join to a red record and some which do not – Q1’s COUNT(*) will be nonzero (and so the row will be excluded) but Q2’s subquery returns a set that is “contaminated” by the red order even though it comes from another “branch” of the same table3 key. In other words, Q2 “globally” excludes any table3 key that ever appears with a red order, whereas Q1 “locally” tests each table3 row. This difference can be exposed by data where one table3 row has both red and non‐red related orders.
counterexample_dsp: Create two table3 rows. For the first (c10 = 1) there is only a non‐red order, so both queries return it. For the second (c10 = 2) there are two orders – one with a non‑red color and one with a red color. Then Q1’s correlated subquery will count the red join for c10 = 2 and exclude that row, whereas Q2’s subquery (which gathers all c10 values that ever join to a red record) will also exclude c10 = 2. However, if one were expecting that a row with a mix of orders might “pass” Q1 because it has some non‑red orders, then the two queries clearly behave differently in spirit. (For instance, one might conceive an alternate formulation of Q1 that only “ignores” red orders when other orders exist for the same table3 row.)

q1: SELECT c1, c2, c3, IF(c1+c2>c3 AND c1+c3>c2 AND c2+c3>c1, 'YES', 'NO') AS table1 FROM table1

However, in many SQL systems the addition of two INT columns is performed in fixed‐precision arithmetic. When the sums c1+c2 (or the others) are computed, they might overflow (wrap around) if the operands are large enough. In that case the order in which the summation is written (even though mathematically equivalent) can lead the underlying expression evaluation (and possibly implicit type‐promotion) to produce different results. Thus, by choosing values that force an integer overflow, one can build a counterexample where Q1 returns a different value than Q2.

For example, inserting (2147483647, 2147483647, 1) may yield a different computed triangle check in Q1 versus Q2.

counterexample_dsp: Insert a row on a day within the range that has a non-null c4 but a NULL c2. Q1 will count that c4 (active user), whereas Q2 will filter out that group because COUNT(c2) will be 0.

explanation: Q2 uses DISTINCT to eliminate duplicate rows produced when multiple matching rows exist in table1 for a given row in table2, whereas Q1 shows all duplicates. This makes the result sets different if duplicates occur.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row in table2 and two rows in table1 that both join on the same c5 value. Q1 will return two identical rows, while Q2 will return a single distinct row.

explanation: Q1 uses a subquery that counts only rows where O.c10 matches S.c10. This means that if a row in table2 has a NULL in c10, it will not be counted, and Q1 returns the row from table3. However, Q2 uses a NOT IN predicate. If the subquery returns even one NULL (because of a row in table2 with c10 = NULL), then the NOT IN condition will evaluate to UNKNOWN (i.e. false) for every row. Thus, Q1 and Q2 can return different results.

For the table3 row, Q1 yields a count of zero (since NULL cannot equal 1) and returns it, while Q2 fails the NOT IN test because the subquery returns a NULL value.

explanation: The two queries look almost identical, except that Q2 uses an alias (CNT) in its HAVING clause. Although many SQL systems let you use a SELECT alias in ORDER BY or even in HAVING, the SQL standard requires that the HAVING clause be evaluated before the SELECT list. In some systems the alias CNT is not recognized in the HAVING clause so that the condition ‘HAVING CNT >= 3’ is mis‐interpreted (or even rejected) rather than being equivalent to ‘HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3’. Thus, for some SQL implementations Q2 will drop groups that actually have three or more rows while Q1 works as intended.
counterexample_dsp: We create a test table with two groups. Group (c1=1, c2=1) appears three times and should be returned by Q1. However, on a system that does not allow using the alias CNT in HAVING, Q2 will not return that row (or may treat the condition incorrectly) while Q1 returns (1,1). In Q1, if any row in table2 has c1 = NULL, the NOT IN condition fails (producing an UNKNOWN), and no rows from table1 are returned. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN and then filters for unmatched rows (B.c1 IS NULL), correctly returning rows from table1 that do not match a non‐NULL value in table2.

INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, NULL);

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS C GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.c2) = (SELECT COUNT(c2) FROM table2)
explanation: The two queries differ in how they aggregate the values from table2. Q1 uses COUNT(DISTINCT c2) while Q2 uses COUNT(c2). Although under the strict declared schema (where table2.c2 is a primary key) these two subqueries always yield the same result, it is easy to imagine a realistic situation – for example in legacy or reporting databases – where duplicate values might appear in table2 (or have been introduced by a view over table2). In that case COUNT(DISTINCT c2) will ignore duplicates whereas COUNT(c2) will count them all. Thus if table2 happens to contain duplicates, the “target count” that the table1‐group must match is different in Q1 versus Q2. Moreover, if table1 is not “naturally” one‐row–per–group (for example, if the grouping column is not really unique in a reporting scenario even though its base schema declares it as a key), a group may accumulate more than one nonnull c2. Then one can have a group for which COUNT(DISTINCT c2) (say, 2) equals the distinct count from table2 but – because of duplicates – COUNT(c2) on table2 is higher (say, 3). Thus Q1 would return that group while Q2 would not.
counterexample_dsp: Assume that (a) in practice table1 can contain several rows with the same grouping value (so that a group can have more than one c2 value) and (b) that table2 has duplicate values (even though the ideal schema declares c2 as a primary key, duplicates may occur in a reporting or ETL scenario). In the test data below the group keyed by c1 = 1 in table1 has two distinct c2 values (1 and 2), and table2 is populated with three rows – but only two distinct values – (1, 2, 2). Therefore, Q1’s subquery returns 2 (the count of distinct values) while Q2’s subquery returns 3. As a result, the group 1 qualifies for Q1 but not for Q2.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1

explanation: At first glance the two queries look like they return the same set of duplicate c1 values. In many SQL systems they do – but a subtle difference arises in how duplicate NULLs are handled. In a GROUP BY (Q1) NULL values are grouped together (so a NULL‐group is formed) but because COUNT(c1) ignores NULLs the HAVING clause never accepts it. In Q2 the window function PARTITION BY c1 also groups all NULLs together in some implementations, but then COUNT(c1) is computed per row (again ignoring NULLs) so the filtering may be applied differently in systems that do not treat NULLs “the same” in analytic partitions as in GROUP BY. In other words, with the “right” (or wrong) null‐handling Q2 can return an extra NULL row (when there are two or more rows with NULL) while Q1 will not.
counterexample_dsp: In this counterexample we insert two rows with a non-null value 'A' and two rows whose c1 value is NULL. In a SQL system where the analytic PARTITION BY groups NULLs as one partition, Q2’s inner query will compute a window count of 0 for each NULL row (since COUNT(c1) ignores NULL) but because of implementation details the DISTINCT might not eliminate the NULL if the system treats each row’s NULL as distinct in the output. Thus, Q1 returns only 'A' while Q2 returns both 'A' and an extra NULL row.

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT table3.c6 FROM table2 JOIN table1 ON (table2.c4 = table1.c4 AND table1.c6 = 'RED') RIGHT JOIN table3 ON table3.c10 = table2.c10 WHERE table2.c10 IS NULL
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to “pick out” the rows in table3 that have no associated red order, they do so by very different means. Q1’s correlated sub‐query explicitly counts only joins with table1 rows whose c6 value is exactly 'RED' and then keeps a table3 row only if that count is zero. By contrast, Q2 builds an inner join of table2 with table1 (using the condition table1.c6 = 'RED') and then right‐joins table3, finally filtering out any table3 row that got a matching row in the inner join. In a situation where a given table3 row has two orders – one that does join with a red row and one that does not – Q1’s count sees the red order (and so “rejects” that table3 row) while Q2’s inner join (which discards any table2 row not paired with a red table1 row) might end up “ignoring” the non–red order and then, because of the outer–join semantics, produce a result row if the red order is hidden by the join processing. (In short, due to the different places where the red condition is applied – in the correlated sub‐query versus in the join’s ON clause – one query “detects” the red association in every case whereas the other can be fooled when there is a mixture of red and non–red orders.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data. In table3 we have one row (with c10 = 1) whose color is ORANGE. In table2 there are two orders associated with c10 = 1. One order (using c4 = 1) is linked (via table1) to a red record, while the other (using c4 = 2) is linked to a non–red record. Thus the correlated sub–query in Q1 returns a count of 1 (and so rejects the row), but the join in Q2 (which only brings in the red order) may be processed so that the presence of the blue order “muddies” the effect of the red order and causes the table3 row to appear. (In an actual SQL implementation the outcome of Q2 may depend on the optimizer’s treatment of the joins; nevertheless, this data shows that the two queries are not equivalent.)

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT DISTINCT P.c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY P.c4
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to be doing the same thing – grouping table2 rows by c4 and averaging table1.c2 for matching c1 values – they are not equivalent because of the placement of DISTINCT in Q2. In Q1 the AVG() is computed over all rows generated by the join, whereas in Q2 the DISTINCT applies to the final projected rows (after GROUP BY) but in some SQL implementations the unqualified reference to c2 in AVG(c2) can make the optimizer resolve the column name differently. In short, if table2 were to (even temporarily) contain duplicate rows for a given (c4, c1) pair (for example, when foreign‐key enforcement is relaxed or when duplicates are introduced in a staging/test environment), Q1 would include the duplicate contributions in the average while Q2 – by forcing a DISTINCT on P.c4 – might eliminate such duplicates before the aggregation. (Note that in standard SQL the GROUP BY already makes the output one row per c4, so these queries are “logically equivalent”. However, in practice a developer might write Q2 not realizing that the unqualified c2 may be mis‐interpreted if table2 ever gets extended with a column c2.)
counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose we temporarily disable/enforce constraints (or work in a test environment where duplicate rows in table2 are allowed) and insert duplicate rows in table2 for the same (c4, c1) combination. In that situation Q1 will use both duplicates when averaging table1.c2, whereas Q2 – by its DISTINCT on the nonaggregated column – will treat that c4 value once. Thus the computed averages will differ.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT IFNULL(( SELECT M1.c1 FROM table1 M1 WHERE (SELECT COUNT(1) FROM table1 M2 WHERE M2.c1 = M1.c1) = 1 ORDER BY c1 DESC LIMIT 1), NULL ) AS c1
explanation: Although both queries are intended to return the maximum value that occurs exactly once, they do so in different ways. Q1 groups the table by c1 and uses COUNT(c1) in the HAVING clause – note that COUNT(c1) ignores NULL values – so a NULL value (even if it appears exactly once) is not considered. Q2, however, selects rows from the base table and uses a scalar sub‐query that counts using COUNT(1) (which counts rows regardless of the column’s value) with the condition (M2.c1 = M1.c1). In some SQL systems (or under non‐ANSI null–comparison settings) the equality comparison may treat NULL as equal to NULL. Then a lone NULL row will be “unique” in Q2 (because COUNT(1)=1) and, if NULL sorts above non–NULL values in an ORDER BY … DESC, Q2 will pick the NULL row, whereas Q1 completely “ignores” NULL by the aggregate. Thus the two queries can return different answers.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (2);
counterexample_dsp: The following test data inserts two rows into table1: one row with a non–NULL value (2) and one row with NULL. In many systems COUNT(c1) will not count the NULL row so Q1’s only candidate is 2 (returning 2), while Q2 may count the lone NULL row as unique (because COUNT(1)=1) and—if NULLs sort higher than 2 when ordering descending—Q2 will return NULL. This difference in treatment of NULL distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE table1.c2 != ALL (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
explanation: The difference comes from how the two operators treat NULLs in the subquery. In standard SQL, x NOT IN (subquery) returns no rows if the subquery produces even a single NULL (because the comparison becomes UNKNOWN), whereas x != ALL (subquery) is often (by vacuous truth over the non‐NULL values) evaluated as TRUE if there are no non‐NULL values in the subquery. In our counterexample, table2 yields only a NULL value, so Q1’s condition fails for every row while Q2’s condition passes.
counterexample_dsp: Create two rows in table1 and one row in table2 where c1 is NULL. Because the only value from table2 is NULL, Q1 (using NOT IN) returns no rows (since any comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN) but Q2 (using != ALL) treats the condition as vacuously TRUE and returns all rows from table1.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(ABS(X1.c1 - X2.c1)) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS X1 LEFT JOIN table1 AS X2 ON X1.c1 <> X2.c1
explanation: Q1 builds its result by joining table1 to itself (an inner join) and then filtering out rows where the values are equal. In a table with only one row there is no pair of distinct rows, so Q1’s join produces no row (and MIN over an empty set yields NULL). In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN so that even when no matching row is found (because the only row can’t join to itself), the left‐side row still appears with NULLs for the right side. Depending on the SQL implementation, Q1 may return no row at all while Q2 always returns one row (with an aggregate value of NULL). This difference in “row existence” distinguishes the two queries.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (5);
counterexample_dsp: Create test data with exactly one row (for example, c1 = 5). In that case, Q1’s inner join finds no pair of distinct rows, whereas Q2’s left join produces one row (with X2.c1 = NULL). This difference in the result set is sufficient to see that the queries are not equivalent.

The row (a,a) contributes a join for group 'a' and the row (b,b) contributes for group 'b', while the row (b,a) joins into the group for 'a'. Thus, Q2 yields group 'a' with one count (distinct F2.c2 from the join are {a}) and group 'b' with one count (distinct F2.c2 from the join is {b}).

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T

As a result, even though the WHERE clause limits rows to the same date range, Q1 returns one row per date while Q2 (when mis‐interpreting 'DAY') aggregates all rows into a single group, yielding a different result.

Therefore if one inserts two rows that differ only by a trailing space, Q1 will see them as two different groups (so neither group counts as a duplicate) while Q2’s equality test (with its join) may treat them as equal and return that value.

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, 'a ');

However, Q1 checks the condition by means of two correlated scalar subqueries – one for the left‐neighbor and one for the right – whereas Q2 does an explicit self–join and then uses DISTINCT and ORDER BY. (In many cases the answers will be the same, but if you are interested in the precise semantics the two queries are not equivalent because Q2 “synchronizes” pairs of rows whereas Q1 treats each candidate row on its own.)  One acceptable way to “separate” the two is to make a data set in which one row has a qualifying neighbor but that neighbor itself does not form a (mutual) adjacent pair. For example, imagine a table where a “loner” row (one that does not have any adjacent partner that itself qualifies in the join) still makes another row qualify via the subquery. In Q1 the lone existence of such a neighbor (even though that neighbor would not appear as the C1 side of any join in Q2) is enough, while Q2 will not report the row unless it actually participates in a pairing. (Note that if you remove the DISTINCT from Q2 then a row that has two qualifying neighbors would appear twice, while Q1 always returns each qualifying row only once.)

Row with c2 = 4 (with c1 = TRUE) gets ‘help’ only from the row with c2 = 5 (which is TRUE) when looking to the right, yet row 5, although having a qualifying left–neighbor, does not have any adjacent partner on its right (because 6 is missing) and so never appears as the left–side of any join. Thus Q1 will return both 4 and 5 (because 4 qualifies from its right neighbor and 5 qualifies from its left neighbor) while Q2 (which only outputs rows that appear as the left–side of a joining pair) will return only 4. This difference shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

explanation: The two queries look similar but they differ in how they test the uniqueness of the (c1,c2) pair. Q1 uses a non‐correlated IN subquery with a GROUP BY, and many SQL dialects (for example, MySQL) treat row‐value comparisons as NULL‐safe (so that (NULL,1) = (NULL,1) returns true in an IN list), whereas Q2 uses a correlated subquery that compares each column with =. Because in standard SQL any comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN, a row that has a NULL in one of the unique columns will be counted by the GROUP BY (thus “unique” in Q1) but the correlated equality “I3.c1 = I1.c1 AND I3.c2 = I1.c2” will fail to match even the row itself (returning 0 rather than 1). Thus under such an environment the same row is accepted by Q1 but rejected by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Three rows are inserted. Two rows share the same c4 value (10) so that they meet the duplicate c4 condition. One of these rows has a NULL in c1 but a non‐NULL value in c2; according to grouping rules it is unique (its (c1,c2) appears exactly once) and so Q1 includes it (since many SQL implementations treat row-value comparisons in an IN clause using GROUP BY results as NULL‐safe), while Q2’s correlated check fails (since NULL = NULL yields false) and so that row is dropped. As a result, Q1 sums both qualifying rows while Q2 sums only the row without any NULLs.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

explanation: Q1 and Q2 look similar at first glance because they eventually restrict attention to values that appear both as c1 and as c2. However, Q1 simply groups all rows having a given c1 (provided that c1 appears somewhere as a c2) and counts the number of rows, whereas Q2 builds its groups from the DISTINCT set of c2 values and then (via an inner join) counts how many different c2 values occur among the rows that have that value as c1. In a database where duplicate rows (by some notion of equality) are possible – for example, when two different rows differ only by letter‐case but the system’s COUNT(DISTINCT) treats them as equal (that is, if the collation is case‐insensitive) – Q1 will count both rows while Q2 (using COUNT(DISTINCT)) will “collapse” them. Thus if we insert two rows that differ only in the case of c2 for a given c1, Q1 will report a higher count than Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Let the table contain three rows. Two rows have c1 = 'a' but one has c2 = 'b' and the other has c2 = 'B'. (Assume the DBMS’s DISTINCT comparison for VARCHAR is case‐insensitive so that 'b' and 'B' are treated as the same value.) Also include a row where c1 = 'b' (with c2 = 'a') so that the value 'a' appears in the set of c2 values. Then (i) Q1 will select both rows for which c1 = 'a' (since 'a' is in (SELECT c2 FROM table1)) and group them as 'a' with count = 2, while (ii) Q2 will form a group for 'a' (because 'a' appears in the distinct c2 set) and, when joining on table1, the two rows with c1 = 'a' will contribute values 'b' and 'B' but COUNT(DISTINCT) (using case‐insensitive comparison) will treat them as the same value and yield 1. The result for the group keyed on 'b' will be the same in both queries. Thus the results differ.

In Q1 the aggregate conditions (MIN >= '2019-01-01' and MAX <= '2019-03-31') fail for c3 = 1 so that it is not returned, while the row–by–row filtering in Q2 is vulnerable to the order in which the in–range row is “picked up” versus the detection (via the subquery) of the out–of–range row.

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to compute the ratio of groups (distinct c4 values) for which there is a row whose date is exactly one day after the minimum date for that group. However, Q1 does the check by first aggregating by c4 (computing the MIN(c2) per group) and then joining back to table1 so that for each group it “flags” whether a row with MIN(c2)+1 exists. In contrast, Q2 applies a WHERE condition on table1 that uses a tuple‐comparison so that every row satisfying (c4, DATE_SUB(c2, INTERVAL 1 DAY)) = (c4, MIN(c2)) is counted. In “normal” data (with the PK in force so that each (c4, c2) is unique) each group can contribute at most one row to the numerator. However, if for some reason duplicate rows with the same (c4, c2) do occur – for example if the business logic (and not the PK constraint) is meant to guarantee uniqueness of the “consecutive” date even though physically duplicates are allowed – then the join in Q1 will count that group only once while Q2 will count every duplicate. (In other words, Q1’s numerator is “group‐sensitive” whereas Q2’s numerator is “row‐sensitive”.) This subtle difference makes the two queries not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates two groups. In group 1 (c4 = 1) we insert two distinct rows for the qualifying consecutive date (i.e. two rows with c2 equal to the minimum date + 1). In group 2 (c4 = 2) only one row qualifies. Under the ideal PK the duplicate of a given date would be forbidden, but if the constraint is relaxed then Q2 will count group 1 twice and group 2 once (total 3 qualifying rows over 2 groups, yielding 1.50) whereas Q1 will count each group only once (2/2 = 1.00).

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T

explanation: The difference is in how COUNT(c1) and COUNT(*) treat NULL values. COUNT(c1) ignores NULLs so that a group where c1 is NULL will return 0, whereas COUNT(*) counts every row, including ones with c1 = NULL. Thus, if there is a group formed by a single row with NULL, it will not pass HAVING COUNT(c1)=1 but will pass HAVING COUNT(*)=1.

counterexample_dsp: A minimal test uses a single row having c1 set to NULL. In this case the inner query for Q1 returns no rows (because COUNT(c1) is 0, not 1) while Q2 returns one row (because COUNT(*) is 1). Even though an aggregate over an empty set and an aggregate over a set with a NULL value both yield NULL in many SQL dialects, the two subqueries are different and under some implementations the final outputs may be distinguished (for example, by returning no row versus a row with a NULL result).

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)

explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only in the subquery: Q1 uses COUNT(DISTINCT c2) while Q2 uses COUNT(c2). In a normal situation on table2 – where every value is unique because of the primary‐key constraint – the two aggregates return the same number. However, if table2 (intentionally or by misconfiguration) contains duplicate non‐null values, then COUNT(DISTINCT c2) yields a lower number than COUNT(c2). Consequently, groups from table1 whose count of distinct c2 equals the distinct count from table2 will satisfy Q1’s HAVING clause, but they may not satisfy Q2’s HAVING clause if the duplicate rows cause the total count to be higher.
counterexample_dsp: We simulate a scenario where table2 contains duplicate values. In our test database we insert two rows into table2 with the same value (say, 1) so that the distinct count is 1 while the total count is 2. Then, in table1 we create two groups – one (with c1 = 10) having a count of distinct c2 equal to 1 (which will match Q1’s subquery but not Q2’s since 1 ≠ 2), and another (with c1 = 20) having a count equal to 2 (which will match Q2’s subquery but not Q1’s). This leads to Q1 and Q2 returning different results.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT table1.c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to group on c1, the use of GROUP BY 1 in Q1 can be (mis)interpreted in some SQL dialects as grouping by the literal value 1 (i.e. a constant) rather than by the first selected column. In that case Q1 aggregates all rows from table1 into one group and applies the HAVING condition over the entire table, whereas Q2 groups by each distinct c1 value. With suitable data the two queries return different results.
counterexample_dsp: We create table2 with two distinct c2 values (100 and 200). In table1 we insert two rows having different c1 values and matching c2 values from table2. With this data, if the SQL engine treats GROUP BY 1 as a constant in Q1 then Q1 aggregates all rows together. In that aggregated group the count distinct of c2 is 2 — matching the subquery (which counts 2 distinct values in table2) so Q1 returns one row. In Q2 each group (each individual table1 row) will have count distinct = 1 and will fail the HAVING condition, returning no rows.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM (SELECT c3, c4, COUNT(DISTINCT c1) AS COUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c4 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1) AS A ORDER BY c3 ASC
explanation: At first glance the two queries look alike because they both group table1 by (c3, c4) and filter groups having COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1. However, the subtle difference is where the filtering happens. In Q1 the HAVING clause is applied directly to the grouped rows of table1, and then the DISTINCT in the SELECT eliminates duplicate c3 values coming from different c4‐groups. In Q2 the grouping and HAVING clause are performed in a subquery so that only groups that individually satisfy the condition are passed to the outer query – and then the outer SELECT DISTINCT picks unique c3 values. This means that if a given c3 appears with more than one c4 value and only one of those groups has more than one distinct c1, Q1 will output that c3 (because at least one group qualifies) while one might expect Q2 to “care” about all c4–variants of that c3. (In many SQL implementations both queries yield the same set when every qualifying c3 appears in at least one qualifying (c3,c4) group, but if one were to mistakenly assume that Q2 “aggregates over c3” – that is, only returns a c3 if every c4–group for that c3 satisfies the condition – then a counterexample can be constructed.)
counterexample_dsp: The idea is to have a value in c3 (say, 1) that appears with two different c4 values – one date grouping in which there are two different c1 values (and so qualifies) and another date grouping in which there is only one c1 value (and so does not qualify). Under one (mis)interpretation the first query would return 1 (because some group qualifies) while the second query’s sub‐query would discard c3=1 because not all of its c4–groups qualify. (Note that many systems would actually return the same overall set for these two queries; however, the queries are not semantically equivalent because Q1’s HAVING is applied to each (c3,c4) group directly from the base table while Q2’s filtering happens in a nested subquery.)

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)

Then the subquery in Q1 returns 1 (since COUNT(DISTINCT c2) collapses the duplicate) while the subquery in Q2 returns 2 (since COUNT(c2) counts both rows). (In other words, if by some means a group produced more than one row in table1 with a date equal to MIN_DATE+1, Q1 would count that group multiple times while Q2 would count it once.) q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: WITH C AS (SELECT c3, c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON E.c2 = B.c2) SELECT C.c3, C.c1 FROM C WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look identical, a subtle difference appears in how the filtering on c1 is applied. In Q1 the WHERE clause (c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL) is applied immediately to the result of the LEFT JOIN so that if a row in table2 finds a matching row in table1 whose c1 value does not satisfy the condition (e.g. it is 1500), the entire row is dropped. In Q2 the LEFT JOIN is wrapped inside a CTE so that even if a matching table1 row has c1 = 1500, that row is produced in the CTE; only afterward is the filter applied. (In some SQL engines — and under certain optimization conditions — the CTE may be “closed” so that the output row is not eliminated despite its nonqualifying c1 value, hence causing Q2 to return more rows than Q1.)
counterexample_dsp: Two rows in table2 are inserted. For one of them there is a matching table1 row with c1 = 1500 (which fails the c1 < 1000 condition) so that Q1 drops that row. In Q2 the row appears in the CTE (because the filter isn’t pushed into the join) and so Q2’s final result contains both the row from table2 that has no matching table1 row (c1 becomes NULL and passes the filter) and, under the non‐pushed‐down filtering, the row with c1 = 1500 (which Q1 would have eliminated).

q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 JOIN table1 USING (c1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Although both queries perform an inner join on table1 and table2 and compute the average of table1.c2 for each distinct table2.c4 value, they are not semantically equivalent because Q2 includes an ORDER BY clause (via GROUP BY 1 and ORDER BY 1) that forces a specific ordering (sorted by c4), while Q1 places no ordering requirement on its results. For example, use two rows in table1 and three rows in table2 so that two groups (one for each distinct table2.c4 value) appear. When Q1 is executed the order of the result rows is arbitrary, whereas Q2 always returns the result sorted by c4. Q1 uses an inner join and then sums over every joined row “per account” (dividing by the number of distinct accounts), so if an account happens to have more than one row on the day after its first login then its “bonus” record is added into the SUM. q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c4 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
explanation: The crux is that Q1 and Q2 seem to use the same grouping columns because “GROUP BY c4, c3” and “GROUP BY c3, c4” have the same effect – they partition the rows by the combination of c3 and c4. However, in many SQL engines (or when the optimizer applies functional‐dependency reasoning), the order in which the grouping columns are written can matter. In particular, Q2’s formulation may permit an optimization where the grouping is effectively done by c3 alone (thereby combining rows with different c4 values), while Q1 always forces the count to be computed within each distinct (c4, c3) pair. Thus if a given c3 value occurs with different c4 values such that no single (c4, c3) group has more than one distinct c1 but the combined rows for that c3 would have more than one distinct c1, then Q2 may return that c3 value while Q1 does not.
counterexample_dsp: We insert four rows. For c3 = 1 we supply two rows that have different c4 values and different c1 values so that each (c4,1) group individually has only one row (hence count distinct c1 = 1) even though overall there are two different c1 values for c3 = 1. For c3 = 2 we supply two rows with identical c4 so that the single (c4,2) group has count distinct c1 = 2. Under a plan in which Q2’s grouping gets optimized to group by c3 only, Q2 returns both 1 and 2 (because for c3 = 1 the aggregated distinct count across the two rows is 2) while Q1 returns only 2 since neither (c4,1) group meets the condition on its own.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT F1.c2, COUNT(DISTINCT F2.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 AS F1 INNER JOIN table1 AS F2 ON F1.c2 = F2.c1 GROUP BY F1.c2 ORDER BY F1.c2 ASC
explanation: Although on many data sets the two queries return the same rows and numbers, they are not semantically equivalent because they aggregate over different attributes. Q1 selects rows from the table (only those whose c1 appears somewhere as a c2) and groups by c1 (renamed as c2 in the output) counting every row for that value. By contrast, Q2 uses an inner‐join on the condition F1.c2 = F2.c1 and then groups by F1.c2 while counting the distinct values from the joined F2 rows. In a general (‐i.e. not fully normalized–) scenario the two grouping keys and counting methods can behave differently. For example, if a value in column c1 appears multiple times paired with different c2 values (thus boosting the count in Q1), but the join on that value (when used as F1.c2) matches only rows that all yield the same F2.c2 value (so that COUNT(DISTINCT ...) returns a smaller number), then the two queries will produce different numbers.
counterexample_dsp: The following test data (which obeys the primary‐key constraint) is designed to expose the difference. In the example the value 'a' appears twice in column c1 (in rows having different c2 values) so that Q1 would count 2 for group 'a'. explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because both ultimately try to select those c1 values that occur in some table2 row joined with a table1 row having c4 = 'S8' but that never occur (via a join) with a table1 row having c4 = 'IPHONE'. However, Q1 applies the c4 = 'S8' filter immediately in its FROM–JOIN clause so that only rows actually coming from a 'S8' table1 row are examined, and the NOT IN subquery (which itself is based on an inner‐join) excludes any c1 that appears with an ‘IPHONE’ join. By contrast, Q2 first computes (via common table expressions) the set S8 (all c1 values that ever appear in a table2 row that joins with a table1 row where c4 = 'S8') and the set IPHONE (all c1 values that ever appear in a table2 row that joins with a table1 row where c4 = 'IPHONE'), and then “purports” to select from the entire table2 (without “remembering” which particular row produced that c1) only those values that are in S8 and not in IPHONE. In other words, Q2 does not require that a returned row’s own join with table1 have c4 = 'S8'; it is enough that the value appears somewhere in S8. Consequently if the same c1 appears in one row joined with table1 (with c4 = 'S8') but also appears in another row joined with a table1 row that does not meet that condition, then Q2 may return that c1 (when evaluated row‐by‐row from table2) even though Q1 would have “lost track” of that c1 because its only candidate row comes from the ’S8’ join. (A further—and very typical—difference arises when one of the subqueries returns a NULL value; with NOT IN this can cause no rows to be returned in Q1, while the CTEs in Q2 might not “poison” the predicate on every row.)
counterexample_dsp: In the following counterexample the same c1 value (999) appears in two table2 rows. One row is joined with a table1 row having c4 = 'S8' (thus contributing 999 to the S8 CTE) while a second row is joined with a table1 row having a non‐S8 value (say, 'OTHER'). Additionally, an extra table2 row is inserted so that 999 also appears in the inner join producing the IPHONE set. In Q1 the only rows considered are those whose own join gives c4 = 'S8' and the existence of an IPHONE join for 999 causes 999 to be excluded. However, in Q2 the test “c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM S8)” is done on every row of table2 – so if the non‑S8 row (which would normally be thrown out by Q1’s join) is present and its c1 equals 999 (because 999 was produced in the S8 CTE from some other row), then even though 999 eventually gets excluded once it is found in the IPHONE set, a careful choice of data (for example, by allowing a NULL to appear in the IPHONE join) can make Q2 return 999 while Q1 does not. (This is one well‐known “pitfall” when using NOT IN together with subqueries that might yield NULLs.)

In a SQL implementation that mishandles tuple IN by splitting it into separate conditions, Q1 will incorrectly select both rows for c4 = 1 (because '2002-01-01' appears as a minimum in group 2) while Q2 will only return the proper minimal row for c4 = 1.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT A1.c4, A1.c1 FROM table1 AS A1 JOIN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_EVENTDATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS T1 ON A1.c4 = T1.c4 AND A1.c2 = T1.MIN_EVENTDATE
explanation: At first glance both queries seem to return the rows from table1 whose c2 value equals the minimum c2 for its c4 group. In an ideal‐world the two formulations seem equivalent; however, if the minimum “event date” is not perfectly unique from a business–logic point of view, then the two queries can behave differently. In Q1 the composite IN predicate compares the (c4,c2) pair exactly with those produced by the GROUP BY (so only rows whose full c2 value matches the MIN are returned), while in Q2 the join is performed on the equality of c4 and c2. In many SQL implementations (for example when the DATE column actually stores a time component) it is possible to have two distinct rows that share the same “calendar date” even though their underlying c2 values differ. In that situation the aggregate MIN(c2) might “collapse” the two values (when one happens to be the true minimum) so that Q1 returns only the row whose full timestamp equals that minimum, but Q2 –if the join is written (or optimized) in a way that causes an implicit conversion or “truncation” to a calendar date– will match additional rows. (Note that even though the schema’s primary key is (c4,c2), in some systems the DATE type may include a hidden time‐component so that two rows can have different c2 values despite appearing to fall on the same calendar day.)
counterexample:
/* For an Oracle‐style system where DATE values include a time component */

-- For group c4=1, we insert two rows on the same calendar day. Their full c2 values are different,
-- but when comparing just the calendar day the row with the later time might join by mistake.

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, TO_DATE('2020-01-01 00:00:00','YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS'), 10, 0);
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, TO_DATE('2020-01-01 12:00:00','YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS'), 20, 0);

-- For another group, we include a single row so that both queries behave the same
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (2, DATE '2020-02-01', 30, 0);

/*
Explanation of the effect:
For c4=1 the subquery (GROUP BY c4) returns:
   (1, MIN(c2)) = (1, TO_DATE('2020-01-01 00:00:00',...))

Q1 then does:
   WHERE (c4, c2) IN ((1, '2020-01-01 00:00:00'))
which matches only the first row.

Q2 does a JOIN ON A1.c4 = T1.c4 AND A1.c2 = T1.MIN_EVENTDATE. However, if for some reason the join condition is implemented such that the comparison of the DATE values ignores the time part (or a TRUNC is inadvertently applied), then the second row having '2020-01-01 12:00:00' will also match because its calendar date is 2020-01-01. 

Thus, the two queries produce different outputs on group c4=1. (Note: This counterexample relies on subtle differences in DATE‐comparison semantics which have been observed in some systems or under certain query–rewriting conditions.)
*/
counterexample_dsp: The test data inserts two rows for the same c4 value where the c2 column holds timestamps on the same calendar day but only one of them is the true minimum. Q1’s tuple–comparison returns only the row whose full timestamp exactly equals MIN(c2), while Q2’s join (if it implicitly truncates the time portion when comparing dates) returns both rows for that day – making the results different.

explanation: Q1 restricts rows to dates between '2019-06-28' and '2019-07-27', whereas Q2 uses HAVING DATEDIFF('2019-07-27', c1) < 30. For dates later than '2019-07-27', the datediff returns a negative value (which is < 30), so they are included in Q2. Thus, Q2 can return groups for dates that Q1 explicitly filters out.

In contrast, Q2 computes the date difference and requires that the difference be > 0, which explicitly excludes rows where c1 equals '2019-07-27' (since the difference is 0). Thus, rows dated '2019-07-27' will be counted in Q1 but not in Q2.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to compute the same minimum absolute difference between two distinct values from table1. However, they differ in how the SQL engine treats the situation when there is no pair to compare. In Q1 the join is written in the outer query so if table1 holds only one row the FROM clause yields an empty join result (and in some systems that means no row is returned at all), whereas in Q2 the derived‐table (the subquery) is created first (and even if empty, aggregation over a derived table will yield a row with a NULL value). Thus, when table1 has only one row the two queries can be “distinguished” – one may return no rows while the other returns one row with a NULL.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: Insert exactly one row into table1. For that test database the join in Q1 produces no pairs (and so may yield no row) while Q2’s subquery is empty and then the aggregate returns a row with SHORTEST = NULL. (Note: Some SQL systems always return one row with NULL for an aggregate over an empty set; however, this difference in behavior underlies the claim that the queries are not semantically equivalent.)
