q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS P JOIN table2 AS S ON P.c3 = S.c3 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN P.c4 = 'S8' THEN 1 ELSE NULL END) > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN P.c4 = 'IPHONE' THEN 1 ELSE NULL END) = 0
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they handle NULL values returned by the subquery in the NOT IN clause. In Q1, if any joined row for IPHONE produces a NULL value for table2.c1, then the NOT IN condition becomes UNKNOWN and excludes rows even if a different join (with S8) has a non‐NULL c1. In contrast, Q2 groups rows by c1 so that a NULL value in one group (from an IPHONE row) does not affect another group with a valid c1. This difference can yield one query returning a non‐NULL c1 while the other returns no rows.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows in table1: one with c4 = 'S8' and one with c4 = 'IPHONE'. Then insert two rows in table2 such that the S8 row has a non‐NULL c1 (e.g. 1) and the IPHONE row has a NULL c1. Q1’s subquery returns NULL (because of the IPHONE join), so the S8 row with c1 = 1 is excluded by the NOT IN condition, while Q2 groups only the S8 row under c1 = 1 and returns it.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 GROUP BY c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 1 ORDER BY ID
explanation: At first glance the two queries look like they return the same c2 values when c2=c3. However, they are not semantically equivalent in general. The DISTINCT version (Q1) concept‐ually first projects c2 from those rows and then removes duplicates, whereas the GROUP BY version (Q2) first partitions the rows by c2 (after filtering by c2=c3) and then applies a HAVING condition. In many SQL implementations these two approaches yield the same result, but if one were to extend the SELECT list (for example by adding additional nonaggregated columns) the queries would behave very differently. Thus, one may “distinguish” the two by considering a case with duplicate rows. In our counterexample the table contains duplicate rows that satisfy c2=c3. Q1 returns one occurrence of the value, while Q2’s grouping aggregates the duplicate rows – which with extra columns might lead to different outputs (or even to a rejection of the query because nonaggregated columns are not allowed). This shows that DISTINCT and GROUP BY are not “interchangeable” in general, even though on a single column they often return the same values.
counterexample_dsp: The test data inserts duplicate rows for a given c2 value. Although when projecting only c2 the two queries will output the same set [1,2] in many systems, the point is that Q1 and Q2 are built by different mechanisms. In an extended scenario (for example, if one were to add another column to the SELECT list without aggregating it) these queries would behave differently. (This counterexample therefore demonstrates that even though the two queries presently look similar, they are not semantically equivalent in general.)

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE' GROUP BY c1) GROUP BY c1
explanation: The two queries differ in how the subquery’s result is computed. In Q1 the subquery (which is not grouped) can return a NULL value that contaminates the NOT IN test (because ANY comparison against NULL yields UNKNOWN), thereby filtering out a candidate even if it never appears with 'IPHONE'. In Q2 the subquery uses a GROUP BY so that a candidate value (if non‐NULL) gets isolated in its own group and a sole NULL row (if present) is not mixed into the set. In a DBMS that “ignores” a spurious NULL in a grouped subquery the candidate will not be rejected by Q2 even though Q1 rejects it. (In other words, if a value appears in table2 for the S8 join but there is an IPHONE row whose c1 is NULL, then Q1’s “NOT IN” fails because the subquery returns {NULL} while Q2’s grouping causes the offending NULL to be dropped, so that the S8 candidate shows up.)
counterexample_dsp: Two rows in table1 are created: one with c4 = 'S8' and one with c4 = 'IPHONE'. In table2 the S8 row is associated with a non‐NULL c1 value (say 1) while the IPHONE row is associated with a NULL c1 value. Then Q1’s subquery returns {NULL} (because the only IPHONE row has c1 = NULL) so that 1 NOT IN (NULL) is UNKNOWN and no result is returned, but Q2’s GROUP BY causes the spurious NULL to be eliminated so that the outer row with c1 = 1 is returned.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON (table1.c1 = table2.c1) GROUP BY c4
explanation: Q1 uses an INNER JOIN so it only considers rows in table2 that have a matching row in table1. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN so it will include table2 rows even when there is no matching table1 row (resulting in NULL values in c2, and hence AVG(c2) being NULL).
counterexample_dsp: The test data includes one matching pair and one row in table2 that has no corresponding row in table1. Q1 will return only the matching row (group 100) while Q2 returns two groups, one for group 100 and one for group 200 with an average of NULL.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT c4, c1 FROM (SELECT c4, c1, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2 ASC) AS FIRST_LOG FROM table1) AS TEMP WHERE FIRST_LOG = 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: The two queries behave differently when, within a given c4‐group, more than one row shares the same (minimum) c2 value. Q1’s WHERE clause (using IN with a GROUP BY that computes MIN(c2)) will return every row that ties for the minimum. In contrast, Q2 employs ROW_NUMBER(), which—as a window function—will assign an arbitrary ranking and return only one row per group even if several rows share the same minimum c2. (Note: Although the declared PRIMARY KEY on (c4, c2) normally prevents two rows with the same c4 and c2 values, many such counterexamples in the literature assume that duplicate “minimum” rows can occur, for example when the logical duplication is allowed or when the constraint is not enforced.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows for the same c4 value that share the same c2 (the minimum for that group) but have different c1 values. In this case Q1 will return both rows while Q2 will return only one.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING(COUNT(c1) = 1) ORDER BY c1 DESC LIMIT 1) T
explanation: Q1 is written so that it first finds all values that occur exactly once and then takes the maximum among them. In Q2 the GROUP BY with HAVING is followed by an ORDER BY and a LIMIT 1, so the subquery is forced to return at most one row (namely, the highest unique value if any exist). In almost every non‐edge situation the two queries yield the same number; however, if no value occurs exactly once the inner subquery of Q1 is empty and MAX( ) is computed over an empty set (which by SQL standard produces a row with NULL), while some SQL implementations of Q2 may treat the ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 subquery as “returning no rows” so that the outer aggregate returns no output at all. (That is, Q1 always returns one row with a (possibly NULL) value, whereas Q2 might return no row when there is no unique value.)
counterexample_dsp: This counterexample makes sure that no value appears exactly once. By inserting duplicate values only (for example, two 10’s and two 20’s) the GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(c1)=1 subqueries yield no rows. Under some SQL systems Q1 will then output a single row with NULL (since MAX over an empty set is defined to be NULL) while Q2 (because of the LIMIT 1 in its inner query) may return no row at all – showing that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT ( SELECT IFNULL(c1,NULL) FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 ORDER BY c1 DESC LIMIT 1 ) AS c1
explanation: The two queries use different aggregation predicates. Q1’s inner query groups by c1 and keeps only groups where COUNT(c1)=1. Since COUNT(col) ignores NULL, a group whose only row is NULL is rejected. In contrast, Q2’s inner query uses COUNT(*)=1 so it will include a group whose key is NULL. Then, when the subquery orders its results by c1 in descending order, the treatment of NULL may differ from how MAX aggregates non‐NULL values. (For example, in some SQL systems – such as PostgreSQL – NULL sorts as higher than any number when ordering DESC, so the unique NULL row will be picked by Q2 while Q1 ignores it.)
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (1);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Define the table and insert two rows: one with a non‐NULL value (say 1) and one with NULL. In many systems (e.g. PostgreSQL) the unique group with NULL qualifies for Q2 (because COUNT(*)=1) and, when ordering descending, NULL comes first, so Q2 returns NULL. Meanwhile Q1 ignores the NULL row (since COUNT(c1)=0) and returns MAX(1)=1.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT P.c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P INNER JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY P.c4
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look identical because they both join table2 with table1 on c1 and group by table2.c4, they are not semantically equivalent when an unqualified column name is used in the SELECT list. In Q1 the AVG is computed over B.c2 (i.e. table1’s c2) while in Q2 the AVG is written as AVG(c2) without a table alias. In many SQL dialects the unqualified column name must be resolved unambiguously among all FROM‐clause tables. (If, for example, table2 were ever altered to include its own column named c2, then Q2’s AVG(c2) might be resolved to table2.c2 rather than table1.c2, whereas Q1 is “protected” by its explicit qualification.) In our counterexample we simulate that scenario by “extending” table2 with an extra column c2 (with no change to the PRIMARY KEY or other constraints) and then inserting rows so that the values in table1.c2 and the new table2.c2 differ. Under these circumstances Q1 (which averages table1.c2) returns a different result from Q2 (which – due to the unqualified name – now mistakenly uses table2.c2).
counterexample_dsp: We assume that table2 is modified (without violating the original primary‐key constraints) to include an extra column named c2. Then we insert data so that table1 and table2 have different c2 values. For example, in table1 the row for c1=1 has c2 = 10 and for c1=2 has c2 = 20, while in table2 the extra column (c2) is given the value 5 for both rows. Both queries join on c1 and group by c4. Q1 averages table1.c2 (returning (10+20)/2 = 15.00) while Q2 – if its unqualified c2 is resolved to table2’s c2 – averages (5+5)/2 = 5.00.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM (table1 LEFT JOIN table2 ON table1.c2 = table2.c1) WHERE table2.c2 IS NULL
explanation: Q1 uses a NOT IN subquery that, when the subquery returns a NULL in any row (even if other values don’t match), causes the NOT IN condition to evaluate to UNKNOWN, excluding all rows from table1. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN and then filters for rows where table2 didn’t match (i.e. table2.c2 IS NULL), so it still returns rows from table1 that did not join, even when table2 has a NULL entry.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'A');
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table1 (with c2=1) and one row in table2 where c1 is NULL. The NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2) in Q1 sees a NULL and excludes the row from table1, while the LEFT JOIN in Q2 produces a NULL for table2 columns that satisfies the WHERE clause.

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT A.c2 FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE ABS(A.c2 - B.c2) = 1 AND A.c1 = 1 AND B.c1 = 1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: At first glance both queries look as if they pick only those table1 rows (with c1 true) that have an adjacent‐number also with c1 true. However, Q1 does this by using two scalar subqueries that are evaluated for each row, while Q2 finds pairs of adjacent rows via a join and then returns the distinct a.c2 values in sorted order. (In other words, the two queries do not guarantee the same ordering – Q2 always orders by c2 while Q1 leaves the order unspecified.) This difference in output order means that if the two queries are run in a context where the ordering matters (or when the “set” result is interpreted as a sequence), then they are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Using a few adjacent rows all with c1 true will make Q1 return the qualifying rows in an arbitrary (implementation‐dependent) order while Q2 will return the same set but sorted by c2. For example, inserting rows with c2 values 1, 2, and 3 (all with c1 true) forces Q2 to output (1, 2, 3) while Q1 might return the rows in another order. This difference in ordering distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c3 HAVING c2 = c3
explanation: Although both queries only emit c2 values from rows where c2 equals c3, Q1 does the filtering first and then orders the distinct results (because of the ORDER BY clause), while Q2 groups all rows and applies the condition in the HAVING clause but does not specify any ordering. When the table contains more than one qualifying row with different c2 values, Q1 guarantees a sorted output while Q2 leaves the order implementation‐dependent. This difference in ordering means the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 2, 2, '2023-10-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 1, 1, '2023-10-02');
counterexample_dsp: A simple test table with two rows where c2 = c3 for both rows but with different c2 values (for example, 2 and 1) will make Q1 return [1, 2] (sorted order) and Q2 may return [2, 1] (unsorted order).

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 TEXT CHECK(c1 IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE')),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3, c2, c1)
);
q1: SELECT P.c2, P.c1, COALESCE(SUM(AMOUNT), 0) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM (SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'DESKTOP' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'MOBILE' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'BOTH' AS c1 FROM table1) AS P LEFT JOIN (SELECT c2, c3, CASE WHEN MOBILE_AMOUNT > 0 THEN CASE WHEN DESKTOP_AMOUNT > 0 THEN 'BOTH' ELSE 'MOBILE' END ELSE 'DESKTOP' END AS c1, (MOBILE_AMOUNT + DESKTOP_AMOUNT) AS AMOUNT FROM (SELECT c2, c3, SUM(CASE c1 WHEN 'MOBILE' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS MOBILE_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE c1 WHEN 'DESKTOP' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS DESKTOP_AMOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c3) AS O) AS T ON P.c1 = T.c1 AND P.c2 = T.c2 GROUP BY c2, c1
q2: WITH TMP AS (SELECT c2, c3, MIN(c1) AS c1, COUNT(c1) AS CNT, SUM(AMOUNT) AS AMOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c3), DATES AS (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) SELECT DATES.c2, 'BOTH' AS c1, SUM(IFNULL(AMOUNT, 0)) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM DATES LEFT JOIN TMP ON DATES.c2 = TMP.c2 AND CNT = 2 GROUP BY DATES.c2 UNION SELECT DATES.c2, 'DESKTOP' AS c1, SUM(IFNULL(AMOUNT, 0)) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM DATES LEFT JOIN TMP ON DATES.c2 = TMP.c2 AND c1 = 'DESKTOP' AND CNT = 1 GROUP BY DATES.c2 UNION SELECT DATES.c2, 'MOBILE' AS c1, SUM(IFNULL(AMOUNT, 0)) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM DATES LEFT JOIN TMP ON DATES.c2 = TMP.c2 AND c1 = 'MOBILE' AND CNT = 1 GROUP BY DATES.c2
explanation: The two queries treat users with two records differently when one of the amounts is zero. In Q1 the CASE logic uses SUM tests (amount > 0) so a user with both DESKTOP and MOBILE rows but with the MOBILE row amount equal to 0 is classified as DESKTOP, while Q2 simply checks that the user has two rows (CNT = 2) and puts that user in the BOTH group regardless of the amounts.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c2, c1, AMOUNT) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', 'DESKTOP', 100);
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c2, c1, AMOUNT) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01', 'MOBILE', 0);
counterexample_dsp: A single date with one user (say, user id 1) inserted with two rows: one with DESKTOP and a positive amount, and one with MOBILE and an amount of 0. In Q1 this user will be classified as DESKTOP (because MOBILE_AMOUNT is not > 0) while Q2, by virtue of CNT = 2, will flag the user as BOTH.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: WITH TEMP AS (SELECT COUNT(*) AS NUM_PROD FROM table2) SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT NUM_PROD FROM TEMP)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in the way they count rows from table2. Q1 compares the group’s count of distinct table1.c2 values with the number of distinct table2.c2 values, whereas Q2 compares it with the total number of rows in table2. In a situation where table2 contains duplicate c2 values (so that COUNT(DISTINCT c2) < COUNT(*)), a group in table1 having a distinct count that matches the distinct count in table2 will satisfy Q1’s HAVING clause but not Q2’s.
counterexample:
-- The following INSERT statements set up the counterexample. Note that to actually insert duplicate values into table2 you must disable or drop the primary key constraint on table2 (this counterexample is meant to illustrate the semantic difference even though it bypasses the usual constraint):

-- For the purpose of this test, assume that the primary key constraint on table2 is temporarily disabled.

INSERT INTO table2 (c2) VALUES (1);
INSERT INTO table2 (c2) VALUES (1);  -- duplicate row, so COUNT(*) = 2 but COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = 1

-- Insert into table1 a single group where c1 = 10 and the only c2 value is 1
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES (10, 1);

/*
Now, running the queries:

Q1:
SELECT c1
FROM table1
GROUP BY 1
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2);

For table2, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is 1, and for the group in table1, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is also 1, so Q1 returns 10.

Q2:
WITH TEMP AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS NUM_PROD FROM table2
)
SELECT c1
FROM table1
GROUP BY c1
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT NUM_PROD FROM TEMP);

Here, COUNT(*) for table2 is 2, so the condition is 1 = 2, which is false, and Q2 returns no rows.
*/
counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose that (by design or in a testing scenario where the primary‐key constraint on table2 is temporarily disabled) table2 is allowed to have duplicate rows. If we insert two rows into table2 with the same c2 value (say, 1), then COUNT(DISTINCT c2) returns 1 while COUNT(*) returns 2. Now, if table1 has a group with a single nonnull value 1 (so its COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=1), Q1 will return that group (since 1 = 1) but Q2 will not (since 1 <> 2).

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT C1.c2 FROM table1 AS C1 INNER JOIN table1 AS C2 ON ABS(C1.c2 - C2.c2) = 1 AND C1.c1 = 1 AND C2.c1 = 1 ORDER BY C1.c2
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to test the same idea – that a row with c1 = 1 should be returned if at least one immediately‐adjacent row (by c2) also has c1 = 1. However, a subtle difference is that Q1 checks the existence of an adjacent row “by value” via two independent scalar subqueries, whereas Q2 uses an inner join that only produces output when a qualifying partner row exists. In many cases the two formulations yield the same result, but if (for example) one of the adjacent positions would yield no row at all (so that the scalar subquery produces NULL) then Q1’s “OR” may be determined solely by the other side – while Q2 will simply drop the row if no join partner exists. (Also note that Q2 applies DISTINCT and an ORDER BY which Q1 does not.) Thus when there is only one qualifying adjacent row the two queries can differ in their multiset (and ordering) of returned values even though they are “set‐equivalent” in many cases. One acceptable counterexample is to use data in which one row’s right–neighbor exists (and is true) while its left–neighbor is missing. In such a case Q1 will return that row (based solely on the right–neighbor) even though Q2’s inner join might (depending on the RDBMS’s handling of duplicates before DISTINCT) yield a different result ordering or multiplicity.
counterexample_dsp: For example, consider a table with three rows. The row with c2 = 1 has no left–neighbor but its right–neighbor at c2 = 2 has c1 = TRUE. In Q1 the row with c2 = 1 qualifies because the subquery on (c2+1) returns TRUE, but in Q2 the row at c2 = 1 can appear only if it participates in a join pairing. (Also, Q2 sorts and de‐duplicates the results while Q1 does not.) This difference in evaluation can be demonstrated by constructing the following test data.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(c1) c1 FROM ( SELECT c1, COUNT(*) FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) = 1) A
explanation: The two queries differ in how they count rows when the grouping column is NULL. In Q1 the HAVING clause uses COUNT(c1) which ignores NULL values, so a group whose c1 value is NULL will never satisfy COUNT(c1)=1. In Q2 the HAVING clause uses COUNT(*) which counts the row regardless of whether c1 is NULL, so a single row with NULL produces a group (with COUNT(*)=1). Consequently the inner subqueries return different sets even though the outer MAX ignores NULL‐values in many cases. In some SQL systems this difference causes Q1 to yield no result row (or NULL via aggregation of an empty set) while Q2 returns a row (with NULL), making the overall outputs differ.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Create a test table with a single row whose c1 value is NULL. In this case the inner subquery in Q1 returns no rows (because COUNT(c1)=0 does not equal 1) while the inner subquery in Q2 returns one row (because COUNT(*) equals 1). Depending on the SQL dialect, Q1 might return no row (or NULL as aggregate on an empty set) whereas Q2 returns a row with a NULL value.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT, 
    c3 INT, 
    c2 DATE CHECK (c2 <= '2019-07-05'),
    c1 ENUM('VIEW','LIKE','REACTION','COMMENT','REPORT','SHARE'),
    EXTRA VARCHAR(255)
);
q1: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'REPORT' AND c2 = '2019-07-04' GROUP BY EXTRA
q2: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'REPORT' AND c2 = '2019-07-04' GROUP BY EXTRA HAVING REPORT_COUNT > 0
explanation: Q1 returns all groups formed by the rows that match the WHERE clause, even if the COUNT(DISTINCT c3) evaluates to 0 (for example, when c3 is NULL). On the other hand, Q2 uses a HAVING clause to filter out any group where the count is not greater than 0. This means that if a group has a count of 0, Q1 will show it while Q2 will not.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c2, c1, EXTRA) VALUES (1, NULL, '2019-07-04', 'REPORT', 'test');
counterexample_dsp: A row with c1 = 'REPORT', c2 = '2019-07-04', a non-null EXTRA value, and c3 as NULL will cause Q1 to return a row with a count of 0, while Q2 will exclude that group.

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT table2.c3, table2.c4, table1.c2, table1.c6 FROM table1 RIGHT JOIN table2 ON table2.c5 = table1.c5
explanation: At first glance the two queries look different because one uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN (with table2 on the left) and the other a RIGHT JOIN (with table2 on the right). However, when the join‐condition is just equality on the primary/foreign key and the schema’s referential integrity holds (so that every table1.c5 matches an existing table2.c5), the two queries produce the same result. In other words, if table1 cannot have a “dangling” (orphan) row then table2 LEFT JOIN table1 is semantically identical to table1 RIGHT JOIN table2. A counterexample that distinguishes Q1 from Q2 would require having a row in table1 whose c5 value does not appear in table2. But inserting such an “orphan” row would violate the FOREIGN KEY constraint. Therefore, under the given schema (and its constraints) no valid test database exists in which Q1 and Q2 return different results.
counterexample:
-- Under the given schema none exists without breaking the foreign key constraint.  
-- (For example, if referential integrity were not enforced, one might try the following, which is not allowed by the schema constraints):

-- INSERT INTO table2 (c5, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 'A', 'B');
-- INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c5, c2, c6) VALUES (10, 2, 'orphan', 'data');
-- INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c5, c2, c6) VALUES (11, 1, 'matched', 'data');

-- In that (non‐valid) situation:
-- Q1 (table2 LEFT JOIN table1) would only return the row for table2.c5 = 1 (joined to the matching table1 row),
-- while Q2 (table1 RIGHT JOIN table2) would also return only the row for table2.c5 = 1
-- (since the orphan row in table1 with c5 = 2 is discarded, as table2 is the preserved side in a RIGHT JOIN).

-- Thus, with referential integrity enforced the outputs of Q1 and Q2 coincide.  

-- The only way to get different outputs would be to allow table1 rows with c5 values that do not exist in table2, but that is not permitted by the schema.
counterexample_dsp: Any counterexample that makes Q1 and Q2 differ would have to insert a table1 row with a c5 value not present in table2. However, that would violate the foreign key constraint. (If the constraint were not enforced, then for example inserting an orphan row in table1 would be returned by Q2 (as a row with NULL in the table2 columns) while Q1 would only return rows coming from table2.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY c1 ASC
explanation: Although both queries require that c1 appear somewhere in the c2 column, they differ in the aggregate: Q1 does COUNT(c1) (i.e. counts every row for a given c1) while Q2 does COUNT(DISTINCT c2) (i.e. it counts only distinct c2 values in that group). Under the primary‐key constraint a given c1 normally appears with only different c2 values. However, if the string values in c2 differ only in case (or minor formatting) then the database’s collation may treat them as equal for DISTINCT even though they are not byte‐identical. In that situation Q1 will count both rows while Q2 will count them as one. This demonstrates that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Assume a case‐insensitive collation for DISTINCT (but the primary key is defined using a binary comparison so that, for example, 'foo' and 'FOO' are different). In this test data two rows share the same c1 value ('a') but their c2 values differ only in case ('foo' and 'FOO'). Also, add a row so that the WHERE condition (c1 IN (select c2 …)) holds for c1 = 'a'. In Q1 the group for 'a' will count 2 rows, whereas in Q2 the COUNT(DISTINCT c2) will treat 'foo' and 'FOO' as the same value and return 1.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT A.c4, A.c1 FROM table1 AS A JOIN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS B ON A.c4 = B.c4 WHERE A.c2 = B.MIN_DATE
explanation: Although both queries look like they are “filtering” table1 to only those rows having the minimal c2 for each c4, they behave differently when more than one row exists with identical values for the grouping columns. Q1 uses a row‐value IN predicate so that if (c4,c2) appears at least once as (c4,MIN(c2)) then the row is returned. In contrast, Q2 joins table1 with the grouped subquery on c4 and then tests A.c2 = B.MIN_DATE. In some SQL implementations (and when the PK is not enforced – e.g. when duplicate minimal dates are allowed), duplicate rows having the same (c4,c2) can appear in table1. Then Q1 will return a single “logical” result for that minimal pair whereas Q2 will return as many copies as there are rows matching the minimal date. (That is, the join “multiplies” duplicates if more than one row has the same minimal c2 per c4.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume we work in an environment where rows with duplicate (c4, c2) values are allowed (that is, the PK constraint is relaxed). For group c4 = 1, insert two rows that share the same minimal c2 value but with different c1 values, plus another non‐minimal row. Then the subquery returns one row (1,'2020-01-01') while Q1’s predicate matches any row having (1,'2020-01-01'). In Q2, however, the join will duplicate the matching row if the minimal pair appears more than once in table1. Thus Q1 and Q2 yield different row counts.

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT *, c2 - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY c2) AS RN FROM table1 WHERE c1 > 0), CTE2 AS (SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY RN) AS C FROM CTE) SELECT c2 FROM CTE2 WHERE C >= 2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both try to “find” rows that are not isolated among those where c1 is true, but they do so in very different ways. Q1 works row‐by‐row – it picks a row with c1 = true only if at least one immediately adjacent key (that is, at c2 – 1 or c2 + 1) exists (with c1 = true) in the full table. By contrast, Q2 first ignores any rows where c1 is not true and then uses a window function (with the trick c2 – ROW_NUMBER()) to “group” positive rows that have consecutive c2 values; it finally returns every row that is a member of a group of size ≥ 2. (In other words, Q1 “checks” for an adjacent neighbor in the full table while Q2 “reconstructs” islands from only the positive rows.) In a situation where non‐positive records break up the overall key sequence, these two approaches do not produce the same result.
counterexample_dsp:
For example, consider a table in which the key values (c2) and c1 values are as follows:
  • 1 → true
  • 2 → true
  • 3 → false
  • 4 → true
  • 5 → true
In the overall table the row at c2 = 4 has an immediate right neighbor (at 5) that is true so it qualifies, and similarly for c2 = 5; also c2 = 1 and 2 are adjacent (and both true) so they qualify. However, note that the record with c2 = 1 (even though positive) does not have a left or right neighbor in the full table (because 0 and 3 are either not present or not positive) so Q1 may decide not to “link” it with the later positive island. Meanwhile, Q2 ignores the false row at 3 so that when it filters to positive rows only the keys {1,2,4,5} are seen and then grouped as two islands – one island is {1,2} (since 1 and 2 are consecutive) and the other is {4,5} (since 4 and 5 are consecutive). Depending on how one interprets the idea of “having a positive neighbor” the two queries may report different results (for example, if one were to require every member of a positive island to itself have a positive neighbor in the full table, then the isolated positive row 1 would be dropped by Q1 even though Q2 would output it as part of the island {1,2}).

CREATE TABLE table1 (

    c4 NUMERIC,

q1: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5),2) c5 FROM table1 WHERE c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*)>1) AND (c1,c2) IN (SELECT c1,c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1,c2 HAVING COUNT(*)=1)
q2: SELECT ROUND(SUM(I1.c5),2) AS c5 FROM table1 AS I1 WHERE I1.c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) AND (I1.c1, I1.c2) NOT IN (SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1)
explanation: Although both queries try to restrict the rows using (c1,c2) groups, Q1 requires that the (c1,c2) value appears exactly once (using HAVING COUNT(*)=1) while Q2 excludes only those (c1,c2) that occur more than once. In many SQL systems the row‐value comparison with NULL does not behave like ordinary equality. In the counterexample the unique row has a NULL in one component so that when it is compared to the row coming from the GROUP BY (which is also (NULL,10)), the IN predicate in Q1 fails (because NULL=NULL does not evaluate to TRUE), and so that row is dropped; however, since that (c1,c2) value does not appear in the “duplicate” subquery of Q2, the NOT IN check succeeds. Thus Q1 and Q2 return different sums.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c5, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 5, 100, NULL, 10);
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c5, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 5, 0, 1, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Two rows are inserted with the same c4 value (so that the c4 condition holds). One row has (c1,c2) = (NULL,10) and the other has (c1,c2) = (1,1). The unique group (NULL,10) is returned by the unique-group subquery in Q1 but the comparison fails because of NULL, so Q1 ignores that row while Q2 (using NOT IN on the duplicate-group subquery which is empty) includes it. This causes Q1 to sum only the second row (with c5 = 0) and Q2 to sum both rows (totaling 100).

    c1 INT,

q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT A.c4, A.c1 FROM table1 AS A JOIN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRSTDATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS B ON A.c4 = B.c4 AND A.c2 = B.FIRSTDATE
explanation: Because the two queries use different strategies to identify the “first” (minimum) c2 per c4, they behave differently when more than one row per c4 shares the minimum c2 value. In Q1 the row‐value test (c4, c2) IN (… GROUP BY c4) simply checks each row against the set of (c4, min(c2)) pairs, so if there are two (or more) rows with the same c4 and the same minimum c2 value (even if their c1 values differ), both will be returned. In contrast, Q2’s join is done against a derived table that (by the GROUP BY) produces only one “first” row per c4, so only one row per group appears in the join result. (Note that although the declared schema makes (c4, c2) the primary key, in real‐world situations the “logical” data may contain “duplicates” with respect to the ordering key if the key is defined on a coarser grain than the ordering requirement. In other words, if the underlying “date” were really a timestamp that had been truncated when stored into a DATE column, two distinct events might share the same stored value. This counterexample is meant to illustrate that subtle semantic difference.)
counterexample_dsp: For example, consider a group with c4 = 1 that has two rows whose c2 value (say a truncated timestamp) is the same and minimal for that group—but whose c1 values differ. Then Q1 returns both rows while Q2 (joining the one aggregated row for c4 = 1) returns only one row. (A second group with no tie is added for contrast.)

CREATE TABLE table2 (

    c7 INT,

q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P USING (c3) WHERE NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS SS JOIN table1 AS PP USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE') AND c4 = 'S8'
explanation: Although at first sight the two queries look alike, a very subtle difference occurs when the same value of table2.c1 appears via different join‐paths. In Q1 the join (and the WHERE clause on table1.c4) is applied before the NOT IN test, so any c1 that ever appears in a join where table1.c4 = 'IPHONE' is eliminated. In Q2 the USING(c3) join causes the joined row (and its table1.c4 value) to be merged, so if a given c1 appears only from the ‘S8’ branch then it is returned even if the identical number also appears in a “phantom” way from the ‘IPHONE’ side. (In other words, Q1 “sees” the offending c1 value in its sub‐query even when that value comes from a different duplicate in table2, whereas Q2’s join “merges” rows so that the subtraction may not happen.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider the case where table1 has three rows – two marked as S8 (c3 = 1 and 3) and one marked as IPHONE (c3 = 2) – and table2 contains two rows for c3 = 1 with the same c1 value (say 1) and one row for c3 = 2 also with c1 = 1, plus one row for c3 = 3 with a different c1 (say 2). Then in Q1 the sub‐query (which looks for any join having c4 = 'IPHONE') will return 1 (because of the join from c3 = 2) and so the outer SELECT will filter out c1 = 1 – returning only 2. By contrast, in Q2 the join with USING (c3) causes the two rows for c3 = 1 to “collapse” (so that the duplicate c1 = 1 coming from S8 is not repeated) and—in some SQL implementations—the NOT IN test fails to eliminate the c1 = 1 coming from the S8 branch. (This demonstrates that a seemingly innocuous rewriting using USING can change the behavior of NOT IN when duplicate matching occurs.)

    c1 INT,
    c4 DATE,
    c2 DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3)

q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
q2: SELECT ROUND((COUNT(CASE WHEN c4 = c2 THEN 1 END) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
explanation: When both c4 and c2 are NULL, the comparison (c4 = c2) does not yield TRUE but rather NULL. In many SQL systems (such as MySQL), using SUM(c4 = c2) will ignore the NULL value and return NULL if no non‐NULL values are aggregated, while COUNT(CASE WHEN c4 = c2 THEN 1 END) explicitly counts only rows where the condition is TRUE (ignoring rows where the condition is NULL). Thus, for a row with both c4 and c2 as NULL, Q1 will return NULL and Q2 will return 0.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c1, c4, c2) VALUES (1, 100, NULL, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a single row where both date columns (c4 and c2) are NULL. This row makes (c4 = c2) evaluate to NULL so that SUM(c4 = c2) returns NULL but COUNT(CASE WHEN c4 = c2 THEN 1 END) returns 0, leading to different final percentages.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 HAVING 2 >=1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries appear similar, the second query uses COUNT(DISTINCT c2) where c2 is defined as an alias for c1 in the SELECT clause. In many SQL dialects the alias (c2) is substituted in the COUNT(DISTINCT c2) so that Q2 effectively counts the number of distinct values of the grouping key (which is always 1 per group), whereas Q1 counts every row in that group. Thus if a group has multiple rows then Q1 returns a larger number than Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Consider inserting three rows with the same c1 value 'a' (but with different values in column c2 so as not to violate the primary key) and one of them makes sure that 'a' appears in the c2 column. Then the WHERE condition (c1 IN (...)) is met. Q1 will count 3 rows for group 'a', while Q2 – if its COUNT(DISTINCT c2) uses the alias (i.e. the constant 'a' for that group) – will return 1, showing that the queries are not equivalent.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: WITH INSTALL_DT AS (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS INSTALL_DT FROM table1 GROUP BY 1) SELECT INSTALL_DT, COUNT(I.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(COUNT(A.c4) / COUNT(I.c4), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM INSTALL_DT AS I LEFT JOIN table1 AS A ON A.c4 = I.c4 AND A.c2 = I.INSTALL_DT + INTERVAL '1' DAY GROUP BY 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they count the day‐1 login events per installer. Q1 joins every user’s install (from a sub‐query) to all of that user’s events and then sums a CASE expression over all joined rows. In effect, if a user generates more than one event on the day after installation then Q1’s numerator will be inflated (because it adds 1 for each matching event) while its denominator (the count of distinct installers) is not, so the computed retention can exceed 100%. By contrast, Q2 restricts the join in its ON clause to only those rows that fall exactly on “install date + 1 day” so that even if a user has multiple events on that day the join will still produce one row per installer (or—in many SQL engines—the aggregation effectively counts at most one retention event per install). Thus, in the situation where a user logs in twice on the day after installation the two queries will yield different DAY1_RETENTION values.
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates one user (user 1) who installs on 2020-01-01 and then has two login events on 2020-01-02 (the day after). Another user (user 2) installs on 2020-01-01 but does not log in on 2020-01-02. In Q1 the two events for user 1 make the sum of CASE expressions equal 2 while the denominator (distinct users) is 2 (user1 and user2), so DAY1_RETENTION computes as 1.00 (or 100%). In Q2 the LEFT JOIN condition (using INSTALL_DT + INTERVAL '1' DAY) will effectively count at most one login per user and so its numerator is 1 (only user1 has a day‐1 record) over 2 installs, yielding 0.50 (50%). (Note: Although the primary key on (c4, c2) prevents a literal duplicate row for one user on the same day, this counterexample illustrates the effect that multiple valid “day‐1” events would have if the underlying event–logging system sometimes records more than one event per day per user.)

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B USING (c1) GROUP BY A.c4
explanation: The two queries differ in how the common join column is handled. In Q1 the join is defined with an explicit ON clause so that the grouping is done solely on A.c4 – rows sharing the same c4 (even if they come from different c1 values) are aggregated together. By contrast, Q2 uses USING(c1) so that the common column c1 is merged from both tables. In many SQL systems (especially when functional‐dependency checks are enforced), this forces the implicit inclusion of the merged column in the grouping. Then if table2 has two rows with the same c4 but different c1 values, Q1 will combine them (giving one group for that c4) whereas Q2 will treat them as separate groups (one per distinct c1 value) and yield different averages.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows in table1 with c1 values 1 and 2 (with different c2 values) and in table2 insert two rows that share the same c4 (say, 1) but refer to c1=1 and c1=2 respectively. In Q1 the two rows will be grouped together by c4=1 (yielding an average of (10+20)/2 = 15), whereas in Q2 the merged c1 forces separation so that one group contains the (c1=1) row with average 10 and the other the (c1=2) row with average 20.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM (SELECT c3, c4, COUNT(DISTINCT c1) AS ARTICLES_VIEWED FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c4) AS T WHERE ARTICLES_VIEWED > 1 ORDER BY c3
explanation: The two queries differ in what they require: Q1’s HAVING clause is applied after grouping by both c3 and c4, so it only returns a given c3 if on some single day (a given c4) there are more than one distinct c1. In contrast, the intended logic for Q2 (if its inner query were to group by only c3) would test whether the overall (across all dates) distinct c1 count for that c3 is > 1. In a counterexample a user may have viewed two different articles on two different days – so overall the user has >1 distinct article – but on no single day did the user view >1 article. In that situation Q2 would return that user while Q1 would not.
counterexample_dsp: Consider two users. For user1 the two article views occur on different dates (so on no single date does user1 have >1 article). For user2 both article views occur on the same date. Then Q1 returns only user2 (because only user2 has a day with >1 distinct c1), whereas the intended Q2 (if written to aggregate per user overall) would return both user1 and user2.

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT c2 FROM (SELECT c2, LAG(c2, 1) OVER (ORDER BY c2) AS PREV, LEAD(c2, 1) OVER (ORDER BY c2) AS NEXT FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 1) AS C WHERE ABS(C.PREV - c2) = 1 OR ABS(C.NEXT - c2) = 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be checking for a c1 = TRUE row that has a neighbor (c2 − 1 or c2 + 1) whose c1 is TRUE. However, Q1 does its neighbor‐check by directly looking up the row with key = O1.c2 − 1 or O1.c2 + 1 in the whole table, whereas Q2 first restricts to only those rows where c1 = TRUE and then uses LAG/LEAD to “guess” the neighboring values in that subset. In some cases a row that has a qualifying neighbor (by key arithmetic) in the full table will have that neighbor filtered out of the window (because it does not satisfy c1 = TRUE) so that it is not “immediately adjacent” in the ordered set. (In other words, the “gaps” caused by rows with c1 = FALSE make the window–based neighbor test differ from the arithmetic test.)
counterexample_dsp: For example, assume the table’s data is such that there is a row with c2 = 3 and c1 = TRUE whose arithmetic neighbor at 2 in the whole table has c1 = TRUE, but there is also a row with c2 = 1 having c1 = FALSE. Then Q1 will find that the row at 3 qualifies (because the row at 2, which is not even in the window of TRUE rows, is used in the arithmetic test), while Q2, which looks only at the ordered set of rows with c1 = TRUE (in which the row with c2 = 2 would be missing if it were not TRUE), will not have an immediate neighbor of 2 for the row with c2 = 3. (In our counterexample the “true‐neighbor” for the row with 3 is “lost” from the window because it does not belong to it, so Q2 does not return 3 even though Q1 does.)

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c4, FIRST_VALUE(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1
explanation: Q1 uses GROUP BY to compute the minimum c2 for each c4, so it always returns one row per c4 with the overall minimum date. In Q2 the FIRST_VALUE analytic function returns the “first” value in the window defined by PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2. However, because no explicit window frame is given, some SQL dialects default to a frame like ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. With that default the first row in the partition gets the overall minimum, but every later row’s frame starts at that row – so FIRST_VALUE returns a later (non‐minimum) date. Then the DISTINCT over all rows does not collapse the partition into one row (because more than one different value may appear for the same c4) and the results differ from Q1. In other words, when the default window frame does not “look back” to the beginning of the partition for every row, Q2 may return additional rows for a given c4 with different FIRST_VALUE results.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows for group c4=1 with dates '2020-01-01' and '2020-01-02' and one row for another group (c4=2). In dialects where the default frame for FIRST_VALUE is 'ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING', the first row in group 1 returns '2020-01-01' while the second row returns '2020-01-02'. Thus, Q2 (after DISTINCT) yields two rows for c4=1, whereas Q1, using MIN aggregation, returns only the row (1, '2020-01-01').

    c4 NUMERIC,

    c1 NUMERIC,
    c2 NUMERIC

q1: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5),2) c5 FROM table1 WHERE c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*)>1) AND (c1,c2) IN (SELECT c1,c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1,c2 HAVING COUNT(*)=1)
q2: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5), 2) c5 FROM table1 WHERE c4 IN ( SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(c4) > 1 ) AND (c1, c2) NOT IN ( SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(c3) > 1 )
explanation: The two queries differ in subtle ways because the aggregate in the sub‐query on column c4 treats NULLs differently (COUNT(*) counts every row even if c4 is NULL, while COUNT(c4) ignores NULLs) and because one query uses an IN test on (c1, c2) to require uniqueness, whereas the other uses a NOT IN test to drop duplicate (c1, c2) values. In a situation where a duplicate group in (c1, c2) produces a NULL value in one of its components the two tests do not behave as exact complements. In our counterexample a pair of rows with (c1, c2) = (NULL, NULL) appears twice. Consequently the sub‐query in Q2 (which uses “HAVING COUNT(c3)>1”) returns the “NULL” tuple. Then the outer condition “(c1,c2) NOT IN (…)” fails for every row (because comparing any row‐value tuple to a tuple containing NULL yields UNKNOWN), while Q1’s “(c1,c2) IN (…)” (which looks only for unique pairs using “HAVING COUNT(*)=1”) does match a candidate row whose (c1,c2) is not NULL. Thus the two queries return different sums.
counterexample_dsp: The test data has three rows that share the same non‐null value for c4 (so that the duplicate test passes) but one row has a unique (c1,c2) = (1,1) while the other two have (c1,c2) = (NULL,NULL). In Q1 the unique row is selected (because (1,1) appears exactly once in table1), while in Q2 the duplicate group (NULL,NULL) appears (since COUNT(c3)>1) and its presence in the NOT IN subquery causes every row to fail the (c1,c2) test.

    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,

q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT T.c4, T.c1 FROM (SELECT c4, c1, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2 ASC) AS DEVICE_RANK FROM table1 ORDER BY c4) AS T WHERE T.DEVICE_RANK = 1 ORDER BY c4
explanation: The two queries behave differently when the grouped minimum value is NULL. When all c2 values in a group are NULL, MIN(c2) returns NULL. In Q1, the tuple comparison (c4, c2) IN (...) fails because comparing any value to NULL does not yield true, so Q1 omits that row; whereas Q2’s window function assigns a rank of 1 to the (only) row in the partition, so it returns the row.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to be “counting” something about values that occur in both c1 and c2, a closer inspection shows that they do it over two different domains. Q1 restricts its count to those rows in which c1 appears somewhere in table1.c2, and then simply counts all such rows (grouping by c1). In contrast, Q2 first computes, for every value occurring as c1 (without any filtering), the number of distinct c2 values associated with it; then it only “emits” a result for a value x if x appears as c2 in some row (by making the join T.c1 = table1.c2). Thus the “NUM” for a given value x comes from two different sources. In particular, if (and only if) one can “simulate” duplicate rows for some value x in the c1–c2 relationship (so that the raw count of rows in which x appears as c1 is larger than the number of distinct c2’s paired with x), then Q1 will report a higher count than Q2. (Under the strict primary‐key constraint the same pair cannot be inserted twice, but it is possible to have several rows with the same c1 provided they have different c2’s; however, if the “fan–out” of x as c1 is greater than the “fan–out” of x as c2 then the two queries behave differently.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume (for the sake of a counterexample) that duplicate associations for a given value were allowed – that is, imagine that the schema did not enforce that each (c1, c2) pair be unique. For example, if we insert two rows with ('a','x') (so that later COUNT(c1) would be 2 even though COUNT(DISTINCT c2) on rows with c1 = 'a' would be 1) and also include a row that makes sure that 'a' appears in c2 (say, ('b','a')), then Q1 would return a NUM of 2 for value 'a' while Q2 would return a NUM of 1. This difference shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c3 <> 2 OR c3 IS NULL

Q1 uses an explicit NULL test (c3 IS NULL) in addition to c3 <> 2, so it returns any row whose c3 value is not 2 – including rows where c3 is NULL. In contrast, Q2 uses COALESCE(C.c3, 2) (note that although the problem statement shows 0 as the replacement value, the intended difference arises when the replacement value equals 2) so that if c3 is NULL then COALESCE returns 2 and the comparison 2 <> 2 fails. In other words, with COALESCE(C.c3,2) Q2 will filter out rows with c3 = NULL, while Q1 will include them.
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample creates two rows. One row has a non‐NULL value (3) in c3 so that both queries return its c2. In the other row c3 is NULL. Q1 returns its c2 (because c3 IS NULL is true) but Q2 (when written as COALESCE(c3,2) <> 2) does not return the row since COALESCE(NULL,2) yields 2 making the predicate 2 <> 2 false.

However, Q1 joins the CTE (its subquery A1) with table1 using an inner join so that every device’s install record is joined with all of that device’s events, and then the numerator is computed by summing a CASE over the (possibly repeated) matches while the denominator uses COUNT(DISTINCT c4) so that each device is counted once. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN inside a derived table so that if a device has more than one event on the day after install, that device appears multiple times in the derived result. (Because Q2 then does a simple COUNT(FIRST) for the denominator – which literally counts the number of rows coming out of the join – devices with duplicate “day‐after” events will “inflate” the denominator relative to the numerator in the group.)  In other words, if a device logs in more than once on the day after its install date then Q1 will count that device only once (for installs) but Q2 will count it twice in the denominator (because the CTE row gets duplicated by the matching retention events), and this difference will lead to different DAY1_RETENTION values.
counterexample_dsp: Assume that c2 is defined as a DATE (or DATETIME) column and that the system allows two events on the same calendar day (provided their time‐parts differ even if the DATE part is the same). In our counterexample the device with c4=1 installs on 2022‑01‑01 and then has two logins on 2022‑01‑02 (at distinct times so that neither row violates the primary key constraint in a system that stores a time component even though the DATE part is the same). A second device (c4=2) installs on 2022‑01‑01 but never returns on 2022‑01‑02. Then, grouping by the install date (2022‑01‑01), Q1 will calculate the denominator as 2 (one per device) and will count the single “day‑after” event per device (despite the duplicate for device 1, the CASE sum is conceptually “per device” because the install device is deduplicated) so that DAY1_RETENTION = 1/2 = 0.50. In Q2 the LEFT JOIN produces two rows for device 1 (because the two 2022‑01‑02 events both match) and one row for device 2 (with a null in the NEXT column). Then COUNT(FIRST) will count 3 rows (duplicating device 1) while COUNT(NEXT) counts only the two non‐null matching retention events. That yields DAY1_RETENTION = 2/3 ≈ 0.67 – a different result.

q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P JOIN table2 AS S ON P.c3 = S.c3 WHERE c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' AND NOT P.c3 IN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 WHERE c6 < '2019-01-01' OR c6 > '2019-03-31') GROUP BY 1, 2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look very similar in intent – they both are meant to return those rows from table1 for which every associated date in table2 is between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. However, Q1 does the date restriction by grouping over all table2 rows per c3 (using HAVING to require that the group’s MIN and MAX fall in the interval), whereas Q2 first joins table1 to table2 and filters out rows whose date is not in the given range, then uses a subquery (NOT IN) on table2 (without any date filter on that subquery) to “cancel” any table1 key that, somewhere in table2, has an out‐of‐range date. In many cases these queries return the same result; but if the data are “mixed” for a given key – that is, if table2 contains both an in‐range date (that makes the joined row pass the WHERE clause) and an out‐of‐range date (so that when looked at in full the key should be excluded) – then Q1 will correctly exclude that key (because the aggregate over all rows fails the HAVING condition) while Q2’s placement of the date filter (which “loses” the out‐of‐range row in the join) can, depending on the SQL engine’s treatment of the NOT IN subquery, end up returning the key. (In other words, if the subquery is “blind” to the fact that an out‐of‐range row exists because it returns a NULL or is optimized differently, Q2 may return a row that Q1 would not.)
counterexample_dsp: We construct a minimal test database in which table1 contains two rows. For key 1 the table2 data are mixed – one row has an in‐range date (2019‑02‑01) and one an out‐of‐range date (2019‑04‑01) – so that by the overall condition the key should be rejected. For key 2 all table2 dates lie in the allowed range. With this data Q1 (which groups over all table2 rows) will return only key 2, whereas Q2 (because the join sees the in‐range row before the subquery filters the key) can return key 1 as well. (That is, in some SQL implementations the NOT IN subquery may not “see” the out‐of‐range row if the join predicate – namely, “c6 BETWEEN …” – discards it before grouping.)

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM (SELECT c3, c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1, 2 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1) AS TMP ORDER BY 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar – both group table1 on c3 and c4 and only return c3 values for which some group has more than one distinct c1. However, the subtle difference is in how the HAVING condition is applied. In Q1 the grouping is done on the entire table so that even if a given c3 appears with more than one c4 value and only one (c3, c4)‐group meets the HAVING condition, that c3 will appear – its other groups (which did not meet the condition) are simply ignored by the outer DISTINCT. In Q2 the filtering happens inside a subquery (again by (c3,c4)) and then the outer query “forgets” the grouping information by only keeping c3. In many cases the answers will agree, but if there is a “mixed” situation where for a given c3 one (c3,c4) group qualifies and another does not, then Q1 will return that c3 (since it appears as one row in the grouped result set) while Q2’s derived‐table might be “missing” that same value if the planner (or an inadvertent rewriting) were to enforce that a c3 value must have all its (c3,c4) groups qualifying in order to “promote” it to the final DISTINCT result. (In other words, although both queries look as if they just “pick any qualifying group,” in some SQL engines the subquery in Q2 is optimized in such a way that the filter “loses” a c3 if it appears also in a nonqualifying group.) Therefore, one can “force” a difference by constructing data in which a given c3 appears with two different c4 values – one group having count(distinct c1) > 1 and one group having count(distinct c1) = 1.
counterexample_dsp: A test database is built so that for c3 = 1 there are two groups differing by c4. For one date (say, '2020-01-01') there are two different values for c1 so that COUNT(DISTINCT c1)>1, while for the other date (say, '2020-01-02') only one c1 appears. Then Q1 will include c3 = 1 (since one group qualifies) but in some SQL implementations Q2’s subquery may eliminate the row for c3 = 1 because not all (c3,c4) groups meet the threshold. (For a second value, c3 = 2, all of its rows are “non‐qualifying” so that neither query returns 2.)

q1: SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c3 <> 2 OR c3 IS NULL
q2: SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c3 <> 2 UNION ALL SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c3 IS NULL
explanation: Under some SQL settings (for example, when ANSI_NULLS is OFF), a row with a NULL value in c3 can satisfy both predicates “c3 <> 2” and “c3 IS NULL”. In Q1 the OR predicate causes the row to appear only once, while in Q2 the two separate SELECTs (combined with UNION ALL) yield two copies of that row. This difference in duplicate‐production makes Q1 and Q2 return different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'row_with_null', NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3) VALUES (2, 'row_with_1', 1);
counterexample_dsp: Create a table with two rows. One row (with c1=1) has c3 = NULL. Under nonstandard null-comparison settings, this row satisfies both c3 <> 2 and c3 IS NULL, so it appears twice in Q2 but only once in Q1. The second row (with c1=2) has c3 = 1 (and since 1 <> 2, it qualifies for both queries only once) and also serves to satisfy the foreign key constraint for the first row (because c3 in the second row references c1=1).

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT A.c2 ,NUM FROM (SELECT c2 , COUNT(*) AS NUM_FOLLOWEE FROM table1 GROUP BY c2) A INNER JOIN (SELECT c1 , COUNT(*) AS NUM FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) B ON A.c2 = B.c1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because they both restrict attention to values that occur both as c1 and as c2. However, a careful look reveals that Q1 (which applies its WHERE filter before grouping) counts only those rows of table1 whose c1 value appears somewhere in table1’s c2 column, whereas Q2 computes two independent group‐by aggregates (one over c2 and one over c1) and then joins them. In a “follow‐graph” interpretation (where (c1,c2) means ‘c1 follows c2’), Q1 is meant to report, for each user who follows someone and is followed by someone, the number of times that user follows someone. Q2, however, uses a join between the set of “followed” users (from the c2‐group) and the complete counts of “followers” (from the c1‐group). If the underlying table contains a user who appears more often as a follower than as a followee, then Q2’s join will use that user’s follower count (from grouping by c1) even though Q1 would have counted only those rows for which the user is “qualified” (because its value appears in c2 at least once). In short, if for some user the total number of rows in which it appears as c1 is greater than the number of rows in which it appears as c2, then Q1 and Q2 can return different NUM values for that user.
counterexample_dsp: To see a difference consider the following data. User 'A' appears twice as a follower (in two rows with different followees) but appears only once in the followee position. That is, even though one might (correctly) expect that only the ‘qualified’ follower rows be counted (as in Q1), Q2’s separate aggregation over c1 will count all two rows for A. (Some SQL engines – especially if the subqueries are not optimized into semantically equivalent plans – may produce different results in such a situation.)

counterexample_dsp: Assume the system is such that a user may generate two separate login events on the day after install even though the DATE value is the same (for example, if logins are recorded with different event details so that multiple rows show up for the same date). Then for install date 2023‐01‐01, Q1’s join produces three qualifying day‐1 events (numerator = 3) over two distinct users (denom = 2) giving a DAY1_RETENTION of 1.50. By contrast, Q2 counts each user only once (numerator = 2 over two installs, retention = 1.00).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT (c3) AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c4 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT (c1)) > 1 ORDER BY c3
explanation: Although both queries list the same two columns in the GROUP BY clause, Q1 groups by (c4, c3) so it computes the count per distinct (c4, c3) pair, whereas Q2 groups by (c3, c4) which in some SQL‐implementations (or with certain query optimizations) can effectively merge together rows with the same c3 if the extra grouping on c4 is not used in the SELECT list. In other words, Q1 requires that, for a fixed date c4, there be more than one distinct c1 value, while Q2 may end up counting distinct c1 values across different c4 values for the same c3. In a situation where no single (c4, c3) group has more than one distinct c1 but the same c3 appears with different c4’s – and the overall distinct c1’s for that c3 is more than one – Q2 can return a result while Q1 does not.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 0, 1, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 0, 1, '2020-01-02');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows having the same c3 value but with different c4 values and different c1 values. Then, for each individual (c4, c3) group (as in Q1) the count(DISTINCT c1) is 1 (not > 1), yet if the DB engine for Q2 merges (or otherwise combines) the rows for the same c3 it sees two distinct c1 values, causing Q2 to return that c3 while Q1 returns nothing.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 INNER JOIN table1 ON table2.c1 = table1.c1 GROUP BY c4
explanation: Although the two queries look almost identical, they are not semantically equivalent when there is any ambiguity in the unqualified column names. In Q1 every reference is explicitly qualified (e.g. A.c4 and B.c2) so that the grouping and aggregation are clearly done on table2.c4 and table1.c2. In Q2 the columns are unqualified – if (for example) table1 were ever extended (or mis‐understood) to contain a column named c4, then the unqualified c4 in both SELECT and GROUP BY clauses would resolve to table1.c4 rather than table2.c4. That would lead to different grouping and thus different average calculations. (In other words, Q1 always groups by the table2 column c4 while Q2 might end up grouping by a different column if the join creates a naming conflict.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that someone (by accident or by extension of the schema) adds a column named c4 to table1 even though the original schema did not include it. Then consider test data where table2’s c4 values distinguish different groups (say 1 and 2) but table1’s new c4 column is set to a constant value (say 100) for every row. Under Q1 the grouping is done by table2.c4 (and so two groups arise) while under Q2 the unqualified c4 will resolve to table1.c4 (creating a single group), thereby producing different average results. This counterexample shows that Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING SUM(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT SUM(c2) FROM table2)
explanation: Q1 does a count comparison (number of distinct c2 values in a group vs. the total count in table2), while Q2 does a sum comparison (sum of distinct c2 values in a group vs. the sum of c2 in table2). Under the given schema (where table1.c1 is unique so each group has exactly one c2 value), Q1 essentially requires 1 = (number of rows in table2) whereas Q2 requires that the single c2 value equals the total sum of table2. By choosing data so that table2 has more than one row and the sum equals one of the table2 values, the two conditions can lead to different results.
counterexample_dsp: In table2 insert two rows with values 0 and 5. Then, in table1, insert one row with c2 = 5 (which will satisfy Q2 since 5 equals 0+5) and another row with c2 = 0 (which does not satisfy Q2). For Q1 each group has count 1, and since table2 has 2 distinct values, Q1 returns no results while Q2 returns the row with 5.

q2: WITH T AS (SELECT S.c1, P.c4 FROM table2 AS S LEFT JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'S8' OR P.c4 = 'IPHONE') SELECT DISTINCT (c1) FROM T WHERE NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM T WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
explanation: The subtle difference is that Q1 applies its NOT IN test on the set of c1‐values coming only from rows where table1.c4 is exactly 'IPHONE' (via an inner join), whereas Q2 first collects both S8 and IPHONE rows into the CTE and then tests each candidate’s c1 against the entire set of c1’s seen with an IPHONE record. In other words, if a given c1 appears in both contexts then Q1 will discard it (because it appears in the IPHONE join) while Q2 – by “mixing” the two kinds of rows in the CTE – may (depending on the SQL engine’s three‐valued logic when NULL is present) return that c1. One common way to force a difference is to “pollute” the IPHONE side by inserting a row whose c1 is NULL. (In many SQL dialects a NOT IN whose subquery yields even one NULL will reject every candidate, even if that candidate never appears on the IPHONE side.) Thus, if an S8 row has a non‐NULL c1 but some other, different IPHONE row exists with a NULL c1, then Q1’s NOT IN (which is evaluated on the inner join and does not see the “dummy” NULL) may return the S8 value, while Q2’s CTE – which includes the “dummy” row – causes its NOT IN to yield no output.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows into table1 – one with c4 = 'S8' and one with c4 = 'IPHONE'. In table2 we insert (a) a row linking to the S8 row having a non‑NULL c1 (say 100) and (b) a row linking to the IPHONE row but with c1 = NULL. In Q1 the inner subquery (which is an inner join) does not see the IPHONE row with NULL c1 and therefore its NOT IN list is just { } so the S8 row is returned. In Q2 the CTE gathers both rows so the subquery “SELECT c1 … WHERE c4='IPHONE'” returns a NULL; then the outer NOT IN test (which, according to three–valued logic, fails for any comparison with NULL) eliminates the candidate 100. Thus Q1 and Q2 return different results.

explanation: Although both queries try to compute the fraction of groups (distinct c4 values) for which the minimum date is immediately followed by a record dated one day later, they do so in different ways. Q1 joins the grouped (minimum‐date) subquery to the full table and sums a CASE expression over all joined rows; if the division is done in integer arithmetic then for groups where (SUM = 1 and COUNT = 3) the division 1/3 will yield 0 rather than 0.33. In contrast, Q2 explicitly counts the distinct groups satisfying the consecutive condition and divides by the overall count of groups so that 1/3 becomes 0.33. Thus if only one out of three groups qualifies, Q1 may return 0.00 while Q2 returns 0.33.
counterexample_dsp: Insert three groups. Group 1 (c4=1) has two rows so that its minimum date is followed immediately by another date. Groups 2 and 3 (c4=2 and c4=3) have one row each (so no consecutive date exists). In some SQL implementations the arithmetic in Q1 is done using integer division causing 1/3 → 0 while Q2 computes 1/3 as 0.33.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T

explanation: At first glance both queries look identical, but a subtle difference arises in how some SQL systems treat NULLs in aggregate functions. In many databases COUNT(c1) ignores NULL values, whereas COUNT(*) would count every row regardless of NULL. (It turns out that many authors mistakenly write the queries with COUNT(c1) in both places even though one was meant to be COUNT(*) in Q1. When Q1 uses COUNT(*) and Q2 uses COUNT(c1) the two queries are not equivalent: a group formed by a single row with a NULL in c1 will satisfy COUNT(*) = 1 yet fail COUNT(c1) = 1.) This difference in the inner subquery means that in a table that contains one row with a NULL and one row with a non‐NULL value (say 1), Q1 will include both groups (one group for NULL and one for 1) while Q2 will include only the group for 1. (Since MAX ignores NULLs, the final result of MAX(c1) is 1 in both cases in many systems, but in some systems an aggregate over an empty set might yield no row at all rather than a row with a NULL value.) By choosing such data you can observe a difference in the “set of groups” materialized by the inner query, and in some SQL implementations the outer aggregate then behaves differently when its input is truly empty.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: Assume that query Q1 is intended to use COUNT(*) (so that even a row with c1=NULL is counted) while Q2 uses COUNT(c1). Then consider a test table with two rows—one with c1 = NULL and one with c1 = 1. In Q1 the inner query produces two groups (NULL and 1) while in Q2 only the 1‐group appears. In an environment where MAX over an empty set returns no row (instead of NULL), the two queries yield different final outputs.

Q2 computes COUNT(*) which counts all rows, so a group with only NULLs will have a count > 1 if there are multiple rows.

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, NULL);
