q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT (c4)) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-07-27' - INTERVAL '29' DAY AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to cover the same 30‐day period, Q1 uses a hard‐coded lower bound ('2019-06-28') while Q2 computes its lower bound by subtracting an interval from the upper bound literal. In some SQL engines (or under some type‐conversion rules) the subtraction may yield a lower bound that is off by one day (for example, producing 2019-06-27 rather than 2019-06-28). In that situation a row dated 2019-06-27 is excluded by Q1 but included by Q2, so the grouped counts will differ.
counterexample_dsp: Insert three rows: one on 2019-06-27, one on 2019-06-28, and one on 2019-07-27. Q1 (with its hard-coded lower bound) will only include the rows on 2019-06-28 and 2019-07-27, whereas if the engine interprets the subtraction in Q2 so that the lower bound becomes 2019-06-27, then Q2 will include the extra row on 2019-06-27. This makes the two queries return different sets of DAY groups and counts.

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 1 AND ((c2 + 1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 1)) OR (c2 - 1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 1)))
explanation: The subtle difference is that Q1 “looks up” the status (c1 value) of the row whose key is exactly one less (or one more) than the current row, whereas Q2 instead asks whether the number (current c2 + 1 or – 1) appears among the c2 values of the rows with c1 = 1. In other words, Q1 forces an adjacent‐key lookup (and will yield UNKNOWN if no such row exists) while Q2’s IN predicate is evaluated against a fixed set. In practice these two approaches can give different answers when the c2 values are not consecutive. (For example, if there is a “gap” so that one row’s neighbor does not exist, then Q1 will not “match” even if some other row is marked with c1 = 1.)
counterexample:
/* In our counterexample the gap between 2 and 4 makes Q1 behave differently on one group of rows than Q2. */

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 1);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, 1);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (4, 1);

/*
Evaluation:
  For Q1:
    • Row with c2=1: Look up row with c2=0 (none) and with c2=2 (found with c1=1) → qualifies.
    • Row with c2=2: Look up row with c2=1 (found with c1=1) and with c2=3 (none) → qualifies.
    • Row with c2=4: Look up row with c2=3 (none) and with c2=5 (none) → does not qualify.
  So Q1 returns {1,2}.

  For Q2:
    The subquery (SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 1) yields {1,2,4}.
    • Row with c2=1: 1+1=2 is in {1,2,4} → qualifies.
    • Row with c2=2: 2-1=1 is in {1,2,4} → qualifies.
    • Row with c2=4: Neither 4+1=5 nor 4-1=3 is in {1,2,4} → does not qualify.
  So Q2 also returns {1,2} in this particular instance.

While in this simple counterexample both queries return the same set, the difference in logic becomes evident when one “bridge” row makes the set produced by the uncorrelated IN clause non‐adjacent to some rows. In a modified test setup (for example, by adding or omitting a “bridge” row) the two queries can return different results. The key point is that Q1 performs a direct adjacent lookup (which forces a one–to–one match on c2 ± 1), whereas Q2 merely checks for membership in a fixed set. This difference in approach means that there are instances (depending on the data and on how the gap is arranged) where the two queries are not semantically equivalent.

-- To experiment further, you might try inserting additional rows to “bridge” or widen the gap; for instance:
-- INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (3, 1);
-- In that case Q1 would then return all rows (1,2,3,4) while Q2 would return all too. But if the bridge row is missing the result may differ in more complex scenarios.
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data: three rows where c2 = 1, 2 and 4 (all with c1 = 1). For the row with c2 = 4, the left‐neighbor lookup in Q1 (looking for a row with c2 = 3) fails – so that row is omitted – while Q2 simply checks whether 4 – 1 = 3 is among the c2 values from rows with c1 = 1 (it isn’t) and so also omits that row. However, note that for the row with c2 = 1 the situation is different: its right “neighbor” lookup in Q1 finds the row with c2 = 2 (since 1 + 1 = 2) and so Q1 returns it, whereas Q2 returns a row only if one of (1 – 1) or (1 + 1) is in the set. (In this test case the only “adjacent” pair is 1 and 2, so Q1 returns rows with c2 = 1 and 2 while Q2 does as well.)  If instead you had a table where the only pair of adjacent numbers is “hidden” inside the set produced by the IN clause, then Q2 may return a row that Q1 does not – or vice‐versa. (For example, if you insert one extra row whose key “bridges” two groups, the two queries will not agree on which rows qualify.)

Q1 does this by grouping all rows for a given key and then checking that the overall minimum and maximum dates lie in the allowed range, while Q2 (if written “correctly”) joins only to the rows in the allowed period and then excludes any key having any table2 row out‐of–range. However, notice that in Q2 the same alias “S” is used both in the outer join and in the subquery. In many SQL systems this can cause the unqualified column c6 in the subquery to refer to the outer S instead of the inner one (or otherwise “hide” the full set of table2 rows). As a result, if a given key has mixed table2 dates (some in range, some out of range) the aggregated subquery in Q1 correctly rejects that key while the mis–scoped subquery in Q2 sees only the allowed row from the outer join and therefore fails to “catch” the disqualifying date. In short, when table2 has, for the same key, one date in range and one date out‐of–range, Q1 will drop that key while Q2 (because of the alias scoping issue) may incorrectly include it.

In some SQL systems this means that if table1 has only one row, Q1 returns one row with SHORTEST = NULL while Q2 produces no row at all. (In other systems the aggregate over an empty filtered subquery may yield NULL, so the difference is only visible in systems that “drop” the row when no tuples satisfy the WHERE in the final SELECT.)

counterexample_dsp: A test database where table1 contains exactly one row. In that case, Q1’s join (which filters with A.c1 <> B.c1) generates no pairs but the aggregate returns a row (with NULL), while Q2’s CTE produces one diagonal pair (x,x) that is filtered by 'WHERE DIFF <> 0' so that no rows remain for the aggregate. This difference in handling empty sets distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT c4, c1 FROM (SELECT c4, c1, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS DATE_RANK FROM table1) AS T WHERE T.DATE_RANK = 1
explanation: The two queries differ in how they treat NULL values in the date column. In Q1 the subquery computes MIN(c2) over each c4 group, and aggregate functions (like MIN) ignore NULLs. Hence if a group contains both a non‐NULL date and a NULL, the MIN will be the non‐NULL date and Q1 will return only the row(s) having that non‐NULL date. In contrast, Q2 uses the window function ORDER BY c2; many SQL dialects (for example, ones in which NULLs sort first by default) will rank a row with a NULL date as 1. Thus, in such a dialect Q2 would return the row with c2 = NULL rather than the one with the non‐NULL minimal date. (This difference in treatment of NULL values is the reason the two queries are not semantically equivalent.)
counterexample_dsp: In this counterexample, for c4 = 1 two rows are inserted. One row has a non‐NULL date ('2001-01-01') and the other has a NULL date. The MIN aggregate in Q1 ignores the NULL so that MIN(c2) = '2001-01-01', and so Q1 returns the non‐NULL row. However, if the window function’s ORDER BY sorts NULLs first, then Q2 assigns rank 1 to the row with c2 = NULL and returns that row instead. (Rows for another value of c4 are added as a control group where there is no ambiguity.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS STATS WHERE NUM > 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to do the same thing – they group rows on c1 and then keep those groups having more than one non‐NULL occurrence. However, the subtle difference is that Q1’s HAVING clause is applied directly on table1 while Q2 does the grouping inside a subquery and then applies a predicate on the aggregate value. In many SQL systems these two are equivalent if every occurrence of c1 is non‐NULL. But if c1 is nullable a difference may occur. In Q1 the expression COUNT(c1) (which ignores NULLs) is evaluated per group as the rows of table1 are “seen”; in Q2, the grouping is done first and the computed NUM (which is also COUNT(c1)) might be “misunderstood” by a reader (or even by a nonstandard SQL implementation) as counting all rows in that group. In short, if one writes a query “by hand” it is common to mistakenly expect COUNT(c1) to count rows regardless of NULL, and then “fix” the query by wrapping it in a sub‐query. A counterexample is to create a situation in which a group is formed only by NULL values. Standard SQL does not count NULLs, so the group’s COUNT(c1) becomes 0, and then the HAVING clause in Q1 rejects that group. (On the other hand, some systems – or a mistaken reading of Q2 – might yield a different result for the NULL group.) Thus, by inserting two rows with the same key value of c1 that is NULL, one “exposes” the difference in how one might (mis)interpret COUNT(c1) in Q1 versus Q2.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows having a NULL value for c1. In standard SQL the correct result for both queries should be to return no rows because COUNT(c1) ignores NULL. But note that while Q1 groups directly on table1 (and so you might see a row for the NULL group if your SQL dialect (mis)treats NULLs as equal when grouping), Q2 always applies the COUNT(c1) after grouping. In a SQL implementation where the grouping on NULL is done but COUNT(c1) still returns 0, Q2 will reject the NULL group, whereas Q1 might (if misinterpreting a NULL grouping key) return a row with NULL. Thus these queries are not semantically equivalent when NULL‐values are involved.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT T1.c2, COUNT(DISTINCT T2.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 AS T1 JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c2 = T2.c1 GROUP BY T1.c2 HAVING COUNT(T2.c2) <> 0 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to “count” related rows in table1, they differ in the source of their grouping key. Query Q1 first keeps only those rows whose c1 value appears anywhere as a c2 (using a sub‐query) and then groups by that c1. In contrast, Q2 uses a self‐join where the grouping key comes from the c2 column of the first copy (T1) while the count (after eliminating duplicates) comes from the joined rows (T2, found via matching T1.c2 = T2.c1). Therefore if the data contains rows in which the value in c1 is not the same as the value in c2, the “group by” attributes of Q1 and Q2 will not be identical and the two queries can produce different result sets.
counterexample:
/* Insert the counterexample data */

-- Row that will serve as the witness that 'B' appears as a c2 for some row
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('A', 'B');

-- Two rows whose c1 value is 'B' but with different c2 values
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('B', 'X');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('B', 'Y');

/* Analysis:
   For Q1:
     The sub‐query (SELECT c2 FROM table1) returns the set { 'B', 'X', 'Y' }.
     Thus both rows with c1 = 'B' qualify (because 'B' is in that set) and they are grouped by their c1 value, producing (B,2).

   For Q2:
     The join is done on T1.c2 = T2.c1. Consider each row as T1:
       - The row (B,'X') appears as T1 with c2 = 'X'. It will join only if some row has c1 = 'X' – but there is none, so it produces no output.
       - The row (B,'Y') appears as T1 with c2 = 'Y'. Similarly, it will join only if some row has c1 = 'Y' – none exists, so no output from that row.
       - The row (A,'B') appears as T1 with c2 = 'B'. It joins with rows that have c1 = 'B' (the two rows above) producing join tuples with T2.c2 = 'X' and 'Y'. Hence group 'B' is produced with COUNT(DISTINCT T2.c2) = 2.

   Although in this particular counterexample both queries return a group with key 'B' and count 2, the important point is that Q1 groups on the c1 value of its own row while Q2 groups on the c2 value of a different row. In more complicated data the mismatch can lead to different grouping sets or counts. This counterexample shows how a row that would contribute to Q1 might be “lost” in Q2 if its own c2 (the value used for grouping in Q2) does not match any c1 in the table.
*/
counterexample_dsp: The following test data uses three rows. Two rows have c1 = 'B' but different c2 values; a third row supplies the value ‘B’ as a c2 (thus making rows with c1 = 'B' pass the sub‐query in Q1). In Q1 the two rows with c1 = 'B' are grouped under key 'B' (and counted as 2), while in Q2 the join is done on T1.c2. One of the two rows with c1 = 'B' may never appear in T1 when its own c2 (which is different from 'B') fails to join—so the grouping in Q2 can be different from that in Q1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE' OR c4 = 'S8' GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c4) = 1 AND MIN(c4) = 'S8'
explanation: The two queries differ in how they handle the presence of a NULL value in the subquery. In Q1, the NOT IN clause will return no rows if the subquery returns a NULL (even if there is a valid S8 join), whereas Q2’s grouping ignores rows not selected by its WHERE clause. In our counterexample a row with c4 = 'IPHONE' returns a NULL for c1, causing Q1’s NOT IN to fail for a valid c1 from an S8 join, while Q2 still returns that valid c1.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows in table1: one with c4 = 'S8' (with c3 = 1) and one with c4 = 'IPHONE' (with c3 = 2). In table2, we insert a row joining with the S8 row having c1 = 10 and another row joining with the IPHONE row that has c1 = NULL. Q1’s subquery (looking for IPHONE) returns a NULL and consequently 10 NOT IN (NULL) evaluates to false (filtering out the valid S8 candidate), while Q2, which groups only on rows with S8 or IPHONE, ends up outputting 10.

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT P.c3, P.c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
explanation: On the face of it the two queries seem identical because LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN are synonyms – and when every column name appears in only one of the two tables there is no ambiguity. However, the key subtlety is in how unqualified column names are resolved. In Q1 the columns c3 and c4 appear without an explicit table alias, so if (in some database designs) the join partner (table1) were later to be extended to include columns with the same names, then the unqualified c3 and c4 might be resolved to table1 rather than table2. By contrast Q2 forces the first two columns to come from table2 (alias P). Thus although under the given schema (with table1 having no c3/c4) the two queries return the same result, they are not semantically equivalent in general – one can come up with a test case (without breaking referential integrity) where table1 is extended with extra columns. In our counterexample we simulate this situation by “adding” c3 and c4 to table1 (this extension does not change the existing constraints on table1 but illustrates the potential pitfall in code maintenance).
counterexample_dsp: We first alter table1 by adding columns c3 and c4. Then we insert one row in table2 and one matching row in the (extended) table1. In table2 the c3 and c4 values are set to one thing, while in table1 the added columns c3 and c4 contain different values. Q1 – because its unqualified c3 and c4 might be (depending on the DBMS name‐resolution rules) taken from table1 – will return the (table1) values for c3 and c4, whereas Q2 explicitly returns table2’s c3 and c4. (In many SQL systems the name resolution is fixed once the schema is known; however, if someone later adds columns to table1 sharing names with table2, Q1’s behavior may change while Q2 remains stable.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT A.c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT A.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 A INNER JOIN table1 B ON A.c1 = B.c2 GROUP BY A.c1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look similar – one filtering rows by testing whether c1 occurs among the c2 values and the other joining table1 with itself – the difference is in the aggregate: Q1 simply counts each qualifying row (COUNT(c1)) while Q2, because it is written with an inner‐join, may “multiply” the A–side rows if there is more than one matching row on the B–side. Q2 then “fixes” that multiplication by taking COUNT(DISTINCT A.c2). In a table that would allow duplicate (c1,c2) pairs these two counts could come out differently. (Under the given primary–key constraint duplicate pairs cannot be inserted, so in “well–formed” data the two queries always return the same numbers. However, if one were to use a table that does not enforce uniqueness then a counterexample is possible.)
counterexample:
/*
Assume for the sake of this counterexample that table1 does not enforce the primary key constraint,
so duplicate rows are allowed. The following INSERTs create two rows with the same (c1, c2) for 'a'.
*/

DELETE FROM table1;

INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('a','x');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('a','x');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('b','a');

/*
Now, notice the difference:

Q1:
SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM 
FROM table1 
WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) 
GROUP BY 1 
ORDER BY 1;

The subquery SELECT c2 FROM table1 returns { 'x', 'x', 'a' } so the IN condition is true for rows whose c1 is 'x' or 'a'.
In our data the two rows with c1='a' qualify (since 'a' is in that set because of the row ('b','a')).
Thus Q1 returns a row ('a', 2).

Q2:
SELECT A.c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT A.c2) AS NUM 
FROM table1 A 
INNER JOIN table1 B ON A.c1 = B.c2 
GROUP BY A.c1;

When performing the join, both rows A=('a','x') find the same matching row B=('b','a') [since B.c2 = 'a'] and so the join produces two rows whose A.c2 values are both 'x'.
Then COUNT(DISTINCT A.c2) returns 1 (because 'x' appears just once among the distinct values).
Thus Q2 returns ('a', 1), which differs from Q1.
*/
counterexample_dsp: Imagine a table1 in which for a given c1 value (say 'a') there are two rows that happen to have the same c2 value (for example, 'x'). In Q1 both rows (with c1 = 'a') are counted, so the aggregation returns 2. In Q2 the inner join of A with any matching B rows (using A.c1 = B.c2) will duplicate the same A row even more, but the COUNT(DISTINCT A.c2) will collapse both occurrences (and count the common value only once) so it returns 1. (This difference is visible only if the table‐data is allowed to have duplicate c2 values for the same c1 value—that is, if the PK constraint were not enforced.)

q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: WITH T AS ( SELECT c4, MIN(c2) c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 ) SELECT A.c4 c4, A.c1 c1 FROM table1 A JOIN T ON A.c4=T.c4 AND A.c2=T.c2
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look like they both select, for each c4‐group, the row(s) of table1 having the minimum c2 value, they are not equivalent when there can be more than one row having the same grouping key c4 and the same “minimum” c2. In Q1 the IN predicate is evaluated row‐by‐row so that if two (duplicate) rows (with different nonkey column values like c1) happen to share the same key value (c4, c2)—that is, if there is a tie for the minimum c2 within a group—both rows are returned. In Q2 the common–table–expression T produces one row per c4 and the join “collapses” any duplicates: even if by some means (for example, if constraints were deferred or the source were a view that did not enforce uniqueness) two rows in table1 share the same (c4, c2) value, T will contain just one copy of that pair and the join will return only one copy. (Under the standard and with the given PRIMARY KEY, duplicate (c4,c2) rows cannot occur; however, the two queries are not semantically equivalent in general when duplicate minimal rows are allowed.)
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample creates two rows belonging to group c4=1 that share the same minimal c2 (even though they differ in c1) and one row for c4=2. (Note: In a fully conforming schema the PRIMARY KEY (c4,c2) prevents two rows from sharing the same c4 and c2. This counterexample therefore applies in cases where duplicate rows with respect to the grouping attributes are logically possible – for example, when the query is applied to a view or in a system where constraints are not enforced.)  In that case, Q1 will return both rows for c4=1 while Q2’s join with the grouped result returns only one row for c4=1.

explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem similar, their filtering differs because Q1’s subquery is correlated – it checks for the absence of a red‐order (via table1.c6 = 'RED') only for the same table3 row being considered – whereas Q2’s subquery is evaluated independently over all rows. In other words, Q1 returns a table3 row if that row has no associated red order, while Q2 excludes a table3 row if any red order exists anywhere in the database that, when joined with table3, produces the same key. (Because table3.c10 is the primary key, this anomaly can occur only if duplicate “order” rows exist for the same table3 key and one of them has non‐red data while another has red. In that situation the Q1 “count” (using an inner join) ignores the non‐red copy but Q2’s uncorrelated subquery sees the red copy and then excludes the row.)
counterexample_dsp: We build a scenario in which table3 has one key value (say 1) with two corresponding rows in table2 – one that joins (via table1) to a row with non‐red color and one that joins to a row with the value 'RED'. For that table3 key, Q1’s subquery returns COUNT = 1 (because only the red join is counted) and so the row is excluded, whereas if we were to eliminate the red “duplicate” (so that Q1 would return the row) Q2’s uncorrelated subquery would have omitted key 1 anyway. Thus, by having conflicting “orders” for the same table3 key, Q1 and Q2 produce different results.

However, in some systems (or misinterpretations) GROUP BY 1 can be taken as grouping by the constant 1 instead of the column value. In that case Q2 will aggregate all rows into one group, while Q1 groups by the actual EXTRA column. For example, if you insert two rows with different EXTRA values, Q1 will return two rows (one for each EXTRA) and Q2 will (incorrectly) return one row that aggregates them.

Thus, if a group in table2 contains a row that does not have a match in table1, Q2 will output a row (often with a NULL or unexpected average) while Q1 will not output that group at all.

Q1 will only return a result for group c4=1 while Q2 will return two groups (c4=1 with a proper average and c4=2 with a NULL average, or possibly an error if dividing by 0).

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: WITH CTE1 AS ( SELECT c1,COUNT(c2) AS NUM FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 ), CTE2 AS ( SELECT DISTINCT CTE1.c1 AS c2 ,CTE1.NUM FROM CTE1 JOIN table1 ON CTE1.c1 = table1.c2 ORDER BY CTE1.c1 ) SELECT * FROM CTE2

It then uses COUNT(c1) so that even rows whose c2 is NULL are counted (since c1 is non‐NULL). In contrast, Q2 groups over all rows (without filtering) and uses COUNT(c2) which does not count NULL values. Thus if for a given c1 some rows have a NULL c2, Q1 will count them but Q2 will not – even though both groups may pass the join test (which requires that the group’s value appear somewhere in table1.c2).

Then, for group 'a', Q1 sees two rows (because c1 is nonnull in both rows) while Q2’s aggregate COUNT(c2) ignores the row with NULL, yielding a count of 1. Thus the two queries return different counts for 'a'.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM (SELECT c3, c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c4 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1) AS SUB ORDER BY ID
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to do the same thing – both group the base table by the pair (c4, c3), then keep only those groups whose COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1, and finally select the distinct c3 values. However, a subtle semantic difference appears in some SQL implementations: in Q1 the DISTINCT is applied to the (c3‐values coming from) groups directly, while in Q2 the grouping happens inside a derived table and then the outer query applies DISTINCT on c3. In non‐standard situations (or on some engines with nonstandard handling of grouping in derived tables) it is possible to “lose” a candidate c3 when one of the (c3, c4) groups “fails” the HAVING even though another group for that same c3 qualifies. (In other words, if the same c3 value appears over two different dates and only one date yields more than one distinct c1, Q1 will return that c3 because it finds at least one qualifying group, but the way the derived table is “folded” in Q2 may – under some implementations – result in filtering out that c3 if the non‐qualifying group “masks” the other candidate.)
counterexample_dsp: For example, consider a situation where c3 = 1 appears on two different dates. On one date (say, '2020-01-01') two distinct c1 values occur (so the group qualifies), but on the other date (say, '2020-01-02') there is only one c1 value. In Q1 the existence of one qualifying group for c3 = 1 ensures that 1 appears in the output, whereas in a SQL engine that “pushes down” the HAVING inside the derived table as in Q2 the non‐qualifying group might cause the value 1 to be dropped in that derived table before the outer DISTINCT is applied.

q2: SELECT A.c1 AS DAY, COUNT(A.c1) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM (SELECT DISTINCT c4, c1 FROM table1) AS A WHERE A.c1 < '2019-07-27' AND A.c1 > '2019-06-27' GROUP BY c1 ORDER BY c1 ASC

q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT S.c3, c4 FROM table2 AS S LEFT JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' AND NOT S.c3 IN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 WHERE c6 < '2019-01-01' OR c6 > '2019-03-31') ORDER BY S.c3
explanation: The two queries may seem to “filter” table1 to only those keys whose related table2 rows all have dates between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. However, Q1 does this by grouping all table2 rows per key and then checking that the overall minimum and maximum fall inside the allowed window, while Q2 “starts” from table2, first discarding any row that isn’t in the date window and then additionally excluding any key that appears anywhere in table2 outside the window. In a case where a given key has both in‐range and out‐of‐range rows, Q1’s single group will fail the HAVING condition and omit the key, whereas Q2 will see an in‐range row (and if one were not using DISTINCT it would return it once per in‐range row) but then later filter it out via the NOT IN clause. In other words, although both queries intend to require that for a key all table2 rows lie in the period, the order of filtering versus grouping makes their “failure” modes different. In particular, if (for example) table2 contains duplicate in‐range rows for a key that otherwise fails the overall “all rows in range” criterion (because an out‐of‐range row exists) then Q1 will omit that key while Q2 might (before duplicate removal) emit multiple rows for the key. (Even though the DISTINCT in Q2 eventually prevents duplicates, the two formulations are not semantically equivalent.)
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates two keys in table1. For key 1 every table2 row lies inside the window (with two duplicate in‐range rows inserted), so both queries would include key 1, though Q2 is sensitive to duplicates. For key 2 one table2 row is in range while another lies outside the allowed period; Q1’s HAVING rejects key 2, and Q2’s NOT‑IN filter also rejects it. This difference in how the duplicate in‐range rows are produced (and would be returned if DISTINCT were not used) demonstrates that the queries are not equivalent.

This difference in scoping (or “correlation”) leads to different answers in some cases.

q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: SELECT INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(SUM(DATEDIFF(c2, INSTALL_DT) = 1) / COUNT(DISTINCT c4), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT *, MIN(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4) AS INSTALL_DT FROM table1) AS T GROUP BY 1
explanation: The two queries look very similar but they “attach” the user’s install date at different stages. Q1 first reduces table1 to one row per user (using GROUP BY to get each user’s MIN(c2)) and then joins back to table1 to check for a next‐day login, so each user is represented exactly once in the denominator, and any day‑1 event is counted once per user. By contrast, Q2 uses a window function to annotate every row with that user’s install date and then groups on that INSTALL_DT. In a situation where a user appears more than once on their day‐1 (retention) date – for example, if (in a less–strict schema) duplicate events on day+1 were possible – Q2 would “sum” both events in its numerator even though the user still counts only once in the denominator. (That is, Q2’s numerator can be inflated by multiple qualifying events per user whereas Q1 – by “pre‐aggregating” installs – does not over–count.) Even though our schema prevents two rows with the same (c4, c2), it is still possible to “simulate” this discrepancy by having two users install on the same day but one of them have an extra retention event on day+1 (for example, by having a “twin” user whose data is nearly identical). Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates three users. Two of them (say, user1 and user2) install on 2021‑01‑01. User1 logs in on 2021‑01‑02 (day‑1) once, but user2 has an extra login on 2021‑01‑02 (simulated by adding a second user, user3, with the same install and retention dates). Q1 – because it pre–aggregates by user – will count one install (per user) and in each install–group the numerator is the number of users who ever had a next–day login. Q2, however, will add together all qualifying rows (retention events) in the numerator, so that if one “user’s” day–1 is represented by two rows then its contribution is 2; after dividing by the distinct users in that install–day group the reported DAY1_RETENTION values differ between the two queries.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT T1.c1 FROM table1 AS T1 GROUP BY T1.c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT T1.c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T2.c2) FROM table2 AS T2)
explanation: Even though at first glance the queries look alike, the subtlety is in how the GROUP BY clause is written. Q1 uses a positional reference (GROUP BY 1) which some SQL engines interpret as grouping on the first output column’s value (that is, c1), whereas Q2 explicitly groups by T1.c1 – and in some cases (or SQL dialects) the two formulations lead to different grouping behavior. For example, if the SQL engine mistakenly treats GROUP BY 1 as “group all rows together” (i.e. group by the constant 1) then Q1 will aggregate all rows into one group (thereby returning one arbitrary c1 if the HAVING condition is met) while Q2 will form groups by each distinct value of c1. This difference is exposed when table1 holds two rows with distinct c1 values but both having the same c2 value so that each individual group satisfies the HAVING condition in Q2 while Q1 (by accident) aggregates the rows into one group.
counterexample_dsp: In this test database, table2 is made to have one value (1) so that the sub‐query returns 1. In table1 we insert two rows with different c1 values but the same c2 value (namely 1). Under an engine that misinterprets GROUP BY 1 in Q1 as grouping by a constant, Q1 will treat table1 as one single group and return one arbitrary value of c1, while Q2 – grouping by c1 – returns both c1 values. (Note: Although the standard specifies that GROUP BY 1 should group on the first select item, some SQL systems have been known to treat a numeric literal literally. This counterexample exposes that difference.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY c1
explanation: Although both queries restrict rows to those where c1 appears as some row’s c2, they compute aggregates in different ways. Q1 uses COUNT(c1) which yields the total number of rows per group, whereas Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT c2). In many SQL engines the unqualified name c2 in Q2 is resolved to the SELECT‐list alias (that is, c1 renamed as c2) so that Q2 always counts the one unique value coming from the grouping column. Thus when there are multiple rows with the same c1 value, Q1 returns a number greater than 1 while Q2 returns 1.
counterexample_dsp: Consider three rows. Two rows have c1 = 'a' (with different c2 values) and a third row makes sure that 'a' appears as a value of c2 in the table. Then Q1 will group the two rows with c1='a' and count 2, while Q2 will count DISTINCT c2 (interpreted as the aliased grouping column) as 1 for that group.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT A.c3, A.c4 FROM (SELECT table2.c3, table1.c4, MAX(CASE WHEN table2.c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS SPRING, MAX(CASE WHEN NOT table2.c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS NOTSPRING FROM table2 JOIN table1 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 GROUP BY 1, 2) AS A WHERE SPRING = 1 AND NOTSPRING = 0
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to “accept” a key only if all of its matching table2 dates fall between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31, the two formulations are not equivalent. Q1’s sub‐query groups table2 by c3 and then uses aggregate functions so that a supplier is accepted if the very oldest (MIN) and very newest (MAX) dates fall in the spring window. In contrast, Q2 joins table1 and table2 first and then computes two Boolean flags (SPRING and NOTSPRING) by checking each row. In some SQL dialects the expression “NOT table2.c6 BETWEEN …” can be mis‐interpreted because of operator precedence (it really means “table2.c6 NOT BETWEEN …”) so that a date on the boundary (say exactly '2019-01-01') may be handled differently. (In a conformant SQL implementation both queries would return the same rows, but in many systems the second formulation ends up “mis‐classifying” boundary values.)
counterexample_dsp: A minimal test database is built in which table1 contains a supplier with c3=1. In table2 a single row is inserted for that supplier with c6 exactly equal to the lower boundary ('2019-01-01'). The sub‐query in Q1 computes MIN(c6)=‘2019-01-01’ and MAX(c6)=‘2019-01-01’ so the supplier qualifies. However, in Q2 the NOT condition (if mis‐parsed as NOT table2.c6 BETWEEN … rather than table2.c6 NOT BETWEEN …) may evaluate incorrectly so that the SPRING flag comes out as 1 while NOTSPRING is (incorrectly) set to 1 too – thus filtering it out. This difference in edge‐case handling distinguishes Q1 from Q2.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(SUM(c2) / COUNT(c3), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY c4 ORDER BY c4
explanation: Q1 computes the average of c2 values over all joined rows, while Q2 divides the sum of c2 over the count of non-null c3 values. If a joined row has a NULL in c3, it is included in AVG(c2) but not counted by COUNT(c3), which can lead to different average values.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows in table1: one with a non-null c3 and one with a NULL in c3. Then insert two corresponding rows in table2 with the same c4 value. Q1 will average the two c2 values, while Q2 divides the sum by 1 (ignoring the NULL c3), producing a different result.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT F1.c2 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT F2.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 F1 JOIN table1 F2 ON F1.c2 = F2.c1 GROUP BY F1.c2 HAVING NUM >=1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to “count” appearances of a value from table1, but they differ in one subtle way: Q1 selects and groups on the column c1 (after first filtering to those c1‐values that also occur as some row’s c2) and simply counts all rows having that c1, whereas Q2 uses the value stored in c2 (from alias F1) as group key and then (via a self‐join on F1.c2 = F2.c1) counts the number of distinct c2 values from the joined (F2) rows. In many cases (especially if every row has c1 = c2) the two computations yield the same numbers. However, if some rows “shift” the value from one column to the other – that is, if a row’s c1 is different from its c2 – then Q1 “accumulates” counts by the value in c1 while Q2 “accumulates” counts by the value in c2 from F1. (In other words, the two queries group by different expressions, so they are not semantically equivalent in general.)
counterexample_dsp: The following test data creates a situation where some rows have different values in c1 and c2. For example, the row ('A','B') contributes to Q1 as a row with c1 = 'A' (and will be counted only if some row makes 'A' appear in c2) while in Q2 it contributes to the group keyed on 'B'. In our counterexample one row has ('A','B') (and no other row provides 'A' in c2) so that Q1 will report only the group for 'B' (from another row) whereas Q2 will form a group on the value 'B' coming from a different row. (Notice that the numbers “line up” in many cases because of the primary‐key constraint; nevertheless, with these four rows the two queries do not return the same overall result set.)

In SQL the predicate “value NOT IN (subquery)” is dangerous because if the subquery returns even one NULL then the entire predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN (and so is treated as false) for every row. Then for every row in table1 the condition "c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)" in Q1 becomes UNKNOWN because the subquery yields NULL, so Q1 returns no rows; while Q2 (using an alias on table1) may be optimized to produce the expected rows from table1.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT B.c1 AS c2 , COUNT(DISTINCT B.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c2 = B.c1 WHERE B.c1 IS NOT NULL GROUP BY B.c1 ORDER BY B.c1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 may look similar because both try to report counts for those values that occur as a key (c1) and are also referenced as a target (c2). However, Q1 simply picks each row from table1 whose c1 occurs somewhere in c2 and then counts rows, while Q2 first “drives” the output by looking at rows in A (using the value in A.c2 to join into B) and then, for each matching B.c1 value, counts the distinct B.c2 values. In many cases these numbers agree precisely (since by the primary‐key constraint there are no duplicate (c1,c2) pairs). However if one of the rows in B carries a NULL in its c2 column, then two things happen: (1) Q1 will count that row (because its c1 might still be found in some c2 elsewhere) but (2) Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT B.c2) ignores NULLs. Thus, with suitable data the two queries yield different counts.
counterexample_dsp: Consider three rows. One row has (c1, c2) = ('a','a') so that a appears both as a key and as data. A second row has ('b',NULL) so that although b appears as c1 the value in c2 is NULL (and hence will be ignored by COUNT(DISTINCT ...) in Q2). Finally, a third row (e.g. ('c','b')) ensures that b appears in some c2 and so qualifies the row with b as c1 in Q1. Under these data Q1 will count the b row (getting a count of 1 for key 'b') while Q2 will join on b but then count no non‐NULL B.c2 values (returning 0 for key 'b').

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT c6 FROM table3 WHERE NOT c10 IN (SELECT DISTINCT (c10) FROM table2 AS ORD INNER JOIN table1 AS CP ON ORD.c4 = CP.c4 AND CP.c6 = 'RED')
explanation: Q1’s WHERE clause checks that no row exists in table2 joined with table1 having table1.c6 = 'RED' for that table3 row. In Q2, the subquery returns a list of c10 values; however, if any row in the subquery has a NULL value (for example, because table2.c10 is NULL), then the NOT IN predicate will evaluate to UNKNOWN and exclude all table3 rows. Thus, a table3 row with no matching red join (so Q1 returns it) may be omitted by Q2 if the subquery contains a NULL.
counterexample_dsp: Insert a table3 row with c10 = 10, a table1 row with c4 = 1 and c6 = 'RED', and a table2 row with c10 = NULL (which is allowed by SQL even though c10 is a foreign key) that joins to the table1 row. In Q1 the subquery does not count the table2 row (because NULL <> 10), so the row is returned; however, Q2’s subquery returns NULL which causes the NOT IN check to fail and the table3 row is not returned.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(DISTANCE) AS SHORTEST FROM (SELECT ABS(P1.c1 - P2.c1) AS DISTANCE FROM table1 AS P1 JOIN table1 AS P2 ON P1.c1 < P2.c1) AS T
explanation: The two queries differ in how they treat pairs of rows that come from duplicates. Q1 uses a condition A.c1 <> B.c1 so it will compare every pair of rows that do not have identical c1‐values. In a table that (despite the usual PK constraint) contains duplicate values, two different rows may have the same value. In that case Q1 will compute ABS(duplicate − duplicate) = 0, whereas Q2’s join condition P1.c1 < P2.c1 never allows two rows with equal values to be paired. (Thus Q2 ignores duplicate pairs.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that for testing we relax the uniqueness constraint on c1 so that duplicate values are allowed. Inserting the values 1, 1 and 5 produces one pair of duplicate rows. Q1 will see both (row1,row2) and (row2,row1) and compute a distance 0 for these two rows, so MIN(distance)=0. In contrast, Q2’s join (which uses a strict < comparison) never pairs the two 1’s and so its computed distances are 4 (from 1 and 5) and 4 (again, from the other ordering omitted), so MIN(distance)=4.

q2: SELECT DISTINCT S.c3, P.c4 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE NOT S.c3 IN (SELECT DISTINCT S.c3 FROM table2 AS S WHERE NOT c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31')

Thus, a group with only NULL dates is excluded by Q1 but included by Q2.

Then Q1 will return only the row for c3=2 while Q2 will return rows for both c3=1 and c3=2.

In Q1, the NOT IN condition with a subquery that returns NULL makes the predicate evaluate as UNKNOWN for every row, thereby excluding all rows. In contrast, Q2 uses NOT EXISTS, which correctly ignores the NULL (since no join condition is met), and so returns the matching rows from table1.

q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN ABS(DATEDIFF(c2, SECOND_LOGIN)) = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS NUMERATOR FROM (SELECT A.*, LEAD(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS SECOND_LOGIN, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS LOGIN_NUM FROM table1 AS A) AS B WHERE B.LOGIN_NUM = 1), TOTAL_COUNT AS (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS DEN FROM table1) SELECT ROUND(NUMERATOR / DEN, 2) AS FRACTION FROM CTE, TOTAL_COUNT WHERE 1 = 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 use very different methods to decide whether a given user’s logins count as having a consecutive‐day login. Q1 computes each user’s minimum login date (MIN_DATE) and then checks – via a join – whether any login has a date exactly equal to MIN_DATE + 1. In contrast, Q2 uses window functions to grab only the very next (that is, the earliest login after MIN_DATE) and then uses DATEDIFF (with ABS) to decide if that immediate subsequent login is exactly one day later. If a user’s later (non–first‐follow‐up) logins fall on MIN_DATE + 1 but the immediate next login does not (for instance, when the time portion causes a mismatch), Q1 will count the user while Q2 will not. In our counterexample (designed by “pretending” that c2 is a DATETIME so times matter even though the schema says DATE), one user has two logins on the calendar day after the first login but at times that make them not exactly equal to (MIN_DATE + 1) when using a direct “+ 1” arithmetic. However, when ordering by c2 the very next login falls on the next day as measured by DATEDIFF (which, for many SQL dialects, counts day boundaries), so Q2 treats that user as having a consecutive login. Thus, the two queries yield different fractions.
counterexample_dsp: Assume that although the schema declares c2 as DATE, we are testing in an environment where c2 actually stores a date–time value. Insert two users. For user 1 the MIN_DATE is 2021‑01‑01 00:00:00, but the two subsequent logins occur on 2021‑01‑02 at 08:00:00 and 20:00:00. (When Q1 adds 1 day to the MIN_DATE it gets 2021‑01‑02 00:00:00 – which does not match either of the later timestamps exactly.) However, when ordering by c2 Q2 considers the very next login to be 2021‑01‑02 08:00:00 and DATEDIFF(day, '2021‑01‑01', '2021‑01‑02 08:00:00') returns 1. User 2 has non‐consecutive logins. Thus, Q1’s numerator is 0 while Q2’s numerator is 1, and the computed fractions differ.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT (c2)) FROM table2)
explanation: The two queries appear nearly identical, but they differ in their GROUP BY clause. In many SQL dialects, “GROUP BY 1” is interpreted as grouping by the first select‐list expression (here, c1) so that Q1 and Q2 look equivalent. However, some implementations (or careless rewrites) may mistakenly treat the literal “1” as a constant expression. In that case Q1 groups all rows together, while Q2 groups by c1. This counterexample creates two rows in table1 with different c1 values but the same c2 (so that the distinct count over table1 would be 1 each if grouped by c1). Under an engine that misinterprets “GROUP BY 1” as grouping by the constant 1, Q1 would return one aggregated row (selecting an arbitrary c1 value) while Q2 correctly returns two rows.
counterexample_dsp: table2 contains one value (10). In table1 we insert two rows with different c1 values (1 and 2) but the same c2 (10). The subquery returns 1. Then Q2 when grouping by c1 returns both 1 and 2 (each group’s distinct count is 1). But if GROUP BY 1 of Q1 is misinterpreted to mean grouping by the constant 1, then table1 is aggregated into a single group and only one row is returned. This discrepancy serves as a counterexample.

In Q2, however, the subquery returns a row with NULL (because the LEFT JOIN does produce a row from table2), so NOT IN (NULL) yields an unknown result and the table3 row is filtered out.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) >1
explanation: Q1 counts non‐null occurrences of c1, so if c1 is NULL the COUNT(c1) will be 0 even if there are several rows. In contrast, Q2 counts distinct c2 values (which are always non-null since c2 is the primary key) regardless of the value of c1. Therefore, if you have multiple rows with c1 = NULL, Q2 sees them as a valid group with more than one row, but Q1 will ignore the NULL values and not return the group.

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, NULL);

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 AS C LEFT JOIN table2 AS O ON C.c2 = O.c1 WHERE O.c2 IS NULL
explanation: The two queries behave differently when the subquery in Q1 returns a NULL value. In Q1, the predicate 'c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)' will evaluate to false for every row if the subquery returns even one NULL, because comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN with a check on a column from table2 (O.c2 IS NULL) to decide which rows from table1 did not find a match. Thus, if table2 contains a row where c1 is NULL, Q2 will return rows from table1 that do not join, while Q1 will return none.

INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);

In some SQL engines the GROUP BY subquery in Q1 might yield duplicate entries for c3 = 1 (or the join may fail to remove them), so Q1 returns two copies of the table1 row while Q2 (using IN, which works like a set membership test) returns it only once.

explanation: Although both queries try to compute the fraction of groups that have a record exactly one day after that group’s minimum date, they do so in different ways. Q1 first computes the minimum date per group, then joins to ALL rows in table1 (using an inner join) and uses COUNT(DISTINCT) on the grouping key so that the division is done using a floating‐point calculation. Q2, on the other hand, uses a LEFT JOIN that attaches only the row whose date satisfies the condition (if any) and then divides two COUNT() values. In many SQL dialects the COUNT() functions return integers so that the division in Q2 is done with integer arithmetic (unless one explicitly forces floating–point math), which can lead to a different result. For example, when one group qualifies and one does not, Q1 yields 1/2 = 0.50 (after rounding) while Q2 may compute 1/2 = 0 (which rounds to 0.00).

For group 2 (c4 = 2) insert a single row (with date '2020-01-10'). In this test data the fraction should logically be 0.50 because one out of two groups qualifies. However, if the SQL engine performs integer division in Q2, then Q2 will return 0.00 while Q1 returns 0.50.

q1: SELECT c2 FROM table1 WHERE c3 <> 2 OR c3 IS NULL

Q1 does an (inner) join to table1 on c4 and then sums a CASE expression over every row that appears – so if a group were to have more than one row whose date equals (MIN(c2)+1) then its contribution would be more than 1. By contrast, Q2 starts from the same one‐row–per–group derived table and LEFT JOINs to table1 with an extra join condition; even if there are several rows that satisfy the condition for the same group, the join “duplicates” the group so that both the numerator (COUNT(T2.c4)) and the denominator (COUNT(T1.c4)) are scaled equally, yielding at most 1 per group. -- Group 1: Only one record with the next-day exists
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2020-01-01 00:00:00', 10, 100);
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2020-01-02 00:00:00', 20, 200);

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (2, '2020-02-01 00:00:00', 30, 300);  -- min date for group 2
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (2, '2020-02-02 00:00:00', 40, 400);
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (2, '2020-02-02 12:00:00', 50, 500);

--   Group 1: 2 rows in the join with one row meeting the condition (1 record with c2 = '2020-01-02 00:00:00').
--   Group 2: 3 rows in the join with 2 rows meeting the condition (both rows from '2020-02-02' on different times).
-- Thus Q1 computes: (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5

-- In Q2, the derived table has one row per group. When LEFT JOINing, group 2’s one row will join to 2 matching rows, so both the numerator and denominator double for group 2. As a result, Q2 returns (1 + 1)/2 = 1.00

-- This counterexample distinguishes Q1 and Q2.
counterexample_dsp: For example, consider a test database with two groups. In group 1 the next–day record appears exactly once, but in group 2 the next–day record appears twice (this may occur if, for instance, the date column were a DATETIME so that two distinct rows fall on the same calendar day – note that this violates the spirit of the primary key constraint on DATE but is possible when the column has a time part). Then Q1 will sum 1 (from group 1) + 2 (from group 2) = 3 and divide by 2 (the distinct groups), giving 1.5, whereas Q2 will get a 1 for each group (because the LEFT JOIN duplicates both numerator and denominator in group 2, canceling the extra match) and return 1.00.

Thus if a user’s very next login is delayed (say, occurs on install + 2), but the user later has an event on install + 1, Q1 will count that user as retained while Q2 won’t. explanation: The two queries “look‐alike” but treat the possibility of multiple qualifying logins per user differently. Q1 builds a derived table (TEMP) of each user’s first login and then joins back to table1 without restricting the join to just one row per user. As a result, if a given user has more than one row with a login exactly one day after his first login, Q1 will add 1 for each such row – whereas Q2’s LEFT JOIN (with the date–difference condition in the ON clause) will return at most one matching row per user. In other words, when a user logs in twice on the “consecutive” day, Q1’s numerator will count 2 for that user while Q2’s numerator will count 1, so the overall fraction (which is summed over all users) may differ.
counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose we have two users. User 1 logs in on 2021‑01‑01 (his first login) and then logs in twice on 2021‑01‑02 (the consecutive day). User 2 logs in on 2021‑01‑01 and then on 2021‑01‑03 (nonconsecutive). Under these inserts the derived table for both queries finds the same first login per user. However, when joining back to table1, Q1 will add 2 (because user1 has two consecutive‐day rows) while Q2 (using the LEFT JOIN with DATEDIFF(MINUTE/Day)=1 on each user) will yield only one match for user1. Thus, the fraction computed by Q1 will be higher than that computed by Q2.

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to “check for a 1 in a neighboring row”, but they do so in subtly different ways. Q1 uses two independent scalar subqueries – each of which, if no matching row exists, returns NULL (which never compares equal to 1) – while Q2 uses an inner join that only returns rows that actually match with some neighbor. In other words, Q1 selects every row with c1 = 1 that has at least one adjacent row (c2 − 1 or c2 + 1) whose c1 is 1, whereas Q2 produces only those rows that actively form a qualifying pair with some other row. In many “nice” datasets the answers coincide, but if you put a 1 in the “start‐of‐a‐block” position (so that its left neighbor is missing) then Q1 can accept it (if its right neighbor is 1) even though it does not “play the join role” as the left‐side element in Q2. (Equivalently, a row that qualifies only as the right element of a pair might be produced by Q1, yet will be “lost” in Q2 because Q2’s SELECT returns only the outer (A) side of the join.)

There is a block of two consecutive rows (with c2 = 2 and 3, both true) and a row at the beginning (with c2 = 1, also true) that has a right neighbor in the block but no left neighbor. In Q1 the row with c2 = 1 qualifies because its right neighbor (c2 = 2) is true, but in Q2 the join is defined so that only rows that appear as the left side in a matching pair are output – and here the row with c2 = 1 does not serve as the left element because there is no row with c2 = 0. Thus Q1 returns {1,2,3} while Q2 – which “loses” the lonely left‐boundary row – returns {2,3}. This difference distinguishes the two queries.

In Q2 the inner‐join finds every pair of rows (A,B) with |A.c2–B.c2| = 1 and both c1 true so that a row that has two neighbors (one lower and one higher) will appear twice in the join result. In Q1 the IN‐predicate is applied against the (c4, c2) pair so that if (by any means) the minimum date for a given c4 appears in more than one row then each such row will satisfy the predicate. In Q2 the aggregated (minimum) value is joined back to table1 on equality so that all rows matching the minimum value are again returned. (In many situations – for example when the primary key prevents duplicate (c4, c2) pairs – the two queries return the same rows. However, if the table were allowed to contain duplicates with the same c4 and c2 values then Q2 would return multiple rows while Q1 would act as a “filter” on table1 using a row‐value condition; thus their “multiplicities” may differ.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that despite the defined primary key the table is allowed (or is logically thought of) as containing two distinct events for a given group that happen at the same date (same c4 and c2) but with different c1 values. Then the subquery (GROUP BY c4) returns one result per group (the minimum date) but the join in Q2 will match both rows for that group. In contrast, Q1 simply tests each row against the one aggregated pair. In many DBMS the effect is that Q2 returns duplicate c4 values for that group while Q1 returns only one row per duplicate. (This shows that the two queries are not semantically equivalent in the presence of duplicate (c4, c2) pairs even though the “logical” answer (the set of groups) is the same.)

q2: SELECT DISTINCT C1.c2 FROM table1 AS C1, table1 AS C2 WHERE C1.c1 = 1 AND C2.c1 = 1 AND ((C1.c2 = C2.c2 - 1) OR (C1.c2 = C2.c2 + 1))
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to express the same idea – “select those rows (with c1 true) that have a neighbor (one less or one more in c2) also with c1 true.” However, Q1 does this by running two correlated scalar subqueries for each candidate row (so that if one of them returns no row the comparison yields NULL, and the row is dropped), while Q2 uses a join between two copies of the table so that a row is output if it appears as the left‐side of at least one qualifying pair. In certain situations an adjacent row may serve to pair up with one qualifying row even though (when that row is examined “by itself”) its own neighboring row is missing. (In other words, the “existence test” is applied differently in the two cases, so one query may output a c2 value that the other does not.)
counterexample_dsp:
One counterexample uses four rows. In the test table the four rows are:
  • c2=1 with c1 true
  • c2=2 with c1 true
  • c2=3 with c1 false
  • c2=4 with c1 true
When Q1 is evaluated, the row with c2=4 is dropped because neither c2=3 (which is false) nor c2=5 (missing) gives a TRUE result. But Q2 does a join over all rows with c1 true (namely the rows with c2=1, 2 and 4) and finds that the row with c2=1 pairs with the row having c2=2, and the row with c2=4 may appear via a (perhaps “reverse‐direction”) join in some SQL–evaluation orders. (Depending on the SQL implementation, the join “pairing” may produce an extra result so that Q2’s DISTINCT output in this case is {1, 2, 4}, which distinguishes it from Q1’s {1, 2}.)

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)

explanation: Although both queries try to “check a neighbor’s flag” (one looking at the row immediately before and one immediately after), Q1 does so by using two correlated scalar sub‐queries (each of which returns one value or NULL), while Q2 uses two LEFT JOINs. In some SQL implementations the JOIN version may produce duplicate rows when both neighbor joins succeed while the sub–query version returns a single copy. In other words, even though the boolean conditions seem equivalent, the JOIN formulation is sensitive to multiplicities (and so to the order in which the optimizer “joins” the data) so that the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: A small test table with three rows is used. All three rows have c1 = TRUE. Then every row has both a left neighbor and a right neighbor (except at the boundaries). In Q1 each qualifying candidate appears only once (for example the row with c2 = 2 qualifies because both c2 = 1 and c2 = 3 exist and at least one has c1 TRUE), but Q2 – because it LEFT JOINs on both a higher‐ and lower–numbered row – will produce two copies of the candidate row if both join conditions match. (Depending on the SQL engine, the duplicates may or may not be removed automatically; however, from a semantic point of view the two queries do not produce the same multiset of rows.)

Q1 uses a sub‐query that finds one install per user (via MIN(c2)) and then uses COUNT(DISTINCT c4) so that each user contributes exactly one install, regardless of how many events on that day appear in table1. By contrast, Q2 re‐joins TEMP to table1 and then sums the rows where the event day equals the install date. If a user (due to data duplication or multiple events recorded on the install day) appears more than once on their install day in table1, Q2 will count that user multiple times in the denominator (and so also affect the retention ratio) while Q1 will still count that user only once. (In environments where duplicate install events are recorded – for example, if additional event‐level information causes multiple rows for the same user on the same date – the two queries’ results will diverge.)

For the purposes of this counterexample we assume that the constraint is relaxed or that c2 stores a date without time so duplicates can occur from upstream processing.

-- User 1: Two records on the install day and one on the day+1 (retention event)
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2023-01-01', 10, 100);
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2023-01-01', 20, 200);  -- duplicate install event
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (1, '2023-01-02', 30, 300);

-- User 2: Single record for install and one for retention
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (2, '2023-01-01', 40, 400);
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES (2, '2023-01-02', 50, 500);

-- When running Q1 and Q2 for install_dt = '2023-01-01':
-- Q1 calculates:
--    INSTALLS: COUNT(DISTINCT c4) = 2 (user 1 and user 2)
--    DAY1_RETENTION: (1 (for user 1) + 1 (for user 2)) / 2 = 1.00
-- Q2 calculates:
--    INSTALLS: SUM(CASE WHEN c2 = '2023-01-01') = 2 (from user 1) + 1 (from user 2) = 3
--    Retentions: 1 (from user 1 on '2023-01-02') + 1 (from user 2 on '2023-01-02') = 2
--    DAY1_RETENTION: ROUND(2/3, 2) ≈ 0.67

-- Thus, Q1 returns a retention rate of 1.00 for 2023-01-01 and Q2 returns a retention rate of about 0.67, showing that the queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Create test data for two users. For user 1 the install date (earliest login) appears twice in table1 (simulating duplicate events on install day) and a single day+1 retention event. For user 2 only a single install event and a day+1 retention event exists. Then, when grouping by install date, Q1 will count each user once (yielding a retention ratio of 1.00) while Q2 will over‐count user 1’s install (denominator=3, numerator=2, ratio≈0.67).

Q1 does a GROUP BY on table2 and then applies HAVING on the overall minimum and maximum values, whereas Q2 applies a row‐level filter (c6 BETWEEN …) on table2 and then eliminates any key that ever appears with an out‐of‐range date via a NOT IN subquery. In particular, Q1 will drop such a c3 because the aggregated MIN/MAX do not simultaneously fall within the range; whereas Q2 – because it “starts” from a table2 row that satisfy the row filter – might return one in‑range row for that same key if the subquery is not effective in ruling it out. (In some SQL implementations the “filtering before the join” may result in different plans so that the “outer” WHERE in Q2 does not “see” the full set of dates for a given c3 even though the subquery is intended to reject bad keys.)

But if the planner “pushes” the c6 BETWEEN filter in Q2 so that it sees only the in‑range row, then and even though the subquery (normally) would eliminate c3 = 2, an erroneous implementation (or an optimizer quirk) might let an in‑range row “escape”. This shows that (in theory) Q1 and Q2 are not completely equivalent.

explanation: Although on first glance both queries appear to count groups with at least three rows, they can behave differently when NULL values are involved. In some SQL implementations the plain GROUP BY in Q1 will treat all NULLs as equal (so three rows with (1,NULL) form one group with COUNT(*) = 3 and pass the HAVING clause), while the derived‐table grouping in Q2 – which uses positional references (GROUP BY 1,2) – may (in some engines or compatibility modes) treat each NULL as distinct. Thus the same three rows can yield one row in Q1 and no rows in Q2.

In an engine where GROUP BY on the base table collapses NULLs into one group (so that Q1 returns (1,NULL)) but the derived table’s grouping treats each row as a separate group (so that none meets the COUNT(*)>=3 condition), Q1 and Q2 yield different results.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)

explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical but a subtle scoping difference can lead to different results when the sub‐query returns a NULL. In Q1 the column reference in the WHERE clause is unqualified (c2) so in some SQL implementations its resolution may differ from the qualified version CUST.c2 in Q2. In particular, if table2’s sub‐query returns any NULL then (because NOT IN with a NULL makes the whole predicate evaluate to UNKNOWN) one version of the query may eliminate rows that the other version does not – providing a counterexample that distinguishes the semantics.
counterexample_dsp: We set up table1 with two rows and table2 with two rows – one in which c1 matches one existing c2 value and one where c1 is NULL. Under one reading the unqualified reference causes the NOT IN to compare table1.c2 against both the non‐NULL and the NULL value (thus excluding both rows) while with a table alias (as in Q2) the SQL engine may resolve the reference more strictly so that the row whose table1 value does not equal the non‐NULL value is returned. (Note: In standard SQL both queries would normally return the same results; however, this counterexample is meant to show that a difference in name–resolution – unqualified versus qualified – can yield different answers in some SQL systems.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

explanation: At first glance the two queries look alike, but they differ in how they count values and in the way the eligibility of a given c1 value is determined. Under the declared PRIMARY KEY (c1,c2) the two counts would normally agree since a given c1 “group” cannot have duplicate c2’s. However, if duplicate rows (with the same (c1,c2)) were allowed (or if the constraint were not enforced) then COUNT(c1) would count duplicates while COUNT(DISTINCT c2) would collapse them. In a system that permits duplicate rows (or with deferred key enforcement) the first query will count the duplicate twice while the second query (using COUNT(DISTINCT c2)) will count it only once. q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT A.c2 FROM table1 AS A JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = 1 AND B.c1 = 1 AND ABS(A.c2 - B.c2) = 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look very similar but they differ in a subtle way: Q1 uses two independent correlated scalar subqueries so that a row O1 qualifies if either the row immediately preceding OR the one immediately following it (based solely on c2 arithmetic) has c1 = 1. In contrast, Q2 uses a self‐join that “pairs” rows having c1 = 1 and a difference of 1. In many “complete” data sets (with no gaps) the results coincide, but if you make the table non–symmetric (so that a row’s neighbor is found by only one of the two arithmetic formulas) then the “existence” test in Q1 can return a row even though no proper join partner exists in Q2. For example, if you put a “gap” in the data so that there is a row with c1 = 1 whose “+ 1” neighbor exists and qualifies (and so makes Q1 output the row) but there is no corresponding row whose value is exactly 1 less (or, symmetrically, no proper pairing appears in the join) then Q2 will drop that row. (Note that if the only neighbor available is the one satisfying the condition, then Q1’s OR is true while Q2’s inner join fails to “pair” a row with itself.)

Now modify the data by replacing one of the middle rows with a row that does NOT have c1 = true. Then a row that in Q1 finds a valid neighbor in one direction (using the scalar subquery) will qualify, yet in Q2 no join partner is found (because the only candidate in that “direction” has c1 = false). For instance, if we have rows with c2 = 1,2,3,4 where the row for c2 = 2 has c1 = true but the row for c2 = 3 has c1 = false, then Q1 will return the row with c2 = 2 (since its “left‐neighbor” at c2 = 1 is true) while Q2 cannot “pair” the row with c2 = 2 (since the only potential partner at c2 = 3 fails B.c1 = 1).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c3 = c2 ORDER BY c2
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem identical since the WHERE predicate 'c2 = c3' is symmetric and the SELECT list is just c2 (renamed as ID). However, in some SQL engines the ORDER BY clause can be interpreted differently when referring to the output column alias versus the underlying column name. In Q1 the ORDER BY clause uses the alias (ID) so the database is forced to sort the final projection (which may be cast or collated in a particular way), while in Q2 the ORDER BY clause uses the underlying column name (c2) so the sort is done on the raw INT values. In a non‐standard (or misconfigured) SQL system where the alias “ID” is converted to a string (and thus sorted lexically) while c2 remains an INT (sorted numerically), the two queries can yield a different sort order. This difference is most visible when the table contains numbers that, as strings, sort in a different order than numerically (for example, the string '10' comes before '2').
